questions.question_md: The movement of the heavenly bodies according to the vedic tradition is guided by :
options: The moral virtues of the people
questions.explanation:
In the Ṛgveda, **Ṛta** is the cosmic law. It is the order that keeps the whole universe regular.

Ṛta makes the sun rise and the seasons change. It also guides the movement of the heavenly bodies. Even the gods follow Ṛta, and Varuṇa protects it. Later, Ṛta also became the base of moral order and of dharma.

The will of the gods is wrong, because the gods themselves obey Ṛta. The moral virtue of people does not move the stars. Prajāpati is a creator god, not the law of cosmic order.

questions.question_md:
Match the **Set-I** with **Set-II** and select the correct code :

| Set - I | Set - II |
|---|---|
| (a) Ṛk | (i) Udgātā |
| (b) Sāma | (ii) Hota |
| (c) Yajuḥ | (iii) Adhvaryu |
| (d) Atharva | (iv) Brahṁā |
questions.explanation:
Each Veda has its own priest in the Vedic sacrifice.

- **Ṛk → Hotā (ii).** The Hotā recites the Ṛgveda hymns to call the gods.
- **Sāma → Udgātā (i).** The Udgātā sings the Sāmaveda chants.
- **Yajuḥ → Adhvaryu (iii).** The Adhvaryu does the actual ritual acts with Yajurveda formulas.
- **Atharva → Brahmā (iv).** The Brahmā watches the whole ritual and corrects mistakes.

So the code is a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv. The first option wrongly gives the Udgātā to the Ṛgveda and the Hotā to the Sāmaveda.

questions.question_md: The absence of horseness in cow according to the Vaiśeṣikas is known as :
questions.explanation:
Vaiśeṣika divides abhāva (absence) into four kinds.

- **Prāgabhāva**: prior absence, before a thing is made.
- **Dhvaṁsābhāva**: absence after a thing is destroyed.
- **Atyantābhāva**: absolute absence of a thing in a place at all times.
- **Anyonyābhāva**: mutual absence, that is, difference. "A cow is not a horse" is the standard example.

The question speaks of the cow and the horse. This is the usual textbook example of **anyonyābhāva**, so it is the suggested answer. The two animals exclude each other's identity.

The question is open to debate. In Navya-Nyāya, the absence of horse*ness* in a cow can also be called atyantābhāva. Prior and posterior absence are clearly wrong, because no making or breaking is involved.

questions.question_md: There are two types of Bandhana of the soul : Bhāvabandhana and dravyabandhana. This view is held by :
questions.explanation:
The **Jainas** explain bondage (bandha) in two levels.

- **Bhāva-bandha** (mental bondage): passions such as anger, pride, deceit and greed arise in the soul.
- **Dravya-bandha** (material bondage): because of these passions, karmic matter flows in and sticks to the soul.

So the passions lead to the real joining of karma-matter with the jīva (soul). This two-fold idea belongs only to Jainism.

Cārvāka does not accept a soul apart from the body, so it has no bondage. Sāṁkhya says that bondage belongs to prakṛti, not to the puruṣa. Mīmāṁsā does not use these terms.

questions.question_md: Which one among the following is **not** acceptable to the Vaiśeṣikas ?
options: Tattvajñāna is not the sufficient condition for niḥśreyasa
Īśvara is a type of ātmā
questions.explanation:
The question asks which view Vaiśeṣika does **not** accept.

- **"Veda is created by none"** is the Mīmāṁsā view. Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika says that Īśvara (God) made the Veda. The Veda is valid because a trustworthy author spoke it. So Vaiśeṣika rejects this statement.
- Abhāva (absence) can be perceived. Vaiśeṣika accepts this.
- Īśvara is a kind of ātmā (self), the supreme self. Vaiśeṣika accepts this.
- Tattvajñāna (knowledge of the categories) works through dharma and needs other aids. So the school can accept that it alone is not enough.

The clearest view that Vaiśeṣika rejects is that the Veda has no author.

questions.question_md:
Which one among the following codes is acceptable to the cārvākas ? Answer considering (a), (b), (c), (d) ?

(a) Kṣti and Kāma
(b) Artha and Puṇya
(c) Sukha and Artha
(d) Marut and Vyoma

**Code :**
questions.notes: 'Kṣti' (sic) in the source, i.e. Kṣiti (earth).
questions.explanation:
Cārvāka is the materialist school. It accepts only what we can perceive.

- **(a) Kṣiti and Kāma: acceptable.** Kṣiti (earth) is one of its four elements. Kāma (pleasure) is the highest goal of life.
- **(b) Artha and Puṇya: not acceptable.** Artha (wealth) is accepted. Puṇya (religious merit) is rejected, because there is no next life.
- **(c) Sukha and Artha: acceptable.** Sukha (happiness) is the aim of life. Artha is the means to it.
- **(d) Marut and Vyoma: not acceptable.** Marut (air) is an element. Vyoma (ākāśa, space) cannot be perceived, so Cārvāka rejects it.

Only (a) and (c) are fully acceptable.

questions.question_md: Select the **correct** sequence with reference to apavarga in Nyāya :
questions.explanation:
Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.2 gives a chain of five links: duḥkha (pain), janma (birth), pravṛtti (activity), doṣa (defect) and mithyājñāna (false knowledge).

Each link causes the next one in this order:

- **Mithyājñāna** (false knowledge) produces doṣa (attachment, hatred and delusion).
- **Doṣa** produces pravṛtti (good and bad action).
- **Pravṛtti** produces janma (rebirth).
- **Janma** produces duḥkha (pain).

Apavarga (liberation) comes when true knowledge removes false knowledge first. Then each later link stops in turn, and pain ends. So the correct sequence starts with mithyājñāna and ends with duḥkha. The other orders break this cause–effect chain.

questions.question_md: Which one among the following is not an avayava of pañcāvayavīnyāya according to the Naiyāyikas ?
questions.explanation:
The Nyāya five-membered inference (pañcāvayava-nyāya) has these parts:

1. **Pratijñā**: the claim (The hill has fire).
2. **Hetu**: the reason (Because it has smoke).
3. **Udāharaṇa**: the example with the general rule (Where there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen).
4. **Upanaya**: the application (The hill has such smoke).
5. **Nigamana**: the conclusion (So the hill has fire).

**Upamāna** is not a part of this inference. It is a separate pramāṇa (source of knowledge), namely comparison. Udāharaṇa, Upanaya and Nigamana are all members of the five-part inference.

questions.question_md: Which one among the following is not a condition of Vākyārtha (sentential meaning) jñāna according to the Naiyāyikas ?
questions.explanation:
Nyāya gives four conditions for understanding the meaning of a sentence (vākyārtha-jñāna).

- **Ākāṅkṣā** (expectancy): one word needs another to complete the sense.
- **Yogyatā** (compatibility): the meanings must fit together. "Wet him with fire" fails.
- **Āsatti** (proximity): the words must come close in time.
- **Tātparya** (intention): we must grasp what the speaker means.

**Vyākaraṇa** (grammar) is not one of these four conditions. Grammar helps us to learn word meanings. But Nyāya does not list it as a condition of sentence meaning.

questions.question_md:
Which type of hetvābhāsa is committed by the following anumāna ? Select the **correct** code :

‘Parvataḥ vahnimān nīladhūmāt’
questions.explanation:
The inference says: "The hill has fire, because it has *blue* smoke."

The word "blue" is an unneeded qualifier (vyartha-viśeṣaṇa). The rule of pervasion (vyāpti) is "wherever there is smoke, there is fire." Blueness adds nothing to this rule. So "blue smoke" as such is not the proper pervaded term (vyāpya). Nyāya calls this defect **vyāpyatvāsiddha**, a kind of asiddha hetu.

- Sādhāraṇa savyabhicāra: the reason is present also where fire is absent. This is not so here.
- Svarūpāsiddha: the reason is not in the subject at all. The hill does have smoke.
- Bādhita: another pramāṇa shows that the conclusion is false. This is also not the case here.

questions.question_md: According to the Naiyāyikas ‘padasákti’ is :
options: A relation between a pada and a padārtha that stands for it
questions.notes: 'padasákti' as printed (diacritic misplaced), i.e. padaśakti.
questions.explanation:
For Nyāya, **padaśakti** (the power of a word) is the relation between a word (pada) and the meaning (padārtha) that the word stands for.

Naiyāyikas say that this relation comes from the will of Īśvara (God). The rule is: "Let this meaning be understood from this word." Because of this relation, the word "cow" makes us think of the animal cow.

Nyāya does not count śakti as an extra padārtha (category); Mīmāṁsā holds that view. Nyāya also denies that śakti is eternal, as Mīmāṁsā claims. It is not a relation between two words, but between a word and its object.

questions.question_md: Which of the following statements is **not** true with regard to Pātanjala Yoga ?
options: Pātanjala Yoga admits prior moral training
questions.explanation:
Pātañjala Yoga accepts the Sāṁkhya metaphysics. So it is **dualist**, not monist. It accepts two separate realities: many puruṣas (selves) and prakṛti (matter). So the statement that Yoga advocates monism is not true.

The other statements are true:

- Yoga Sūtra 1.24 calls Īśvara a special puruṣa (puruṣa-viśeṣa). So God is one among the puruṣas.
- Yoga accepts three pramāṇas: perception, inference and testimony (YS 1.7).
- Yoga asks for moral training first. Yama (restraints) and niyama (observances) are the first two limbs of the eight-limbed path.

questions.question_md: ‘‘The silver that appears in a shell cannot be unreal because it appears ; that silver cannot also be real because it is found to be not there when we see the shell properly’’. This is the view of :
questions.explanation:
This is the **anirvacanīya-khyāti** of Śaṁkara's Advaita Vedānta.

- The silver is not unreal, because we see it. A wholly unreal thing, like a hare's horn, never appears.
- The silver is not real, because correct seeing later removes it.

So the silver is "anirvacanīya": we cannot describe it as real or as unreal. Śaṁkara uses the same idea for the world, which is neither real nor unreal.

Rāmānuja holds satkhyāti: all knowledge is of the real. Īśvarakṛṣṇa is the author of the Sāṁkhya Kārikā. Nāgārjuna is a Mādhyamika Buddhist, and the Mādhyamika error theory is asatkhyāti.

questions.question_md:
Match **List - I** and **List - II** and choose the correct answer with the help of the code given below :

| List - I | List - II |
|---|---|
| (a) Jivanmukti | (i) Nyāya - Vaiśeṣikas |
| (b) Videhamukti | (ii) Early Mīmāṁsakas |
| (c) Niḥśreyasah | (iii) Śaṁkara |
| (d) Svarga | (iv) Madhva |
questions.explanation:
Each idea of the final goal belongs to one school.

- **Jīvanmukti → Śaṁkara (iii).** Śaṁkara says that a person can be free while still living in the body.
- **Videhamukti → Madhva (iv).** Madhva accepts liberation only after the death of the body.
- **Niḥśreyasa → Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika (i).** Their sūtras call the highest good niḥśreyasa. They describe it as the end of all pain.
- **Svarga → Early Mīmāṁsakas (ii).** Early Mīmāṁsā made heaven (svarga) the goal of Vedic ritual.

So the code is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii. The other codes give jīvanmukti to Madhva or Nyāya, which is wrong.

questions.question_md:
Given below are **Assertion (A)** and **Reason (R)**. Consider them and select the correct code given below, in the context of Śaṁkara’s Philosophy :

**Assertion (A) :** Śaṁkara’s philosophy denies the world outright

**Reason (R) :** The fact is that there is a real external world

**Code :**
options: (A) and (R) are both true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
(A) and (R) are both true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation:
- **(A) is false.** Śaṁkara does not deny the world outright. He accepts its vyāvahārika (practical or empirical) reality. The world is māyā only from the highest (pāramārthika) point of view. It is not a pure nothing like a hare's horn.
- **(R) is true** at the practical level. Śaṁkara criticises the Yogācāra Buddhists, who say that only ideas exist. Against them he says that external objects really exist for our experience.

So (A) is false and (R) is true. Since Śaṁkara accepts the empirical world, the claim that he denies it outright fails.

questions.question_md: The correct sequence of evolution according to Sāṁkhya is :
questions.explanation:
Sāṁkhya gives this order of evolution from prakṛti:

1. **Mahat** (buddhi, the cosmic intellect) comes first.
2. **Ahaṁkāra** (ego) comes from mahat.
3. From the sāttvika ahaṁkāra comes **manas** (mind). The five **jñānendriyas** (sense organs) and the five **karmendriyas** (organs of action) also come from it.
4. From the tāmasa ahaṁkāra come the five tanmātras (subtle elements), and then the gross elements.

Only the last option starts with mahat and then ahaṁkāra. The other options put the products before their causes. For example, they put the indriyas before mahat.

questions.question_md: Prakṛti in Sāṁkhya philosophy is :
questions.explanation:
In Sāṁkhya, **prakṛti** (primal matter) is **unconscious** (acetana). Only puruṣa (the self) is conscious.

Prakṛti is also **active**. It has three guṇas (sattva, rajas and tamas), which are always changing. When the balance of the guṇas breaks, prakṛti evolves into the world. Puruṣa is conscious but passive.

Prakṛti is independent (svatantra), not dependent, so the first option is wrong. Options that call it conscious describe puruṣa, not prakṛti.

questions.question_md: In Mīmāṁsā philosophy, all the following propositions are true except :
options: Mīmāṁsā upholds the theory of Svataḥ prāmāṇyavāda
The perceptual error in case of shell-silver illusion is because of adhyāsa
questions.explanation:
The question asks for the statement that is **not** true for Mīmāṁsā.

- **Svataḥ prāmāṇyavāda: true.** Mīmāṁsā says that knowledge is valid by itself.
- **The self is active: true.** The self is the doer (kartā) and enjoyer of ritual action.
- **The Vedas are apauruṣeya: true.** No person, human or divine, wrote them.
- **Shell-silver error comes from adhyāsa: not true.** Adhyāsa (superimposition) is Śaṁkara's Advaita idea.

Mīmāṁsā explains error in its own ways. Prabhākara gives akhyāti, the failure to see a difference. Kumārila gives viparīta-khyāti, seeing one real thing as another.

questions.question_md:
Given below are **Assertion (A)** and a **Reason (R)**. Consider them and select the correct code in the context of Buddhism :

**Assertion (A) :** Nirvāṇa is momentary

**Reason (R) :** Sarvam Kṣaṇikaṁ Kṣaṇikaṁ

**Code :**
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation:
- **(R) is true.** "Everything is momentary" (sarvaṁ kṣaṇikam) is a core Buddhist teaching. All conditioned things arise and pass away every moment.
- **(A) is false.** Nirvāṇa is not a conditioned thing. Buddhist schools call it asaṁskṛta (unconditioned). It is the end of craving and rebirth, not a passing moment.

The law of momentariness applies to conditioned things. So it cannot make nirvāṇa momentary. Thus (A) is false and (R) is true.

questions.question_md:
Match **List - I** with **List - II** and choose the correct answer with the help of code given below :

| List - I | List - II |
|---|---|
| (Writer) | (Writing) |
| (a) Sri Aurobindo | (i) Freedom from the known |
| (b) J. Krishnamurti | (ii) The Recovery of Faith |
| (c) K.C. Bhattacharya | (iii) Studies in Vedantism |
| (d) S. Radhakrishnan | (iv) Savitri, a Legend and a symbol |
questions.explanation:
Match each thinker with the book.

- **Sri Aurobindo → *Savitri: A Legend and a Symbol* (iv).** This is his long spiritual poem.
- **J. Krishnamurti → *Freedom from the Known* (i).**
- **K.C. Bhattacharya → *Studies in Vedantism* (iii).** This is one of his early works.
- **S. Radhakrishnan → *Recovery of Faith* (ii).**

So the code is a-iv, b-i, c-iii, d-ii. The other codes link *Savitri* to the wrong author, so they fail.

questions.question_md: Which among the following is **not** correctly matched with Sri Aurobindo’s concept of three poises of Supermental consciousness ?
questions.explanation:
In *The Life Divine*, Sri Aurobindo describes three poises (states) of the Supermind.

- **Comprehending consciousness**: the Supermind holds all things in one unity.
- **Apprehending consciousness**: it stands back a little and views each thing within the whole.
- **Projecting consciousness**: it enters into each form as the individual Divine.

**Analytical consciousness** is not one of the three poises. Analysis splits things apart, which is the way of the lower mind. The Supermind sees unity in all things.

questions.question_md: Who among the following has addressed supreme reality as ‘Jeevana Devatā’ ?
questions.explanation:
**Rabindranath Tagore** called the Supreme "Jīvan Devatā" (the Lord of Life). For him, this divine presence lives inside the person. It guides the whole of the poet's life and gives it unity. This idea is central to his *Religion of Man*.

Sri Aurobindo speaks of the Supermind. S. Radhakrishnan speaks of the Absolute and God. B.R. Ambedkar did not describe reality in such theistic terms.

questions.question_md: Who among the following has said that ‘It is better that mankind should become atheist by following reason than blindly believe in two million of gods’ ?
questions.explanation:
**Swami Vivekananda** said these words. He said that it is better to become an atheist through reason than to believe blindly in millions of gods on someone's authority.

Vivekananda wanted religion to stand the test of reason and experience. He did not want people to accept religion on blind faith.

Ambedkar also valued reason, but this sentence is famous from Vivekananda's lectures. Gandhi and Tagore did not say this.

questions.question_md:
Given below are an **Assertion (A)** and a **Reason (R)**. Consider them and select the correct code given below in the context of K.C. Bhattacharya :

**Assertion (A) :** Judgements of Philosophy are Pseudo Judgements.

**Reason (R) :** In all Judgements Predicate is Contained in the Subject

**Code :**
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation:
- **(A) is true** for K.C. Bhattacharya. In *The Concept of Philosophy*, he says that philosophy is not literal knowledge of facts. Its contents are not literally thinkable, unlike scientific judgements. So philosophical judgements are not true judgements. In this sense they are pseudo-judgements.
- **(R) is false.** The view that the predicate is always in the subject belongs to Leibniz. It is not KCB's theory. It is also not true of all judgements. Synthetic judgements add something new.

So (A) is true and (R) is false. The reasoning for (A) is a little open to debate, but (R) is clearly false.

questions.question_md: Who among the following holds the view that : ‘Divine knowledge is creational, and as there is nothing outside God. He himself is the object of his knowledge. He creates as he knows, and knows as he creates.
questions.notes: The opening quotation mark is not closed in the source.
questions.explanation:
**Muhammad Iqbal** wrote this in *The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam*.

For Iqbal, God's knowledge is not like human knowledge. Human knowledge looks at an object that is already outside. Nothing is outside God. So God's knowing and God's creating are the same act. God creates as he knows, and knows as he creates.

Tagore, Vivekananda and K.C. Bhattacharya do not use this argument. The idea of creative divine knowledge is a key point in Iqbal.

questions.question_md:
Match **List - I** with **List - II** and choose the correct answer with the help of code given below :

| List - I | List - II |
|---|---|
| (Thinker) | (Thought) |
| (a) S. Radhakrishnan | (i) What is spoken must be in the first instance believed |
| (b) Vivekananda | (ii) The destiny of the human soul is to realise its oneness with the Supreme |
| (c) K.C. Bhattacharya | (iii) The infinite and finite are one as song and singing are one |
| (d) Tagore | (iv) Immortality is the realisation of oneness with everything |
questions.explanation:
Match each thinker with the thought.

- **S. Radhakrishnan → (ii).** The human soul is destined to realise its oneness with the Supreme.
- **Vivekananda → (iv).** Immortality means realising oneness with everything.
- **K.C. Bhattacharya → (i).** "What is spoken must be first believed." This comes from his idea of speakable, believed content.
- **Tagore → (iii).** The finite and the infinite are one, as the song and the singing are one.

So the code is a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii. The second option is close, but it gives (iii) to KCB and (i) to Tagore. That is wrong.

questions.question_md: According to the ex nihilo theory of St. Augustine ;
options: God created the world out of the existent
God created the world out of nothing
God created the evil out of something
God created himself out of nothing
questions.explanation:
*Creatio ex nihilo* means "creation out of nothing." St. Augustine holds that God created the world from nothing. God did not use any pre-existing matter, and the world did not flow out of God's own being.

- God did not create from something already existing. That would make matter co-eternal with God.
- God did not create evil. For Augustine, evil is only an absence of good (privatio boni).
- God did not create himself. God is eternal and uncreated.

questions.question_md: ‘‘If there are no individual circular things ; there would be no such thing as the form called circularity’’, can be attributed to ;
questions.explanation:
This is **Aristotle's** view of forms. For him, a form (universal) exists only in individual things. Circularity exists only in circular things. If no circular things existed, there would be no circularity. This view is "universals in things" (universalia in rebus).

Plato holds the opposite view. His Forms exist apart from particular things. They would exist even if no particular things existed. Socrates looked for definitions but did not hold this theory. Augustine put the Forms in God's mind.

questions.question_md:
Consider the following statements in the light of Plato’s metaphysics and mark the correct code :

(a) What is truly real is not the objects we encounter in sensory experience
(b) Forms can only be grasped intellectually
(c) Forms are just ideas or concepts in the mind of some one

**Code :**
questions.explanation:
Check each statement for Plato.

- **(a) True.** The objects of sense experience change and are only copies. The truly real things are the Forms.
- **(b) True.** We grasp Forms only by the intellect (reason), not by the senses.
- **(c) False.** The Forms are not just ideas in someone's mind. They exist objectively and independently of any mind.

So only (a) and (b) are true.

questions.question_md: Who among the following holds the view that ‘‘Things are things because they can be ennumerated’’ ?
questions.notes: 'ennumerated' (sic) in the source.
questions.explanation:
**Pythagoras** and his followers held that number is the basic reality. Things are what they are because of number. So things exist as things because we can count (enumerate) them. They also saw number and ratio in music and in the heavens.

Anaximander took the apeiron (the boundless) as the first principle. Heraclitus spoke of fire, flux and the logos. Parmenides taught that Being is one and does not change.

questions.question_md:
Given below are **Assertion (A)** and **Reason (R)**. Consider them in the light of Thomas Aquinas and mark the correct code :

**Assertion (A) :** God is the uncaused cause of the world.

**Reason (R) :** Anything that begins to exist has to be caused to exist by something that already exists.

**Code :**
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation:
Thomas Aquinas proves God by the argument from causes, his "second way."

- **(R) is true** for Aquinas. A thing cannot bring itself into existence. Anything that comes to exist needs a cause that already exists.
- **(A) is true.** The chain of causes cannot go back without end. So there must be a first cause that no other thing causes. This first cause is God.

(R) is the principle that leads to (A). It shows why the world needs a cause, and the cause must stop in an uncaused cause. So (R) correctly explains (A).

questions.question_md:
Which one of the following early Greek Philosophers held that ;

‘‘You can not know what is not, nor can you express it. What can be thought of and what can be - they are the same’’.
questions.explanation:
This is **Parmenides**. In his poem, he says that "what is not" cannot be known or spoken. Thinking and being are the same. So only Being is real, and change and plurality are illusions.

Heraclitus taught that everything changes, which is the opposite view. Empedocles spoke of four roots with Love and Strife. Democritus spoke of atoms and the void. He even gave the void (what is not) a kind of reality, so he could not hold this view.

questions.question_md:
Match **List - I** with **List - II** and choose the correct answer with the help of code given below :

| List - I | List - II |
|---|---|
| (a) Anaximenes | (i) Nous |
| (b) Anaximander | (ii) Air |
| (c) Thales | (iii) Apeiron |
| (d) Anaxagoras | (iv) Water |
questions.explanation:
Match each early Greek thinker with his first principle.

- **Anaximenes → Air (ii).**
- **Anaximander → Apeiron (iii),** the boundless or the unlimited.
- **Thales → Water (iv).**
- **Anaxagoras → Nous (i),** mind, which orders all things.

So the code is a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.

questions.question_md: Which of the following sequence correctly represent the successive stages of the Absolute mind according to Hegel ?
questions.explanation:
For Hegel, Absolute Spirit (Absolute mind) knows itself in three forms, in rising order.

1. **Art**: the Absolute appears in sense form, in beauty.
2. **Religion**: the Absolute appears in images and pictorial thought.
3. **Philosophy**: the Absolute knows itself in pure concepts. This is the highest stage.

So the order is art, religion, philosophy. The option with religion before art reverses the first two steps. Psychology belongs to subjective spirit, not to Absolute spirit.

questions.question_md:
In the light of Kant’s philosophy, match **List - I** with **List - II** and choose the correct answer with the help of code given below :

| List - I | List - II |
|---|---|
| (a) The Problematical Judgement | (i) Heat is a form of motion |
| (b) The Infinite Judgement | (ii) This may be poison |
| (c) The Apodictic Judgement | (iii) Mind is unextended |
| (d) The Affirmative Judgement | (iv) Every effect must have a cause |
questions.explanation:
Kant's table of judgements groups judgements by quality and modality.

- **Problematic → "This may be poison" (ii).** It states only a possibility.
- **Infinite → "Mind is unextended" (iii).** The form is affirmative, but the predicate is negative ("un-extended").
- **Apodictic → "Every effect must have a cause" (iv).** It states a necessity.
- **Affirmative → "Heat is a form of motion" (i).** It simply affirms a predicate.

So the code is a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.

questions.question_md:
In the light of Heidegger’s thought match the following **List - I** with **List - II** and choose the correct answer with the help of code given below :

| List - I | List - II |
|---|---|
| (a) Phenomenon | (i) Possibility |
| (b) Fear | (ii) That which reveals itself |
| (c) Ready - to - hand | (iii) A mode of man’s being |
| (d) Existenz | (iv) Circumspection |
questions.explanation:
Match the terms from Heidegger's *Being and Time*.

- **Phenomenon → that which reveals itself (ii).** Heidegger defines it as what shows itself in itself.
- **Fear → a mode of man's being (iii).** Fear is a mood, a way in which Dasein (human being) finds itself in the world.
- **Ready-to-hand → circumspection (iv).** We deal with tools through circumspection, a practical looking-around.
- **Existenz → possibility (i).** Dasein is always its own possibilities.

So the code is a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.

questions.question_md:
Given below are **Assertion (A)** and **Reason (R)**. Consider them and select the correct code :

**Assertion (A) :** According to Gilbert Ryle, to say of someone that ‘x’ is intelligent implies

**Reason (R) :**

(i) It is an assertion about x’s mind
(ii) It is our knowledge of x’s public performance

**Code :**
options: Both (A) and (R) (i), (ii) are true and (R) (i), (ii) both are correct explanations of (A)
(A) and (R) are true but (R) (i) only is the correct explanation of (A)
(A) and (R) are true but (R) (ii) only is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are false and (R) (i), (ii) is not a correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation:
The question is badly printed, but its meaning is clear. It asks what "x is intelligent" means for Gilbert Ryle.

- **(i) is wrong for Ryle.** In *The Concept of Mind*, Ryle rejects the idea of a "ghost in the machine". Calling x intelligent is not a report about hidden events in x's private mind.
- **(ii) is right.** The word refers to x's dispositions, shown in public performance. For example, x solves problems well and corrects mistakes.

So only (R)(ii) correctly explains (A). The option that also includes (i) is wrong. It brings back the mind–body dualism that Ryle attacks.

questions.question_md: Which of the following statement is **incorrect** in the context of Nietzsche :
options: Slave morality settles for the imaginary revenge of the after life
Slave morality is inauthentic because it is always a reaction, never originating impulse
Slave morality immediately says yes to what comes from outside, to what is different, to what is not oneself
Slave morality is a morality of resignation, deferment and prohibition
questions.explanation:
Nietzsche contrasts master morality with slave morality in *On the Genealogy of Morals*.

Slave morality says **"No"** to what is outside, to what is different, to what is not itself. This "No" is its creative act. So the statement that slave morality says "yes" to what comes from outside is **incorrect**. Master morality is the one that says yes to itself.

The other statements are correct:

- Slave morality takes an imaginary revenge through the afterlife.
- It is a reaction (ressentiment), never an original impulse.
- It is a morality of resignation, delay and prohibition.

questions.question_md: In the light of William James, which of the following is **not** a correct statement ?
options: False ideas are those that we cannot verify
Theories are only man - made language, in which we write our reports of nature
questions.explanation:
William James gives a pragmatic theory of truth. He says that true ideas are those that we can assimilate, validate, corroborate and verify. False ideas are those that we cannot verify. So the statement "true ideas cannot be validated" is **not** correct.

The other statements are James's views:

- In "The Will to Believe," life gives us forced options. We must choose.
- In *Pragmatism*, he says that theories are only a man-made language. We write our reports of nature in it.
- False ideas are those we cannot verify.

questions.question_md: Phenomenology, according to Husserl, rests upon which of the following radical conviction ?
options: Meaning is in the mind alone
Meaning is in the world alone
Meaning is neither in the mind nor in the world
Meaning is in the intentional relationship between the mind and the world
questions.explanation:
Husserl builds phenomenology on **intentionality**. Consciousness is always consciousness *of* something.

So meaning is not in the mind alone, as subjectivism says. It is not in the world alone, as naive realism says. Meaning arises in the intentional relation between the act of consciousness and its object.

The option that puts meaning in neither mind nor world denies meaning altogether. Husserl does not hold this view.

questions.question_md:
Given below are **Assertion (A)** and **Reason (R)**. Consider them and select the **correct** code :

**Assertion (A) :** According to Kant, though we cannot directly experience Noumena, a special class of Transcendental Ideas bridges the gap between the Phenomenal and Noumenal Worlds

**Reason (R) :**

(i) Ideas are called Transcendental because they are products of reason alone and not the result of the mind’s interaction with sensation
(ii) They ‘Unify’ or ‘make possible’ having experience in the first place.

**Code :**
options: Both (A) and (R) (i), (ii) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
(A) and (R) (i) are true and (R) (i) is the only correct explanation of (A)
(A) and (R) (ii) are true and (R) (ii) alone is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) (i), (ii) are false and (R) does not provide a correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation:
The wording follows a popular textbook account of Kant.

- **(A) is true in that account.** We cannot experience noumena. But reason forms Transcendental Ideas (soul, world and God). They point beyond the phenomenal world.
- **(R)(i) is true.** These ideas come from reason alone, not from the meeting of mind and sensation.
- **(R)(ii) is also accepted.** The ideas "unify" our knowledge. Kant says that without this unity of reason, there is no coherent use of the understanding.

So the expected answer is that (A) and both parts of (R) are true, and (R) explains (A). The question is open to debate. Strictly, the categories make experience possible, and the ideas are only regulative.

questions.question_md:
Match **List - I** with **List - II** and mark the correct code from given below :

| List - I | List - II |
|---|---|
| (a) Epoche | (i) The intending consciousness |
| (b) Eidos | (ii) Suspension of the empirical and metaphysical presupposition |
| (c) Intuition | (iii) The invariant structure |
| (d) Noesis | (iv) An active repossession of the passive play of possibilities, reuniting them in a single grasp |
questions.explanation:
Match the terms of Husserl's phenomenology.

- **Epoché → (ii).** It is the suspension of empirical and metaphysical presuppositions, or "bracketing."
- **Eidos → (iii).** It is the essence, the invariant structure found by free variation.
- **Intuition → (iv).** It actively grasps the play of possibilities and unites them in one grasp.
- **Noesis → (i).** It is the intending act of consciousness. Its object side is the noema.

So the code is a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.

questions.question_md:
Which one of the following code is correct with reference to the thought given below ? Answer considering (a), (b), (c) and (d) :

Thought : ‘‘.... mind and body, extension and thought as two of the many inseparable aspects of a single, all - inclusive reality. Being co - existent attributes of the substance, thought and extension cannot interact’’.

(a) Descartes
(b) Leibnitz
(c) Spinoza
(d) Berkeley

**Code :**
questions.explanation:
This is **Spinoza**. He holds that there is only one substance, God or Nature. Thought and extension are two of its infinite attributes. They are two aspects of the same reality. So mind and body do not interact; they run in parallel.

- Descartes treats mind and body as two separate substances that interact.
- Leibniz explains mind and body by pre-established harmony between monads.
- Berkeley denies material substance, so extension is not an attribute of reality for him.

questions.question_md: For Leibnitz, monads are :
questions.explanation:
For Leibniz, monads are the simple units of reality.

- **Indivisible**: they have no parts.
- **Self-active**: each monad changes from its own inner principle. Monads "have no windows."
- **Spiritual**: they are centres of force and perception, not bits of matter.

So all three features apply. The options with "only" leave out one feature. The option "material" is wrong, because monads are not extended matter.

questions.question_md:
Match **List - I** with **List - II** and choose the correct answer by using code given below :

| List - I | List - II |
|---|---|
| (a) Hume | (i) The idea of causality is not necessarily connected with uniformity |
| (b) Locke | (ii) God is the real cause of spirits and things |
| (c) Berkeley | (iii) The relation of the soul to the body is of the nature of the pilot and his machine |
| (d) Descartes | (iv) Past experience of constant conjunction. |
questions.explanation:
Match each thinker with the view.

- **Hume → (iv).** Our idea of cause comes from past experience of constant conjunction, along with habit.
- **Locke → (i).** Locke gets the idea of cause from seeing one thing produce another. He does not base it on uniformity.
- **Berkeley → (ii).** God is the real cause of ideas. Only spirits are active causes.
- **Descartes → (iii).** The soul–body relation is compared to a pilot and his ship (machine). Descartes uses this image, though he says the union is closer.

So the code is a-iv, b-i, c-ii, d-iii.

questions.question_md:
Which one among the following code is acceptable to John Locke ? Answer considering (a), (b), (c) and (d) :

(a) Only Agreement of Ideas is Knowledge
(b) Only Agreement of Sensations is Knowledge
(c) Agreement or Disagreement of Ideas is Knowledge
(d) Agreement or Disagreement of Sensations is Knowledge

**Code :**
questions.explanation:
Locke defines knowledge in Book IV of the *Essay*. Knowledge is "the perception of the connection and agreement, or disagreement and repugnancy, of any of our ideas."

- **(c) is fully correct.** Knowledge is the agreement or disagreement of ideas.
- **(a) is partly correct.** Agreement of ideas is knowledge, but the word "only" leaves out disagreement.
- **(b) and (d) are wrong.** Locke speaks of ideas, not sensations.

Only the code (c) and (a) avoids sensations. So it is the best choice. It is open to debate, because the "only" in (a) does not fit Locke exactly.

questions.question_md:
Which one among the following code is acceptable to Spinoza ? Answer considering (a), (b), (c), (d) :

(a) Nature as a self-creating reality is known as Natura Naturans.
(b) Nature as a self-creating reality is known as Natura Naturata.
(c) In its aspect of a creative product, Nature is known as Natura Naturata.
(d) In its static aspect, Nature is known as Natura Naturans.

**Code :**
questions.explanation:
Spinoza uses two Latin terms for Nature (God).

- **Natura naturans** ("nature naturing"): Nature as active and self-creating. This is God as substance with its attributes. So **(a) is true** and (b) is false.
- **Natura naturata** ("nature natured"): Nature as the product, the world of modes. So **(c) is true**.
- **(d) is false.** Natura naturans is the active side of Nature, not the static side.

So (a) and (c) are acceptable to Spinoza.

questions.question_md: In the philosophy of Berkeley, all the following statements are true except :
options: What we call objects are only ideas
There are ideas of flying horses
questions.explanation:
Berkeley denies **material substance**. This is matter that exists without being perceived. But he does not deny the things we see and touch. He says that he does not argue against anything we can perceive by sense. Tables and trees are real collections of ideas. So "there are no physical objects" does not state his view exactly.

The other statements are true for Berkeley:

- What we call objects are only ideas (esse est percipi).
- God produces the ideas of sense in us.
- We can form ideas of imagination, such as a flying horse, by combining ideas.

This answer is open to debate. Some textbooks loosely say that Berkeley denies physical objects.

questions.question_md: Select the **correct** sequence of process of evolution regarding Sri Aurobindo’s philosophy :
questions.explanation:
Sri Aurobindo describes a triple process in evolution.

1. **Widening**: each new principle that appears enlarges the field of existence.
2. **Heightening**: consciousness rises to a higher level, such as from life to mind.
3. **Integration**: the higher principle takes up and changes the lower levels.

So the order is widening, heightening, integration. The other orders do not follow the sequence that Aurobindo gives in *The Life Divine*.

papers.instructions_note: 75 compulsory questions, 2 marks each

questions.question_md: The cause of the apprehension of past and present according to the Vaiśeṣikas is :
questions.explanation:
Vaiśeṣika lists nine substances (dravya). Kāla (time) is one of them. It is one, eternal and all-pervading.

Vaiśeṣika infers Kāla from notions such as "past", "present", "future", "older", "younger", "at once" and "slowly". These notions need a common cause, and that cause is Kāla.

- **Dik** (space or direction) explains "here", "there", "east" and "west". It does not explain past and present.
- **Ākāśa** (ether) is the substrate of sound.
- **Manas** (mind) is the inner organ that links the self with the senses. It explains why we know one thing at a time.

questions.question_md: According to Rāmānuja, apṛthaksiddhi is a relation between :
options: Between Brahman and Jiva on the one hand and between Brahman and Jagat on the other.
questions.explanation:
Apṛthaksiddhi means "inseparable relation". Rāmānuja uses it in place of the Nyāya relation called samavāya (inherence).

For Rāmānuja, Brahman is a qualified whole. Cit (conscious selves, the jīvas) and acit (unconscious matter, the jagat) are its body. They cannot exist apart from Brahman. So the relation holds in two directions:

- between Brahman and the jīvas, and
- between Brahman and the world (jagat).

The options that say "only" leave out one side of this relation. Rāmānuja also uses apṛthaksiddhi for a substance and its attributes, but the main use is Brahman and its body.

questions.question_md: What is the asamavāyikāraṇa of a dvyaṇuka according to the Vaīśeṣikas ?
questions.explanation:
Vaiśeṣika names three kinds of cause:

- **Samavāyi kāraṇa** (inherent cause): the material in which the effect inheres.
- **Asamavāyi kāraṇa** (non-inherent cause): a quality or action that inheres in the material cause and helps to make the effect.
- **Nimitta kāraṇa** (efficient cause): the agent or instrument.

For a dvyaṇuka (dyad, a pair of atoms):

- The two paramāṇus (atoms) are the inherent cause.
- The saṁyoga (conjunction) of the two atoms is the non-inherent cause.
- Īśvara (God) and adṛṣṭa (unseen merit) are efficient causes.

The parimāṇa (size) of an atom does not produce the size of the dyad. Vaiśeṣika says the dyad's size comes from the number two, not from atomic size.

questions.question_md: According to the Vaiśeṣikas sattā sāmānya exists in :
options: Dravya, Guṇa, Karma and Sāmānya only
questions.explanation:
Sattā is the highest universal (para sāmānya), "being" or "existence".

In Vaiśeṣika, sattā inheres only in the first three categories:

- Dravya (substance)
- Guṇa (quality)
- Karma (action)

These three are called "sattāvat", that is, things that have existence through the universal sattā.

Sāmānya, viśeṣa and samavāya do not have the universal sattā. They have only "svātmasattva", their own nature as real. If a universal had a universal in it, an infinite regress would follow. So the options that add Sāmānya, or that leave out Dravya or Karma, are wrong.

questions.question_md: Which one among the following is **not** a mūrtadravya ?
questions.explanation:
In Vaiśeṣika, a mūrta dravya is a substance with limited size (it is not all-pervading). It can move.

The five mūrta dravyas are:

- Kṣiti or pṛthvī (earth)
- Ap (water)
- Tejas (fire)
- Marut or vāyu (air)
- Manas (mind), which is atomic in size

The Ātman (self) is vibhu, that is, all-pervading. So it has no limited size and does not move. Ākāśa, Kāla and Dik are also all-pervading. Therefore Ātman is not a mūrta dravya.

questions.question_md: Who among the following Early Greek Philosophers distinguished between appearance and reality as a contrast between apparent permanence and hidden reality of continuous change ?
questions.explanation:
Heraclitus taught that everything is in constant flux. His famous image is the river: "you cannot step into the same river twice."

For Heraclitus, things look stable to our senses. This permanence is only an appearance. The hidden reality is continuous change, held in order by the logos (rational law). So he contrasts apparent permanence with a hidden reality of change.

- **Anaxagoras** and **Empedocles** held that real elements do not change. Only their mixtures change.
- **Democritus** contrasted sense qualities with atoms and the void.

These thinkers take the opposite view: hidden reality is permanent, and change is the appearance.

questions.question_md:
Consider the following statements in the light of the philosophy of Locke and mark the correct code :

(a) Primary qualities are sensible qualities that depend on the perceiver.
(b) Primary qualities are Color, Sound, Taste and Texture.
(c) Secondary qualities are those whose existence is independent of any perceiver.
(d) Primary qualities are objective properties of things whereas secondary qualities are subjective properties.

**Code :**
questions.explanation:
Locke divides the qualities of objects into two kinds.

- **(a) False.** Primary qualities do not depend on the perceiver. They are in the object itself.
- **(b) False.** Primary qualities are solidity, extension, figure, motion or rest, and number. Colour, sound and taste are secondary qualities.
- **(c) False.** Secondary qualities are powers in objects to produce ideas in us. The ideas of these qualities exist only in the perceiver.
- **(d) True.** Primary qualities are objective, and the ideas of them resemble the object. Secondary qualities are subjective. Their ideas do not resemble anything in the object.

So only (d) is true.

questions.question_md: According to Cartesian dualism human beings are a combination of :
options: Incorporeal and corporeal substances each operating according to separate sets of laws.
Corporeal substances operating according to the same set of laws.
Incorporeal substances each operating according to separate sets of rules.
Incorporeal and corporeal substances both operating to the same set of laws.
questions.explanation:
Descartes holds that there are two kinds of finite substance:

- **Mind**: an incorporeal (non-bodily) thinking thing. Its essence is thought.
- **Body**: a corporeal (bodily) extended thing. Its essence is extension.

A human being is a union of the two. The body follows mechanical laws of physics. The mind is free and follows the laws of thought and will. So each substance works by its own set of laws.

The options with only corporeal or only incorporeal substances miss the dualism. The option with "the same set of laws" goes against Descartes' sharp division of mind and matter.

questions.question_md: An individual for Plato can be :
options: Sensible object that can be known by perception.
Image that can be known by perception.
Sensible object that can be known by reason.
Sensible object that can be known by imagination.
questions.explanation:
For Plato, an individual is a particular thing in the sensible world, such as this horse or this chair. It is a sensible object.

Plato's Divided Line (in the *Republic*) places sensible objects in the lower part, the world of opinion (doxa). We grasp them through sense perception. Reason grasps only the Forms, which are universal and unchanging.

- "Image known by perception" describes shadows and reflections. These are copies of individuals, not the individuals themselves.
- "Sensible object known by reason" is wrong because reason knows Forms, not particulars.
- Imagination (eikasia) grasps images, not real objects.

questions.question_md: Which one of the following can be placed under "Opinion", according to Plato ?
questions.explanation:
In the *Republic*, Plato divides cognition into two parts:

- **Knowledge (epistēmē)** has the Forms as its objects. "Chairness" is the Form of chair. So it belongs to knowledge, not to opinion.
- **Opinion (doxa)** deals with the changing sensible world. It has two stages: eikasia (imagination of images) and pistis (belief about physical things).

A belief about a chair is a case of pistis. So "Belief of Chair" falls under opinion.

The blackness or whiteness of a chair are sensible qualities. The options present them as general features, like "chairness", so they do not name a state of opinion. The question is loosely worded, but "belief" matches Plato's term for the upper part of opinion.

questions.question_md: According to Nichomachean Ethics phronesis refers to :
questions.explanation:
In the *Nicomachean Ethics*, Aristotle uses phronesis for practical wisdom. It is an intellectual virtue. It helps a person to think well about what is good to do in a given situation.

Aristotle says that a person cannot have full moral virtue without phronesis. Phronesis finds the right mean between excess and deficiency.

- **Cardinal virtue** is a later term for courage, temperance, justice and prudence.
- **Natural excellence** is a natural tendency, not a virtue built by reason and habit.
- **Happiness** is eudaimonia, the final end of life. It is not phronesis.

questions.question_md: "The mind creates the ideas of causality and necessity ; we do not observe them." This statement can be attributed to which one of the following modern western philosophers ?
questions.explanation:
Hume argues that we never observe a necessary connection between a cause and its effect. We see only that one event comes before the other, that they are close, and that they always occur together.

After many repetitions, the mind forms a habit (custom). It expects the effect when it sees the cause. The idea of necessity comes from this feeling of expectation in the mind. It is not a property that we observe in objects.

- **Locke** and **Descartes** accept real causal powers or necessary connections.
- **Mill** gives methods to find causes. He does not hold that the mind creates necessity.

questions.question_md:
Consider the following statements in the context of William James' pragmatism and mark the correct code :

(a) Universalist notion of truth is rejected
(b) Truth is contextless
(c) Truth happens to an idea

**Code :**
questions.explanation:
William James is an American pragmatist. For him, an idea is true if it "works" in experience.

- **(a) True.** James rejects a fixed, absolute or universal notion of truth. Truth changes as experience grows.
- **(b) False.** Truth is not contextless. It depends on the situation and on the practical results of an idea.
- **(c) True.** In *Pragmatism*, James writes that "truth happens to an idea". An idea becomes true, or is made true, by events.

So only (a) and (c) are true.

questions.question_md: According to which one of the following Western Philosophers "Truth is a subjective condition, not an objective one."
questions.explanation:
Kierkegaard wrote that "truth is subjectivity". This appears in his *Concluding Unscientific Postscript*.

For Kierkegaard, the important truth is not an objective fact. It is the truth that a person lives by with passion and commitment. Faith is his main example. So truth is a subjective condition of the existing person.

- **Hume** is an empiricist who studies how ideas come from impressions.
- **Kant** looks for universal and necessary conditions of knowledge.
- **William James** links truth to practical results, not to inward passion.

questions.question_md: 'Self' according to Hume is :
questions.explanation:
Hume looks inside himself for an impression of the self. He finds only particular perceptions, such as heat, cold, love or pain.

So Hume says that the self is "a bundle or collection of different perceptions". These perceptions follow one another very quickly. We have no impression of one simple self that stays the same over time. Personal identity is a product of the imagination.

- "A static subject" and "a persistent identity" describe the substance view that Hume rejects.
- "A static physical entity" is a materialist view. It does not fit Hume either.

questions.question_md: Which of the following is **not** a correct statement ?
options: Sāṁkhya holds that a word signifies a particular.
Kumārila holds that word cannot mean particular.
Early Mimāṁsakās hold that word means Ākṛti.
Naiyāyikās hold that word does not mean Jāti
questions.explanation:
Indian schools debate what a word (pada) means: the particular (vyakti), the form (ākṛti) or the universal (jāti).

- **Sāṁkhya and particular.** Older accounts name Sāṁkhya among those who say a word means the particular. This is accepted as correct.
- **Kumārila.** He holds that a word means the universal (jāti), not the particular. This is correct.
- **Early Mīmāṁsā.** The *Mīmāṁsā Sūtra* says that a word means ākṛti. This is correct.
- **Nyāya.** The *Nyāya Sūtra* says that a word means the individual, the form and the universal together. So Nyāya does accept jāti as part of word meaning.

Therefore the statement that Naiyāyikas say a word does not mean jāti is not correct.

questions.question_md: In Indian logic vācyārtha does not mean :
questions.explanation:
Indian theories of meaning name different kinds of meaning (artha).

- **Vācyārtha** is the direct meaning of a word. It comes from abhidhā, the primary power of a word.
- **Abhidheyārtha**, **mukhyārtha** and **śakyārtha** are other names for the same direct meaning. Śakti is the power of a word to mean its object.
- **Vyaṅgyārtha** is the suggested meaning. It comes from vyañjanā (suggestion), not from abhidhā. Poetics treats it as a separate level of meaning.

So vācyārtha does not mean vyaṅgyārtha.

questions.question_md: According to which one of the following schools, Truth of Pramā is considered to be 'Abādhitārtha - Viṣayakatva' ?
questions.explanation:
Advaita Vedānta defines valid knowledge (pramā) in the *Vedānta Paribhāṣā*. Pramā is knowledge of an object that is:

- **anadhigata**: not already known, and
- **abādhita**: not contradicted later.

"Abādhitārtha-viṣayakatva" means "having an uncontradicted object". This is the Advaita mark of truth.

Advaita uses this mark because empirical knowledge is valid only until Brahman-knowledge cancels it. So truth is a matter of non-contradiction.

- **Cārvāka** accepts only perception.
- **Jaina** and **Sāṁkhya** have their own accounts of pramāṇa. They do not use this formula.

questions.question_md: 'The name and the universal concept are supplied by our imagination' is the view of :
questions.explanation:
The Buddhist logicians Dignāga and Dharmakīrti hold that perception is "kalpanāpoḍha", that is, free from conceptual construction.

What is real is only the unique momentary particular (svalakṣaṇa). Names (nāma) and universals (jāti) are not real. The mind adds them later through kalpanā (imagination or conceptual construction).

- **Naiyāyikas** and **Vaiśeṣikas** are realists. They hold that universals are real and that we perceive them.
- **Advaitins** accept universals in the empirical world. They do not reduce them to imagination.

questions.question_md: Which one of the following theory of Khyāti illustrates that "Khyāti is non-apprehension' of the distinction between two cognitions which are partial and imperfect" ?
questions.explanation:
Akhyāti is the theory of error of Prabhākara Mīmāṁsā. It means "non-apprehension".

Take the error "this is silver" when we see shell. Prabhākara says that two cognitions are present:

- a perception of "this" (the shining object in front), and
- a memory of silver seen before.

Both cognitions are true but partial. The error comes because we fail to grasp the distinction between them. So error is non-apprehension of the difference, not a wrong apprehension.

- **Anyathā khyāti** (Nyāya) says that we wrongly perceive one thing as another.
- **Viparīta khyāti** (Kumārila) is similar to anyathā khyāti.
- **Yathārtha khyāti** (Rāmānuja) says that all knowledge is real.

questions.question_md: Upamāna is considered as a case of Pratyabhijñā by :
questions.explanation:
The Jainas divide valid knowledge into pratyakṣa (direct) and parokṣa (indirect). Parokṣa includes smṛti (memory), pratyabhijñā (recognition), tarka, anumāna and āgama.

Pratyabhijñā combines a present perception with a memory. Examples are "this is that Devadatta" or "this is like that".

The Jainas include upamāna (comparison) under pratyabhijñā. For example, "the gavaya is like a cow" joins a present perception with a memory of the cow.

- **Naiyāyikas** treat upamāna as a separate pramāṇa.
- **Sāṁkhya** and **Vaiśeṣika** include it under other pramāṇas, such as perception, inference or testimony. They do not call it pratyabhijñā.

questions.question_md:
Consider the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) and select the correct code given below :

**Assertion (A) :** Advaitins accept only 'Anvayī' but not 'Kevalānvyī' Anumāna.

**Reason (R) :** The thing to be inferred must not be the counter positive of non-existence.

**Code :**
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not a correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation:
Nyāya names three kinds of inference. Kevalānvayī is one of them. It is inference with only positive examples, such as "this is nameable because it is knowable".

- **(A) is true.** The *Vedānta Paribhāṣā* says Advaita accepts only the anvayi form of inference. It rejects kevalānvayī and kevala-vyatirekī.
- **(R) is true.** It states the condition that a kevalānvayī sādhya must meet. The thing to be inferred must never be the counter-positive (pratiyogī) of absolute non-existence.

Advaita says that no such sādhya exists. Everything other than Brahman is negated in Brahman. So every possible sādhya is the counter-positive of some non-existence.

This is why Advaita rejects kevalānvayī. So (R) explains (A). The wording of (R) is compressed, and the question is open to some debate.

questions.question_md: According to Advaita Vedānta, the term Antaḥ-Karaṇa-Vṛtti refers to :
questions.explanation:
In Advaita Vedānta, the antaḥkaraṇa is the inner organ, or mind. In perception, the antaḥkaraṇa goes out through a sense organ to the object. It takes the form of the object.

This modification is called antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti. It removes the ignorance that covers the object. Then consciousness reveals the object. So in Advaita theory of knowledge, the vṛtti is the cognitive mode of the mind. Knowledge through it is called vṛtti-jñāna.

Desire and will are also states of the mind. So "All of the above" is tempting. But the term antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti appears mainly in the theory of knowledge. The answer is open to debate.

questions.question_md:
Consider the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) and select the correct code given below :

**Assertion (A) :** According to Advaita, anything perceived is not revealed by Pramātṛ - Caitanya.

**Reason (R) :** Anything Unperceived is veiled by Ajñāna .

**Code :**
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true but (R) is false and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation:
Advaita perception theory (*Vedānta Paribhāṣā*) speaks of three forms of consciousness:

- pramātṛ-caitanya: the knower
- pramāṇa-caitanya: the mental mode
- viṣaya-caitanya: the object

- **(A) is false.** In perception, the vṛtti (mental mode) goes out to the object. Object-consciousness then becomes one with knower-consciousness. So a perceived object is revealed by pramātṛ-caitanya.
- **(R) is true.** An unperceived object is veiled by ajñāna (ignorance). The witness knows it only as "unknown". Advaita says that everything is an object of the witness, either as known or as unknown.

So (A) is false and (R) is true.

questions.question_md:
Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer by using code given below :

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| (a) Sākṣātpratitīh Pratyakṣaṁ | (i) Dingnāga |
| (b) Viśeṣāvadhāraṇa-Pradhāna Pratyakṣaṁ | (ii) Gangeśa |
| (c) Pratyakṣaṁ kalpanapodhaṁ jñānaṁ | (iii) Prabhākara |
| (d) Jñānākarṇakaṁ jñānaṁ Pratyakṣaṁ | (iv) Yoga |

**Code :**
questions.explanation:
Each definition of perception belongs to a known school.

- **(a) Sākṣāt pratītiḥ pratyakṣam** means "perception is direct apprehension". This is the Prabhākara definition, from Śālikanātha. So a–iii.
- **(b) Viśeṣāvadhāraṇa-pradhānā vṛttiḥ pratyakṣam** means "perception mainly grasps the particular". This comes from Vyāsa's *Yoga Bhāṣya*. So b–iv.
- **(c) Pratyakṣaṁ kalpanāpoḍham** means "perception is free from conceptual construction". This is Dignāga's definition. So c–i.
- **(d) Jñānākaraṇakaṁ jñānaṁ pratyakṣam** means "perception is knowledge that does not have knowledge as its instrument". This is Gaṅgeśa's Navya-Nyāya definition. So d–ii.

The code a–iii, b–iv, c–i, d–ii fits all four.

questions.question_md: Lokasaṁgraha is meant for :
questions.explanation:
Lokasaṁgraha is a key idea of the *Bhagavad Gītā* (3.20, 3.25). It means "holding the world together", that is, the welfare of the people as a whole.

Kṛṣṇa tells Arjuna to act without selfish desire. A wise person should keep working to set an example and keep society in order. So lokasaṁgraha is for the benefit of the masses, the whole of society.

- It is not for a selected few. That would go against its universal aim.
- It is not mainly for victims or for ancestors. Duties to ancestors belong to the idea of the debts (ṛṇa).

questions.question_md: Which one does **not** represent triratna ?
questions.explanation:
Triratna (the "three jewels") of Jainism are the path to liberation. Tattvārtha Sūtra 1.1 states them:

- **Samyak darśana**: right faith
- **Samyak jñāna**: right knowledge
- **Samyak cāritra**: right conduct

Samyak karmānta means "right action". It is a step of the Buddhist Noble Eightfold Path, not a Jaina jewel. So it does not belong to the Jaina triratna.

Buddhism also has "three jewels" (Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha), but none of the options name them.

questions.question_md: Select the **correct** sequence :
questions.explanation:
The four puruṣārthas are the four aims of human life in Indian thought. The standard order is:

1. **Dharma**: duty and moral order
2. **Artha**: wealth and material means
3. **Kāma**: pleasure and desire
4. **Mokṣa**: liberation

Dharma comes first because it guides how a person should pursue artha and kāma. Mokṣa is the highest and final goal. So the order is Dharma, Artha, Kāma, Mokṣa.

The other options change this order.

questions.question_md: Observation of brahmacarya is a means of meeting :
questions.explanation:
Hindu tradition speaks of three debts (ṛṇa) that every person owes:

- **Ṛṣi-ṛṇa**: the debt to the sages. A person pays it by study of the Vedas during brahmacarya (the student stage).
- **Deva-ṛṇa**: the debt to the gods. A person pays it by sacrifice (yajña).
- **Pitṛ-ṛṇa**: the debt to the ancestors. A person pays it by having children in the householder stage.

Brahmacarya is the stage of Vedic study. So it meets only the ṛṣi-ṛṇa. Pitṛ-ṛṇa needs marriage and children, so it cannot belong to the student stage.

questions.question_md:
Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer from the code given below :

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| (Writer) | (Writing) |
| (a) Broad | (i) *Language of Morals* |
| (b) Urban | (ii) *Five types of Ethical Theory* |
| (c) Hare | (iii) *Metaphysics of Morals* |
| (d) Kant | (iv) *Fundamentals of Ethics* |

**Code :**
questions.explanation:
Match each writer with his book.

- **(a) C. D. Broad** wrote *Five Types of Ethical Theory* (1930). So a–ii.
- **(b) W. M. Urban** wrote *Fundamentals of Ethics*. So b–iv.
- **(c) R. M. Hare** wrote *The Language of Morals* (1952). So c–i.
- **(d) Kant** wrote *The Metaphysics of Morals*. He also wrote the *Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals*. So d–iii.

The code a–ii, b–iv, c–i, d–iii fits. Another option also starts with a–ii and b–iv. But it gives *Metaphysics of Morals* to Hare, which is wrong.

questions.question_md:
Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer with the help of code given below :

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| (Philosopher) | (View) |
| (a) Zeno | (i) Sense of dignity |
| (b) Hegel | (ii) Social equilibrium |
| (c) J.S. Mill | (iii) Be a person |
| (d) Samuel Alexander | (iv) Life according to nature |

**Code :**
questions.explanation:
Match each thinker with his moral formula.

- **(a) Zeno** of Citium founded Stoicism. The Stoic ideal is "life according to nature". So a–iv.
- **(b) Hegel** gives the command "Be a person, and respect others as persons" in the *Philosophy of Right*. So b–iii.
- **(c) J. S. Mill** says that people prefer higher pleasures because of a "sense of dignity". So c–i.
- **(d) Samuel Alexander** explains moral good as an equilibrium (balance) of interests in society. So d–ii.

The code a–iv, b–iii, c–i, d–ii fits. The other options with a–iv swap Hegel and Alexander.

questions.question_md: According to Ayer, when you say 'This is good' you are :
questions.explanation:
A. J. Ayer is a logical positivist. In *Language, Truth and Logic*, he gives the emotive theory of ethics.

For Ayer, "This is good" does not state a fact. It is neither true nor false. It expresses the speaker's feeling of approval, like a cry of "Hurrah!".

- **Describing** is wrong, because Ayer denies that moral words describe anything.
- **Communicating** feelings is wrong, because Ayer separates expressing a feeling from asserting that one has it.
- **Influencing others' feelings** is a secondary aim in Ayer. It is the main point of C. L. Stevenson's version of emotivism.

questions.question_md:
Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer with the help of code given below :

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| (a) Legal theory | (i) Practical Reason is the true source of moral obligation |
| (b) Kant's view | (ii) The state is the source of moral obligation |
| (c) Intentionist view | (iii) The self is the source of moral obligation |
| (d) Eudaemonist view | (iv) Moral obligation is imposed by conscience, which is the supreme authority |

**Code :**
questions.explanation:
Ethics textbooks list several theories about the source of moral obligation.

- **(a) Legal theory**: the state, through its laws, is the source of obligation. So a–ii.
- **(b) Kant**: practical reason gives the moral law to itself. So b–i.
- **(c) "Intentionist"**, likely a misprint for Intuitionist. Butler and others say that conscience is the supreme authority. So c–iv.
- **(d) Eudaemonist view**: the self, seeking its own full realisation, is the source of obligation. So d–iii.

The code a–ii, b–i, c–iv, d–iii fits all four pairs.

questions.question_md: Who among the following has said that 'Punishment brings wisdom. It is the healing art of Wickedness' ?
questions.explanation:
Plato sees punishment as a kind of medicine for the soul. In the *Gorgias*, Socrates (Plato's speaker) says that just punishment makes the wrongdoer better. It frees the soul from injustice, as a doctor frees the body from disease.

So the saying "Punishment brings wisdom; it is the healing art of wickedness" fits Plato's reformative theory of punishment. Quote collections attribute it to Plato.

- **Socrates** speaks in Plato's dialogues, but the saying is credited to Plato.
- **Aristotle** treats punishment as a kind of corrective justice.
- **Nietzsche** criticises punishment and the morality of revenge.

questions.question_md: Who among the following has said that "True law is the right" reason in agreement with nature; it is of universal application, unchanging and everlasting" ?
questions.explanation:
This famous definition of natural law comes from Cicero. It appears in *De Re Publica* (On the Republic), Book III.

Cicero was a Roman statesman who followed Stoic ideas. He says that true law is right reason in agreement with nature. It applies to all people, and it does not change. No human law can cancel it.

- **Kant** grounds morality in practical reason, not in nature.
- **Hegel** sees law as part of the development of Spirit in the state.
- **Darwin** is a biologist, not a theorist of natural law.

questions.question_md: Definition of 'good' in terms of self realisation according to Moore would be :
questions.explanation:
G. E. Moore, in *Principia Ethica*, holds that "good" is a simple, indefinable quality. Any attempt to define good by another property commits the naturalistic fallacy.

Moore applies this to "metaphysical ethics" also. Idealists such as Green and Bradley define good as self-realisation or as a relation to a supersensible reality. Moore says that these theories commit the same naturalistic fallacy. He does not name a separate "metaphysical fallacy".

So defining good as self-realisation is a naturalistic fallacy. The options with "metaphysical fallacy" are tempting because Moore calls these theories "metaphysical ethics". But his name for the error stays the same.

questions.question_md: Which philosopher among the following has classified 'Adjectives' in three categories (A - words, D - words, G - words) as per their functions ?
questions.explanation:
P. H. Nowell-Smith, in his book *Ethics* (1954), sorts value adjectives by their function:

- **A-words** (aptness words), such as "appropriate" or "suitable". They show that something fits a situation.
- **D-words** (descriptive words), such as "red" or "heavy". They describe properties.
- **G-words** (gerundive words), such as "right" or "obligatory". They say what ought to be done.

He used this to show that moral language has many jobs, not only one.

- **Ayer** and **Stevenson** are emotivists.
- **Hare** is a prescriptivist. None of them uses this A, D and G scheme.

questions.question_md: Which one of the following is consistent regarding moral Judgement ?
questions.explanation:
A moral judgement says what ought to be done, or what is right, wrong, good or bad. It sets a norm or standard for conduct. So it is a normative judgement.

- An **"is" judgement** states a fact. Hume and others separate "ought" from "is".
- A **logical judgement** concerns validity or truth in reasoning.
- A **"natural" judgement** would describe natural facts. To reduce moral judgement to natural facts is the naturalistic fallacy, according to Moore.

questions.question_md: According to which one of the following views value-judgements are essentially imperative ?
questions.explanation:
Prescriptivism is the view of R. M. Hare (*The Language of Morals*, 1952). For Hare, value judgements are prescriptive. They work like imperatives. "You ought to tell the truth" guides action, much like "Tell the truth". Hare adds that moral judgements are also universalizable.

- **Descriptivism** says that value judgements describe facts.
- **Emotivism** (Ayer, Stevenson) says that they express or arouse feelings.
- **Intuitionism** (Moore, Ross) says that we know moral truths by intuition.

questions.question_md: Find out the fallacy committed in the syllogistic form : AAI-1
questions.explanation:
AAI-1 is the first figure with two A premises and an I conclusion:

- All M are P.
- All S are M.
- Therefore, some S are P.

On the Aristotelian view, this mood (Barbari) is valid. On the Boolean view, universal propositions (A and E) do not claim that anything exists. But a particular proposition (I) does claim that some S exists. So the conclusion says more than the premises.

This is the existential fallacy. The middle term M is distributed in the first premise. No term is distributed in the conclusion. So there is no undistributed middle, illicit major or illicit minor.

questions.question_md:
Given below are an **Assertion (A)** and a **Reason (R)**, consider them and select the correct answer from code given here under :

**Assertion (A) :** A Categorical syllogism commits a fallacy of four terms if more than three terms are used.

**Reason (R) :** In a standard form of categorical syllogism, there are three and only three terms occurring twice each in the same meaning.

**Code :**
options: (A) and (R) both are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) and (R) both are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation:
- **(A) is true.** A categorical syllogism must have exactly three terms. If it has four, it commits the fallacy of four terms (quaternio terminorum). This often happens when a word changes its meaning (equivocation).
- **(R) is true.** A standard-form categorical syllogism has three terms: major, minor and middle. Each term occurs twice and keeps the same meaning.

(R) gives the rule that (A) applies. Because a syllogism must have only three terms, a fourth term breaks the rule. So (R) correctly explains (A).

questions.question_md: The difference between Aristotlean and Boolean interpretation of categorical propositions is as follows :
options: Aristotlean accepts contrary, sub - contrary, sub-alternation and contradictory relations whereas Boolean accepts only contradictory relations.
Aristotlean accepts contrary, sub - contrary and Boolean accepts only contradictory relations.
Aristotlean and Boolean both accepts all the above relations.
Aristotlean and Boolean both accept none of the above relations.
questions.explanation:
The traditional square of opposition has four relations: contradiction, contrariety, sub-contrariety and subalternation.

- **Aristotelian interpretation**: universal propositions assume that their subjects exist. So all four relations hold.
- **Boolean interpretation**: universal propositions (A and E) do not assume existence. So contrariety, sub-contrariety and subalternation fail. Only the contradictory relations (A–O and E–I) remain.

The second option leaves out subalternation for the Aristotelian side. The options that say "both accept all" or "both accept none" are wrong.

questions.question_md: If 'A' proposition is converted to 'A' and 'E' proposition is contraposited to E, what kind of fallacy is commited according to Boole ?
questions.explanation:
In Boolean logic, A and E propositions have no existential import. They do not claim that any member of the subject class exists. I and O propositions do make such a claim.

So any inference that goes from a universal premise to a conclusion with existential import is invalid. This error is the existential fallacy. Copi names it for conversion by limitation (A to I) and contraposition by limitation (E to O).

The question seems to refer to these two inferences. "A converted to A" and "E contraposed to E" are odd wording. Undistributed middle, illicit major and illicit minor are fallacies of syllogism, not of immediate inference. So existential fallacy is the best answer, though the wording is open to debate.

questions.question_md: Which of the following is a correct statement in the light of truth and validity ?
options: The truth or falsity of an argument's conclusion does by itself determine the validity or invalidity of that argument.
The validity of an argument does guarantee the truth of its conclusion.
Truth and falsity are attributed to the arguments while validity and invalidity are attributed to the propositions.

The truth or falsity of an argument's conclusion does not by itself determine the validity or invalidity of that argument and the fact that an argument is valid does not guarantee the truth of its conclusion.
questions.explanation:
In logic, truth and validity are different properties.

- Truth and falsity belong to propositions.
- Validity and invalidity belong to arguments.

A valid argument can have a false conclusion if a premise is false. An invalid argument can have a true conclusion by chance. So the truth of the conclusion does not by itself decide validity. Validity alone does not guarantee a true conclusion. Only a sound argument (valid with true premises) guarantees it.

- The first two options state these points the wrong way.
- The third option swaps the bearers of truth and validity.

questions.question_md: Which one of the following is not the correct formulation of De morgan theorems ?
questions.explanation:
De Morgan's theorems are:

- ~(p ∨ q) ≡ (~p · ~q). "Not (p or q)" means "not p and not q".
- ~(p · q) ≡ (~p ∨ ~q). "Not (p and q)" means "not p or not q".

The first option is the first theorem. The second and fourth options are the second theorem, written in either direction.

~(p · q) ≡ ~(p ∨ q) is not a theorem. Test it with p true and q false. Then ~(p · q) is true, but ~(p ∨ q) is false. So the two sides are not equivalent.

questions.question_md:
Match the List-I with List-II and select the correct answer from the code given here under in the argument and argument form :

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| (Arguments) | (Argument form) |
| (a) A / ∴ A∨B | (i) (p ⊃ q).(r ⊃ s) / p ∨r / ∴ q∨s |
| (b) C·D / ∴ C | (ii) p / ∴ p ∨q |
| (c) H / I / ∴ H.I | (iii) p.q / ∴ p |
| (d) (A ⊃ B).(C ⊃ D) / A∨C / ∴ B∨D | (iv) p / q / ∴ p.q |

**Code :**
questions.notes: Each argument / argument form is printed on separate lines (premises then conclusion); shown here separated by " / ".
questions.explanation:
Match each argument with its form by replacing letters with variables.

- **(a) A, so A ∨ B** has the form p, so p ∨ q. This is Addition. So a–ii.
- **(b) C · D, so C** has the form p · q, so p. This is Simplification. So b–iii.
- **(c) H, I, so H · I** has the form p, q, so p · q. This is Conjunction. So c–iv.
- **(d) (A ⊃ B) · (C ⊃ D), A ∨ C, so B ∨ D** has the form of Constructive Dilemma. So d–i.

The code a–ii, b–iii, c–iv, d–i fits all four.

questions.question_md: What are the correct symbolization of the paradoxes of material implication ?
questions.explanation:
The paradoxes of material implication show odd results of the truth table for "⊃".

- **p ⊃ (q ⊃ p)**: a true proposition is implied by any proposition. If p is true, then q ⊃ p is true for any q.
- **~p ⊃ (p ⊃ q)**: a false proposition implies any proposition. If p is false, then p ⊃ q is true for any q.

These two formulas are the standard paradoxes. They are tautologies but look strange in ordinary language.

The other options use ~p ⊃ (q ⊃ p) or p ⊃ (p ⊃ q). These are not tautologies. For example, ~p ⊃ (q ⊃ p) is false when p is false and q is true.

questions.question_md: A statement form is said to be tautologous :
options: If all of its substitution instances are false.
If its substitution instances are admixture of true and false.
If all of its substitution instances are true.
If its substitution instances are neither true nor false.
questions.explanation:
A statement form is tautologous when every substitution instance is true. Its truth table shows "T" in every row of the main column. Example: p ∨ ~p.

- All substitution instances false: this is a contradictory form, such as p · ~p.
- A mix of true and false instances: this is a contingent form, such as p ⊃ q.
- "Neither true nor false" does not apply. Every substitution instance is a statement, and it is either true or false.

questions.question_md: Two statements are said to materially equivalent if :
options: Both are true and both are false.
One is true and another is false.
One is false and another is true.
There is no question of truth and falsity is involved.
questions.explanation:
Two statements are materially equivalent when they have the same truth value. That is, both are true, or both are false. Then the biconditional "p ≡ q" is true.
