groups.md:
Read the below passage and answer the five questions that follow:

There are several reasons why " Know yourself " has obscured " Take care of yourself ". We are more inclined to see taking care of ourselves as an immorality, as a means of escape from all possible rules. We inherit the tradition of Christian morality which makes self-renunciation the condition for salvation. To know oneself was, paradoxically, a means of self-renunciation. We also inherit a secular tradition that sees in external law the basis for morality. How then can respect for the self be the basis for morality? We are the inheritors of a social morality that seeks the rules for acceptable behavior in relations with others. Since the 16th century, criticism of established morality has been undertaken in the name of the importance of recognizing and knowing the self. Therefore, it is difficult to see the care of the self as compatible with morality. "Know thyself" has obscured "Take care of yourself" because our morality, a morality of asceticism, insist that the self is that which one can reject.

...To summarize: There has been an inversion in the hierarchy of the two principles of antiquity, "Take care of yourself" and "Know yourself". In Greco-Roman culture, knowledge of oneself appeared as the consequence of the care of the self. In the modern world, knowledge of oneself constitutes the fundamental principle".

Read the below passage and answer the following five questions.

Summing up, then, it should first of all, be borne in mind that the norms and tendencies of the Deep Ecology movement are not derived from ecology or logic or induction. Ecological knowledge and the life style of the ecological field worker have suggested, inspired and fortified the perspectives of Deep Ecology movements. Secondly, it should be fully appreciated that the significant tenets of the Deep Ecology movement are clearly and forcefully normative. They express a value priority system only in part based on result(or law of results) of scientific research. Today, ecologists try to influence policy-making bodies largely through threats, through predictions concerning pollutants and resource depletion, knowing that policy makers accept at least certain minimum norms concerning health and just distribution. There are political potentials in this movement which have little to do with pollution and resource depletion. Thirdly, in so far as ecology movements deserve our attention, they are ecophilosophical rather than ecological. Ecology is a limited science which makes use of scientific methods. Philosophy is the most general forum of debate on fundamentals, descriptive as well as prescriptive, and political philosophy one of its subsections. By an ecosophy, I mean a philosophy of ecological harmony or equilibrium. A philosophy as a kind of Sofia wisdom, is openly normative; it contains both norms, rules, postulates, value priority announcements and hypotheses concerning the state of affairs in our universe... An ecosophy is more like a system of the kind constructed by Aristotle or Spinoza... The basic relation is that between subsets of premises and subsets of conclusions, that is, the relation of derivability. At the moment, ecosophy might profitably use models of systems, rough approximations of global systemizations.... under the name of ecologism, various deviations from the deep movement have been championed - primarily with a one sided stress on pollution and resource depletion...."

questions.question_md: According to Merleau Ponty, perception is :
questions.notes: Dropped in the NTA final answer key (marks awarded to all).
questions.explanation:
Merleau-Ponty wrote *Phenomenology of Perception* (1945). In the Preface, he says that perception is not a science of the world. He adds that it is not even an act, that is, a deliberate taking of a position. Perception is the background from which all our acts stand out.

For Merleau-Ponty, perception is also **embodied** (it happens through the living body). It is **perspectival** (we always see from one point of view).

- "A science of the world" – he denies this directly.
- "Not embodied" and "Not perspectival" – these are the opposite of his view.
- "A conscious act" – he denies that perception is a deliberate act. It is a pre-reflective (before thinking) bodily contact with the world.

So no option states his view correctly. This is the likely reason why NTA dropped the question. "A conscious act" is the least wrong choice, because perception still involves a lived awareness. But this choice is open to debate.

questions.question_md: Which one of the following presents Kierkegaard's philosophy appropriately ?
questions.explanation:
Søren Kierkegaard is the father of existentialism. His key claim is that **"subjectivity is truth"**. Truth that matters is not an objective fact. It is the truth that a person lives with passion and commitment, especially in faith.

- **Hegelianism and Rationalism** – Kierkegaard attacked these. He said that Hegel's system forgets the single, existing person.
- **Being of the human being** – this phrase fits Heidegger's question of *Dasein* (human existence) better.
- **Reality of the Universal** – Kierkegaard stresses the single individual, not the universal.

questions.question_md: Wittgenstein is convinced that the particular employment of words are deemed to be one of the following :
questions.notes: Dropped in the NTA final answer key (marks awarded to all).
questions.explanation:
The later Wittgenstein (*Philosophical Investigations*) says that the meaning of a word is its use in a language-game. He wants to bring words back from their **metaphysical** use to their **everyday** (ordinary) use.

So for Wittgenstein, the right description of a particular use of words is "ordinary use" or "a language-game". No option gives this. The options name only ontological, metaphysical, axiological (value) and ethical uses. Wittgenstein rejects or questions all of these as ways to describe how words work.

The question wording is also unclear. These are the likely reasons why NTA dropped it. If one option must be chosen, "metaphysical use of language" is the term that Wittgenstein himself uses. He uses it for the misuse of words that he wants to cure. This choice is open to debate.

questions.question_md: According to P. F. Strawson, the concept of a person that is embodied mind is a primitive concept and through this argument, Strawson rejected one of the following :
questions.explanation:
In *Individuals* (1959), P. F. Strawson says that the concept of a **person** is primitive. A person is one thing. We apply to it both mental predicates (thinks, feels) and physical predicates (weighs 60 kg, is in a room). We cannot break this concept into a mind plus a body.

With this argument, Strawson rejects two views:

- **Cartesian dualism** – it splits a person into a pure mind and a separate body.
- **Behaviourism** and the "no-ownership" view – they reduce mental states to bodily behaviour or deny that a person owns them.

Empiricism, rationalism and idealism are theories of knowledge or reality. They are not the target of the person argument.

questions.question_md: What is multiculturalism ?
options: It is the existence of cultural diversity within a given society.
It is the existence of minority groups in a society.
It is the existence of political diversity in a society.
It is the existence of ethnic minority groups in a society.
questions.explanation:
**Multiculturalism** means that many cultures exist side by side in one society. It also means that the society respects and accepts this cultural diversity. Different languages, religions and ways of life all have a place.

- "Minority groups" and "ethnic minority groups" are only one part of the picture. Multiculturalism covers all cultural groups, not only minorities.
- "Political diversity" is about different political views and parties. That is pluralism in politics, not cultural diversity.

questions.question_md: Who propounded the ethics of ambiguity ?
questions.explanation:
**Simone de Beauvoir** wrote *The Ethics of Ambiguity* (1947). She says that human beings are both free and limited, both subjects and objects. This is the "ambiguity" of human life. Ethics must accept this fact and not escape it. My freedom also needs the freedom of others.

- **Sartre** was her partner and fellow existentialist. He wrote *Being and Nothingness*, not this book.
- **Heidegger** and **Jaspers** were German existential thinkers. They did not write an ethics of ambiguity.

questions.question_md: What is the concern of the ethics of Levinas ?
questions.explanation:
Emmanuel Levinas makes ethics the "first philosophy". The **face of the Other** person calls on me. It makes me **responsible for the Other** before any choice or contract. This responsibility has no limit, and I cannot refuse it.

- "Regulation with oneself" – Levinas moves the centre of ethics away from the self to the Other.
- "Charity to the other" – charity is a voluntary gift. Levinas speaks of a responsibility that comes before any choice.
- "Unconditional faith to the other" – this is a religious idea. It is not his ethical term.

questions.question_md: Dworkin proposed that rights should be thought of as :
questions.explanation:
Ronald Dworkin, in *Taking Rights Seriously* (1977), says that **rights are trumps**. In a card game, a trump card beats ordinary cards. In the same way, an individual right beats an ordinary argument based on general welfare. The state cannot override a right just because many people would gain.

The option prints "Triumphs", but it means "trumps". This is a printing or spelling mistake. "Privileges", "opportunities" and "wealth" are not Dworkin's terms.

questions.question_md: Which one of the following is consistent with Spinoza ?
options: *Mind* and *Matter* are the parallel attributes of substance
questions.explanation:
Spinoza holds that there is only **one substance**: God or Nature. This substance has infinite attributes. We know two of them: **thought** (mind) and **extension** (matter).

These two attributes run in **parallel**. Every mental event matches a bodily event. But one does not cause the other. They are two ways of expressing the same reality. We call this view psycho-physical parallelism.

- "Two distinct substances" is Descartes' dualism.
- "Mind derived from matter" is materialism.
- "Matter derived from mind" is idealism.

questions.question_md: The division of qualities into *primary* and *secondary* is unphilosophical. Who held this view?
questions.explanation:
**Locke** divided qualities into two kinds:

- **Primary qualities** (shape, size, motion, number) – they really exist in objects.
- **Secondary qualities** (colour, taste, sound) – they exist only as ideas in the mind.

**Berkeley** rejected this division. He argued that primary qualities are also known only as ideas. We never see shape without colour. So if colour exists only in the mind, shape also exists only in the mind. Thus the division has no philosophical basis.

Locke and Descartes both accepted the division. So any option that includes them is wrong.

questions.question_md: Which of the following is not acceptable to Kant ?
options: Knowledge consists of synthetic *a priori* judgements
Analytic judgements do not add to our knowledge
Synthetic judgements give cent percent sure knowledge
questions.explanation:
Kant divides judgements into analytic and synthetic.

- **Analytic judgements** – the predicate is already in the subject. They are always *a priori* (known before experience). They do not add new knowledge. Kant accepts both of these points.
- **Synthetic judgements** – the predicate adds something new. Most of them are *a posteriori* (based on experience), for example "The table is brown". Such judgements are not necessary or certain.
- Kant holds that real scientific knowledge consists of **synthetic *a priori*** judgements, such as "7 + 5 = 12".

So Kant does **not** accept that all synthetic judgements give 100% certain knowledge. Only synthetic *a priori* judgements are necessary and universal.

questions.question_md: According to whom -'One idea cannot perceive another idea. Therefore there should exist a soul which perceives ideas'.
questions.explanation:
**Berkeley** holds that ideas are passive. An idea cannot perceive anything, including another idea. But ideas exist only when someone perceives them (*esse est percipi*). So there must be an active being that perceives ideas. Berkeley calls this being a **spirit** or soul.

- **Hume** found only a bundle of perceptions. He denied a soul substance.
- **Locke** accepted a soul, but not by this argument about ideas.
- **Leibniz** spoke of monads, not of ideas that need a perceiver in this way.

questions.question_md: Which of the following statement is incompatible with Hegel's view ?
options: Contradiction is the root of all life and movement
Everything tends to change into its opposite
The seed for example contradicts itself and transcends itself
questions.explanation:
For Hegel, reality is the **Absolute** (Absolute Spirit). The Absolute develops through a dialectic: thesis, antithesis and synthesis. So Hegel accepts these points:

- Contradiction is the root of all life and movement.
- Everything tends to change into its opposite.
- A seed contradicts itself and goes beyond itself when it becomes a plant.

But the Absolute is the central reality of Hegel's whole system. So the statement "The Absolute is a myth" is incompatible with his view.

questions.question_md: In Vaiśeṣika metaphysics, which *dravyas* can be both *nirāvayava* and *sāvayava*?
questions.explanation:
In Vaiśeṣika, a *dravya* (substance) can be *nirāvayava* (without parts) or *sāvayava* (with parts).

- ***Kṣiti*** (earth), ***ap*** (water), ***teja*** (fire) and ***marut*** (air) exist in two forms. Their atoms are partless and eternal. Their products, such as a pot, have parts and are not eternal. So these four are both *nirāvayava* and *sāvayava*.
- ***Vyoma*** (*ākāśa*, ether) is one, all-pervading and partless. It never has parts.
- ***Manas*** (mind) is atomic and partless. It also never has parts.

So only the four elements fit. Any option with *vyoma* or *manas* is wrong.

questions.question_md: Which one among the following is NOT a means of *Śaktigraha* ?
questions.explanation:
*Śaktigraha* means grasping the *śakti* (meaning-power) of a word. That is, we learn which object a word stands for. Indian logicians list several means for this:

- ***Vyākaraṇa*** – grammar.
- ***Āptavākya*** – the word of a trusted person.
- ***Vṛddhavyavahāra*** – the use of words by elders.
- Others are *upamāna* (comparison), *kośa* (dictionary), *vākyaśeṣa* (the rest of a sentence), *vivṛti* (explanation) and nearness to a known word.

***Sāmānyalakṣaṇa pratyakṣa*** is an extraordinary perception of a whole class through its universal. Nyāya uses it to grasp *vyāpti* (the universal relation in inference). It is not a means of *śaktigraha*.

questions.question_md: Which system of Vedānta, postulates the conception of three grades of *Sattā (Sattātraya)?*
questions.explanation:
**Advaita Vedānta** accepts three grades of *sattā* (reality):

- ***Pāramārthika*** – the highest reality. Only Brahman has it.
- ***Vyāvahārika*** – the empirical reality of the everyday world. It is real until knowledge of Brahman arises.
- ***Prātibhāsika*** – illusory reality, such as the snake seen in a rope. It lasts only while the illusion lasts.

Viśiṣṭādvaita, Dvaita and Dvaitādvaita hold that the world is fully real. So they do not need grades of reality.

questions.question_md: By which relation, the relation between a pot and its colour is related with the pot according to the Vaiśeṣikas?
questions.explanation:
Read the question carefully. It does not ask how the colour relates to the pot. It asks how the **relation itself** relates to the pot.

- The colour is a quality. It is in the pot by ***samavāya*** (inherence).
- Now, how is *samavāya* linked to the pot? If we say "by another *samavāya*", we need a third relation, then a fourth. This is an infinite regress.
- To stop the regress, Vaiśeṣika says that *samavāya* links itself to its terms by ***svarūpa sambandha*** (self-linking relation). It needs no further relation.

***Saṁyoga*** (conjunction) is a quality that holds only between two substances. ***Tādātmya*** (identity) is not a Vaiśeṣika relation for this case. *Samavāya* is the tempting answer, but it is the relation between pot and colour, not the link of that relation to the pot.

questions.question_md: Which one among the following is the direct knowledge of the thoughts of others in Jaina epistemology ?
questions.explanation:
Jainism names five kinds of knowledge. ***Manaḥparyāya*** is direct knowledge of the thoughts of other people. It does not use the senses or the mind as tools.

- ***Pratyakṣa*** is the general name for direct knowledge. It is not the special name for knowing other minds.
- ***Avadhi*** is direct knowledge of distant or hidden physical objects ("clairvoyance").
- ***Kevala*** is complete knowledge of everything. Only a liberated soul has it.

questions.question_md: In Vedic literature *Ṛta* is equated with :
questions.explanation:
*Ṛta* is the cosmic and moral order of the Vedas. It is the law behind both nature and right conduct.

- *Ṛta* is closely linked with ***satya*** (truth). Vedic hymns often name them together.
- *Ṛta* is also the source of the later idea of ***dharma*** (moral and social law). In time, the word *dharma* took over the meaning of *ṛta*.

So the Vedas equate *ṛta* with both *satya* and *dharma*. The options with "only" or "neither" leave out one of these links.

questions.question_md: By begetting off-spring one can repay :
questions.explanation:
Hindu texts speak of three *ṛṇas* (debts) that every person is born with:

- ***Devaṛṇa*** – debt to the gods. One repays it by *yajña* (sacrifice).
- ***Ṛṣiṛṇa*** – debt to the sages. One repays it by study of the Vedas.
- ***Pitṛṛṇa*** – debt to the ancestors. One repays it by begetting children and continuing the family line.

So begetting offspring repays only *pitṛṛṇa*.

questions.question_md: According to the *Cārvākas* fire burns because :
options: It is the nature of fire
The burning power is the essence of fire
questions.explanation:
The *Cārvākas* reject God and any unseen force. To explain events, they use ***svabhāvavāda*** (the doctrine of nature). Things act as they do because of their own nature. Fire is hot and water is cold by nature. Nobody makes them so.

- "Divine will" – the *Cārvākas* reject God.
- "Cosmic order" – this is like *ṛta* or *karma*. They reject such unseen forces too.
- "The burning power is the essence of fire" – this speaks of a hidden power (*śakti*) or essence behind the thing. The *Cārvākas* do not accept such unseen powers. They simply say that burning is fire's nature.

questions.question_md: Which school is of the opinion that there is no contradiction in holding the judgement that a *ghataḥ* is and is not at the same time ?
questions.explanation:
**Jainism** holds *anekāntavāda* (many-sidedness of reality). It uses ***syādvāda*** (the doctrine of "in some respect") to state this.

A pot exists in respect of its own form, place, time and material. The same pot does not exist in respect of another object's form, place, time and material. So "the pot is" and "the pot is not" are both true, each from its own point of view. There is no contradiction.

- **Nyāya** accepts the law of non-contradiction strictly.
- **Bauddha** and **Advaita Vedānta** do not hold that a thing both is and is not at the same time in this sense.

questions.question_md: In Nyāya epistemology, by which *sannikarṣa* do we perceive the relation between my hand and the pen I am writing with ?
questions.explanation:
In Nyāya, the relation between my hand and the pen is ***saṁyoga*** (contact). *Saṁyoga* is a quality (*guṇa*). It inheres in the hand (and in the pen) by *samavāya* (inherence).

To perceive this relation, Nyāya uses ***saṁyukta samavāya*** (inherence in what is in contact):

- My eye is in contact (*saṁyoga*) with the hand.
- The *saṁyoga* quality inheres (*samavāya*) in the hand.

So the eye perceives the contact through *saṁyukta samavāya*.

- We use ***saṁyoga*** alone to perceive a substance, such as the hand itself.
- We use ***samavāya*** alone to perceive sound by the ear.
- We use ***viśeṣaṇatā*** to perceive absence and inherence.

questions.question_md: Which of the following philosophers advocate a distinction between *Anumāna* and *Arthāpatti pramāṇa*?
questions.explanation:
*Arthāpatti* (postulation) is knowing a fact that alone can explain another fact. For example, Devadatta is fat but does not eat by day. So he must eat at night.

- **Kumārila** (Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṁsā) accepts *arthāpatti* as a separate *pramāṇa* (means of knowledge). He says it is different from *anumāna* (inference).
- **Śaṁkara's** Advaita follows the Bhāṭṭa list of six *pramāṇas* for practical life. So it also keeps *arthāpatti* apart from *anumāna*.
- **Rāmānuja**, **Madhva** and **Nimbārka** accept only three *pramāṇas*: perception, inference and testimony. They include *arthāpatti* under inference.

So only Śaṁkara and Kumārila make the distinction.

questions.question_md: In Nyāya philosophy of language *Iśvarecchā* is :
questions.explanation:
*Śakti* is the meaning-relation between a word and its object. The old Naiyāyikas say that ***Īśvarecchā*** (the will of God) **is** *śakti* itself. God willed: "Let this object be understood from this word". This divine will fixes the meaning of each word.

- God's will is not the cause of *śabda* (word). Human speech produces words.
- It is not just the cause of *śakti*. Nyāya identifies the will with *śakti* itself.
- It is not *śabda* itself. *Śabda* is the sound or word.

Later Naiyāyikas extend *śakti* to any will, including human will, as in technical names.

questions.question_md: Which type of *hetvābhāsa* is committed by the *anumāna: Śabdaḥ nityaḥ śabdatvāt* ?
questions.explanation:
The inference is "Sound is eternal, because it has soundness (*śabdatva*)".

- *Śabdatva* is found only in sound, which is the *pakṣa* (subject).
- It is not found in any *sapakṣa* (similar case: other eternal things).
- It is not found in any *vipakṣa* (dissimilar case: non-eternal things).

A *hetu* (reason) that exists only in the *pakṣa* is ***asādhāraṇa savyabhicāra*** (the "too narrow" reason). It cannot prove anything.

- ***Sādhāraṇa*** is the "too wide" reason. It is found in both *sapakṣa* and *vipakṣa*.
- ***Svarūpāsiddha*** – the reason is absent in the *pakṣa*. Here *śabdatva* is present in sound.
- ***Viruddha*** – the reason proves the opposite. *Śabdatva* does not prove non-eternity.

questions.question_md: Which one among the following is *NOT* a characteristic of *sat hetu*?
questions.explanation:
In Nyāya, a *sat hetu* (valid reason) has five marks:

- ***Pakṣasattva*** – it is present in the subject (*pakṣa*).
- ***Sapakṣasattva*** – it is present in similar cases.
- ***Vipakṣāsattva*** – it is **absent** in dissimilar cases.
- ***Abādhita viṣayatva*** – its conclusion is not contradicted by stronger proof.
- ***Asatpratipakṣatva*** – no equal counter-reason exists.

***Vipakṣasattva*** means "presence in dissimilar cases". This is the opposite of a valid mark. It makes the reason *savyabhicāra* (wandering). So it is not a characteristic of a *sat hetu*.

questions.question_md: Which type of cause is *Kapālasaṁyoga* in the production of *ghataḥ?*
questions.explanation:
Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika names three kinds of cause for a pot (*ghaṭa*):

- ***Samavāyi kāraṇa*** (inherent cause) – the two halves (*kapāla*). The pot inheres in them.
- ***Asamavāyi kāraṇa*** (non-inherent cause) – the **conjunction of the halves** (*kapālasaṁyoga*). This quality inheres in the halves and helps produce the pot.
- ***Nimitta kāraṇa*** (efficient cause) – the potter, the stick and the wheel.

So *kapālasaṁyoga* is the *asamavāyi* cause. "*Nimitta–upādāna*" (efficient and material cause together) is a Vedānta idea for Brahman, not for a pot.

questions.question_md: What is the nature of *jīva* (individual self) according to Rāmānuja?
options: *Jīva* is fundamentally non dual with Brahman.
*Jīva* is both fundamentally non dual and absolutely different from Brahman.
*Jīva* is existentially different but inseparably connected with Brahman.
questions.explanation:
Rāmānuja teaches *Viśiṣṭādvaita* (qualified non-dualism). Brahman is the whole. The *jīvas* (selves) and matter are its body and attributes.

- The *jīva* is **really different** from Brahman. It is finite, atomic and dependent.
- But the *jīva* is **inseparable** from Brahman (*apṛthak-siddhi*). It cannot exist apart from Brahman, as a body cannot live apart from its soul.

Other options:

- "Fundamentally non-dual with Brahman" is Śaṅkara's Advaita.
- "Absolutely different from Brahman" is Madhva's Dvaita.
- "Both non-dual and absolutely different" mixes the two views. It is closer to Bhedābheda, not to Rāmānuja.

questions.question_md: Kumārila's advocacy of *pramāṇas* was endorsed by which of the following systems?
questions.explanation:
Kumārila Bhaṭṭa accepts six *pramāṇas* (means of knowledge): perception, inference, comparison, testimony, postulation (*arthāpatti*) and non-cognition (*anupalabdhi*).

**Advaita Vedānta** accepts the same six *pramāṇas* for empirical life. Advaitins say: "In practical matters, we follow the Bhāṭṭa method" (*vyavahāre bhāṭṭanayaḥ*).

- **Nyāya** accepts four *pramāṇas*.
- **Sāṁkhya** accepts three.
- **Śuddhādvaita** (Vallabha) does not follow Kumārila's list.

questions.question_md: Figures of categorical syllogism are determined on the basis of :
options: Position of the major term in the premises.
Position of the minor term in the premises.
Position of the middle term in the premises.
Position of the major term in the conclusion.
questions.explanation:
A categorical syllogism has three terms: major, minor and middle. The **figure** of a syllogism depends on the position of the **middle term** in the two premises.

- Figure 1 – the middle term is the subject of the major premise and the predicate of the minor premise.
- Figure 2 – the middle term is the predicate of both premises.
- Figure 3 – the middle term is the subject of both premises.
- Figure 4 – the middle term is the predicate of the major premise and the subject of the minor premise.

The major and minor terms always have fixed places in the conclusion. So they cannot mark the figure.

questions.question_md: Which one of the following is the obversion of the proposition "All residents are voters" ?
questions.explanation:
To **obvert** a proposition, do two things:

1. Change its quality (affirmative to negative, or negative to affirmative).
2. Replace the predicate with its complement (add "non-").

"All residents are voters" is an A proposition. Its obverse is the E proposition **"No residents are non-voters"**. The meaning stays the same.

- "All voters are residents" swaps subject and predicate. That is conversion, and it is not valid for A.
- "No voters are residents" and "No residents are voters" change the meaning. They are not equivalent to the original.

questions.question_md: Which one of the following does not fall under the category of Fallacies of Relevance ?
questions.explanation:
**Fallacies of relevance** use premises that do not bear on the conclusion. They include:

- **Red herring** – it moves attention to a different topic.
- **Straw man** – it attacks a weak, false version of the opponent's view.
- **Appeal to emotion** – it uses feelings instead of reasons.

**Begging the question** (*petitio principii*) is different. Its premise is relevant, but it already assumes the conclusion. Copi places it among the **fallacies of presumption**. So it does not fall under fallacies of relevance.

questions.question_md: If A and B are true statements and X,Y and Z are false statements, determine which one of the following is true.
questions.explanation:
Put A, B = T and X, Y, Z = F. Then check each option.

**Option (1):** [A ⊃ (X·Y)] ⊃ [(A ⊃ X) ∨ (A ⊃ Y)]
- X·Y = F, so A ⊃ (X·Y) = T ⊃ F = **F**.
- A conditional with a false antecedent is true. So the whole is **T**.

**Option (2):** [(A·X) ⊃ B] ⊃ (A ⊃ X)
- A·X = F, so (A·X) ⊃ B = T.
- A ⊃ X = T ⊃ F = F.
- T ⊃ F = **F**.

**Option (3):** [(X ⊃ Z) ⊃ B] ⊃ Y
- X ⊃ Z = T, then T ⊃ B = T.
- T ⊃ Y = T ⊃ F = **F**.

**Option (4):** [(A·X) ⊃ Y] ⊃ (A ⊃ X)
- (A·X) ⊃ Y = F ⊃ F = T.
- A ⊃ X = F.
- T ⊃ F = **F**.

Only option (1) is true.

questions.question_md: Which one of the following is the correct combination of moods in the fourth figure ?
questions.explanation:
The valid moods of the **fourth figure** are: **Bramantip, Camenes, Dimaris, Fesapo** and **Fresison**.

- **Camenes, Dimaris and Fresison** are all on this list.
- **Datisi** and **Disamis** belong to the third figure.
- **Ferison** also belongs to the third figure.
- **Ferio** belongs to the first figure.
- **Festino** belongs to the second figure.

So only the set Camenes, Dimaris and Fresison is fully from the fourth figure.

questions.question_md:
Which one of the following represents the relation between propositions provided below?

Some pens are red.

Some pens are not red.
questions.explanation:
"Some pens are red" is an **I** proposition. "Some pens are not red" is an **O** proposition. They have the same subject and predicate.

In the square of opposition, I and O are **sub-contraries**. Both can be true together. But both cannot be false together.

- **Contraries** are A and E (both universal).
- **Contradictories** are A–O and E–I.
- **Sub-alterns** are A–I and E–O (a universal and its particular).

questions.question_md:
Consider the following syllogism and identify the fallacy involved in it:

- Some friends are rich.
- No rich persons are helpful.
- ∴ No helpful persons are friends.
questions.explanation:
First find the terms from the conclusion: "No helpful persons are friends".

- Minor term = "helpful persons" (subject of the conclusion).
- Major term = "friends" (predicate of the conclusion).
- Middle term = "rich persons".

Now check distribution:

- The conclusion is an E proposition. So it distributes "friends".
- In the premise "Some friends are rich" (I), "friends" is **not** distributed.

If the conclusion distributes a term, its premise must also distribute that term. The major term breaks this rule. This is the **illicit major**.

- "No rich persons are helpful" distributes the middle term. So there is no undistributed middle.
- The E premise distributes "helpful persons". So there is no illicit minor.
- There are only three terms, so there is no fallacy of four terms.

questions.question_md:
Consider the following syllogism and identify the fallacy in it.

- No dogs are bipeds.
- No cats are bipeds.
- ∴ No cats are dogs.
questions.explanation:
Both premises are negative:

- "No dogs are bipeds" (E).
- "No cats are bipeds" (E).

A rule of the syllogism says that **no conclusion follows from two negative premises**. The premises only say that both dogs and cats are outside the class of bipeds. They tell us nothing about how dogs and cats relate to each other.

- Both E premises distribute the middle term "bipeds". So there is no undistributed middle.
- Each term has one clear sense. So there is no fallacy of ambiguity.
- Its premise distributes the minor term "cats". So there is no illicit minor.

questions.question_md:
Identify the contraposition of the proposition

"Some philosophers are not-scientists"
questions.explanation:
Read the proposition as "Some philosophers are not scientists". This is an **O** proposition. The printed hyphen in "not-scientists" seems to be a typing slip.

Contraposition has three steps:

1. **Obvert:** "Some philosophers are non-scientists" (I).
2. **Convert:** "Some non-scientists are philosophers" (I).
3. **Obvert again:** "Some non-scientists are not non-philosophers" (O).

So the contrapositive is "Some non-scientists are not non-philosophers". The O proposition has a valid contrapositive.

- "Some non-philosophers are non-scientists" does not follow.
- "No non-scientists are non-philosophers" and "All scientists are non-philosophers" are universal. A particular premise cannot give a universal conclusion.

questions.question_md: Who said that " I don't care of God, if he is anything but truth "?
questions.explanation:
**M. K. Gandhi** placed truth above everything. He first said "God is Truth". Later he said "Truth is God". He wrote that he would not care for God if God were anything other than Truth. For Gandhi, the search for truth is the search for God.

- **K. C. Bhattacharya** wrote on the subject as freedom.
- **Iqbal** wrote on the ego and the Ultimate Ego.
- **Vivekananda** taught Vedānta and service.

None of them made this statement.

questions.question_md: Which of the following philosophers conceptualized God as "personal being" or "supreme person".
questions.explanation:
**Rabindranath Tagore**, in *The Religion of Man*, speaks of God as the **Supreme Person** or "Man the Eternal". God is a personal being who relates to human beings in love and creative joy. Human personality finds its fulfilment in this Supreme Person.

- **Radhakrishnan** sees the Absolute as beyond personality. God is the Absolute in relation to the world.
- **Ambedkar** rejected a personal creator God. He followed Buddhism.
- **Iqbal** calls God the "Ultimate Ego". But the exam links the term "Supreme Person" with Tagore.

questions.question_md: Who among the following Contemporary Indian Thinkers expresses the view that self knowledge is equivalent to knowing oneself in relation?
questions.explanation:
**Jiddu Krishnamurti** teaches that we can know ourselves only in **relationship**. He says that relationship is a mirror. In it we see our own anger, fear and desire. Self-knowledge does not come from books or a guru. It comes from watching ourselves in our daily relations with people and things.

- **M. N. Roy** taught radical humanism.
- **K. C. Bhattacharya** wrote on the subject as freedom and stages of self-knowledge, but not in terms of relationship.
- **Jyotiba Phule** was a social reformer against caste.

questions.question_md: Who among the following is the ancient Greek pluralist?
questions.explanation:
The ancient Greek **pluralists** said that reality has many basic elements.

- **Empedocles** named four "roots": earth, water, air and fire. Love joins them, and Strife separates them. So he is a pluralist.
- **Parmenides** said that Being is one and unchanging. He is a monist.
- **Zeno** was Parmenides' pupil. He defended monism with his paradoxes.
- **Anaximander** said that everything comes from one source, the *apeiron* (the boundless). He is also a monist.

questions.question_md: Which of the following is philosophically unacceptable to St Anselm ?
questions.explanation:
St Anselm's motto is "**faith seeking understanding**" (*fides quaerens intellectum*). He also wrote: "I believe so that I may understand."

- Anselm starts with **faith**.
- He then uses reason to **understand** that faith.
- He tries to show **why revealed truth is true**, as in his ontological argument.

So he accepts faith, understanding and reasoning about revelation. **Giving up reason** goes against his whole method. That is the view he would not accept.

questions.question_md: "The so called cause is nothing but one event immediately succeeded by another event, the succeeded event may be called effect. That is all". Who among the following holds this view?
questions.explanation:
**Hume** says that we never perceive a necessary link between cause and effect. We only see one event followed by another, again and again. From this habit, we expect the second event when we see the first. So "cause" means only constant conjunction and succession.

- **Locke** accepted real causal powers.
- **Descartes** accepted causation as a rational, necessary link.
- **Kant** made causality an *a priori* category of the understanding. He wrote partly to answer Hume.

questions.question_md: Which of the following statement is incompatible with Descartes?
options: Taking mathematics as the model of philosophical method
Setting the face against old authorities
Viewing sense-experience as a gateway to all knowledge
Reconciliation of mechanism and the notions of God, Soul and Freedom
questions.explanation:
Descartes is a **rationalist**. He holds that reason, not the senses, is the source of true knowledge. He doubts sense experience because the senses sometimes deceive us. So "sense-experience as the gateway to all knowledge" is incompatible with his view. That is an empiricist claim.

Descartes does accept the other points:

- He takes **mathematics** as the model of method: clear, distinct and step by step.
- He **rejects old authorities**, such as scholastic tradition, and starts from doubt.
- He tries to **reconcile** a mechanical view of nature with God, the soul and freedom.

questions.question_md: What of the following is incorrect as far as Rationalism is concerned (as a Philosophical theory)?
options: Reason and Reason alone is the source of all philosophical knowledge
Sense experience is deceptive and therefore cannot act as a source of philosophical knowledge
Reason limits itself and is defective
questions.explanation:
**Rationalism** holds that reason is the main source of knowledge.

- Reason alone gives philosophical knowledge – rationalists accept this.
- Reason is permanent and does not change – they accept this too.
- Sense experience can deceive, so it cannot give philosophical knowledge – they accept this as well.

The claim that **reason limits itself and is defective** is not a rationalist view. It comes from Kant's critical philosophy. Kant showed the limits of pure reason. So this statement is incorrect for rationalism.

questions.question_md: Berkeley is called as Idealist because :
options: There is no knowledge which is not in the form of ideas.
He postulated the principle : Think with the learned and speak with the vulgar.
questions.explanation:
Berkeley is an **idealist** because he holds that everything we know exists as **ideas** in a mind. His famous principle is *esse est percipi* (to be is to be perceived). There is no knowledge that is not in the form of ideas.

- He was a bishop, but that has nothing to do with his idealism.
- "Matter matters least to him" is a joke. Berkeley actually denied the existence of material substance.
- "Think with the learned and speak with the vulgar" is a rule about language. It is not the reason he is an idealist.

questions.question_md: "Men may come and men may go, but the man-type, the human race goes on forever". Whose view is this?
questions.explanation:
This view comes from **Plato's** theory of Ideas (Forms). Individual men are born and die. But the **Idea of Man** (the "man-type") is eternal and does not change. Particular things are only copies of the eternal Ideas.

- **Aristotle** denied that Forms exist apart from particular things.
- **Protagoras** and **Gorgias** were Sophists. They denied any eternal, universal standard.

questions.question_md: Who held the view that 'God is the Unmoved Mover'.
questions.explanation:
**Aristotle** calls God the **Unmoved Mover** (Prime Mover). Everything in the world moves and changes. But a chain of movers cannot go on forever. So there must be a first mover that moves others but is not moved itself. It moves the world as an object of love and desire. It is pure thought, "thought thinking itself".

- **Socrates** focused on ethics and self-knowledge.
- **Plato** spoke of the Demiurge (a divine craftsman) and the Idea of the Good.
- **Thales** said that water is the basic stuff of the world.

questions.question_md: Which of the following is the correct view of Anaxagoras ?
options: Elements are only four in number.
Mind initiates motion in the elements.
questions.explanation:
**Anaxagoras** said that the world contains countless tiny "seeds" of every kind of stuff. At first they were all mixed together. **Nous** (Mind) started a whirling motion in this mixture. This motion separated the seeds and formed the world. So Mind initiates motion in the elements.

- "Elements without qualities" fits the atoms of Democritus, not the seeds of Anaxagoras. His seeds have qualities.
- "Only four elements" is Empedocles' view.
- "Change is impossible" is the view of Parmenides.

questions.question_md: "Knowledge is possible : It is concerned with the general and typical, not the particular and accidental". Who among the following holds this view ?
questions.explanation:
**Socrates** held that real knowledge is possible. It is knowledge of **concepts** (general definitions), such as "What is justice?". A concept grasps what is common and essential in many cases. It ignores the particular and accidental details.

- The **Sophists** said that knowledge is relative to each person. So they denied universal knowledge.
- The **Atomists** explained the world by atoms and the void. This is not a theory of concepts.
- **Empedocles** wrote on the four roots, not on general concepts.

questions.question_md: "The impulse towards pleasure, if too predominant, defeats its own aim ". Who among the following holds this view ?
questions.explanation:
This is the **paradox of hedonism**. If a person seeks pleasure too directly and too strongly, the person finds less pleasure. Pleasure comes best as a by-product of other aims. **Henry Sidgwick** states this in *The Methods of Ethics* with these words.

- **Bentham** treated pleasure as something to calculate and seek directly.
- **J. S. Mill** made a related point in his *Autobiography*, but the quoted words are Sidgwick's.
- **Kant** rejected pleasure as the basis of morality.

questions.question_md: Who amongst the following criticized Cartesian Rationalism ?
questions.explanation:
Cartesian rationalism holds that reason gives certain knowledge through innate ideas. **Hume**, an empiricist, criticized this view. He held that all ideas come from impressions (sense experience). There are no innate ideas. Reason alone cannot prove matters of fact, such as cause and effect or the self.

- **Spinoza** and **Leibniz** were rationalists. They developed Descartes' method further.
- **St. Augustine** lived long before Descartes. He could not criticize him.

questions.question_md: Which of the following aim is NOT conducive to Immanuel Kant ?
options: To prove that reason was all in all
To show the possibility of *synthetic apriori* propositions
questions.explanation:
Kant's *Critique of Pure Reason* had these aims:

- To answer **Hume's scepticism** and show that necessary knowledge is possible.
- To limit **dogmatism**, that is, rationalist claims to know God, soul and world by pure reason.
- To show how **synthetic *a priori*** judgements are possible.

Kant did **not** try to prove that reason is all in all. He showed the opposite. Reason has limits. It cannot know things-in-themselves. So this aim is not Kant's.

questions.question_md: Who among the following is inclined to accept Transcendental Idealism?
questions.explanation:
**Kant** called his own view **transcendental idealism**. We know things only as they appear to us (phenomena). Space, time and the categories come from the mind. Things-in-themselves (noumena) exist, but we cannot know them.

- **Hegel** held **absolute idealism**. He rejected Kant's unknowable thing-in-itself.
- **Descartes** was a rationalist and a dualist.
- **Hume** was an empiricist and a sceptic.

questions.question_md: Who is the chief architect for the reconciliation between Rationalism and Empiricism?
questions.explanation:
**Kant** brought rationalism and empiricism together. He said: "Thoughts without content are empty; intuitions without concepts are blind."

- From **empiricism**, he took the idea that knowledge starts with experience.
- From **rationalism**, he took the idea that the mind supplies *a priori* forms and categories.

Both are needed for knowledge. So Kant is the chief architect of the synthesis.

- **Locke** and **Hume** were empiricists.
- **Spinoza** was a rationalist.

questions.question_md: For Kant, what is the faculty that coordinates sensations and perception?
questions.explanation:
For Kant, the mind must join many sensations and perceptions into one experience. The **transcendental unity of apperception** does this. It is the "I think" that must be able to go with all my ideas. It is the highest point of synthesis in the mind.

- **Space** and **time** are forms of intuition. They only arrange what the senses receive.
- The **categories** are concepts of the understanding. They work under the unity of apperception, which is the final source of their unity.

questions.question_md: Which of the following position is incompatible with the view of Berkeley?
options: Acceptance of the existence of soul
questions.explanation:
Berkeley **rejected abstract ideas**. In the Introduction to the *Principles*, he argues that we cannot form an idea of "man in general" or "triangle in general". Every idea is of a particular thing. A general word only stands for many particular ideas.

Berkeley accepts the other points:

- **Ideas** – everything we perceive is an idea.
- **Soul** – spirits exist and perceive ideas.
- **Nominalism** – general words have no general idea behind them.

So acceptance of abstract ideas is incompatible with Berkeley.

questions.question_md: What is the place of God in Plato's philosophy?
options: God is the cause of Idea
God is the same as Idea
Idea is the cause of God
questions.explanation:
In the standard textbook reading of Plato, the highest Idea is the **Idea of the Good**. It is the source of all other Ideas and of all being and knowledge. This reading identifies Plato's God with this highest Idea. So God is the same as the Idea (of the Good).

- "God is the cause of Idea" makes God stand above the Ideas. But for Plato, the Ideas are eternal and uncaused.
- "God is different from Idea" fits the Demiurge of the *Timaeus*. But the exam follows the reading that identifies God with the Good.
- "Idea is the cause of God" has no basis in Plato.

questions.question_md: Which one of the following is unacceptable to David Hume?
options: Knowledge of Soul, World and God is possible
questions.explanation:
Hume is an empiricist and a sceptic.

- He divides knowledge into **relations of ideas** (mathematics) and **matters of fact** (based on experience). He accepts both.
- He **criticizes the causal relation**. We never perceive a necessary link between cause and effect. Only habit leads us to expect it.
- He denies that we can know the **soul** (only a bundle of perceptions), the **external world** as a substance, or **God**. We have no impressions of these things.

So the claim that knowledge of soul, world and God is possible is unacceptable to Hume.

questions.question_md:
Who holds the following view about emotive theory?

"Only the propositions of the mathematics and empirical sciences have sense, and all other propositions are without senses".

A. A. J. Ayer

B. R. Carnap

C. G. E. Moore

D. B. Russell

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
These words come from **Rudolf Carnap**, in *Philosophy and Logical Syntax* (1935). He says that only the propositions of mathematics and empirical science have sense. All other propositions, such as those of metaphysics and ethics, are without sense. Ethical sentences only express feelings or commands. This supports the **emotive theory**.

- **A. J. Ayer** held a very similar view in *Language, Truth and Logic*. But the quoted words are Carnap's. So the key gives "B only".
- **G. E. Moore** held that "good" is a real but indefinable quality. He was not an emotivist.
- **Bertrand Russell** did not state this principle in these words.

questions.question_md:
"Self-realization is the highest good". This view is maintained by:

A. Rigorism

B. Eudaemonism

C. Emotivism

D. Egoism

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Indian ethics textbooks often describe theories of the moral standard in terms of self-realization:

- **Eudaemonism** (perfectionism) – the highest good is the realization of the **whole self**, both reason and feeling. Aristotle and T. H. Green hold this.
- **Rigorism** – the highest good is the realization of the **rational self**. One must control or suppress the feelings and desires. The Stoics and Kant hold this.

So both A and B treat some kind of self-realization as the highest good. This is the examiner's reasoning.

- **Emotivism** says that moral words only express feelings. It names no highest good.
- **Egoism** seeks one's own pleasure or interest. That is not self-realization in this sense.

questions.question_md:
Consider the following and select the code stating Bahiranga Limbs of *Aṣṭāṅga yoga*:

A. *Yama, Niyama, Āsana*

B. *Dhyāna , Dhāraṇā*

C. *Prāṇāyāma, Pratyāhāra*

D. *Dhāraṇā, Dhyāna, Somādhi*

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Patañjali's *Aṣṭāṅga yoga* has eight limbs. They fall into two groups.

- ***Bahiraṅga*** (outer limbs): *yama*, *niyama*, *āsana*, *prāṇāyāma* and *pratyāhāra*. They prepare the body, breath and senses.
- ***Antaraṅga*** (inner limbs): *dhāraṇā* (concentration), *dhyāna* (meditation) and *samādhi* (absorption).

Check each item:

- A (*Yama, Niyama, Āsana*) – outer. Correct.
- B (*Dhyāna, Dhāraṇā*) – inner. Wrong.
- C (*Prāṇāyāma, Pratyāhāra*) – outer. Correct.
- D (*Dhāraṇā, Dhyāna, Samādhi*) – inner. Wrong.

So the answer is A and C only.

questions.question_md:
*Lokasaṁgraha* stands for :

A. Fruitless activities

B. Moral activities

C. Religious activities

D. Public welfare activities

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
*Lokasaṁgraha* is a key idea in the *Bhagavad Gītā*. It means the welfare and unity of the world. Kṛṣṇa tells Arjuna to act for *lokasaṁgraha*, as King Janaka did. A wise person works to keep society together and to set a good example.

- A – "Fruitless activities": wrong. *Niṣkāma karma* means action without desire for fruit. It does not mean useless action.
- B – "Moral activities": too general.
- C – "Religious activities": too narrow.
- D – "Public welfare activities": this is the meaning of *lokasaṁgraha*.

So D only.

questions.question_md:
We can perceive, according to Nyāya, the external substances by:

A. Visual sense organ

B. Tactual sense organ

C. Gustatory sense organ

D. Internal sense organ

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
In Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, we can perceive a substance (*dravya*) only through two external senses:

- **Sight** – if the substance is large and has manifest colour.
- **Touch** – if it is large and has manifest touch.

The other senses grasp only qualities. The tongue grasps taste, the nose grasps smell and the ear grasps sound. They do not grasp the substance itself.

The **internal sense** (*manas*) perceives inner states, such as pleasure, pain and the self. It does not perceive external substances.

So only A (visual) and B (tactual) are correct.

questions.question_md:
Who among the following admits both Jīvanmukti and Videhamukti

A. Śankara

B. Buddha

C. Rāmānuja

D. Madhva

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
***Jīvanmukti*** is liberation while still alive in the body. ***Videhamukti*** is final liberation after death.

- A – **Śaṅkara** accepts both. Knowledge of Brahman frees a person in this life. The body continues until past *karma* runs out. Then *videhamukti* follows.
- B – **Buddha** accepts both: *nirvāṇa* in this life, and *parinirvāṇa* at death.
- C – **Rāmānuja** rejects *jīvanmukti*. Liberation comes only after death, by God's grace.
- D – **Madhva** also rejects *jīvanmukti*.

So only A and B admit both.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following text is composed by Maulana Azad ?

A. *Ghubar-e-Khatir*

B. *Education and Religious Identity*

C. *India Wins Freedom*

D. *Tarjumanul Quran*

E. *Tarjumanul Geeta*

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
options: A, B, C, D and E
questions.explanation:
Maulana Abul Kalam Azad wrote these works:

- A – ***Ghubar-e-Khatir*** – letters he wrote in Ahmednagar Fort prison. Correct.
- C – ***India Wins Freedom*** – his autobiographical account of the freedom struggle. Correct.
- D – ***Tarjuman-ul-Quran*** – his Urdu translation of and commentary on the Quran. Correct.

The other two are not his books:

- B – *Education and Religious Identity* is not a known title by Azad.
- E – *Tarjumanul Geeta* is not a known work of Azad. His famous commentary is on the Quran.

So the answer is A, C and D only.

questions.question_md:
Who among the following are votaries of *caturvarṇya* system?

A. M. K. Gandhi

B. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan

C. Narayana Guru

D. Deendayal Upādhyāya

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
*Caturvarṇya* is the fourfold *varṇa* order: Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya and Śūdra.

- A – **Gandhi** defended *varṇa* as a division of duties by birth. He said that it implies no high or low. Votary.
- B – **Radhakrishnan** defended *varṇa* as a scheme based on a person's nature and aptitude. Votary.
- D – **Deendayal Upadhyaya** (Integral Humanism) saw the *varṇas* as organic, cooperating parts of society, like limbs of a body. Votary.
- C – **Narayana Guru** opposed caste. His motto was "One caste, one religion, one God for man". Not a votary.

So the answer is A, B and D only.

questions.question_md:
Consider the following statements with reference to conjunction and choose the correct combination :

A. If ' p ' is true and ' q' is true, then ' p·q ' is true

B. If ' p ' is false and ' q' is true, then ' p·q ' is false

C. If ' p ' is true and ' q' is false, then ' p·q ' is true

D. If ' p ' is false and ' q' is false, then ' p·q ' is true

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
A conjunction "p · q" is true only when **both** p and q are true. In every other case, it is false.

- A – p true, q true → p · q **true**. Correct.
- B – p false, q true → p · q **false**. Correct.
- C – p true, q false → the statement says "true". But p · q is false. Wrong.
- D – p false, q false → the statement says "true". But p · q is false. Wrong.

So A and B only.

questions.question_md:
Consider the following with reference to distribution of terms in categorical propositions :

A. A proposition distributes only its predicate term.

B. E proposition distributes both its subject and predicate terms.

C. I proposition distributes its only subject term.

D. O proposition distributes only its predicate term.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
The rules of distribution are:

- **A** (All S is P) distributes the subject only.
- **E** (No S is P) distributes both subject and predicate.
- **I** (Some S is P) distributes neither term.
- **O** (Some S is not P) distributes the predicate only.

Check each statement:

- A – "A distributes only its predicate": wrong. A distributes its subject.
- B – "E distributes both terms": correct.
- C – "I distributes its subject": wrong. I distributes neither term.
- D – "O distributes only its predicate": correct.

So B and D only.

questions.question_md:
Match **List I** with **List II**

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
options: A - I , B - II, C - III, D - IV

A - IV, B - III , C - I, D - II
A - I, B - III, C - IV, D - II
questions.explanation:
- A – **Advaita Vedānta** → **Self-realization** (III). Liberation is knowing that the self (*ātman*) is Brahman.
- B – **Buddhism** → **Noble Truth** (IV). The Four Noble Truths are the core of the Buddha's teaching.

So the match is A–III, B–IV, C–II, D–I.

questions.explanation:

questions.question_md:
Match **List I** with **List II**

| B. Parallelism | II. Descartes |
| C. Pre-established harmony | III. Spinoza |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
options: A - III, B - II , C - I , D - IV
A - II, B - III, C - IV, D - I
A - III , B - I, C - II, D - IV
A - I, B - II, C - III, D - IV
questions.explanation:
These are theories of the mind–body relation, plus one theory of knowledge.

- A – **Interactionism** → **Descartes** (II). Mind and body are two substances that act on each other through the pineal gland.
- B – **Parallelism** → **Spinoza** (III). Thought and extension are parallel attributes of one substance. They do not act on each other.
- C – **Pre-established harmony** → **Leibniz** (IV). God set the monads in harmony from the start, like clocks that keep the same time.
- D – **Scepticism** → **Hume** (I). He doubted causation, the self and the external world.

So the match is A–II, B–III, C–IV, D–I.

questions.question_md:
Match **List I** with **List II**

| List I | List II |
|---|---|
| A. Self is active and conscious | I. Advaita Vedānta |
| B. Self is inactive and conscious | II. Sāṁkhya |
| C. Self is the body itself | III. Vaiśeṣika |
| D. Self is knowledge itself | IV. Cārvāka |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
options: A - I, B - II, C - III, D - IV
A - I, B - II, C - IV, D - III
A - III, B - II, C - IV, D - I
A - III, B - IV, C - I, D - II
questions.explanation:
- A – **Self is active and conscious** → **Vaiśeṣika** (III). The self is a substance that knows, wills and acts. Consciousness is its quality, which arises when the self joins the mind and body.
- B – **Self is inactive and conscious** → **Sāṁkhya** (II). *Puruṣa* is pure consciousness. It is a mere witness and never acts. *Prakṛti* does all the acting.
- C – **Self is the body itself** → **Cārvāka** (IV). The self is just the living, conscious body.
- D – **Self is knowledge itself** → **Advaita Vedānta** (I). The self (*ātman*) is pure consciousness and is identical with Brahman.

So the match is A–III, B–II, C–IV, D–I.

questions.question_md:
Match **List I** with **List II**

| List I | List II |
|---|---|
| A. The effect is produced in the presence of its cause | I. Vaiśeṣika |
| B. The effect is produced in the absence of its cause | II. Advaita Vedānta |
| C. The effect preexists in its cause before its production | III. Bauddha |
| D. The effect is not real but the cause is real | IV. Sāṁkhya |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
options: A - I , B - II, C - III, D - IV
A - I, B - III, C - IV, D - II
A - II, B - III, C - IV, D - I
A - I , B - II, C - IV, D - III
questions.explanation:
These are views on causation:

- A – **Effect produced in the presence of its cause** → **Vaiśeṣika** (I). By *ārambhavāda*, the material cause, such as threads, stays present while it produces a new effect, the cloth.
- B – **Effect produced in the absence of its cause** → **Bauddha** (III). By momentariness, the cause perishes in one moment and the effect arises in the next.
- C – **Effect pre-exists in its cause** → **Sāṁkhya** (IV). This is *satkāryavāda*: curd is already present in milk.
- D – **Effect not real, but the cause is real** → **Advaita Vedānta** (II). This is *vivartavāda*: the world is only an appearance of Brahman.

So the match is A–I, B–III, C–IV, D–II.

questions.question_md:
Consider the following and select the code consistent with Kant's Categorical Imperative:

A. Internal law of conscience

B. Apriori

C. Moral law

D. Natural law

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Kant's **Categorical Imperative** is the supreme moral law. It commands without any condition: "Act only on that maxim which you can will as a universal law."

- A – **Internal law of conscience**: correct. Reason gives this law to itself (autonomy). It is not imposed from outside.
- B – ***A priori***: correct. It comes from pure reason, not from experience.
- C – **Moral law**: correct. It is the basic law of morality.
- D – **Natural law**: wrong. Natural laws describe what happens by necessity in nature. The moral law commands what ought to be, through freedom.

So A, B and C only.

questions.question_md:
Consider the following and select the correct sequence from the codes given below :

A. *Artha*

B. *Dharma*

C. *Mokṣa*

D. *Kāma*

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below
questions.explanation:
The four ***puruṣārthas*** (goals of human life) come in this traditional order:

1. ***Dharma*** – duty and moral order.
2. ***Artha*** – wealth and material means.
3. ***Kāma*** – desire and pleasure.
4. ***Mokṣa*** – liberation.

*Dharma* comes first because it guides how we seek wealth and pleasure. *Mokṣa* is the final and highest goal. So the order is B, A, D, C.

questions.question_md:
Select the correct sequence :

A. *Avagraha*

B. *Dhāraṇā*

C. *Ihā*

D. *Avāya*

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below
questions.explanation:
In Jaina epistemology, ***mati jñāna*** (sense knowledge) develops in four stages:

1. ***Avagraha*** – the first bare grasp of an object: "something is there".
2. ***Īhā*** – the wish to know more: "Is it a man or a post?"
3. ***Avāya*** (*apāya*) – the definite judgement: "It is a man".
4. ***Dhāraṇā*** – retention, so that we can remember the knowledge later.

So the order is A, C, D, B.

questions.question_md:
Consider the following explanation of the fallacies :

**Statement I:** The deliberate misrepresentation of opponent's position is the fallacy of straw man

**Statement II:** An attack upon the character or special circumstances of the opponent involves fallacy of *Ad hominem*

In light of the above statements, choose the ***most appropriate*** answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation:
- **Statement I is correct.** The **straw man** fallacy happens when we twist or misstate an opponent's view. Then we attack that weak version instead of the real view.
- **Statement II is correct.** The ***ad hominem*** fallacy attacks the person, not the argument. The abusive form attacks the opponent's character. The circumstantial form points to the opponent's special situation or interests.

Both are fallacies of relevance, and both descriptions are standard. So both statements are correct.

questions.question_md:
Given below are two statements :

**Statement I:** Radhakrishnan rejects naturalistic explaination of the world as it fails to appreciate the nature of the ultimate reality

**Statement II:** The absolute is conceived by Radhakrishnan as pure consciousness, pure freedom and infinite possibility.

In light of the above statements, choose the ***correct*** answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.explanation:
Both statements match S. Radhakrishnan's *An Idealist View of Life*.

- **Statement I is true.** Radhakrishnan rejects naturalism (the view that only nature and matter are real). Naturalism cannot explain life, mind and values. So it misses the spiritual nature of ultimate reality.
- **Statement II is true.** He describes the Absolute as **pure consciousness, pure freedom and infinite possibility**. Our world is one possibility that the Absolute has made real.

questions.question_md:
Consider the following statements with reference to Iqbal's intuition.

**Statement I:** Intuition is an immediate knowledge of reality.

**Statement II:** Intuition is the property of heart.

In light of the above statements, choose the ***correct*** answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.explanation:
Muhammad Iqbal, in *The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam*, gives intuition a high place.

- **Statement I is true.** For Iqbal, intuition is a direct, immediate grasp of reality as a whole. It does not move step by step like the intellect.
- **Statement II is true.** Iqbal follows the Quran and the Sufis. He calls intuition the work of the **heart** (*qalb*). The heart is a kind of inner sight that reaches aspects of reality hidden from the senses.

So both statements are true.

questions.question_md:
Given below are two statements :

**Statement I:** Gandhian trinity of development consists in *Sarvodaya, Swadeshi* and *Swaraj*

**Statement II:** Gandhian trinity of development consists in *Swadeshi, Swaraj* and *Asteya*

In light of the above statements, choose the ***correct*** answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.explanation:
The Gandhian **trinity** of development is ***Sarvodaya***, ***Swadeshi*** and ***Swaraj***.

- **Sarvodaya** – the welfare of all, including the last person.
- **Swadeshi** – self-reliance and use of local goods and resources.
- **Swaraj** – self-rule, both for the nation and for each person over oneself.

So **Statement I is true**.

**Statement II is false.** It replaces *Sarvodaya* with ***Asteya*** (non-stealing). *Asteya* is one of Gandhi's ethical vows. It is not part of this development trinity.

questions.question_md:
Given below are two statements, one is labelled as **Assertion A** and the other is labelled as **Reason R**

**Assertion A :** According to Madhva, Jīva (individual self) is not the same as *Brahman.*

**Reason R :** *Jīva* (individual self) entirely depends on *Brahman* for its existence (*sattā*), Knowledge (*pramiti*) and action (*kriyā*).

In light of the above statements, choose the ***correct*** answer from the options given below
options: Both **A** and **R** are true and **R** is the correct explanation of **A**
Both **A** and **R** are true but **R** is NOT the correct explanation of **A**
questions.explanation:
Madhva teaches *Dvaita* (dualism).

- **A is true.** For Madhva, the *jīva* (individual self) is always different from Brahman (Viṣṇu). This difference stays even in liberation.
- **R is true.** Madhva calls Brahman *svatantra* (independent). The *jīva* is *paratantra* (dependent). It depends on Brahman for its existence (*sattā*), knowledge (*pramiti*) and action.
- **R explains A.** Brahman is fully independent, and the *jīva* is fully dependent. A dependent being cannot be the same as the independent one. So this dependence shows why the *jīva* is different from Brahman.

questions.question_md:
Given below are two statements, one is labelled as **Assertion A** and the other is labelled as **Reason R**

**Assertion A :** *Vedas* cannot be a ground for God's existence.

**Reason R :** God is the author of the Vedas.

In light of the above statements, choose the ***correct*** answer from the options given below
options: Both **A** and **R** are true and **R** is the correct explanation of **A**
Both **A** and **R** are true but **R** is NOT the correct explanation of **A**
questions.explanation:
Read this question from the Nyāya point of view.

- **R is true.** Nyāya holds that God (*Īśvara*) is the author of the Vedas. Every text needs an author. The Vedas are fully reliable, so their author must be all-knowing. That author is God.
- **A is false.** Because the Vedas need such an author, Nyāya uses the Vedas as a ground (*śruteḥ*) to prove God's existence. Udayana gives this as one of his proofs in *Nyāyakusumāñjali*.

Mīmāṁsā would accept A, because it says that the Vedas are authorless. But then it would reject R. The pair "A false, R true" fits only the Nyāya view.

questions.question_md:
Given below are two statements, one is labelled as **Assertion A** and the other is labelled as **Reason R**

Answer with reference to Mill's, *Utilitarianism*

**Assertion A :** The general happiness is good to the aggregate of all persons.

**Reason R :** Each person's happiness is good to the person concerned.

In light of the above statements, choose the ***correct*** answer from the options given below
options: Both **A** and **R** are true and **R** is the correct explanation of **A**
Both **A** and **R** are true but **R** is NOT the correct explanation of **A**
questions.explanation:
In *Utilitarianism*, Chapter 4, Mill gives his "proof" of the principle of utility. He says that each person desires his own happiness. So **each person's happiness is a good to that person** (R). Therefore, **the general happiness is a good to the aggregate of all persons** (A).

- **A is true.** It is Mill's conclusion.
- **R is true.** It is Mill's premise.
- **R explains A.** Mill derives A from R. Critics say that this step commits the fallacy of composition. But the question asks about Mill's own argument.

questions.question_md: What do you understand as the import of this paragraph?
options: Compatibility of the care of the self with morality
Development of the understanding of Self
Self as the ultimate moral principle
questions.explanation:
The passage is from Michel Foucault. It traces how two old principles changed places over time:

- In Greco-Roman culture, "Take care of yourself" came first. Self-knowledge followed from it.
- In modern culture, "Know yourself" came first. Christian self-renunciation and modern morality caused this change.

So the main import is the **development of the understanding of the self**.

- "Greco-Roman understanding of Self" covers only the first stage.
- "Compatibility of care of the self with morality" – the passage says the opposite: it is hard to see them as compatible today.
- "Self as the ultimate moral principle" – the passage does not claim this.

questions.question_md: "Know yourself" has obscured " Take care of yourself " because:
options: Our morality is able to appropriate the Self
A morality of asceticism rejects the Self
We inherited the tradition of Christian morality
Morality is recognized in terms of knowing the Self
questions.explanation:
The passage gives the reason at the end of the first paragraph. "Know thyself" has obscured "Take care of yourself" **because our morality, a morality of asceticism, insists that the self is that which one can reject**.

- "Our morality is able to appropriate the Self" – the passage says that morality rejects the self.
- "We inherited the tradition of Christian morality" – this is one of the reasons in the passage. But the final, summing-up reason is asceticism that rejects the self.
- "Morality is recognized in terms of knowing the Self" – the passage does not give this as the cause.

questions.question_md: Select tradition advocates one of the following :
options: External circumstances as the basis for morality.
Internal circumstances as the basis for morality.
Respect for law as the basis for morality.
External law as the basis for morality.
questions.notes: "Select tradition" as printed (probably meant "Secular tradition").
questions.explanation:
"Select tradition" is a misprint for "**secular tradition**". The passage says: "We also inherit a **secular tradition that sees in external law the basis for morality**."

- "External circumstances" – the passage speaks of external law, not circumstances.
- "Internal circumstances" – it is not mentioned.
- "Respect for law" – this is close, but the passage uses the exact words "external law". It also asks how respect for the **self** can be the basis of morality.

questions.question_md: According to Michel Foucault :
options: Renouncing the world is a path towards salvation.
Self-renunciation is the condition to salvation.
Self-knowledge is the condition for salvation.
questions.explanation:
The passage speaks of the tradition of Christian morality. This tradition makes **self-renunciation the condition for salvation**. The question asks what Foucault states in this passage.

- "Renouncing the world is a path towards salvation" – the passage speaks of renouncing the self, not the world.
- "Self-realization and self-renunciation are the same" – the passage does not say this.
- "Self-knowledge is the condition for salvation" – the passage says that self-knowledge was a **means** of self-renunciation. Self-renunciation, not self-knowledge, is the condition for salvation.

questions.question_md: According to Foucault, social morality implies one of the following :
options: Importance of recognizing and knowing the Self
Seeks rules for acceptable behaviour in realtion with others
Importance of the knowledge of oneself
questions.explanation:
The passage says: "We are the inheritors of a **social morality that seeks the rules for acceptable behavior in relations with others**."

- "Importance of recognizing and knowing the Self" – the passage links this to the criticism of established morality since the 16th century.
- "Importance of external law" – this belongs to the secular tradition.
- "Importance of the knowledge of oneself" – this is the modern principle "Know yourself". It is not the meaning of social morality.

questions.question_md: In the name of ecologism, deep movement has various deviations which are one sided and laid emphasis on:
questions.explanation:
The last sentence of the passage gives the answer. Under the name of **ecologism**, some deviations from the deep movement appeared. They put a **one-sided stress on pollution and resource depletion**.

- "Ecological harmony" is the aim of ecosophy, which Naess supports.
- "Ecological knowledge" inspires the deep movement. It is not the one-sided deviation.
- "A theory of ecologism" is just the name of the deviation, not what it stresses.

questions.question_md: What does Arne Naess intend to convey in this paragraph?
options: Advocating a philosophy of ecological harmony.
Advocating the limitation of ecology as a science.
Advocating the perspective of Deep Ecology movement that has normative and ecophilosophical dimensions.
questions.explanation:
Arne Naess sums up his main points in this passage:

- The norms of Deep Ecology are **normative** (about values). They do not come from ecology or logic.
- The movement is **ecophilosophical** rather than just ecological.
- It needs an **ecosophy**, a philosophy of ecological harmony.

So the overall aim is to advocate the perspective of Deep Ecology, with its normative and ecophilosophical sides.

- "A theory of ecologism" – Naess criticizes ecologism as a deviation.
- "A philosophy of ecological harmony" and "the limits of ecology as a science" – these are parts of his argument, not the whole message.

questions.question_md: Deep Ecology movement is fortified by one of the following:
options: A movement that culminated in ecosophy.
Ecological knowledge and the life style of the ecological field workers.
A policy that emphasizes ecological harmony.
questions.explanation:
The passage says: "**Ecological knowledge and the life style of the ecological field worker** have suggested, inspired and **fortified** the perspectives of Deep Ecology movements."

- "Policy-making bodies by ecologists" – ecologists try to influence such bodies. But they do not fortify the movement.
- "A movement that culminated in ecosophy" – the passage does not say this.
- "A policy that emphasizes ecological harmony" – ecological harmony is the aim of ecosophy, not what fortifies the movement.

questions.question_md: According to Naess, Deep Ecology movement involves:
options: Value priority system based on results of scientific research.
Scientific potentials based on scientific research.
A philosophical outlook that implies ecological harmony.
questions.explanation:
The passage says that the tenets of Deep Ecology "express a **value priority system** only in part based on results of scientific research". So Deep Ecology involves a value priority system, and science gives part of its basis. The first option is closest to this. The passage, however, says "only in part".

- "Scientific potentials" – the passage speaks of **political** potentials, not scientific ones.
- "Policy-making bodies of ecologists" – ecologists only try to influence policy makers.
- "A philosophical outlook that implies ecological harmony" – this describes **ecosophy**. Naess's own term for the movement's content here is the value priority system.

questions.question_md: According to Naess, ecosophy is :
options: A limited science based on scientific methods.
questions.explanation:
Naess defines the term directly: "By an **ecosophy**, I mean a **philosophy of ecological harmony** or equilibrium."

- "A theory of ecologism" – ecologism is the one-sided deviation that Naess criticizes.
- "A limited science based on scientific methods" – this is how Naess describes **ecology**, not ecosophy.
- "A normative theory on ecology" – ecosophy is openly normative. But Naess defines it as a philosophy of ecological harmony, not as a theory **about** ecology.

groups.md:
Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow:

There is on the one hand the thing of which we are aware -- say the colour of my table -- and on the other hand the actual awareness itself, the mental act of apprehending a thing. The mental act is undoubtedly mental, but is there any reason to suppose that the thing apprehended is in any sense mental?... This question of the distinction between the act and the object in our apprehending of things is vitally important, since our whole power of acquiring knowledge is bound up with it. The faculty of being acquainted with things other than itself is the main characteristic of a mind. Acquaintance with objects essentially consists in a relation between the mind and something other than the mind; it is this that constitutes the mind's power of knowing things. If we say that the things known must be in the mind, we are either unduly limiting the mind's power of knowing, or we are uttering a mere tautology. We are uttering a mere tautology if we mean by 'in the mind' the same as by 'before the mind', i.e. if we mean merely being apprehended by the mind. But if we mean this, we shall have to admit that what, in this sense, is in the mind, may nevertheless be not mental... If I am acquainted with a thing which exists, my acquaintance gives me the knowledge that it exists. But it is not true that, conversely, whenever I can know that a thing of a certain sort exists, I or someone else must be acquainted with the thing.

Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow:

I would like to defend the notion of applied philosophy, and from the defence there emerge several important points about its nature. One is that it is essentially interdisciplinary, for the problems with which it deals are usually complex practical ones to which more than one kind of expertise is relevant. This means that in these days of necessary specialization, applied philosophy will have to be a cooperative venture if it is to be done properly. Such cooperation between experts is by no means easy, and the philosopher could make himself useful just by helping each expert to interpret his discipline to the others.
