In matters of social justice and of scientific truths alike, the legitimation of that power is based on its optimizing the system's performance-efficiency. The application of this criterion to all of our games necessarily entails a certain level of terror, whether soft or hard: be operational (i.e., commensurable) or disappear........ The operativity criterion is technological, it has no relevance for judging what is true or just. Is legitimacy to be found in consensus obtained through discussion .........? Such consensus does violence to the heterogeneity of language games. And invention is always born of dissension.

Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow:

The philosophy of technology is a branch of philosophy that examines the nature, development and impacts of technology on society and human life. This field explores the ethical, social and existential questions raised by technological advancements and seeks to understand how technology shapes and is shaped by human values and practices.

One of the central themes in the philosophy of technology is the relationship between humans and technology. Philosophers debate whether technology is a neutral tool that humans use to achieve their goals or it actively shapes human behavior and society. The instrumentalist view considers technology as a means to an end, emphasizing human control over technological tools. In contrast, the determinist perspective argues that technology has its own logic and momentum, significantly influencing human actions and social structures. Another critical aspect of the philosophy of technology is the ethical implications of technological innovation. For instance, the rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine-learning raises questions about autonomy, responsibility and the potential for biased decision-making. The concept of technological mediation is also significant here, which refers to the ways in which technology influences human perception and interactions with the world. For instance, smartphone and social media platforms alter how people communicate, form relationships and perceive reality.

The philosophy of technology also addresses the notion of: technological utopianism and dystopianism. Utopian-views see technology as a force for positive charge. Dystopian perspectives, on the other hand, warn of potential dangers and negative consequences of unchecked technological advancements, such as loss of privacy, dehumanization and environmental degradation.

questions.question_md:
Match the **List-I** with **List-II**

| LIST I (Naya) | LIST II (Description) |
|---|---|
| A. Sangraha- naya | I. A name should be applied to an object only when its meaning is fulfilled |
| B. Rjusūtra- naya | II. When particulars alone are viewed as real and universals are rejected as unreal |
| C. Evambhūta- naya | III. The particulars are reduced to a series of moments and any given moment is regarded as real |
| D. Vyavahāra- naya | IV. When universals alone are treated as absolutely real and particulars are rejected as unreal |

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Jainism uses **nayas** (partial standpoints) to look at an object. When a naya claims to be the whole truth, it becomes a false naya.

- **A. Saṅgraha-naya** looks at the general class. In its extreme form, only universals are real → **IV**.
- **B. Ṛjusūtra-naya** looks only at the present moment. A thing becomes a series of moments → **III**.
- **C. Evambhūta-naya** uses a name only when the thing does the act that the name means. For example, "Indra" applies only when he rules → **I**.
- **D. Vyavahāra-naya** looks at practical, particular things. In its extreme form, only particulars are real → **II**.

Only option (1) gives A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II.

questions.question_md:
Which among the following can be correctly claimed

A. Sāṁkhya upholds the plurality of Puruṣas

B. Evolution, according to Sāṁkhya is linear

C. Sāṁkhya posits the theory of Saṁyogābhāsa (semblance of contact) between Puruṣa and Prakṛti

D. The second evolute of Prakṛti is Ṃahat

E. Buddhi, for Sāṁkhya, is essentially conscious

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Check each statement about Sāṁkhya.

- **A is true.** Sāṁkhya accepts many Puruṣas (selves). Birth, death and bondage differ from person to person.
- **B is false.** Evolution in Sāṁkhya is cyclic. Creation (sṛṣṭi) and dissolution (pralaya) follow each other.
- **C is true.** Puruṣa is free from all attachment. So its contact with Prakṛti is only an apparent contact (saṁyogābhāsa).
- **D is false.** Mahat (Buddhi) is the first evolute, not the second. Ahaṅkāra (ego) comes second.
- **E is false.** Buddhi comes from Prakṛti, so it is unconscious. It only seems conscious because Puruṣa's light reflects in it.

So only A and C are correct.

questions.question_md:
What among the following can be correctly claimed

A. Prabhākara and Kumārila both accept Anuplabdhi as an independent Pramāṇa

B. For, Kumārila, Anuplabdha padārtha cannot be perceived, for there is no sense- object contact

C. The Naiyāyikās reduces Arthāpatti to Anumāna

D. Prabhākara and Kumārila both admit Aṛthāpatti as an independent Pramāṇa

E. For Kumārila, Anuplabdha padārtha can be known through inference.

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
This question is about Anupalabdhi (non-cognition) and Arthāpatti (postulation) in Mīmāṁsā.

- **A is false.** Only Kumārila (Bhāṭṭa school) accepts Anupalabdhi as a separate pramāṇa. Prabhākara rejects it.
- **B is true.** For Kumārila, an absence has no sense-object contact. So we cannot perceive it.
- **C is true.** Nyāya treats Arthāpatti as a kind of inference (a negative, vyatireki inference).
- **D is true.** Both Prabhākara and Kumārila accept Arthāpatti as a separate pramāṇa.
- **E is false.** Kumārila says that inference cannot give knowledge of absence. That is why he needs Anupalabdhi.

So B, C and D are correct.

questions.question_md:
Madhva Vedānta distinguishes into four orders of Mukti, the correct sequence is:-

A. Karma- kṣaya

B. Utkrānti- laya

C. Acirādigaman

D. Bhoga

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.notes: Options 2 and 4 are identical in the source.
questions.explanation:
Madhva describes the path of the liberated soul in four steps.

1. **Karma-kṣaya** — the soul's binding karma comes to an end. This follows the direct vision of God.
2. **Utkrānti-laya** — the soul leaves the body at death.
3. **Arcirādi-gamana** — the soul travels by the path of light (arcis) to the world of Viṣṇu.
4. **Bhoga** — the soul enjoys the bliss of liberation.

So the order is A, B, C, D. The other options put the departure from the body before the end of karma. In the source, options (2) and (4) are the same, and both are wrong.

questions.question_md:
Match the **List-I** with **List-II**

| LIST I (Authors) | LIST II (Books) |
|---|---|
| A. Bhāsarvajña | I. Padārthatattva- nirūpaṇam |
| B. Raghunāth Śiromaṇi | II. Nyāya- Bhūṣaṇam |
| C. Vallabhācārya | III. Tarkabhāṣā |
| D. Keśava Miśra | IV. Nyāya- Līlāvati |

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
These are well-known Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika authors and their works.

- **A. Bhāsarvajña** wrote the *Nyāyasāra*. He also wrote its own commentary, the *Nyāya-bhūṣaṇa* → **II**.
- **B. Raghunātha Śiromaṇi** was a Navya-Nyāya thinker. He wrote the *Padārtha-tattva-nirūpaṇa* → **I**.
- **C. Vallabhācārya** (the Vaiśeṣika writer, not the Vedānta teacher) wrote the *Nyāya-līlāvatī* → **IV**.
- **D. Keśava Miśra** wrote the *Tarkabhāṣā*, a short handbook of Nyāya → **III**.

Only option (2) gives A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the underneath philosophers in chronological sequence in an ascending order:-

A. Udyotkara

B. Udayanācārya

C. Vācaspati Miśra

D. Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya

E. Vardhamāna Upādhyāya

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Place each Nyāya thinker in his period.

- **Udyotakara** (about 6th–7th century CE) wrote the *Nyāya-vārttika*.
- **Vācaspati Miśra** (about 9th–10th century) wrote a commentary on Udyotakara's work.
- **Udayanācārya** (about 10th–11th century) wrote a commentary on Vācaspati's work.
- **Vardhamāna Upādhyāya** (about 14th century) was the son of Gaṅgeśa, the founder of Navya-Nyāya.
- **Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya** (about 17th century) was a late Navya-Nyāya writer.

So the order is A, C, B, E, D. The chain of commentaries (Udyotakara → Vācaspati → Udayana) helps to fix the first three.

questions.question_md:
Match the **List-I** with **List-II**

| LIST I (Author) | LIST II (Book) |
|---|---|
| A. Citsukha | I. Bhagwad- Bhakti- Rasāyana |
| B. Sureśvara | II. Pañcapādikā Vivaraṇa |
| C. Madhusudan Saraswati | III. Naiṣkarmya- Siddhi |
| D. Prakāśātma Yati | IV. Tattva- Pradīpikā |

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
These are Advaita Vedānta authors and their works.

- **A. Citsukha** wrote the *Tattva-pradīpikā*, also called *Citsukhī* → **IV**.
- **B. Sureśvara**, a direct pupil of Śaṅkara, wrote the *Naiṣkarmya-siddhi* → **III**.
- **C. Madhusūdana Sarasvatī** wrote the *Bhagavad-bhakti-rasāyana*, a work on devotion → **I**.
- **D. Prakāśātma Yati** wrote the *Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇa*. This work started the Vivaraṇa school → **II**.

Only option (4) gives A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II.

questions.question_md: The knowledge of the non-dual relation between Brahma and Jīva, through Mahāvākyas is through the following pramāṇa in Vedānta- Paribhāṣā:
questions.explanation:
In the *Vedānta-Paribhāṣā*, Dharmarāja treats knowledge of an immediately present object as **perception** (pratyakṣa). This is true even when words produce it.

- A mahāvākya such as "Tat tvam asi" (That thou art) shows the identity of Jīva and Brahman.
- Consciousness is always immediately present. So this knowledge is perceptual, not verbal.
- It grasps pure identity, with no relation between two things. So it is **nirvikalpaka** (non-relational) perception.
- Dharmarāja gives a similar example: "This is that Devadatta."

Śabda (testimony) is the tempting answer, because the knowledge comes through a sentence. But Vedānta-Paribhāṣā calls the result perception. Savikalpaka perception grasps a relation, so it does not fit.

questions.question_md:
In the context of Purva-Mimāṁsā, what among the following can be claimed

A. For Kumārila, knowledge leads to successful activity.

B. For Prabhākara, all knowledge, vedic or secular, points to activity

C. A Varṇa is non-eternal but Śabda is eternal

D. A word signifies a particular object.

E. The relation between word and its meaning is natural, necessary and internal.

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Check each claim about Pūrva-Mīmāṁsā.

- **A is false.** Kumārila holds that knowledge is valid by itself (svataḥ prāmāṇya). Its validity does not depend on successful activity. That is the Nyāya view.
- **B is true.** Prabhākara says that all knowledge, Vedic or worldly, points to something to be done (kārya).
- **C is false.** Mīmāṁsā holds that the letters (varṇas) are eternal.
- **D is false.** For Mīmāṁsā, a word means the universal (jāti or ākṛti), not a particular object.
- **E is true.** The word–meaning relation is natural (autpattika), necessary and internal. No person makes it.

So B and E are correct.

questions.question_md:
Which among the following do not affirm the existence of Prakṛiti.

A. Evolution means manifestation of the implicit as the explicit

B. The unity of the universe points to a single cause.

C. The finite cannot be the cause of the universal. The infinite, independent, unlimited is the source of universe.

D. All objects are composed of three guṇās and it logically presuppose the existence of an entity that is wittness to them

E. All compound objects exist for the sake of Prakṛti

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Sāṁkhya gives five proofs for **Prakṛti** (Kārikā 15). It gives five other proofs for **Puruṣa** (Kārikā 17).

- **A** affirms Prakṛti. An effect is the manifest form of what was hidden in the cause.
- **B** affirms Prakṛti. The unity of the world points to one cause.
- **C** affirms Prakṛti. Finite things need an unlimited cause.
- **D** does not affirm Prakṛti. Things made of the three guṇas need a witness who is free from the guṇas. This proves Puruṣa.
- **E** does not affirm Prakṛti. Compound things exist for the sake of another, that is, for Puruṣa. They do not exist for Prakṛti.

So D and E are the items that do not support Prakṛti.

questions.question_md:
Consider the following about texts of Indian-Philosophy and identify the correct items:-

A. “Laukiko- mārgo- anusartavyaḥ” is the view seconded by Jayarāśi

B. ‘Tttvopplavasiṁha’ is a Vaitaṇḍika text

C. Vaidalya- sūtra supports the assertion of Nyāya- Sūtra

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
- **A is true.** Jayarāśi was a Cārvāka thinker. His *Tattvopaplavasiṁha* ends with "laukiko mārgo 'nusartavyaḥ". It means "one should follow the worldly path".
- **B is true.** A Vaitaṇḍika only attacks other views and sets up no view of its own. Jayarāśi's book refutes all pramāṇas in this way.
- **C is false.** Nāgārjuna's *Vaidalya-sūtra* (Vaidalya-prakaraṇa) attacks the sixteen categories of the Nyāya-sūtra. It does not support them.

So A and B only.

questions.question_md: Which of the following is incorrect?
options: For Vaibhāṣika, perception as a source of external world's knowledge cannot be conciliated with kṣaṇikavāda
questions.explanation:
Check each statement.

- **(1) is true.** Vijñānavāda holds that cognition reveals itself (sva-prakāśa).
- **(2) is true.** Buddhists reject pramāṇa-samplava, that is, one object known by many pramāṇas. Each pramāṇa has its own object (pramāṇa-vyavasthā).
- **(3) is true.** Nyāya holds that another cognition reveals a cognition (para-prakāśa). This is anuvyavasāya (after-cognition).
- **(4) is incorrect.** The Vaibhāṣika is a direct realist. It accepts both momentariness and direct perception of external things. The Sautrāntika says that momentary objects cannot be perceived directly. So the Sautrāntika infers them.

So statement (4) is the incorrect one.

questions.question_md:
Identify the consistent items with the vedāntic- view of perception

A. Kedārī- kulyā- Nyāya

B. Transcendental knowledge is related to Vrtti Caitanya

C. Pramātṛ- Caitanya is related to subject

D. Pramātṛ- Caitanya is related to object

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Advaita explains perception in the *Vedānta-Paribhāṣā*.

- **A is consistent.** In Kedāra-kulyā-nyāya, water flows from a tank through channels into fields. In the same way, the mind (antaḥkaraṇa) goes out through the senses and takes the form of the object.
- **B is not consistent.** Vṛtti-caitanya is consciousness limited by a mental mode. It gives empirical knowledge, not transcendental knowledge.
- **C is consistent.** Pramātṛ-caitanya is consciousness limited by the mind. It is the knowing subject.
- **D is not consistent.** Consciousness limited by the object is viṣaya-caitanya, not pramātṛ-caitanya.

So A and C only.

questions.question_md: You explain the meaning of the term hyena to your friend by giving its description since you are quite familiar with hyenas. Two of you go to a jungle and see a creature, your friend recalls your description and compares it to the creature and knows, “this is 'hyena', ” in that situation your knowledge, “this is hyena” is through (as per nyāya) :-
questions.explanation:
Read the question carefully. It asks about **your** knowledge, not your friend's knowledge.

- You already know hyenas well. You have seen them before.
- When you see the creature, your senses grasp it directly. So your knowledge "this is a hyena" is **Pratyakṣa** (perception).
- Your friend learns from your description and then compares it with the creature. For the friend, the knowledge is **Upamāna** (comparison).

Upamāna is the trap. It fits the friend, but not you. Anumāna and Śabda do not fit, because you see the animal directly.

questions.question_md:
Which among the following are incorrect

A. For Leibniz, our ideas of space, figure, motion have their origin, in the common sense, in the mind itself

B. For Spinoza, thought and extension are separate substances

C. According to Hegel, concrete universal notion is the synthesis of opposites

D. According to Kant, all synthetic judgements give us genuine knowledge

E. According to Berkeley, the idea of soul can be formed on the basis of its acts.

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
The question asks for the **incorrect** statements.

- **A is correct.** Leibniz says ideas of space, figure and motion come from the "common sense", that is, from the mind itself.
- **B is incorrect.** For Spinoza, thought and extension are two attributes of one substance (God). They are not separate substances.
- **C is correct.** Hegel's concrete universal unites opposites in a higher synthesis.
- **D is incorrect.** For Kant, only synthetic a priori judgements give knowledge that is both new and necessary. Synthetic a posteriori judgements lack necessity.
- **E is incorrect.** Berkeley says we have no **idea** of the soul, because ideas are passive. We have only a "notion" of spirit.

So B, D and E are incorrect.

questions.question_md:
Match the **List-I** with **List-II**

| LIST I (Huṁean View) | LIST II (Its justification) |
|---|---|
| A. Empirical | I. Our knowledge is limited to the world of phenomena. |
| B. Positivistic | II. Our knowledge has its source in experience |
| C. Agnostic | III. We know nothing of the ultimates |
| D. Humanistic | IV. The human mental world is the only legitimate sphere of science and enquiry |

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Hume's philosophy has several sides. Each name has its own reason.

- **A. Empirical** — all our knowledge comes from experience → **II**.
- **B. Positivistic** — our knowledge stays within the world of phenomena (appearances) → **I**.
- **C. Agnostic** — we know nothing about ultimate things like substance, self or God → **III**.
- **D. Humanistic** — the study of human nature is the main field of enquiry → **IV**.

Only option (4) gives A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV.

questions.question_md:
Match the **List-I** with **List-II**

| LIST I (Kant's Judgment) | LIST II (Example) |
|---|---|
| A. The Particular Judgment | I. Every effect must have a cause. |
| B. The Infinite Judgment | II. If the air is warm, the thermometer rises. |
| C. The Hypothetical Judgment | III. Mind is unextended |
| D. The Apodictic Judgment | IV. Some animals are herbivores. |

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Kant's table of judgements has four groups: quantity, quality, relation and modality.

- **A. Particular** (quantity): "**Some** animals are herbivores" → **IV**.
- **B. Infinite** (quality): "Mind is **un**extended". It has the form "S is non-P" → **III**.
- **C. Hypothetical** (relation): "**If** the air is warm, the thermometer rises" → **II**.
- **D. Apodictic** (modality): "Every effect **must** have a cause". It states necessity → **I**.

Only option (4) gives A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I.

questions.question_md: The crux of Kant's Transcendental Method lies in the argument that it leads:
options: From the presuppositions to their logical outcomes
From experience to its necessary presuppositions
From individual experiences to general experiences
From one postulate to several other leading postulates
questions.explanation:
Kant's **transcendental method** starts from the fact of experience. Then it asks what makes this experience possible.

The answer gives the **necessary presuppositions** (a priori conditions) of experience. Examples are the forms of space and time and the categories.

- Option (1) goes the other way. It starts from presuppositions and draws results, like ordinary deduction.
- Option (3) describes induction, from single cases to general ones.
- Option (4) describes a chain of postulates, as in an axiom system.

So the method goes from experience to its necessary presuppositions.

questions.question_md:
The following assertions are attributed to Rene Descartes:

(A) I know that I perceive the truth clearly and distinctly, because God exists and is not a deceiver.

(B) I know that God exists and is not a deceiver because I perceive this truth clearly and distinctly.

In the logical terms, the above mentioned assertions commit the informal fallacy called as:
questions.explanation:
Look at how the two claims support each other.

- (A) uses God's existence to prove that clear and distinct ideas are true.
- (B) uses a clear and distinct idea to prove that God exists.

Each claim depends on the other. So the argument assumes what it wants to prove. This is **circular reasoning** (petitio principii). Critics call it the "**Cartesian Circle**". Antoine Arnauld raised this objection.

There is no appeal to an authority, no loaded question and no appeal to lack of proof. So the other options do not fit.

questions.question_md: According to John Locke, sometimes the mind perceives the agreement or disagreement of two ideas by direct inspection, without the intervention of any other ideas. Such knowledge is called:
questions.explanation:
Locke names three degrees of knowledge.

- **Intuitive knowledge**: the mind sees the agreement or disagreement of two ideas **directly**. It needs no other idea in between. For example, white is not black. This is the most certain knowledge.
- **Demonstrative knowledge**: the mind needs other ideas in between, as in a proof. So option (4) is wrong.
- **Sensitive knowledge**: it is knowledge of particular external things through the senses. So option (2) is wrong.

"Hypothetical knowledge" is not one of Locke's degrees.

questions.question_md:
Rene Descartes defends the external world by posing following arguments:

A. Belief in an external world is not natural.

B. The mind is primarily its conceptions.

C. Imagination and perception do not depend just on conception.

D. Belief in an external world is required to explain the phenomena of imagination and perception.

E. The existence of an all-perfect God is the surest guarantee of the external world.

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
In Meditation VI, Descartes argues for the existence of the external world.

- **A is wrong.** Descartes says that we have a strong **natural** inclination to believe in bodies. So statement A goes against his argument.
- **B is right.** The essence of the mind is thinking, that is, its conceptions.
- **C is right.** Imagination and sense perception are not part of the mind's essence. They need something more than pure conception.
- **D is right.** The best way to explain imagination and perception is that bodies exist.
- **E is right.** God is perfect and is not a deceiver. So our natural belief in bodies cannot be false.

So B, C, D and E only.

questions.question_md:
Match the **List-I** with **List-II**

| LIST I (Thinkers) | LIST II (Ancient School of Philosophy) |
|---|---|
| A. Hippo, Idaeus, Diogenes | I. The Stoics |
| B. Xenophanes, Parmenides, Zeno | II. The Atomists |
| C. Leucippus and Democritus | III. The Ionic School |
| D. Zeno, Cleanthes, Chrysippus | IV. The Eleatic School |

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Each group of thinkers belongs to one ancient Greek school.

- **A. Hippo, Idaeus, Diogenes (of Apollonia)** were later Ionian nature-thinkers. They looked for one basic stuff → **III. Ionic School**.
- **B. Xenophanes, Parmenides, Zeno (of Elea)** → **IV. Eleatic School**. They held that reality is one and unchanging.
- **C. Leucippus and Democritus** → **II. Atomists**.
- **D. Zeno (of Citium), Cleanthes, Chrysippus** → **I. Stoics**.

Note: there are two Zenos. Zeno of Elea is an Eleatic, and Zeno of Citium founded Stoicism.

questions.question_md:
The philosophic knowledge that stands as the preserve of ‘philosopher- rulers’ is expressed in:

A. The Simile of the Sun

B. The Divided Line

C. The Story of the Flying arrow

D. The Simile of the Cave

E. The Parable of the Beast

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
In the *Republic*, Plato explains the knowledge of the philosopher-rulers with three famous images (Books VI–VII).

- **A. The Simile of the Sun**: the Form of the Good is like the sun. It gives truth and being.
- **B. The Divided Line**: it shows the levels of knowledge, from images up to the Forms.
- **D. The Simile (Allegory) of the Cave**: it shows the soul's journey from shadows to the light of the Good.

**C** is wrong. The Flying Arrow is a paradox of Zeno of Elea. **E** is not one of these three images. So A, B and D only.

questions.question_md: Modern ‘Brain in a Vat’ arguments are direct descendants of :
questions.explanation:
The **Brain in a Vat** argument asks a question. How can you know that you are not a brain in a vat? A scientist could feed it false experiences.

This is a modern form of **Cartesian doubt**. In Meditation I, Descartes imagines an **evil demon**. The demon could deceive him about the whole external world. The vat scientist plays the same role as the demon.

- Hume's doubt is about causation and induction, not a total deceiver.
- Akrasia is weakness of will.
- Hegel's Geist is world-spirit.

questions.question_md:
Match the **List-I** with **List-II**

| LIST I (Aristotelian Terms) | LIST II (Meaning of the Term) |
|---|---|
| A. Phronesis | I. Flourishing |
| B. Arete | II. Weakness of the will |
| C. Akrasia | III. Virtue or Excellence |
| D. Eudaimonia | IV. Practical Wisdom |

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
These are key terms of Aristotle's ethics.

- **A. Phronesis** — practical wisdom. It is the ability to see what is right in a situation → **IV**.
- **B. Arete** — virtue or excellence → **III**.
- **C. Akrasia** — weakness of the will. A person knows the good but does not do it → **II**.
- **D. Eudaimonia** — flourishing or well-being. It is the highest human good → **I**.

Only option (4) gives A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I.

questions.question_md: Which of the following is not in line with the philosophical thought of St. Thomas Aquinas
options: Faith is a gift from the creator
It is better to know an object of greatest magnitude imperfectly than to love it
Indetermination is one of the characteristics of the will
Grace is a bridge between an infinite creator and a finite creation
questions.explanation:
Aquinas holds that, in this life, it is better to **love** God than to know Him imperfectly. Knowledge brings the object down to the level of the knower. Love goes out to the object as it is in itself. So for things higher than us, love is nobler than knowledge.

Statement (2) says the opposite. So it is not in line with Aquinas.

- (1) is in line. Faith is a gift of God.
- (3) is in line. The will can choose among goods, so it is free.
- (4) is in line. Grace links the infinite God and finite creatures.

questions.question_md: “Credeut Intelligas” (Believe in order that you may understand) is a dictum of
questions.explanation:
**St. Augustine** taught that faith comes before understanding. In his sermons he wrote "Crede, ut intelligas" (believe, so that you may understand). He based this on a verse of Isaiah: "Unless you believe, you will not understand."

St. Anselm is the tempting option. He later used the first-person form "**Credo ut intelligam**" (I believe so that I may understand). His motto follows Augustine's dictum.

Aquinas gave reason a wider role. Protagoras was a sophist ("Man is the measure of all things").

questions.question_md: What among the following can not be attributed to Leibniz
options: The source of mechanics lies in metaphysics
Bodies act according to the laws of final causes, by means of desire, ends and means.
Every Monad is ‘charged with the past’ and and 'big with the future.
questions.explanation:
In the *Monadology*, Leibniz separates two kinds of causes.

- **Souls** act by the laws of **final causes**, through desires (appetitions), ends and means.
- **Bodies** act by the laws of **efficient causes**, that is, by motions.

Statement (2) gives final causes to bodies. So Leibniz would not accept it.

- (1) is Leibniz's view. The laws of motion rest on metaphysics, for example on force.
- (3) is his view. Monads are simple, soul-like substances.
- (4) is his view. Each monad's present state carries its past and contains its future.

questions.question_md:
Match the **List-I** with **List-II**

Match the definition of happiness with the system of philosophies

| LIST I | LIST II |
|---|---|
| A. Psychophysical happiness | I. Nyāya |
| B. Absolute absence of misery | II. Vedānta |
| C. Absolute separation of soul from Body | III. Cārvāka |
| D. Blissfulness | IV. Jainism |

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Each school has its own idea of the highest goal.

- **A. Psychophysical happiness** → **III. Cārvāka**. The goal is bodily and mental pleasure in this life.
- **B. Absolute absence of misery** → **I. Nyāya**. Apavarga (liberation) is the complete end of all pain.
- **C. Absolute separation of soul from body** → **IV. Jainism**. The soul becomes free from all karmic matter.
- **D. Blissfulness** → **II. Vedānta**. Mokṣa is the bliss (ānanda) of Brahman.

Only option (1) gives A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

questions.question_md: Which among the following Āśrama is also known as “Vaikhānasa”?
questions.explanation:
**Vaikhānasa** is an old name for the forest hermit. The *Vaikhānasa* rules give the code of life for a person who lives in the forest. So the term refers to **Vānaprastha**, the third āśrama (stage of life).

- Brahmacarya is the student stage.
- Gṛhastha is the householder stage.
- Sannyāsa is the stage of full renunciation. A sannyāsin has other names, such as parivrājaka (wandering monk).

questions.question_md:
Which combination among the following constitutes the meaning of 'Karma"?

A. You reap what you sow.

B. The present life is a by chance occurrence.

C. You don't get the result of an unperformed Karma.

D. All our decisions are entirely determined by previous Karma.

E. The law of causation is compatible with the theory of Karma.

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
The law of Karma is a moral law of cause and effect.

- **A fits.** You reap what you sow. Every action brings its result to the doer.
- **B does not fit.** Under Karma, the present life comes from past actions. It is not chance.
- **C fits.** You do not get the result of an action that you did not do (no akṛtābhyāgama).
- **D does not fit.** Past karma shapes our situation, but it does not fix every decision. We stay free to act now. Otherwise moral effort would have no meaning.
- **E fits.** Karma is the law of causation applied to moral life.

So A, C and E only.

questions.question_md:
Match the **List-I** with **List-II**

| LIST I | LIST II |
|---|---|
| A. Nitya Karṁa | I. We should take bath daily. |
| B. Naimittika Karma | II. If we want to clean ourselves, we should take bath daily |
| C. Kāmya Karma | III. We should take bath after eclipse |
| D. Niṣiddha Karma | IV. We should avoid stale food. |

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
The Mīmāṁsā and Dharmaśāstra texts sort actions into four kinds.

- **A. Nitya karma** — a daily duty with no special cause: "take a bath daily" → **I**.
- **B. Naimittika karma** — a duty on a special occasion: "take a bath after an eclipse" → **III**.
- **C. Kāmya karma** — an act done for a wish: "**if** we want to be clean, we should bathe" → **II**.
- **D. Niṣiddha karma** — a forbidden act: "avoid stale food" → **IV**.

Only option (3) gives A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV.

questions.question_md:
What are the factors of Cikīrṣā, according to Nyāya philosophy, among the following?

A. Balavad aniṣṭa asambhāvyatā jñāna

B. Prārabdha phala jñāna

C. Kṛtisādhyata jñāna

D. Iṣṭasādhanatā jñāna

E. Akarmasādhyatā jñāna

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
For Nyāya, **Cikīrṣā** (the wish to act) arises from three kinds of awareness.

- **Kṛti-sādhyatā jñāna** (C) — "I can do this by my effort."
- **Iṣṭa-sādhanatā jñāna** (D) — "This act is a means to what I want."
- **Balavad-aniṣṭa-ananubandhitva jñāna** (A) — "This act will not bring a greater harm." The option calls it "asambhāvyatā" (unlikeliness) of strong harm.

**B** (knowledge of fruits that have already started) and **E** (knowledge that something needs no action) are not causes of the wish to act.

So A, C and D only.

questions.question_md: In which, among the following sense Apūrva is not considered
options: Relation between Karma and its result
questions.explanation:
**Apūrva** is the unseen power that a Vedic ritual produces. It joins the act to its later result, such as heaven.

- **(2) is a sense of Apūrva.** It is the link between karma and its fruit.
- **(3) is a sense of Apūrva.** Kumārila treats it as a potency in the soul, like a saṁskāra (impression).
- **(4) is a sense of Apūrva.** Prabhākara treats it as kārya (what must be done) or niyoga. The Vedic command reveals it.
- **(1) is not a sense of Apūrva.** The act itself perishes at once. Apūrva is the new power that the act leaves behind.

So Apūrva is not the karma (act) itself.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following elements of Pratītyasamutpāda in correct cause- effect order:

A. Nāma- rūpa

B. Vedanā

C. Ṣaḍāyatana

D. Tṛṣṇā

E. Sparśa

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
The twelve links of **Pratītyasamutpāda** (dependent origination) run in this order:

Avidyā → Saṁskāra → Vijñāna → **Nāma-rūpa** → **Ṣaḍāyatana** (six sense bases) → **Sparśa** (contact) → **Vedanā** (feeling) → **Tṛṣṇā** (craving) → Upādāna → Bhava → Jāti → Jarā-maraṇa.

Apply this to the five given links:

- A. Nāma-rūpa
- C. Ṣaḍāyatana
- E. Sparśa
- B. Vedanā
- D. Tṛṣṇā

So the order is A-C-E-B-D. The senses must exist before contact, and feeling comes before craving.

questions.question_md: No one can stay without action even for a moment due to ................, according to the Bhagavadgītā.
questions.explanation:
The Bhagavadgītā (3.5) says that no one can stay without action even for a moment. The **guṇas** (sattva, rajas and tamas) of **Prakṛti** force every being to act.

So action belongs to our nature. That is why the Gītā does not teach giving up action. It teaches action without attachment to its fruits (niṣkāma karma).

The verse does not mention divine will, compassion or cowardice as the cause.

questions.question_md:
Match the **List-I** with **List-II**

| LIST I (Authors) | LIST II (Books) |
|---|---|
| A. Henery Sidgwick | I. Data of Ethics |
| B. Herbert Spencer | II. Ethics |
| C. J.S. Mill | III. Outlines of the History of Ethics |
| D. G. E. Moore | IV. Utilitarianism |

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
These are well-known books in ethics.

- **A. Henry Sidgwick** wrote *Outlines of the History of Ethics*. His main work is *The Methods of Ethics* → **III**.
- **B. Herbert Spencer** wrote *The Data of Ethics*, an evolutionary ethics → **I**.
- **C. J.S. Mill** wrote *Utilitarianism* → **IV**.
- **D. G.E. Moore** wrote the short book *Ethics*, as well as *Principia Ethica* → **II**.

Only option (3) gives A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

questions.question_md: What is the “naturalistic fallacy”?
options: A problem created by the Nature
Human being is by nature problematic
Mistaking an ethical judgement with a factual one
Focusing on the good of nature
questions.explanation:
G.E. Moore named the **naturalistic fallacy** in *Principia Ethica*. The fallacy defines "good" by a natural property, such as "pleasant" or "more evolved".

For Moore, "good" is a simple, non-natural quality. A factual statement about natural properties cannot give its meaning. So the fallacy mixes up an ethical judgement with a factual one. This links with Hume's point that we cannot get an "ought" from an "is".

The other options use the word "nature" in its everyday sense. They have nothing to do with Moore's idea.

questions.question_md: What is not true to Utilitarianism?
options: An action is good if it produces useful things.
An action is intrinsically good or bad.
The merit of Law is due to its effect.
questions.explanation:
Utilitarianism is a **consequentialist** theory. An act is right or wrong only because of its results, that is, the happiness it produces.

- **(2) is not true to Utilitarianism.** It says an act is good or bad in itself (intrinsically). That is the view of deontology or intuitionism.
- (1) fits. Good acts are useful.
- (3) fits. Bentham judged laws by their effects on happiness.
- (4) fits. Classical utilitarians equate good with pleasure.

questions.question_md:
Match the **List-I** with **List-II**

| LIST I (Thinkers) | LIST II (Thoughts) |
|---|---|
| A. Jeremy Bentham | I. Good means I approve it. |
| B. J.S. Mill | II. Quantitative distinction of pleasure. |
| C. C.L. Stevenson | III. Good means I prescribe it. |
| D. R.M. Hare | IV. Quantitative distinction of pleasure |

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.notes: In the English source, List-II items II and IV both read “Quantitative distinction of pleasure”; the Hindi version has item IV as qualitative distinction of pleasure (सुख का गुणवत्तापरक प्रभेद).
questions.explanation:
Note: in the English source, items II and IV both read "Quantitative". The Hindi version shows that item IV means **qualitative** distinction of pleasure.

- **A. Bentham** — pleasures differ only in **quantity** → **II**.
- **B. J.S. Mill** — pleasures also differ in **quality** → **IV**.
- **C. C.L. Stevenson** (emotivist) — "This is good" means "I approve of this; do so as well" → **I**.
- **D. R.M. Hare** (prescriptivist) — moral words prescribe. "Good" works like "I prescribe it" → **III**.

Only option (1) gives A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

questions.question_md:
Match the **List-I** with **List-II**

| LIST I (Thinkers) | LIST II (Thoughts) |
|---|---|
| A. Henry Davie Thoreau | I. Be a member of a kingdom of ends. |
| B. G.E. Moore | II. That government is best which governs the least |
| C. Immanuel Kant | III. My station and its duties |
| D. F.H. Bradley | IV. Good is simple and indefinable |

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Each thought is a famous line or idea of one thinker.

- **A. Thoreau** — *Civil Disobedience* starts with the motto "That government is best which governs least" → **II**.
- **B. G.E. Moore** — "good" is simple and cannot be defined → **IV**.
- **C. Kant** — act as a member of a **kingdom of ends**, a union of rational beings under moral laws → **I**.
- **D. F.H. Bradley** — "My Station and Its Duties" is an essay in his *Ethical Studies* → **III**.

Only option (2) gives A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements are correct?

A. Highest good in Kant is goodwill.

B. Henry Sidgwick's view of utilitarianism is Rational Utilitarianism.

C. J.S. Mill does not accept quantitative differences in pleasures.

D. The number of virtues in socrates is ‘one’.

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
- **A is false.** For Kant, the good will is the only thing good without limit. But the **highest good** (summum bonum) is virtue joined with happiness in proportion to it.
- **B is true.** Sidgwick based utilitarianism on rational, self-evident principles. So people call his view rational (or ethical) utilitarianism.
- **C is false.** Mill accepts differences of quantity in pleasures. He adds differences of quality.
- **D is true.** For Socrates, virtue is knowledge. So all the virtues are at bottom **one** (the unity of virtue).

So B and D only.

questions.question_md: Which theory among the following is not compatible with capital punishment?
questions.explanation:
The **reformative theory** says that punishment should change the criminal into a better person. A dead person cannot reform. So this theory cannot support capital punishment.

- The **deterrent** theory can support it. The death penalty may frighten others away from crime.
- The **retributive** theory can support it. A person who takes a life deserves to lose his own.
- The **preventive** theory can support it. Death stops the criminal from doing the crime again.

questions.question_md: Which one among the following is not a Metaethical question?
options: What is the meaning of a moral judgement?
What is the right thing to do?
questions.explanation:
**Metaethics** studies the nature of moral words and judgements. It asks what they mean and whether we can prove them.

- (1) asks about the meaning of a moral judgement. This is metaethics.
- (2) asks about the meaning of "good". This is metaethics.
- (4) asks whether we can prove moral judgements. This is metaethics.
- (3) "What is the right thing to do?" asks for a moral answer, not for the nature of morality. So it is a **normative** question.

questions.question_md: Which among the following is not a true statement with reference to Metaethics?
options: For an emotivist, “Killing is bad” means “Killing, boo!”
C.L. Stevenson is not an emotivist.
According to G.E. Moore, the meaning of an ethical term can be intuited.
questions.explanation:
**C.L. Stevenson** is one of the main **emotivists**. With A.J. Ayer, he gave the classic form of emotivism in *Ethics and Language*. So statement (3) is plainly false.

- (2) is true. Emotivism is sometimes called the "boo–hurrah" theory. "Killing is bad" expresses disapproval, like "Killing, boo!"
- (4) is true. Moore held that we know "good" by intuition, not by definition.
- (1) has loose wording. Most writers class intuitionists as cognitivists. But the examiner seems to mean that intuition is not a process of reasoning.

The clear factual error is statement (3).

questions.question_md:
Which among the following are true to Intuitionism?

A. Conscience is a universal faculty of all persons.

B. Rightness and wrongness are inherent qualities of actions.

C. Actions are intrinsically right or wrong.

D. The moral merit of an action is dependent on its result.

E. Conscience reveals the rightness of an action by way of perceiving its consequence.

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
**Intuitionism** says that we know right and wrong directly, by moral intuition or conscience. We do not need to look at results.

- **A fits.** Conscience is a faculty that all people have.
- **B fits.** Rightness and wrongness belong to actions themselves.
- **C fits.** Actions are right or wrong in themselves (intrinsically).
- **D does not fit.** Merit that depends on results is the teleological (consequence-based) view.
- **E does not fit.** Intuition sees rightness directly, not by looking at consequences.

So A, B and C only.

questions.question_md: Which among the following is an inconsistent thought in the light of Swami Vivekananda
options: No distinction of qualifications can be ascribed to Reality
As a pantheist, he holds God to be personal
questions.explanation:
Swami Vivekananda follows Advaita Vedānta. The ultimate Reality (Brahman) is beyond all qualities and limits. So Reality is **indeterminate** (nirguṇa). It is not determinate.

- (1) is consistent. His view is monistic idealism: only one spiritual Reality exists.
- (3) is consistent. We cannot apply any distinction of qualities to the Absolute.
- (4) is consistent with the examiner's view. He accepts a personal God (Īśvara) as the Absolute seen through the human mind.

So "Reality is determinate" is the inconsistent thought.

questions.question_md: Which among the following is incorrect in the light of Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan
options: Man is a combination of egoism and self-transcendence.
The created world is not an illusion
questions.explanation:
Radhakrishnan sees the universe as a **creative process**, not a fixed plan. New forms of life, mind and spirit keep emerging. The world is "not a finished product". So the claim that the universe is a planned activity goes against his view.

- (1) fits. Man has an ego, but he also has a drive to go beyond himself.
- (3) fits. Radhakrishnan rejects the idea that māyā makes the world false. The world depends on the Absolute, but it is not an illusion.
- (4) fits. The world is an ordered, meaningful whole.

questions.question_md: Annihilation of Caste of Ambedkar has a detailed response to:-
questions.explanation:
Ambedkar prepared *Annihilation of Caste* (1936) as a speech for the Jat-Pat-Todak Mandal. The Mandal cancelled the event, so he printed it himself.

**Gandhi** criticised the text in his paper *Harijan*. He defended varṇa as an ideal. Ambedkar then wrote a long **reply to Gandhi**. Later editions of the book include this reply.

So the book contains a detailed response to Gandhi, not to M.N. Roy, Nehru or D.P. Chattopadhyaya.

questions.question_md: The following from Upaniṣad-s encapsulates the entire message of Hindu religion as per Gandhi:-
questions.explanation:
Gandhi said that the **first verse of the Īśa Upaniṣad** sums up all of Hinduism. He said that if all the scriptures were lost and only this verse remained, Hinduism would still live.

The verse begins "Īśāvāsyam idaṁ sarvam" (all this is covered by God). It continues "enjoy through renunciation; do not covet anyone's wealth".

The other passages are famous, but Gandhi did not give them this special place.

questions.question_md: The following is not a feature of Gnostic Being in Sri Aurobindo:-
options: He relentlessly works for materializing the divine life
There are types of Gnostic Beings, such as intuitional, overmental, etc.
He is same as Jīvanmukta of Vedānta
questions.explanation:
For Sri Aurobindo, the **Gnostic Being** is a person who has gone through the **supramental transformation**. Such a being lives and works to bring the divine life into matter. Aurobindo also speaks of grades of gnostic beings, such as intuitive and overmental ones.

So (1), (2) and (3) are features of the Gnostic Being.

Statement (4) is not a feature. The Jīvanmukta of Vedānta is free within, but his body, mind and life stay as they were. He seeks release from the world. The Gnostic Being changes mind, life and body themselves. He does not leave the world.

questions.question_md: The following is not true about Radical Humanism of MN Roy:-
options: It is basically a type of speculative ontology
The ethical norms are this- worldly
To be moral one needs to be only human
questions.explanation:
M.N. Roy's **Radical (New) Humanism** rests on materialism and modern science. Roy rejects speculative metaphysics. So the claim that it is "basically a speculative ontology" is not true.

- (2) is true. Moral norms belong to this world. They do not come from God or the beyond.
- (3) is true. Humans have reason, and reason makes them moral. No religion is needed.
- (4) is true. Roy treats freedom as the highest value. The quest for freedom drives all human progress.

questions.question_md:
Which among the following can be claimed in the context of Neitzche's moral thought

A. The idea of superman is an attempt to restore the ideals of master morality.

B. Master morality asks the man to be empathetic.

C. The values of the master are expressions of the will to power.

D. Master-morality creates its own values.

E. The slave can one day become the master.

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Check each claim about Nietzsche.

- **A can be claimed.** The Übermensch (superman) creates his own values. This revives the spirit of master morality.
- **B cannot be claimed.** Pity and empathy belong to **slave** morality. Master morality values strength and pride.
- **C can be claimed.** The values of the master express the **will to power**.
- **D can be claimed.** The master creates his own values. He calls "good" what he himself is.
- **E cannot be claimed.** Nietzsche does not teach that the slave will one day become the master. The slave's "revolt" only changes values out of resentment.

So A, C and D only.

questions.question_md: Which of the following is incorrectly matched
options: 'Here is a Hand' argument- G.E. Moore
questions.explanation:
**Virtue epistemology** judges knowledge by the intellectual virtues of the knower. **Ernest Sosa** introduced it around 1980. Linda Zagzebski and John Greco developed it. A.J. Ayer was a logical positivist. He did not found virtue epistemology. So (3) is the wrong pair.

- (1) is right. Moore's "Here is one hand" argument answers the sceptic.
- (2) is right. Ryle wrote "Systematically Misleading Expressions" (1932).
- (4) is right. Quine's essay "Epistemology Naturalized" (1969) makes epistemology a part of psychology.

questions.question_md: The idea through which Husserl dispels solipsism is
questions.explanation:
In the fifth *Cartesian Meditation*, Husserl faces the charge of **solipsism**. The charge says that, after the reduction, only my own ego seems to remain.

He answers with the experience of other egos (empathy). The ego knows other egos as other centres of experience. Together they form a community of monads. Husserl calls this **transcendental monadology** (transcendental intersubjectivity).

- **Lebenswelt** (life-world) belongs to his later work, the *Crisis*.
- Phenomenological reduction is the step that **raises** the solipsism problem. It does not solve it.
- "Ego–cogito–cogitata" is the structure of consciousness, not an answer to solipsism.

questions.question_md:
In the context of ‘Phenomenological Reduction’ what can not be claimed

A. The act by which bracketing is made possible is called ‘epoche’

B. According to Husserl, there is only one type of reduction i.e. Phenomenological

C. ‘Epoche’ is going to be a position of the origin of our knowledge

D. ‘Cartesian doubt’ and ‘Epoche’ are essentially same for Husserl.

E. ‘Epoche’ eliminates all elements which make doubt possible.

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
The question asks what **cannot** be claimed.

- **A can be claimed.** The act that brackets the natural attitude is **epoché**.
- **B cannot be claimed.** Husserl speaks of several reductions, for example the eidetic reduction and the transcendental reduction.
- **C can be claimed.** Epoché takes us back to the source of our knowledge, that is, pure consciousness.
- **D cannot be claimed.** Husserl says that epoché is **not** Cartesian doubt. Doubt denies or questions the world. Epoché only suspends our belief in it and does not deny it.
- **E can be claimed.** After epoché, only what is given to consciousness remains. So nothing is left that we could doubt.

So B and D only.

questions.question_md:
Which among the following cannot be claimed in the light of Heidegger's thought

A. Philosophy committed a mistake by dissociating itself from the notion of Being since the time of Plato

B. The real self is ethical, not cognitive.

C. Being must be approached through an investigation into Dasein.

D. Being is God.

E. The world can be bracketed or doubted.

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
The question asks what **cannot** be said about Heidegger.

- **A can be said.** Heidegger says that Western philosophy forgot the question of Being from Plato onwards.
- **B can be said** in the examiner's view. Dasein is first a being that cares and acts. It is not first a knowing subject.
- **C can be said.** *Being and Time* approaches Being through an analysis of **Dasein** (the human being).
- **D cannot be said.** Heidegger does not equate Being with God. God would be one being among beings.
- **E cannot be said.** Dasein is always **being-in-the-world**. So the world cannot be bracketed, as Husserl tries to do.

So D and E only.

questions.question_md: Which is not correct about Sartre:-
options: “Being and nothingness” demolishes the spirit of seriousness
The aim of “Transcendence of Ego” is to respond to the misgivings about Existentialism.
A comrade believing in ‘all is well’ owing to his egalitarian dream is a case of bad faith owing to denial of facticity
questions.explanation:
Sartre wrote *The Transcendence of the Ego* (1936–37) as a study in phenomenology. He argued against Husserl's **transcendental ego**. The ego is an object in the world, not a resident of consciousness. The book does not reply to critics of existentialism. Sartre did that in *Existentialism Is a Humanism* (1946). So statement (2) is not correct.

- (1) is correct. *Being and Nothingness* attacks the "spirit of seriousness". This spirit treats values as fixed facts.
- (3) is correct in the examiner's view. The comrade denies the hard facts of his situation (facticity). This is bad faith.
- (4) is correct. My body is part of my facticity.

questions.question_md: The central conception in Kierkegaard's “Sickness unto Death” is:-
questions.explanation:
Kierkegaard's *The Sickness unto Death* (1849) is a study of **despair**. The "sickness unto death" is despair. It is the failure of the self to be itself before God. The book examines its forms, for example not wanting to be oneself and wanting to be oneself in defiance.

- **Dread** (anxiety) is the theme of another book, *The Concept of Anxiety* (*The Concept of Dread*).
- The three stages (aesthetic, ethical, religious) belong mainly to *Either/Or* and *Stages on Life's Way*.

questions.question_md: Which of the following is incorrect about Wittgenstein's philosophy:-
options: There is no example of object in the text of tractatus
There is no example of name in the text of tractatus
Resolute and Irresolute readings are methods to read “Philosophical Investigation”
“New Wittgenstein” is a book by group of Wittgensteinian scholars
questions.explanation:
The **resolute** and **irresolute** (standard) readings are two ways to read the ***Tractatus***. They are not ways to read the *Philosophical Investigations*.

The resolute reading comes from Cora Diamond and James Conant. It says that the nonsense in the Tractatus is plain nonsense. It does not hint at deep truths that cannot be said. So statement (3) is incorrect.

- (1) and (2) are common points in the literature. The Tractatus speaks of objects and names, but it gives no actual example of either.
- (4) is true. *The New Wittgenstein* (2000) is a collection of essays. Alice Crary and Rupert Read edited it.

questions.question_md: A.J. Ayer's approach regarding ‘non-sensical nature of certain observations’ was shaped by Willgenstein's famous remark at the end of:
questions.explanation:
The **Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus** ends with two famous remarks.

- 6.54: the reader must throw away the ladder after climbing up it. The Tractatus's own sentences are nonsensical.
- 7: "Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent."

The Vienna Circle used this idea. Statements of metaphysics, ethics and religion are not about facts, so they are nonsense. A.J. Ayer took this view into *Language, Truth and Logic*.

The *Investigations*, *On Certainty* and the *Blue Book* come from Wittgenstein's later period. They did not shape Ayer's early positivism.

questions.question_md: Doing anything with language- whether making statements or promising, commanding, asking and so forth are all:
questions.explanation:
J.L. Austin points out that every use of language involves a **locutionary act**. This act is saying something meaningful, with sense and reference. Making a statement, promising, commanding and asking all start with such an act. So the examiner treats "doing anything with language" as a locutionary act.

- The **illocutionary** act is what we do **in** saying something, for example promising or warning. Some students choose it because the examples name such forces. The item is open to debate, but the key takes the general act of saying.
- The **perlocutionary** act is the effect **by** saying something, such as persuading or frightening.
- "Nonsensical act" is not one of Austin's terms.

questions.question_md:
.Which of the following statements can be credited to Ayer's Emotivism?

A. Ethical statements are neither laute logics nor empirically verifiable

B. Ethical statements are unsayable ‘pseudo concepts’.

C. Ethical statements simply evince i.e. indicate approval or disapproval.

D. Ethical statements express feeling, but cannot arouse feeling in others

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
A.J. Ayer gives his emotive theory in *Language, Truth and Logic*, chapter 6.

- **A is Ayer's view.** Ethical statements are neither tautologies nor empirically verifiable.
- **B is Ayer's view.** He calls ethical concepts **pseudo-concepts**. They add no factual content, so they cannot be analysed.
- **C is Ayer's view.** Ethical words only **evince** (show) the speaker's approval or disapproval.
- **D is not Ayer's view.** Ayer says that ethical words also aim to **arouse** feeling in others and to make them act.

So A, B and C only.

questions.question_md:
Put the following analytical philosophers in the correct chronological order:

A. Carnap

B. Quine

C. Ryle

D. Moore

E. Frege

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Use the birth years of these analytic philosophers.

- **E. Frege** — 1848
- **D. Moore** — 1873
- **A. Carnap** — 1891
- **C. Ryle** — 1900
- **B. Quine** — 1908

So the order is E, D, A, C, B. Their main works follow the same order. Examples are Frege's *Begriffsschrift* (1879), Moore's *Principia Ethica* (1903) and Quine's "Two Dogmas" (1951). In the other options, Moore or Quine is in the wrong place.

questions.question_md: Which among the following is incorrect in the context of Tagore's philosophy
options: The reason for creation is joy
Metaphysically, man in many respects is God- like
The ‘Surplus’ in man indicates the finite aspect of man's nature
The infinite nature of man's personality is dynamic
questions.explanation:
Tagore says in *The Religion of Man* that man has a "**surplus**". He has more than he needs for mere survival. This surplus shows itself in art, love and religion. It shows the **infinite** side of man, not the finite side. So statement (3) is incorrect.

- (1) is Tagore's view. God creates out of joy (ānanda).
- (2) is his view. Man's creative personality reflects the divine.
- (4) is his view. The infinite in man is always growing and active.

questions.question_md:
Match the **List-I** with **List-II**

| LIST I | LIST II |
|---|---|
| A. Sādhāraṇa Dharma | I. Telling lie to save the life of an innocent |
| B. Rājadharma | II. The nature of a person should be determined by the proportion of Sattva, Rajas and Tamas guṇa |
| C. Āpaddharma | III. Every person must practice non-violence |
| D. Varṇāśrama Dharma | IV. The behaviour of a king should be guided by moral excellance |

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Indian ethics speaks of several kinds of dharma (duty).

- **A. Sādhāraṇa dharma** — duties common to all people, such as non-violence → **III**.
- **B. Rājadharma** — the duty of the king. His rule should show moral excellence → **IV**.
- **C. Āpaddharma** — duty in an emergency. Rules may relax, for example a lie to save an innocent life → **I**.
- **D. Varṇāśrama dharma** — duty by one's varṇa and stage of life. The Gītā links varṇa with the mix of sattva, rajas and tamas → **II**.

Only option (1) gives A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

questions.question_md:
Match the **List-I** with **List-II**

| LIST I (Article) | LIST II (Subject matter) |
|---|---|
| A. Art. 21A | I. Right to Equality |
| B. Art.14 | II. Right to Life |
| C. Art. 21 | III. Abolition of Untouchability |
| D. Art. 17 | IV. Right to Education |

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
These are articles of the Indian Constitution.

- **A. Article 21A** — right to free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 → **IV**.
- **B. Article 14** — equality before the law → **I**.
- **C. Article 21** — protection of life and personal liberty → **II**.
- **D. Article 17** — abolition of untouchability → **III**.

Only option (2) gives A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.

questions.question_md: Which one among the following is not included as the parts (limbs) of State, according to Kautilya
questions.explanation:
Kauṭilya's *Arthaśāstra* gives the **saptāṅga** (seven limbs) theory of the state:

1. Svāmī — the king
2. Amātya — the ministers
3. **Janapada** — the territory and people
4. **Durga** — the fort
5. **Kośa** — the treasury
6. Daṇḍa — the army or force
7. Mitra — the ally

A written **constitution** (saṁvidhāna) is not one of the seven limbs. It is a modern idea.

questions.question_md:
The correct sequence in Gandhian scheme of social change in the order of succession is

A. Swadeshi

B. Swarājya

C. Sarvodaya

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Gandhi's plan for social change moves from the local to the universal.

- **Swadeshi** comes first. People use local goods and serve their neighbours. This gives economic self-reliance.
- **Swarāj** (self-rule) comes next. It is self-control in the person and self-government in the village and the nation.
- **Sarvodaya** (the welfare of all) is the final goal. It is a society in which all people rise together.

So the order is A, B, C. Swadeshi is the base, so it cannot come after Swarāj or Sarvodaya.

questions.question_md:
According to the Mahābhārata, which of the following four are included in the means to achieve the end of the State

A. Truth (Satya)

B. Reasoning (Upapatti)

C. Expediency (Upāya)

D. Good conduct (Sadācāra)

E. Punishment (Daṇḍa)

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
The official key accepts **truth (satya)**, **reasoning (upapatti)**, **expediency (upāya)** and **good conduct (sadācāra)** as the four means.

The Mahābhārata (Śānti Parva) holds that the state should rest on truth and right conduct. It should also use sound reasoning and suitable methods.

Daṇḍa (punishment) is very important in the Mahābhārata's theory of kingship. But the key does not count it among these four means. This item depends on the examiner's source text, so learn the key's list as it stands.

questions.question_md:
Match the **List-I** with **List-II**

| LIST I (Political Ideology) | LIST II (Nature of the State) |
|---|---|
| A. Liberalism | I. Denial |
| B. Conservatism | II. Common Good |
| C. Socialism | III. Coercion |
| D. Anarchism | IV. Weak paternalism |

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Each ideology has its own view of the state.

- **D. Anarchism** rejects the state completely → **I. Denial**.
- **C. Socialism** wants the state to work for the **common good** of all → **II**.
- **B. Conservatism** values order and authority. The state must use **coercion** to keep order → **III**.
- **A. Liberalism** wants a limited state. It accepts only **weak (soft) paternalism**. The state may step in only to protect people who do not act with full knowledge or freely → **IV**.

Only option (4) gives A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I. The pairs for anarchism and socialism alone are enough to fix this option.

questions.question_md:
Consider the following statements about Judith Butler

A. There is an unchallenged distinction between sex and gender

B. Gender may be seen as a cultural interpretation of sex

C. Gender is not to culture as sex is to nature

D. “Gender Trouble” is one of the masterpiece works by Butler

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Judith Butler questions the usual feminist split between **sex** (biology) and **gender** (culture).

- **A is false.** Butler challenges the sex–gender distinction. She does not accept it without question.
- **B is false for Butler.** "Gender is a cultural reading of sex" is the older view that she criticises. She says that sex itself is already shaped by gender.
- **C is true.** Butler writes that gender is **not** to culture as sex is to nature.
- **D is true.** *Gender Trouble* (1990) is her best-known work. It gives her theory of gender as performative.

So C and D only.

questions.question_md:
Consider the following statements and identify the correct ones:

A. In Hobbes, the contract leads to both society and state

B. In John Locke, there are two contracts - one gives rise to the state, the other to the government

C. In Locke as well as Rousseau, state is an organism.

D. Hobbes belongs to rational natural traditions of political philosophy.

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
- **A is correct.** For Hobbes, one contract creates both civil society and the sovereign state together.
- **B is not correct.** Locke's contract forms civil society. Government comes from a **trust**, not from a second contract. Even books that speak of "two contracts" say the first creates society, not the state.
- **C is not correct.** Locke sees the state as a tool to protect rights, not as an organism. Rousseau's general will is closer to an organic idea, but Locke's view is not.
- **D is not correct.** Michael Oakeshott names three traditions of political philosophy. He places Hobbes in the tradition of **"Will and Artifice"**, not in "Reason and Nature".

So only A is correct.

questions.question_md:
Consider the following statements about Miranda Fricker's conception of Epistemic Injustice

A. The conception could be a way to understand epistemic ideas through the feminist lens.

B. There are two types of epistemic injustice hermeneutic and testimonial

C. In order to ensure epistemic justice, one must be a virtuous hearer

D. The concept of testimony is revisited from a virtue epistemological perspective by Fricker

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
options: A, B, C and D Only
questions.explanation:
Miranda Fricker's *Epistemic Injustice* (2007) supports all four statements.

- **A is true.** Her work comes from feminist philosophy. It studies how social power affects knowing.
- **B is true.** She names two types. **Testimonial** injustice is when prejudice lowers the credibility that a hearer gives to a speaker. **Hermeneutical** injustice is when a group lacks the shared concepts to make sense of its experience.
- **C is true.** To avoid testimonial injustice, the hearer must have the virtue of **testimonial justice**. In short, one must be a virtuous hearer.
- **D is true.** She treats testimony from the point of view of virtue epistemology.

So A, B, C and D.

questions.question_md:
The correct sequence of imperfect societies, as per Plato, in the progression of imperfection is:-

A. Oligarchy

B. Timocracy

C. Tyranny

D. Democracy

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.notes: Dropped in the NTA final answer key.
questions.explanation:
In *Republic* Book VIII, Plato describes how the ideal state (aristocracy) declines step by step:

Aristocracy → **Timocracy** → **Oligarchy** → **Democracy** → **Tyranny**

So the correct order of the four given forms is **B, A, D, C**.

None of the four options gives this order. That is why NTA dropped the question and gave marks to all.

The nearest option is **A, B, D, C**. It only swaps the first two forms, and it puts democracy and tyranny in the right places. The other options put democracy first or timocracy after democracy. So they are further from Plato's order.

questions.question_md: What is not true of a valid argument among the following
options: If its conclusion is false, then all the premises cannot be true together
If all its propositions are true, then it is a sound argument
If any of the premises is true, then its conclusion is necessarily true
It's conclusion necessarily follows from its premises
questions.explanation:
An argument is **valid** when the premises cannot all be true while the conclusion is false.

- **(1) is true.** If the conclusion is false, the premises cannot all be true together.
- **(2) is true.** A valid argument with all true propositions has true premises. So it is **sound**.
- **(4) is true.** In a valid argument, the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises.
- **(3) is not true.** One true premise is not enough. Validity guarantees a true conclusion only when **all** the premises are true.

So statement (3) is the answer.

questions.question_md:
Name the fallacy committed in the following argument:

No poets are accountants

Some artists are poets

Therefore, some artists are accountants
questions.explanation:
Write the argument in standard form.

- Major premise: No poets (M) are accountants (P). This is an **E** proposition (negative).
- Minor premise: Some artists (S) are poets (M). This is an **I** proposition.
- Conclusion: Some artists are accountants. This is an **I** proposition (affirmative).

The rule says: if a premise is negative, the conclusion must be negative. Here the conclusion is affirmative. So the argument breaks a rule about **negative premises**.

Strictly, logicians call this the fallacy of an affirmative conclusion from a negative premise. Exclusive premises means two negative premises. None of the options names the exact fallacy. The key takes "exclusive premises" as the nearest negative-premise fallacy.

- The middle term is distributed in the E premise, and there is no illicit process.
- No universal premise leads to a particular conclusion, so it is not existential.
- There are only three terms.

questions.question_md: What can be correctly said for argument from “some reformers are fanatics, so some idealists are fanatics, because all reformers are idealists”.
questions.explanation:
First find the conclusion. The word "so" marks it: "Some idealists are fanatics".

- Minor term (S) = idealists; major term (P) = fanatics; middle term (M) = reformers.
- Major premise (has P): "Some reformers are fanatics" = **I**.
- Minor premise (has S): "All reformers are idealists" = **A**.
- Conclusion = **I**.

So the mood is **IAI**. The middle term "reformers" is the subject of both premises. So it is in the **third figure**.

IAI-3 is **Disamis**, a valid form. Check the rules: the middle term is distributed in the A premise. No term is distributed in the conclusion. So the argument is valid.

questions.question_md:
Match the **List-I** with **List-II**

| LIST I (Definition) | LIST II (Description) |
|---|---|
| A. Stipulative | I. A definition devised to eliminate ambiguity or vagueness by delineating a concept more sharply |
| B. Lexical | II. A definition that encapsulates an understanding of the theory in which the definiendum term is a key element |
| C. Precising | III. A definition that reports the meaning that the definiendum already has |
| D. Theoretical | IV. A definition in which a new symbol is introduced to which some meaning is arbitrarily assigned |

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
These are the kinds of definition in Copi's logic.

- **A. Stipulative** — gives a new term a meaning by choice → **IV**.
- **B. Lexical** — reports the meaning that a word already has in use → **III**.
- **C. Precising** — removes vagueness or ambiguity and makes a concept sharper → **I**.
- **D. Theoretical** — gives a theory of the thing that the word names, for example "heat" in physics → **II**.

Only option (4) gives A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II.

questions.question_md:
Match the **List-I** with **List-II**

| LIST I (Fallacy) | LIST II (Description) |
|---|---|
| A. Accident | I. When correct reasoning is undermined by the deliberate misrepresentation of the opponent's position |
| B. Equivocation | II. When a shift of meaning arises within an argument as a consequence of changes in the emphasis given to its words or parts. |
| C. The Strawman | III. When one mistakenly applies a generalization to an individual case that it does not properly govern |
| D. Accent | IV. When the same word/phrase is used with two or more meanings in formulating an argument. |

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
These are informal fallacies.

- **A. Accident** — a person applies a general rule to a special case that it does not cover → **III**.
- **B. Equivocation** — one word or phrase has two meanings in the same argument → **IV**.
- **C. Straw man** — a person attacks a false, weaker picture of the opponent's view → **I**.
- **D. Accent** — the meaning shifts because of a change in emphasis on words or parts → **II**.

Only option (3) gives A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

questions.question_md:
Match the **List-I** with **List-II**

| LIST I (Proposition) | LIST II (Example) |
|---|---|
| A. Contrary | I. If ‘E’ is false; ‘O’ is undetermined |
| B. Sub- Contrary | II. If ‘I’ is true; ‘A’ is undetermined |
| C. Sub-Altern | III. If ‘A’ is true; ‘E’ is false |
| D. Super- Altern | IV. If ‘O’ is false; 'I' true |

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Use the traditional square of opposition.

- **A. Contraries** (A and E) cannot both be true. If A is true, E is false → **III**.
- **B. Sub-contraries** (I and O) cannot both be false. If O is false, I is true → **IV**.
- **C. Subaltern** (going from I up to A): if I is true, A is undetermined → **II**.
- **D. Superaltern** (going from E down to O): if E is false, O is undetermined → **I**.

Only option (2) gives A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I.

questions.question_md:
(P ∨ Q) ⊃ (R · S), ~ P ⊃ (T ⊃ ~ T), ~ R

Given the above three are consistent what all is entailed by these:

A. ~ P

B. ~ Q

C. ~ S

D. ~ T

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Work step by step from the premises.

1. ~R is given.
2. If R is false, then R·S is false: ~(R·S).
3. Premise 1 is (P ∨ Q) ⊃ (R·S). By Modus Tollens, ~(P ∨ Q).
4. By De Morgan, ~P · ~Q. So **~P (A)** and **~Q (B)** follow.
5. Premise 2 is ~P ⊃ (T ⊃ ~T). With ~P, we get T ⊃ ~T.
6. T ⊃ ~T is false only when T is true. So **~T (D)** follows.

**~S (C) does not follow.** We only know that R·S is false, and R is already false. So S can be true or false.

So A, B and D only.

questions.question_md:
If a valid argument form is converted into a Statement form, then:-

A. Such a statement form must be a conditional statement

B. Such a statement form is always a tautology

C. The truth value of such statement form is indeterminate

D. In forming such a statement form conjunction must be used

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
A valid argument form becomes a statement form like this: (conjunction of premises) ⊃ conclusion. This is the "corresponding conditional".

- **A is correct.** The result is a conditional statement.
- **B is correct.** The argument is valid. So the conditional can never have true antecedent and false consequent. It is a **tautology**.
- **C is wrong.** A tautology is always true, so its truth value is fixed.
- **D is wrong.** We need conjunction only when there is more than one premise. With one premise, we need no conjunction. So "must" is too strong.

So A and B only.

questions.question_md:
Consider the following statements about Deductive systems

A. The method of 19 rules in Copi's method of deduction is incomplete minus the rule of Absorption.

B. ‘Post Criterion’ is criterion for consistency.

C. If an axiom is derivable as a theorem from some other axioms outside the given axiomatic system, such an axiom is definitely ‘independent’.

D. All logistic systems are types of deductive system.

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
- **A is true.** Copi includes Absorption among his nineteen rules. Without conditional proof, some valid arguments cannot be proved without it. So the list is incomplete without Absorption.
- **B is true.** Post's criterion is a test of consistency. A system is consistent in Post's sense if at least one formula is not a theorem.
- **C is false.** An axiom is **independent** if we cannot derive it from the **other axioms of the same system**. Axioms outside the system have nothing to do with it.
- **D is true.** A logistic system is a formal deductive system. It has exact rules of formation and inference.

So A, B and D only.

questions.question_md: The following is incorrect about Quantification Theory
options: A proposition can be obtained from a propositional function by two processes- Instantiation and Generalization
A singular proposition is a substitution instance of propositional functions
Propositional functions are neither true nor false
questions.explanation:
In quantification theory, the universal and existential quantifiers can be defined by each other:

**(x)(φx) ≡ ~(∃x)~(φx)**

"Everything is φ" means the same as "Nothing is not-φ". So statement (4) says they are **not** equal, and this is incorrect.

- (1) is correct. We get a proposition from a propositional function by instantiation or by generalization (quantification).
- (2) is correct. A singular proposition such as "Socrates is mortal" is a substitution instance of "x is mortal".
- (3) is correct. A propositional function such as "x is mortal" has a free variable. So it is neither true nor false.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following is correct regarding the methods of proving validity in Propositional Logic

A. The Rule of I.P. (Indirect Proof) could be used to prove the validity of argument form

B. Reductio- Ad- Absurdum could be used to prove the inconsistency of premises.

C. The Rule of conditional proof could be used for only such Argument forms whose conclusion is a conditional statement

D. The strengthened Rule of conditional proof permits any assumption of limited scope.

Choose the *correct* answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
All four statements are correct.

- **A is correct.** Indirect proof (I.P.) assumes the denial of the conclusion. Then it derives a contradiction. This proves that the argument is valid.
- **B is correct.** If we can derive a contradiction from the premises alone (reductio ad absurdum), the premises are inconsistent.
- **C is correct.** The basic rule of conditional proof (C.P.) works only when the conclusion is a conditional. We assume its antecedent and derive its consequent.
- **D is correct.** The strengthened rule of C.P. allows any assumption, but only within a limited scope. We must discharge the assumption before the proof ends.

So A, B, C and D.

questions.question_md: Which among the following is not an implication of the statement ~[(P ⊃ Q) ⊃ P]
questions.explanation:
Simplify the statement step by step.

1. ~[(P ⊃ Q) ⊃ P]
2. A conditional is false only when its antecedent is true and its consequent false. So this equals (P ⊃ Q) · ~P.
