groups.md:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the following questions based on the passage:

“ It being an established fact that the object and the subject, that are fit to be the contents of the concepts ‘you’ and ‘we’, and are by nature as contradictory as light and darkness, cannot logically have any identity, it follows that their attribution can have it still less. Accordingly the superimposition of the object, referable through the concept ‘you’, and its attributes on the subject that is conscious by nature and is referable through the concept ‘we’ and contrariwise the superimposition of the subject and its attributes on the object should be impossible. (Ādi Śaṁkarāchārya, Brahmasūtrabhāṣya)

Read the following passage carefully and answer the following questions based on the passage:

**Socrates:** Let us consider the matter in this way: If a person knows the way to Larissa, or anywhere else, and goes there, shall we call him a right and good guide?

**Meno:** Certainly.

**Socrates:** And a person who has a right opinion as to the way, but has never been there, may he not also be a good guide?

**Meno:** Certainly.

**Socrates:** Then true opinion is as good guide to correct action as knowledge. And the man who has true opinion will be just as good a guide as the man who has knowledge.

**Meno:** That appears to be true

**Socrates:** The right opinion is not less useful than knowledge.

**Meno:** That is correct.

**Socrates:** But true opinion so long as they stay, are fine thing and do all sorts of good. But, they are not willing to remain long. They escape from a man’s mind, so they are not of much value until one ties them down by giving an account of reason. This act of tying them down is called “recollection” and when bound, they become knowledge.

**Meno:** I understand.

**Socrates:** Therefore, we must say that knowledge differ from true opinion, not in usefulness but in stability.

**Meno:** That seems to be well put, Socrates.

**Socrates:** Then the person who has knowledge is more stable and reliable than one with mere opinion, even if both may guide correctly.

questions.question_md: The Cārvāka Darśana defines Ātman as :
questions.explanation:
Cārvāka is the materialist school of Indian philosophy. It accepts only perception as a source of knowledge. So it rejects a soul that is separate from the body.

For Cārvāka, the self is **only the body that has consciousness** (*caitanya-viśiṣṭa-deha*). Consciousness appears when the four elements combine in a special way. When the body dies, the self ends too.

The full phrase *caitanya-viśiṣṭa-deha-mātra-eva-ātmā* says this exactly: "the self is nothing but the body qualified by consciousness".

- "Caitanya-ātmā" (the self is consciousness) is closer to Vedānta.
- The other two phrases are incomplete forms. They do not say that the self is *only* the body.

questions.question_md: According to Dharmakīrti, Pratyakṣa means:
options: Apprehending a thing as it appears
Apprehending a thing as it is conceptually constructed
Apprehending a thing as an ābhāsa
questions.explanation:
Dharmakīrti is a Buddhist logician. For him, **pratyakṣa** (perception) is *kalpanāpoḍha* and *abhrānta*. This means it is free from concepts and free from error.

Perception grasps the **svalakṣaṇa**. This is the unique particular, the thing as it is in itself. Names, kinds and other concepts come later, from the mind.

- "As it is conceptually constructed" describes *savikalpa* (conceptual) cognition. Dharmakīrti does not call this perception.
- "As an ābhāsa" means an appearance or a false show. That is pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).
- "As it appears" is too loose. An appearance can be mixed with mental construction.

questions.question_md: ‘Prakriti parināmavāda’ is the theory of causation propounded by
questions.explanation:
**Pariṇāmavāda** is the theory that the effect is a real change (*pariṇāma*) of the cause. Sāṁkhya says that the whole world is a real transformation of **Prakṛti** (primal matter). Prakṛti changes into mahat, ahaṁkāra, the senses and the elements.

This theory rests on *satkāryavāda*: the effect already exists in the cause before it appears.

- Nyāya holds *ārambhavāda* (asatkāryavāda): the effect is a new thing.
- Advaita holds *vivartavāda*: the world is only an appearance of Brahman, not a real change.
- Cārvāka does not build a theory of causation of this kind.

questions.question_md: ‘Athāto Brahma Jijñāsā’ is taken from the primary text called:
questions.explanation:
*Athāto Brahma-jijñāsā* means "Now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman". It is the **first sūtra of the Brahmasūtra** of Bādarāyaṇa.

The Brahmasūtra sums up the teaching of the Upaniṣads in short aphorisms. All Vedānta schools (Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, Madhva and others) wrote commentaries on it.

The Upaniṣads and the Gītā are the two other sources of Vedānta. But this exact sentence opens the Brahmasūtra. The Atharvaveda is a Vedic Saṁhitā and has no link to it.

questions.question_md: The notion of ‘saptabhangi-naya’ is propounded by
questions.explanation:
**Saptabhaṅgī-naya** (the seven-fold predication) is a Jaina doctrine. It belongs to the Jaina theory of *syādvāda*.

Jainism says that reality has many aspects (*anekāntavāda*). So every statement is true only from one point of view. Each statement starts with *syāt* ("in some respect"). The seven forms are: is, is not, is and is not, is indescribable, and three more mixed forms.

Buddhism, Mīmāṁsā and Nyāya do not use this seven-fold scheme.

questions.question_md: 'Ekaṁ Sat viprā bahudhā vadanti' is an extract from
questions.explanation:
*Ekaṁ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti* means "Truth (Being) is one; the wise call it by many names".

This line comes from the **Ṛg Veda** (Book 1, hymn 164, verse 46). The hymn says that the one reality is called Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni and other names.

The line is often used to show the unity behind the many Vedic gods. The Yajur, Sāma and Atharva Vedas are not the source of this line.

questions.question_md: ‘Citta-vritti nirodhaśca yogaḥ’ is the definition of Yoga given in
questions.explanation:
*Yogaś citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ* means "Yoga is the stopping of the changes (*vṛtti*) of the mind (*citta*)". This is the second sūtra of the first chapter of **Patañjali's Yoga Sūtra**.

The Gītā also speaks of yoga, but it defines it in other ways. For example, it says *yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam* (yoga is skill in action). The Pañcadaśī is a later Advaita text by Vidyāraṇya. The Rāmāyaṇa is an epic, not a source of this definition.

questions.question_md: 'Ananta dharmakaṁ vastu’ means:
options: A thing has both finite and infinite properties.
A thing has neither finite nor infinite properties.
questions.explanation:
*Anantadharmakaṁ vastu* is a basic Jaina idea. It means "**a thing has infinite properties**" (*ananta* = infinite, *dharma* = property, *vastu* = thing).

This idea is the basis of *anekāntavāda*, the Jaina view that reality has many sides. An ordinary person knows only some of these properties. So each judgement is partial, and this leads to *syādvāda* and *nayavāda*.

The other options change the meaning of *ananta*. They do not match the Jaina phrase.

questions.question_md: Who among the following philosophers rejected the Platonist view about existence of an evil as substance and endorsed the Neo-Platonist view that evil is unsubstantial?
questions.explanation:
**St. Augustine** first followed the Manichaeans. They said that evil is a real substance or power. Later he accepted the Neo-Platonist view of Plotinus. In this view, **evil is not a substance**. It is a *privation* (lack) of good.

All that God creates is good. Evil is only the absence of a good that should be present, like blindness in an eye.

- Anselm is famous for the ontological argument.
- Aquinas later took the privation view from Augustine. But the question asks who first moved from the substance view to the Neo-Platonist view.
- St. John the Evangelist is a Gospel writer, not a philosopher of evil.

questions.question_md: Who among these philosophers believed that self is nothing but a bundle of impressions?
questions.explanation:
**David Hume** says that when he looks into himself, he never finds a "self". He finds only some particular perception, such as heat, cold, love or pain.

So the self is "nothing but a **bundle or collection of different perceptions**". These perceptions follow one another very fast. This is the *bundle theory* of the self, in Hume's *Treatise of Human Nature*.

- Berkeley accepts a spiritual substance (mind) that perceives ideas.
- Locke bases personal identity on consciousness and memory.
- Leibniz sees the self as a monad, a simple spiritual substance.

questions.question_md: Which among the following statements shall not align with Kant’s thought?
options: Reason forms the basis of our faculties and of things.
The legislation of will is practical reason.
questions.explanation:
Kant limits the power of reason. In the *Critique of Pure Reason*, reason cannot know *things-in-themselves*. Our knowledge comes from the senses and the categories of the understanding together. So Kant would not say that reason is "the basis of our faculties and of things". This statement does **not** fit Kant.

The other statements fit Kant:

- **Will is practical reason.** Kant says that the will is nothing but practical reason. It gives the moral law to itself.
- **Physical laws are inexorable.** In nature, events follow causal laws with necessity.
- **Moral laws do not compel.** The moral law says "ought". A rational being can still disobey it. So the moral law commands but does not force.

questions.question_md: Which among the followings is a correct explanation of monads according to Leibnitz?
questions.explanation:
**Leibniz** says that the world is made of *monads*. Monads are simple substances with no parts. They have perception and appetite, so they are like minds.

Leibniz calls monads **metaphysical points**. They are exact like mathematical points. They are also real like physical points.

- **Mathematical points** are exact but not real. They are only abstractions.
- **Physical points** are real but not exact. Matter can always be divided.

Only a metaphysical point is both real and exact. "Scientific points" is not Leibniz's term.

questions.question_md: According to Democritus’ Atomism, what are the fundamental substances?
questions.explanation:
**Democritus** (with Leucippus) said that reality has two basic parts: **atoms and the void**.

Atoms are tiny, solid bodies that cannot be cut (*atomos* = uncuttable). They differ in shape, size and position. The void is empty space. Atoms move in the void. They join and separate to form all things.

- Fire, water, air and earth are the four roots of Empedocles.
- "Energy particles" is a modern idea.
- "Continuous uniform matter" is the opposite of atomism. Atomism says matter is made of separate units.

questions.question_md: What problem does Aristotle’s ‘Third Man argument’ raise concerning Plato’s theory of form?
options: It demonstrates that Forms are constantly changing.
It shows that Forms are material.
It implies an infinite regress of Forms, making it impossible to explain the relationship between forms and particulars.
It shows that Forms are subjective mental constructs.
questions.explanation:
Plato says that many large things are large because they share in the **Form** of Largeness.

The **Third Man argument** asks a question. The large things and the Form of Largeness are all large. So, by Plato's own rule, there must be a second Form that they all share. Then a third Form is needed, and so on without end.

This is an **infinite regress**. It shows that Plato cannot clearly explain how Forms relate to particular things. Aristotle used this argument against Plato. Plato also discusses a version of it in the *Parmenides*.

The argument does not say that Forms change, are material or are only in the mind.

questions.question_md: According to Parmenides, which of the following does not follow from his claim that “what is, is and what is not, is not”?
options: Being comes into existence and passes away.
questions.explanation:
**Parmenides** says: "What is, is; what is not, is not." Non-being cannot exist and cannot be thought.

From this, several results follow:
- **Change is illusory.** Change means something comes from what is not.
- **Plurality is impossible.** Many things would need empty space (non-being) between them.
- **Non-being is inconceivable.** We cannot think of what is not.

But "**being comes into existence and passes away**" does not follow. It is the opposite. Coming into being needs non-being before it. Passing away needs non-being after it. So Parmenides says that Being is ungenerated and imperishable.

questions.question_md: The prayojana of all acts according to Nyāya school is:
questions.explanation:
In Nyāya, *prayojana* means the purpose that moves a person to act. Every act aims either to **gain pleasure** (*sukha-prāpti*) or to **avoid pain** (*duḥkha-parihāra*).

- *Pravṛtti* and *nivṛtti* are the acts themselves: going towards a thing or turning away from it. They are not the purpose.
- *Rāga* and *dveṣa* (attachment and aversion) are causes inside us. They are faults (*doṣa*), not the goal.
- *Āvaraṇa* and *vikṣepa* (concealing and projecting) are the two powers of *māyā* in Advaita.

questions.question_md: According to the Nyāya school of philosophy, the two ideals open to human beings are:
questions.explanation:
Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika speaks of two ideals for human beings:

- **Abhyudaya**: worldly well-being and prosperity in this life and the next.
- **Niḥśreyasa**: the highest good, that is, liberation (*apavarga*).

The Vaiśeṣika Sūtra defines dharma as that which brings abhyudaya and niḥśreyasa. Nyāya accepts this pair too.

- *Śreyas* and *preyas* (the good and the pleasant) come from the Kaṭha Upaniṣad.
- *Jīvanmukti* and *videhamukti* are two kinds of liberation, mainly discussed in Vedānta.
- Kāma and dharma are two of the four *puruṣārthas*, not this pair of ideals.

questions.question_md: Among the four Puruṣārthas, which one is context free?
questions.explanation:
The four *puruṣārthas* (goals of human life) are dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa.

**Dharma, artha and kāma** depend on context. Right duty changes with a person's caste, stage of life, time and place. Wealth and pleasure also depend on situation and rules.

**Mokṣa** (liberation) is the final goal. It is the same for all people and does not change with situation. It is the end of all bondage. So mokṣa is the **context-free** goal. The other three serve it or are judged by it.

questions.question_md: Deontological theory of moral goodness is associated with:
questions.explanation:
A **deontological** theory judges an act by its duty (*deon* = duty), not by its results.

**Kant** is the main deontologist. An act is morally good when it is done **from duty**, by following the categorical imperative. Results do not decide its moral worth.

- **Aristotle** gives a virtue ethics based on *eudaimonia* (flourishing).
- **Moore** is an ideal utilitarian. Right acts produce the most good.
- **Spinoza** bases ethics on reason and self-preservation, not on duty.

questions.question_md: Which among the following most appropriately defines the idea of eudemonia?
options: Happiness is driven by the spirit of celibacy.
Happiness is driven by the sense of excellence.
Happiness is gained through pleasurable sensation.
Happiness is gained by the avoidance of pleasure.
questions.explanation:
*Eudaimonia* is the Greek word for happiness or human flourishing. For **Aristotle**, it is "activity of the soul in accordance with **virtue** (*aretē*, excellence)".

So happiness is not a feeling of pleasure. It comes from living well and doing one's proper function with excellence over a whole life.

- "Pleasurable sensation" is hedonism, such as the Cyrenaic view.
- "Avoidance of pleasure" and "celibacy" are ascetic ideas. Aristotle accepts that good activity brings fitting pleasure.

questions.question_md: “we must tolerate the view point of the other even if those view points go strongly against our view points; because, in the past, we have made wrong judgements about things/action/events, and there is possibility that the view I hold to be true now may turn out to be wrong later.” With whom is the above argument on toleration associated with?
questions.explanation:
This argument says that we can be wrong. Our past judgements were sometimes false. So the view we now hold may also be false. Therefore we must tolerate other views.

This is an argument from **human fallibility** (the fact that we can make mistakes). It belongs to **John Locke**. In *A Letter Concerning Toleration* and the *Essay*, Locke says that no person or ruler has certain knowledge of the true religion. So force cannot make people believe, and the state must tolerate different faiths.

- Aristotle and Machiavelli did not develop a theory of toleration.
- Kant stresses respect for persons and autonomy, not this argument from past errors.

questions.question_md: Which proofs for the existence of the God did Swami Vivekananda relied upon?
questions.explanation:
**Swami Vivekananda** followed Vedānta. He said that we cannot prove God fully by logic. God must be **directly realised**. Religion is "realisation", that is, a direct experience of the Divine.

So he relied on **intuition** (*anubhūti*, inner experience). He pointed to the experience of saints and yogis as the main proof of God.

- The cosmological, ontological and moral proofs are arguments of reason from Western philosophy.
- Vivekananda thought that these arguments can at most point towards God. They cannot give certainty.

questions.question_md: What is the ultimate objective of Integral Humanism in the philosophy of Deendayal Upadhyaya?
options: The state policy must ensure safety, dignity and freedom of individual over and above everything.
The state policy must ensure balance development of individual with the welfare of the group.
The state policy must ensure primary welfare of the group which structurally includes the individual welfare.
The state policy must ensure the intra-individual development that will ensure stability and growth of various psychological development in an individual.
questions.explanation:
**Deendayal Upadhyaya** proposed **Integral Humanism** (*Ekātma Mānavavāda*). It sees the human being as a whole of body, mind, intellect and soul.

The person is also part of larger wholes: family, society, nation and humanity. These are not in conflict. So state policy must ensure the **balanced development of the individual together with the welfare of the group**.

- The first option puts the individual above everything. That is close to Western individualism, which Upadhyaya rejected.
- The third option puts the group first. That is close to collectivism, which he also rejected.
- The fourth option speaks only of inner psychological growth. It leaves out society.

questions.question_md: Who among the following philosophers emphasized the primacy of ethics?
questions.explanation:
**Emmanuel Levinas** said that **ethics is first philosophy**. For him, ethics comes before ontology (the study of being) and before knowledge.

The face of the Other person makes a demand on me: "Do not kill." My responsibility for the Other comes before any theory. His main works are *Totality and Infinity* and *Otherwise than Being*.

- **Husserl** gave priority to the study of consciousness.
- **Heidegger** gave priority to the question of Being.
- **Merleau-Ponty** gave priority to perception and the lived body.

questions.question_md: Which among the following philosophers preaches theistic existentialism?
questions.explanation:
**Søren Kierkegaard** is called the father of existentialism. He is a **theistic** (religious) existentialist. For him, the individual reaches true selfhood through a "leap of faith" into a personal relation with God. The highest stage of life is the religious stage.

- **Nietzsche** said that "God is dead". He is an atheistic thinker.
- **Sartre** is the leading atheistic existentialist.
- **Levinas** speaks of God through ethics. But he is a phenomenologist, not an existentialist in this sense.

questions.question_md: Things seen in theoretical mode bracketed from their connections and engagements with Dasein’s interest are called
questions.explanation:
In *Being and Time*, **Heidegger** describes two ways in which things show themselves to Dasein (the human being).

- **Ready-to-hand** (*Zuhandenheit*): things in use, like a hammer while we work. We see them through our tasks and interests.
- **Present-at-hand** (*Vorhandenheit*): things seen in a detached, **theoretical** way. We look at them as mere objects with properties. They are cut off from our practical concerns.

The question describes the second mode. So the answer is **present-at-hand**.

- "Being-in-the-world" is the basic structure of Dasein itself, not a mode of things.
- "Being-about-the-world" is not Heidegger's term.

questions.question_md: Which among the followings is true regarding ‘Epoché’?
questions.explanation:
**Epoché** is a method of **Husserl's** phenomenology. It is also called "bracketing".

In the epoché, we **suspend** our natural belief that the world exists outside us. We also suspend our presuppositions about it. We do not deny them or reject them. We only put them aside for a time. Then we can describe pure experience as it appears to consciousness.

- "Rejected" and "prohibited" are too strong. Husserl does not say that our beliefs are false.
- "Accepted" is the opposite of epoché.

questions.question_md: In Russell’s view, definite descriptions are:
questions.explanation:
In "On Denoting" (1905), **Russell** says that a definite description, such as "the present King of France", is **not a name**.

It is an "incomplete symbol". It has no meaning by itself. When we analyse a sentence with it, the description disappears. It becomes a set of **quantified** statements.

"The King of France is bald" makes three claims. There is at least one King of France. There is at most one. Whoever is King of France is bald.

So definite descriptions are **disguised quantifier phrases**. They are not names, referring expressions or indexicals (words like "I", "here", "now").

questions.question_md: W.V.O. Quine’s concept of radical translation most notably implies:
options: That actual translation is always possible due to universal grammar.
That there is no fact of matter about what a speaker means, and thus, no way to choose a single correct translation.
That the accuracy of translation is ensured by the objective nature of meaning.
That translation is possible between languages with a common ancestor.
questions.explanation:
In *Word and Object* (1960), **Quine** imagines **radical translation**. A linguist must translate a totally unknown language. He has only the speaker's behaviour and the situations around it.

Quine's famous example is "Gavagai", said when a rabbit runs by. It could mean "rabbit", "rabbit-part" or "rabbit-stage". All the evidence fits each translation equally.

So Quine draws the thesis of the **indeterminacy of translation**. There is **no fact of the matter** about what the speaker means. Many translation manuals fit all the facts, yet they differ from one another.

- Universal grammar is Chomsky's idea, not Quine's.
- Quine denies that meanings are objective entities.
- A common ancestor language does not solve the problem.

questions.question_md: Why did Moore defend commonsense beliefs in his philosophical writings?
options: Because commonsense beliefs are self-evident truth that we directly experience
Because commonsense beliefs provide practical foundation to our knowledge
questions.explanation:
**G. E. Moore** wrote "A Defence of Common Sense" (1925). He listed beliefs such as "I have a body" and "the earth has existed for many years".

Moore said that he **knows these truths with certainty**. They are more certain than any premise of a sceptical or idealist argument. If a philosophical argument denies them, the argument must be wrong.

So for Moore, common-sense beliefs are **certain, evident truths** that we know directly.

- Moore did not defend them because they are popular or simple.
- He did not defend them only as a practical base. He claimed that they are known to be true.

questions.question_md: According to Gottlob Frege, what is the primary distinction between sense and reference of a term?
options: Sense refers to the object, while reference refers to the way the object is presented.
Sense is subjective meaning, while reference is logical meaning.
Sense is the mode of presentation of an object, while reference is the actual object itself.
Sense and reference are the same.
questions.explanation:
**Frege** separates two parts of meaning:

- **Reference** (*Bedeutung*): the object that a term picks out.
- **Sense** (*Sinn*): the **mode of presentation**, that is, the way in which the object is given.

His example: "the Morning Star" and "the Evening Star". Both refer to the same object, the planet Venus. But their senses differ. So "the Morning Star is the Evening Star" gives new information.

- The first option reverses the two ideas.
- Frege says that sense is objective, not subjective. A private idea is a different thing.
- Sense and reference are clearly not the same.

questions.question_md: Which of the followings is the most appropriate definition of ‘satyāgraha’?
questions.explanation:
**Satyāgraha** is Gandhi's word. It joins *satya* (truth) and *āgraha* (firm holding, insistence).

So satyāgraha means "**holding firmly to truth**" or "truth-force". A satyāgrahī clings to truth and resists injustice by non-violent means. He accepts suffering on himself rather than causing it to others.

- "Experiments with truth" is the title of Gandhi's autobiography. It is not the meaning of satyāgraha.
- "Welcoming" and "abode" do not translate *āgraha*.

questions.question_md: Which of the followings is the most appropriate explanation of the concept ‘sarvodaya’?
options: Upliftment of all, addressing to the least privileged
Food and security for the homeless
Universal brotherhood and oneness of humankind
questions.explanation:
**Sarvodaya** means "the **upliftment (rise) of all**" (*sarva* = all, *udaya* = rise). Gandhi took the idea from Ruskin's *Unto This Last*.

The welfare of all must start with the **last and least privileged** person. Gandhi's "talisman" says: when in doubt, recall the face of the poorest person. Then ask whether your step will help that person. Vinoba Bhave later led the Sarvodaya movement.

- "Social justice for all" and "universal brotherhood" are related ideals. But they miss the special focus on the least privileged.
- "Food and security for the homeless" is too narrow.

questions.question_md: In the second priority rule devised by John Rawls, fair opportunity is lexically prior to -----
questions.explanation:
In *A Theory of Justice*, **Rawls** gives two priority rules.

- **First priority rule**: the priority of **liberty**. The first principle (equal basic liberties) comes before the second principle.
- **Second priority rule**: justice comes before efficiency and welfare. Also, **fair equality of opportunity** comes before the **difference principle**.

"Lexically prior" means that the first must be fully met before we move to the second.

So fair opportunity is lexically prior to the **difference principle**. Liberty is prior to fair opportunity, not after it.

questions.question_md: Who among the following philosophers considers justice as only a ‘remedial’ virtue?
questions.explanation:
A "remedial" virtue is needed only to repair a defect in society.

**Marx** sees justice in this way. Questions of justice arise only in class society, because of scarcity and conflict over property. In a future communist society, there will be plenty and no classes. Then the idea of justice will no longer be needed. People will live by the rule "from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs".

- **Plato** sees justice as the highest virtue of the soul and the state.
- **Rawls** calls justice "the first virtue of social institutions".
- **Locke** bases justice on natural rights to property.

questions.question_md: Which among the statements best explains ‘politics of recognition’?
options: Focus on socioeconomic injustice rooted in the economic structure of the society
Focus on cultural injustice rooted in social patterns of representation
Distribute all the resources equally among all the citizens
questions.explanation:
The **politics of recognition** is linked to Charles Taylor, Axel Honneth and Nancy Fraser.

It focuses on **cultural injustice**. This injustice comes from social patterns of representation, interpretation and communication. Examples are disrespect, cultural domination and non-recognition of a group's identity. The remedy is to recognise and value group differences.

- Socioeconomic injustice in the economic structure is the concern of the **politics of redistribution**. Fraser contrasts the two.
- Equal sharing of resources is also redistribution.
- Recognition does not aim to reduce group differences. It aims to respect them.

questions.question_md: Which among the following list of the moods in the first figure is valid in Aristotelian Syllogism?
questions.explanation:
In Aristotelian syllogism, the **first figure** has the middle term as subject of the major premise and predicate of the minor premise.

Its four valid moods have the names **Barbara, Celarent, Darii and Ferio**. A medieval verse lists them first.

The other lists belong to other figures:
- Cesare, Camestres, Festino, Baroco: **second figure**.
- Darapti, Disamis, Datisi, Felapton: **third figure**.
- Bramantip, Camenes, Dimaris, Fesapo: **fourth figure**.

Note: "Cesere" in option (1) is a misprint for Cesare.

questions.question_md: Which among the following is a proposition in predicate logic?
questions.notes: In the source the variables after f, G and ∃ are printed as subscripts. Options 1 and 4 are printed identically in the source.
questions.explanation:
In predicate logic, a formula is a **proposition** only when it has no **free variable**. Every variable must be bound by a quantifier. Otherwise it is a *propositional function*.

- **(x)(Fx ⊃ Gx)**: both x's are bound by (x). It is a proposition ("All F are G").
- **(∃x)(Fa · Gx)**: "a" is a constant and x is bound. This is also a closed formula, so it is a proposition.
- **(∃x)(Fy · Gx)**: y is free. So this is a propositional function, not a proposition.

The intended answer is **(x)(Fx ⊃ Gx)**, the standard form of a universal proposition.

**Why it was dropped:** options (1) and (4) are printed exactly the same. So two options are correct. Option (2) is also a proposition. The question has more than one correct answer, so all candidates got the marks.

questions.question_md: Which among the followings is true regarding the relation between theory and practice according to Peter Singer?
options: Practices do not stem from theories.
Theories, which are not practiced, are not theories.
Theories and practices are not related.
questions.explanation:
**Peter Singer** wrote *Practical Ethics*. He says that ethics is not an ideal system that is good in theory but useless in practice.

The whole point of an ethical judgement is to **guide practice**. So if a theory cannot work in practice, it has a defect as a theory too. In this sense, "a theory that is not practised is not a (real) theory".

- The other options separate theory from practice. Singer rejects such a split.

questions.question_md: While consent is not obtained from a patient either because he is not asked for or has not decided yet, the type of euthanasia executed is called
questions.explanation:
Euthanasia is divided by the patient's consent.

- **Voluntary**: the patient asks for death.
- **Non-voluntary**: the patient **cannot** give consent. Examples: a person in a coma or a newborn baby.
- **Involuntary**: the patient **could** consent, but is **not asked**, or has not agreed. Peter Singer gives this definition.

Here the patient is able to decide but was not asked or has not decided yet. So it is **involuntary** euthanasia.

- Non-voluntary is the most tempting option. But it applies only when the patient lacks the capacity to choose.
- "Active" refers to the method (a direct act that causes death), not to consent.

questions.question_md:
Identify the correct sequencing that make up ‘sādhana catuṣṭaya’

A. Iha mutrārtha-bhoga-virāgah

B. mumukśutvaṁ

C. Śamadamādi sādhana saṁpat

D. Nityānityā vastu Vivekaḥ

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
**Sādhana-catuṣṭaya** is the four-fold discipline that Śaṅkara requires before the study of Vedānta. The order is:

1. **D. Nityānitya-vastu-viveka**: telling apart the eternal (Brahman) from the non-eternal.
2. **A. Ihāmutrārtha-bhoga-virāga**: giving up desire for enjoyment here and in heaven.
3. **C. Śamadamādi-ṣaṭka-sampat**: the six virtues, such as calm (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*).
4. **B. Mumukṣutva**: an intense desire for liberation.

Each step grows out of the one before it. Discrimination produces detachment. Detachment helps the virtues. These lead to a longing for freedom. So the order is **D, A, C, B**.

questions.question_md:
Identify the correct sequencing of the following tattvas in Sāṁkhya philosophy.

A. Tanmātras, Bhutas

B. Prakriti, Mahat

C. Ahaṁkāra, Manas

D. Sensory organs, Motor organs

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
In **Sāṁkhya**, the world evolves from Prakṛti step by step.

1. **B. Prakṛti → Mahat** (cosmic intellect, buddhi).
2. **C. Ahaṁkāra** (ego) comes from mahat. **Manas** (mind) comes from the sattva side of ahaṁkāra.
3. **D. Sense organs and motor organs** also come from the sattva side of ahaṁkāra, along with manas.
4. **A. Tanmātras** (subtle elements) come from the tamas side of ahaṁkāra. The **bhūtas** (gross elements) come from the tanmātras.

The gross elements are the last products. So the standard order of the 25 tattvas is **B, C, D, A**.

questions.question_md:
Based on Plato’s metaphor of the Divided Line, arrange the stages of knowledge from lower to higher

A. Belief

B. Imagination

C. Intelligence

D. Thinking

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
In the *Republic*, **Plato's Divided Line** shows four stages of the mind, from lowest to highest:

1. **B. Imagination** (*eikasia*): seeing shadows and images.
2. **A. Belief** (*pistis*): opinion about physical things.
3. **D. Thinking** (*dianoia*): mathematical reasoning from assumptions.
4. **C. Intelligence** (*noēsis*): direct grasp of the Forms, up to the Form of the Good.

The first two belong to opinion (*doxa*). The last two belong to knowledge. So the order is **B, A, D, C**.

questions.question_md:
Sequence the following ideas in order of their emergence in the western thought.

A. Mind and body are two attributes human intellect knows

B. God alone is a substance in the real sense of the term

C. No body without movement, No substance without effort

D. Thinking substance alone can be the cause of the ideas

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Each statement belongs to a modern rationalist or idealist thinker.

- **B. Descartes** (1596–1650): only God is a substance in the strict sense, because only God depends on nothing else.
- **A. Spinoza** (1632–1677): God has infinite attributes. The human intellect knows only two: thought (mind) and extension (body).
- **C. Leibniz** (1646–1716): substance is active force. No body is without motion, and no substance is without effort (striving).
- **D. Berkeley** (1685–1753): only a thinking spirit can cause ideas. Matter cannot cause them.

So the historical order is **B, A, C, D**. Berkeley's main works came after Leibniz's early writings on force.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following statements in terms of thoughts and arguments:

A. Hegel’s idea of real is different from what the empiricists call as empirically ‘real’.

B. The idea of absolute spirit manifests in the form of *Geist*.

C. Hegel’s famous slogan is: ‘the real is rational, the rational is real’.

D. His idea of rational, on the other hand, leads to the idea of spirit, i.e. absolute.

E. For Hegel, empiricists would be irrational.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
The statements form one argument about **Hegel**. The logical order is:

1. **C.** Hegel's famous slogan: "the real is rational, and the rational is real".
2. **A.** His idea of the "real" differs from the empirical real of the empiricists.
3. **E.** So, for Hegel, the empiricists' view of the real would be irrational.
4. **D.** His idea of the rational leads to the idea of spirit, the Absolute.
5. **B.** This Absolute Spirit shows itself as *Geist* in history and culture.

The slogan opens the argument. The other statements explain the "real" first and then the "rational". So the order is **C, A, E, D, B**.

questions.question_md:
Identify the correct chronological order of the works cited below:

A. *Pañcatantra*

B. *I am Thou*

C. *Swaraj in Ideas*

D. *Hind Swaraj*

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
The *Pañcatantra* is an ancient Indian book of animal fables. It is many centuries older than the other three works. So it must come first. Only one option starts with A.

The rest follow in the modern period:
- **D. *Hind Swaraj*** by Gandhi was written in 1909.
- **C. *Swaraj in Ideas*** is a lecture by K. C. Bhattacharya. It came after Gandhi's work, in the period of the freedom movement.
- **B. *I am Thou*** is the latest of the four according to the key.

So the order is **A, D, C, B**.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following ideas based on chronology of their emergence

A. Moral first principles as intuitively known

B. Parable of Divided Line

C. Weakness of will

D. Goodwill as duty for the sake of duty

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
The ideas came from these thinkers:

- **B. Divided Line**: Plato, *Republic* (4th century BCE).
- **C. Weakness of will** (*akrasia*): Aristotle discussed it in the *Nicomachean Ethics*, after Plato.
- **D. Good will and duty for the sake of duty**: Kant, *Groundwork* (1785).
- **A. Moral first principles known by intuition**: ethical intuitionism of Moore, Prichard and Ross (early 20th century).

So the order is **B, C, D, A**. Socrates and Plato also discussed akrasia, but Aristotle gave the classic analysis after the Divided Line.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following in terms of hierarchy of aesthetic joy from lower to the higher according to K. C. Bhattacharya

A. Contemplating joy

B. Initial joy associated with an aesthetic object

C. Sympathetic joy

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
**K. C. Bhattacharya**, in "The Concept of Rasa", describes levels of aesthetic feeling. They rise from lower to higher:

1. **B. Primary feeling**: the first joy linked with the aesthetic object itself.
2. **C. Sympathetic feeling**: the viewer feels with the feeling of another, such as a character or the artist.
3. **A. Contemplative feeling**: the viewer enjoys the feeling in a detached, universal way. This is the level of *rasa*.

As the feeling becomes more detached and universal, it rises higher. So the order is **B, C, A**.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following steps as ways to the realization of Saccidānanda in the philosophy of Sri Aurobindo:

A. Negation of Ascetic spiritualism

B. Principles of reconciliation

C. Negation of materialistic denial

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
In *The Life Divine*, **Sri Aurobindo** discusses two errors before he gives his own view.

1. **C. The materialist denial**: matter alone is real, and spirit is denied.
2. **A. The refusal of the ascetic**: spirit alone is real, and the world is denied as illusion.
3. **B. Reconciliation**: Aurobindo joins matter and spirit. Both are real expressions of **Saccidānanda** (Being–Consciousness–Bliss).

The book treats the materialist denial first and then the ascetic refusal. Then it reconciles them. So the order is **C, A, B**.

questions.question_md:
Find out proper progression in Husserl’s phenomenological engagement:

A. Epoché

B. Transcendental Ego

C. Life World

D. Intentionality

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
**Husserl's** phenomenology moves in these steps:

1. **A. Epoché**: we bracket the natural belief in the world.
2. **B. Transcendental Ego**: the bracketing reveals the pure ego as the source of all meaning.
3. **D. Intentionality**: this consciousness is always "consciousness of something". Husserl then studies its structure.
4. **C. Life-world** (*Lebenswelt*): in his late work, *The Crisis of European Sciences* (1936), Husserl turns to the shared world of everyday life.

The life-world is clearly the last stage. Only one complete option puts it last. So the order is **A, B, D, C**. Option (1) lists only three items, so it cannot be right.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following books in terms of their year of publication:

A. *The Concept of Mind*

B. *Language, Truth and Logic*

C. *Philosophical Investigations*

D. *Individuals*

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
The years of publication are:

- **B. *Language, Truth and Logic*** by A. J. Ayer: 1936.
- **A. *The Concept of Mind*** by Gilbert Ryle: 1949.
- **C. *Philosophical Investigations*** by Wittgenstein: 1953, after his death.
- **D. *Individuals*** by P. F. Strawson: 1959.

So the order is **B, A, C, D**. Options that put the *Investigations* before Ryle's book are wrong. Wittgenstein wrote it earlier, but it was published only in 1953.

questions.question_md:
Sequence the order of the following stages for achieving an ideal society in Marxist Philosophy

A. Socialism

B. Capitalism

C. Primitive Communism

D. Feudalism

E. Communism

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
**Marx** describes history as a series of stages. Each stage is based on a mode of production. The order is:

1. **C. Primitive communism**: no private property and no classes.
2. **D. Feudalism**: lords and serfs. (Marx also names a slave society before feudalism, but it is not in this list.)
3. **B. Capitalism**: the bourgeoisie and the proletariat.
4. **A. Socialism**: the workers control the means of production. This is the lower stage of communism.
5. **E. Communism**: a classless, stateless society, the ideal end.

So the order is **C, D, B, A, E**.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following the steps of proving the valid argument: ~(A ⊃ B) / ∴ A in sequence:

A. ~~A · ~B

B. ~(A ⊃ B)

C. A

D. ~(~A v B)

E. ~~A

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
We must prove A from ~(A ⊃ B). The steps are:

1. **B. ~(A ⊃ B)**: the premise.
2. **D. ~(~A v B)**: by Material Implication, A ⊃ B is the same as ~A v B.
3. **A. ~~A · ~B**: by De Morgan's rule, ~(p v q) is ~p · ~q.
4. **E. ~~A**: by Simplification, we take the left part of the conjunction.
5. **C. A**: by Double Negation.

So the order is **B, D, A, E, C**. Every proof starts with the premise and ends with the conclusion. Only one option does both.

questions.question_md:
What is the correct sequence of proving validity of an argument through truth table method?

A. Assignment of truth-value under columns

B. Deciding the numbers of rows

C. Examining the rows where there are Ts under premises and F under conclusion

D. Calculating truth-value of the premises and the conclusion

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
The truth-table test of validity has these steps:

1. **B. Decide the number of rows.** With n simple statements, we need 2ⁿ rows.
2. **A. Assign truth-values** (T and F) under the columns of the simple statements.
3. **D. Calculate the truth-values** of each premise and of the conclusion, row by row.
4. **C. Examine the rows.** Look for a row with T under all premises and F under the conclusion. If there is such a row, the argument is invalid. If there is none, it is valid.

So the order is **B, A, D, C**.

questions.question_md:
Find the correct order in the development of anthropocentric approach in the history of western philosophy:

A. Man tops the pyramid of teleology

B. Man is the measure of everything

C. Man is the end in-itself

D. Man is made in the God’s own image

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
The idea that the human being is at the centre has a history in Western thought.

1. **B. "Man is the measure of all things"**: Protagoras, the Sophist (5th century BCE).
2. **A. Man tops the pyramid of teleology**: Aristotle. In his ordered nature, plants exist for animals and animals for man.
3. **D. Man is made in God's own image**: the Judaeo-Christian view of medieval thinkers such as Augustine and Aquinas.
4. **C. Man is an end in himself**: Kant (18th century).

So the order is **B, A, D, C**.

questions.question_md:
Identify the appropriate combination from the lists given below:

A. The Naiyāyikas assume vyāpti to be universals that are facts of reality.

B. The Naiyāyikas claim that universal relations are logical and not real.

C. The Buddhist logicians regard universal propositions as ideal constructions and not real relations.

D. For the Buddhists the universal is but a name and the identity, a fiction.

E. The Cārvākas accept vyāpti but negate anumāna.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
This question compares Nyāya, Buddhist and Cārvāka views on **vyāpti** (invariable relation, the basis of inference).

- **A is true.** Naiyāyikas are realists. For them, vyāpti rests on real universals (*jāti*) in things.
- **B is false.** Naiyāyikas say these relations are real, not only logical.
- **C is true.** Buddhist logicians say that universal propositions are mental constructions (*kalpanā*), not real relations.
- **D is true.** For Buddhists, the universal is only a name. They explain it by *apoha* (exclusion of others). Identity is a fiction.
- **E is false.** Cārvāka rejects vyāpti, because no one can perceive all cases. So it rejects inference too.

So the answer is **A, C, D**.

questions.question_md:
Prābhākara Mīmāṁsā accepts only the following categories:

A. Substance, quality, action, generality, inherence, force, similarity, number only

B. Quality, action, substance, inherence, force only

C. Number, similarity, force, inherence, generality, action, substance only

D. Action, quality, substance, generality, force only

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
**Prābhākara Mīmāṁsā** accepts **eight** categories (*padārthas*):

1. Substance (*dravya*)
2. Quality (*guṇa*)
3. Action (*karma*)
4. Generality (*sāmānya*)
5. Inherence (*samavāya*)
6. Force or potency (*śakti*)
7. Similarity (*sādṛśya*)
8. Number (*saṁkhyā*)

Only list **A** has all eight. B and D leave out several categories. C has seven items and leaves out **quality**. The question says "only", so an incomplete list is wrong. So the answer is **A only**.

questions.question_md:
Which among the following statements follow from the fact that extension constitutes the essence of body?

A. Extension has limit

B. There is no empty space, nor bodies without atoms

C. The corporeal world is illimitable

D. The body has no centre

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
This is **Descartes'** view. For him, the essence of body is **extension** (length, breadth and depth). Several results follow:

- **B is true.** Wherever there is extension, there is body. So there is **no empty space** (vacuum). Extension can always be divided, so there are no indivisible atoms. The wording of B is odd, but it states this Cartesian point.
- **C is true.** We cannot think of a limit to extension. So the corporeal world is **indefinitely extended**.
- **D is true.** An unlimited world has **no centre**.
- **A is false.** Saying that extension has a limit goes against C.

So the answer is **B, C and D**.

questions.question_md:
Read the following statements about St. Thomas Aquinas and choose the correct statements:

A. One of the many objectives of St. Thomas Aquinas, philosophy is to negotiate Averroist reading of Aristotle with the Christian reading

B. To prove the existence of the God was another objective

C. The ideas of essence and existence are the same

D. If we know God’s essence, we come to know His existence

E. Aquinas also propagated the idea of evil, which is an essence and intentional in nature

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
**St. Thomas Aquinas**:

- **A is not accepted.** Aquinas did not try to blend the Averroist reading with Christianity. He argued **against** the Latin Averroists, for example on the unity of the intellect.
- **B is true.** He gave the "Five Ways" to prove the existence of God.
- **C is true for God.** In God, essence and existence are the same. God is pure existence (*ipsum esse*).
- **D is true.** Since God's essence is His existence, anyone who knew God's essence would know that He exists. We do not know God's essence, so we prove God from His effects.
- **E is false.** Aquinas, like Augustine, says that evil is a **privation** of good. It has no essence.

So the answer is **B, C, D**.

questions.question_md:
Identify the correct combination of ontological positioning of śreyas and preyas with reference to Kaṭhopaniṣad:

A. Preyas over śreyas

B. Neither preyas nor śreyas

C. Equipositioning of śreyas and preyas

D. Supremacy of śreyas over preyas

E. Inferiority of preyas to śreyas

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
In the **Kaṭha Upaniṣad**, Yama tells Naciketas that two paths come before a person:

- **Śreyas**: the good, which leads to liberation.
- **Preyas**: the pleasant, which leads to worldly enjoyment.

The wise person chooses śreyas. The foolish person chooses preyas. So śreyas is **supreme** (D), and preyas is **inferior** (E).

- A puts preyas above śreyas, which is the reverse.
- B and C deny any ranking. The Upaniṣad clearly ranks them.

So the answer is **D, E**.

questions.question_md:
According to Ādi Śankara, if all that exists is Braman and the world of plurality is mithyā, then there cannot be any real distinction between good and evil. Based on this, choose the correct combination from below :

A. Because a confusion exists between reality and existence, the eternal and the temporal

B. Because a confusion that essentially imperfect and incomplete series of temporal events is the same as the true timeless Brahman

C. The metaphysical truth of oneness of Brahman does not violate the validity of ethical distinctions

D. If life is unreal, then moral distinctions are not valid

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
The question states an objection to Śaṅkara. If only Brahman is real and the world is *mithyā* (false appearance), then good and evil seem to have no real difference.

- **D** states this objection: if life is unreal, moral distinctions are not valid.
- **A** shows the error in it. The objection confuses **reality with existence**, and the **eternal with the temporal**. The world is not ultimately real, but it exists at the empirical level.
- **C** gives the result. The oneness of Brahman does not cancel ethical distinctions. They stay valid in the empirical world (*vyavahāra*), where we live and act.
- **B** is not part of the answer. Śaṅkara never says that the imperfect series of temporal events is the same as the timeless Brahman.

So the key takes **A, D, C**. This follows S. Radhakrishnan's defence of Śaṅkara's ethics.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements are true of Kant?

A. Good will, according to Kant, is guided by the conditions on which man is posited

B. Good Will’s only motive is to do duty for the sake of doing its duty

C. The test of a genuine moral imperative is that I can universalize it, that I can will for a universal law

D. However, Kant also recognizes aberrations to good will, what he called the ‘weakness of will’

E. Therefore, according to Kant, hypothetical imperative is categorical imperative

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
**Kant's** ethics:

- **A is false.** The good will is good in itself, without conditions. It does not depend on a person's situation.
- **B is true.** The good will acts **from duty, for the sake of duty**.
- **C is true.** The test of a moral rule is the categorical imperative. I must be able to **will my maxim as a universal law**.
- **D is false.** "Weakness of will" (*akrasia*) is a theme of Aristotle, not a central idea of Kant.
- **E is false.** Kant clearly separates hypothetical imperatives ("if you want X, do Y") from the categorical imperative.

So the answer is **B, C**.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements are true of Rabindranath Tagore?

A. Rabindranath Tagore is often described as a mystic

B. His mysticism is well amalgamated with his nationalist ethos

C. He accepted two aspects of the self - the physical and the spiritual

D. According to Tagore, man’s individual peculiarities are the aspects of his finite self and his universal nature is the infinite aspect of his personality

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
**Rabindranath Tagore**:

- **A is true.** Tagore is often called a mystic poet and thinker. His *Gitanjali* expresses a deep, personal union with the Divine.
- **B is false.** Tagore strongly criticised **nationalism**, in his book *Nationalism* (1917). His mysticism was universal, not tied to a nationalist ethos.
- **C is true.** In *The Religion of Man*, he describes two sides of the self: the physical (finite) and the spiritual (infinite).
- **D is true.** Individual peculiarities belong to the finite self. Man's universal nature is the infinite side of his personality.

So the answer is **A, C, D**.

questions.question_md:
Read the following statements carefully:

A. In the ‘Parable of the Cave’, Plato highlights the necessity of the human life to be guided by the idea of transcendental knowledge

B. Aristotle critiques Plato for his inability to account for the diversity of uses of good

C. For Aristotle, therefore, there is no distinction between different types of actions, whether guided by reason, will, or weakness of will

D. On the other hand, for Epicurus, virtue is simply the art of pleasure

E. However, Stoics ultimately aim at withdrawal from public life and leading towards ethical solipsism

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
These statements are about Greek ethics:

- **A is true.** In the Cave, Plato shows that life must be guided by knowledge of the Good, which lies beyond the senses.
- **B is true.** In the *Nicomachean Ethics*, Aristotle criticises Plato's single Form of the Good. "Good" is said in many ways, in many categories.
- **C is false.** Aristotle clearly separates kinds of action, such as voluntary and involuntary acts, choice, and *akrasia* (weakness of will).
- **D is true.** For Epicurus, virtue is the means and art of living pleasantly.
- **E is false.** The Stoics did not aim at withdrawal or "ethical solipsism". They taught duty to the world community (cosmopolitanism). Many Stoics, like Seneca and Marcus Aurelius, served in public life.

So the answer is **A, B, D**.

questions.question_md:
Which among the following statements are true of J.S. Mill?

A. J.S. Mill abandons the view that the comparison among pleasures is or can be purely quantitative.

B. He , however, makes no distinction between higher and lower pleasures.

C. Therefore, all pleasures are qualitatively same.

D. Ultimate objective of Mill was to bring all the objects and goals of human desires under a single concept, of pleasure.

E. He treats pleasure as a unitary concept.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
**J. S. Mill**, in *Utilitarianism*:

- **A is true.** Mill rejects Bentham's purely quantitative comparison of pleasures. He adds **quality**.
- **B is false.** Mill clearly separates **higher** (intellectual) and **lower** (bodily) pleasures. "Better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied."
- **C is false.** It follows from B, which is false. Pleasures differ in quality.
- **D is true.** Mill tries to show that all things people desire, such as virtue or money, are desired as parts of happiness (pleasure).
- **E is true.** So pleasure, or happiness, is the single, unifying concept of his ethics.

So the answer is **A, D, E**.

questions.question_md:
Choose the correct combination of the statements from those given below:

A. M.K. Gandhi was deeply influenced by Tolstoy’s *The Kingdom of God is within You* as new interpretation of Christianity.

B. Gandhi’s religious orientation was deeply influenced by Vaiṣṇava ethos.

C. When Gandhi explains the notion ‘God is Truth’, his idea of truth is oriented towards the truth of the mundane reality.

D. According to Gandhi, ahimsā and truth are intertwined, and are like two sides of a coin.

E. Gandhi derived the idea of ahimsā from the traditional worldview of Mīmāṁsā.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
**Gandhi**:

- **A is true.** Tolstoy's *The Kingdom of God Is Within You* deeply influenced him. Gandhi said so in his autobiography.
- **B is true.** He grew up in a Vaiṣṇava family in Gujarat. Its devotion and non-violence shaped him.
- **C is false.** In "Truth is God", Truth means the absolute, eternal **Sat**. It is not mundane, worldly truth.
- **D is true.** Gandhi said that ahiṁsā and truth are so linked that they are like two sides of a coin.
- **E is false.** Gandhi drew ahiṁsā from Jainism, the Gītā, Vaiṣṇavism and the Sermon on the Mount. Mīmāṁsā even allows killing in Vedic sacrifice.

So the answer is **A, B, D**.

questions.question_md:
Which among the followings are true about existentialism?

A. It theorizes the nature of pure ego.

B. It prioritizes existence over essence.

C. It rejects the possibility of freedom in human life.

D. It revolts against speculative philosophy.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
**Existentialism**:

- **A is false.** The study of the pure (transcendental) ego belongs to Husserl's phenomenology, not to existentialism.
- **B is true.** Sartre's slogan is "**existence precedes essence**". A person first exists and then makes himself.
- **C is false.** Existentialism stresses **freedom**. Sartre says that man is "condemned to be free".
- **D is true.** Kierkegaard and others revolted against abstract, speculative systems, such as Hegel's. They focused on the concrete individual.

So the answer is **B, D**.

questions.question_md:
Who among the following have refuted idealism?

A. Russell

B. Berkeley

C. G. E. Moore

D. H.P. Grice

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
At the start of the 20th century, British philosophy turned against the idealism of Bradley and others.

- **G. E. Moore** wrote "**The Refutation of Idealism**" (1903). He argued that the object of awareness is different from the act of awareness.
- **Bertrand Russell** joined Moore. He rejected idealism and developed realism and logical analysis.
- **Berkeley** is himself an idealist ("to be is to be perceived").
- **H. P. Grice** worked on meaning and conversation. He is not known for refuting idealism.

So the answer is **A, C** (Russell and Moore).

questions.question_md:
Which of the following combinations constitute the principle of Nītisāra of Kamandaki?

A. Theories of social order

B. Structure of the state

C. Inter-state relationship

D. Detailed internal administration

E. Criminal law

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Kāmandaka's **Nītisāra** is a work on statecraft, based on Kauṭilya's *Arthaśāstra*. Its main themes are:

- **A. Social order**: the duties of the varṇas and āśramas.
- **B. Structure of the state**: the seven limbs (*saptāṅga*), such as king, minister, territory and army.
- **C. Inter-state relations**: the *maṇḍala* (circle of states) and the six policies of foreign relations.

The *Nītisāra* gives little space to the detailed internal administration and criminal law of the *Arthaśāstra*. So the key gives **A, B, C**.

questions.question_md:
Which among the following are the four purposes of Daṇḍanīti?

A. Acquisition of the unacquired

B. preservation of the acquired

C. Augmentation of the preserved

D. Distribution of the augmented

E. Taxation on the distributed

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Kauṭilya's *Arthaśāstra* gives the four aims of **daṇḍanīti** (the science of government):

1. **A.** To acquire what is not yet acquired (*alabdha-lābha*).
2. **B.** To preserve what is acquired (*labdha-parirakṣaṇa*).
3. **C.** To increase what is preserved (*rakṣita-vivardhana*).
4. **D.** To distribute what is increased to worthy recipients (*vṛddhasya tīrtheṣu pratipādana*).

**E. Taxation** is not one of the four aims. So the answer is **A, B, C, D**.

questions.question_md:
Which among the following statements are true about social contract theory?

A. The state of nature was gloomy, nasty and dark

B. The state existed before the state of nature

C. The state is the result of a hypothetical agreement

D. The state was created by God

E. There was no rights in the state of nature

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
**Social contract** theory (Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau):

- **A is true** (mainly for Hobbes). In the state of nature, life is "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short".
- **B is false.** The state of nature comes **before** the state.
- **C is true.** The state comes from an agreement (contract) among people. Many thinkers treat it as a hypothetical agreement.
- **D is false.** The divine-right theory says God created the state. Contract theory rejects it.
- **E is false.** Locke says that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property in the state of nature. Hobbes also speaks of a "right of nature".

So the answer is **A, C**.

questions.question_md:
Which among the following activities best characterizes the ‘ethics of care’ according to Carol Gilligan?

A. Learning moral principles

B. Developing moral dispositions

C. Solving moral problems by application of universal principles

D. Seeking contextual responses

E. Attending to responsibilities and relationships

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
**Carol Gilligan** wrote *In a Different Voice* (1982). She contrasts the **ethics of care** with the **ethics of justice**.

- **A and C are false.** Learning abstract principles and applying **universal rules** describe the justice approach of Kohlberg.
- **B is true.** Care ethics stresses moral dispositions, such as empathy and attentiveness.
- **D is true.** It seeks responses that fit the **context** of each case.
- **E is true.** It attends to **responsibilities and relationships** with concrete persons.

So the answer is **B, D, E**.

questions.question_md:
Which among the following propositions are tautologies?

A. ~(A ≡ ~A)

B. A ≡ (B v A)

C. A ⊃ (A v B)

D. (B ⊃ A) ⊃ (A ⊃ B)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
A **tautology** is true in every row of its truth table. Test each formula.

- **A. ~(A ≡ ~A)**: A and ~A always have opposite values. So A ≡ ~A is always false. Its negation is always true. **Tautology.**
- **B. A ≡ (B v A)**: let A be false and B be true. Then B v A is true, so F ≡ T is false. **Not a tautology.**
- **C. A ⊃ (A v B)**: if A is true, then A v B is also true. So it can never be T ⊃ F. **Tautology.**
- **D. (B ⊃ A) ⊃ (A ⊃ B)**: let A be true and B be false. Then B ⊃ A is true and A ⊃ B is false. So the whole is T ⊃ F, which is false. **Not a tautology.**

So the answer is **A, C**.

questions.question_md:
Which are the restrictions of the rule of Universal Generalisation(UG)?

A. There are no restriction on UG.

B. An UG must not be done to an individual constant.

C. An UG cannot be done to a variable under an assumption.

D. An UG must not be done on a quasi variable in a line that is justified by Existential Instantiation ( EI ).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
**Universal Generalisation** (UG) lets us move from Φy to (x)Φx. It is valid only when y stands for "any individual". So it has restrictions (as in Copi's system):

- **A is false.** UG does have restrictions.
- **B is true.** We cannot generalise from an **individual constant**, such as "a". From "Socrates is mortal" we cannot infer "everything is mortal".
- **C is true.** We cannot use UG on a variable that is free in an **undischarged assumption** (inside a conditional or indirect proof).
- **D is true.** We cannot use UG on a variable that was brought in by **Existential Instantiation** (EI). That variable names one particular thing, not any thing.

So the answer is **B, C, D**.

questions.question_md:
Which among the followings are true in regard to the relationship between law and morality?

A. Moral principles are dependent on legal principles.

B. Moral principles are independent of legal principles.

C. Legal principles are necessarily moral principles.

D. Moral principles with legal sanctions turns to be legal principles.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Law and morality are related, but they are not the same.

- **A is false.** Morality does not depend on law. Many moral duties, like gratitude, have no law behind them.
- **B is true.** Moral principles are **independent** of legal principles. We can even judge a law as immoral.
- **C is false.** Not every law is a moral rule. For example, a traffic rule about driving on the left is a convention. Some laws can even be unjust.
- **D is true.** When the state adds a legal sanction (penalty) to a moral principle, it becomes a **law**. "Do not murder" is an example.

So the answer is **B, D**.

questions.question_md:
Match the **LIST-I** with **LIST-II**

| LIST-I | LIST-II |
|---|---|
| A. Yuṣmad-Aṣmad-pratyaya-gocara | I. Nyāyasūtra, Gotama |
| B. Samyagjñana-pūrvikā-puruṣārtham-siddhiriti-tad-vyutpādhyate | II. Vedāntaparibhāṣā, Dharmarāja Adhvarīn |
| C. Brahma-bhinnaṁ-sarvaṁ-mithyā | III. Nyāyabindu, Dharmakīrti |
| D. Indriyārtham sannikarṣaṁ jñānaṁ pratyakṣaṁ | IV. Brahma-sūtra-Śāṁkara-Bhāṣyaṁ |

Choose the ***correct*** answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Each line is the opening or a famous definition from a classical text.

- **A – IV.** *Yuṣmad-asmat-pratyaya-gocara* ("the object of 'you' and 'we'") opens **Śaṅkara's commentary on the Brahmasūtra** (the *adhyāsa-bhāṣya*).
- **B – III.** "All human goals are reached through right knowledge, so it is explained" opens **Dharmakīrti's *Nyāyabindu***.
- **C – II.** "All that is different from Brahman is false" is a line of **Dharmarāja Adhvarin's *Vedāntaparibhāṣā***.
- **D – I.** "Cognition from the contact of sense and object is perception" is the definition of perception in **Gotama's *Nyāyasūtra*** (1.1.4).

So the match is **A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I**.

questions.question_md:
Match the **LIST-I** with **LIST-II**

| LIST-I | LIST-II |
|---|---|
| A. Parmenides | I. Nous |
| B. Anaximander | II. Logos |
| C. Heraclitus | III. Being |
| D. Anaxagoras | IV. Apeiron |

Choose the ***correct*** answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Each early Greek thinker has a key concept:

- **A – III. Parmenides: Being.** Only Being is; non-being is not.
- **B – IV. Anaximander: Apeiron.** The "boundless" or unlimited is the source of all things.
- **C – II. Heraclitus: Logos.** The rational law or order behind constant change.
- **D – I. Anaxagoras: Nous.** Mind starts and orders the motion of the world.

So the match is **A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I**.

questions.question_md:
Match the **LIST-I** with **LIST-II**

| LIST-I | LIST-II |
|---|---|
| A. Conscience is our own opinion, of our own actions | I. Berkeley |
| B. All we see, hear and feel is but a phantom | II. Locke |
| C. Religions are anything but sick men’s dream | III. Kant |
| D. If there is no God, we should have to invent one | IV. Hume |

Choose the ***correct*** answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
- **A – II. Locke.** In the *Essay*, Locke says that conscience is "nothing else but our own opinion or judgement" of our own actions.
- **B – I. Berkeley.** Berkeley denies matter outside the mind. So, to a critic, all we see, hear and feel seems only a "phantom" of ideas. Berkeley discusses this charge in his *Dialogues*.
- **C – IV. Hume.** In *The Natural History of Religion*, Hume says that popular religions seem to be nothing but "sick men's dreams".
- **D – III. Kant.** The famous line "If God did not exist, we would have to invent him" is really Voltaire's. The examiner links it to Kant. For Kant, we cannot prove God by theory, but practical reason must postulate God for morality.

So the match is **A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III**.

questions.question_md:
Match the **LIST-I** with **LIST-II**

| LIST-I | LIST-II |
|---|---|
| A. Ethical Egoism | I. Auguste Comte |
| B. Altruism | II. Immanuel Kant |
| C. Ethical universalism | III. R. M. Hare |
| D. Non-cognitivism | IV. Henry Sidgwick |

Choose the ***correct*** answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
- **A – IV. Ethical egoism: Henry Sidgwick.** In *The Methods of Ethics*, Sidgwick studies egoism as one of three main methods. He gives its classic analysis.
- **B – I. Altruism: Auguste Comte.** Comte coined the word "altruism" (living for others).
- **C – II. Ethical universalism: Kant.** The categorical imperative asks us to act on maxims that we can will as universal laws.
- **D – III. Non-cognitivism: R. M. Hare.** Hare's prescriptivism says that moral judgements are prescriptions, not statements of fact.

So the match is **A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III**.

questions.question_md:
Match the **LIST-I** with **LIST-II**

| LIST-I | LIST-II |
|---|---|
| A. Deterrent Theory of Punishment | I. To maintain social order and ensure absence of crime in the society |
| B. Retributive Theory of Punishment | II. To stop others from committing similar crimes |
| C. Reformative Theory of Punishment | III. To return the same quantum of harm inflicted by the convict |
| D. Preventive Theory of Punishment | IV. To improve the mindset of the convict and ensure rightful thinking |

Choose the ***correct*** answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Theories of punishment differ by their purpose.

- **A – II. Deterrent:** to **stop others** from doing similar crimes, by making an example of the offender.
- **B – III. Retributive:** to give the offender **the same amount of harm** that he caused ("an eye for an eye").
- **C – IV. Reformative:** to **improve the mind** of the offender, so that he thinks rightly.
- **D – I. Preventive:** to keep **social order** and stop crime, for example by keeping the offender away from society.

So the match is **A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I**.

questions.question_md:
Match the **LIST-I** with **LIST-II**

| LIST-I | LIST-II |
|---|---|
| A. *Savitri* | I. Sir Mohammad Iqbal |
| B. *Assar-e-Khudi* | II. M. N. Roy |
| C. *Science and Philosophy* | III. B. R. Ambedkar |
| D. *Riddles in Hinduism* | IV. Śri Aurobindo |

Choose the ***correct*** answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
- **A – IV.** *Savitri* is a long epic poem by **Sri Aurobindo**.
- **B – I.** *Asrar-e-Khudi* (Secrets of the Self) is a Persian poem by **Muhammad Iqbal**. It develops his idea of *khudi* (selfhood).
- **C – II.** *Science and Philosophy* is a book by **M. N. Roy**, the radical humanist.
- **D – III.** *Riddles in Hinduism* is a critical work by **B. R. Ambedkar**.

So the match is **A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III**.

questions.question_md:
Match the **LIST-I** with **LIST-II**

| LIST-I | LIST-II |
|---|---|
| A. Satyasodhak Samāj | I. Santh Kabi Bhima Bhoi |
| B. Vaikom Satyāgraha | II. Jyotiba Phule |
| C. Mahima Dharma | III. Swami Dayananda Saraswati |
| D. Traitavāda | IV. Narayana Guru |

Choose the ***correct*** answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
- **A – II. Satyashodhak Samāj:** founded by **Jyotiba Phule** in 1873. It fought caste and Brahmin dominance.
- **B – IV. Vaikom Satyāgraha** (1924–25): a struggle for the right of lower castes to use temple roads in Kerala. **Narayana Guru** supported it, and his followers took part.
- **C – I. Mahima Dharma:** a reform faith in Odisha. The poet-saint **Bhima Bhoi** spread it.
- **D – III. Traitavāda:** the theory of three eternal realities (God, soul and Prakṛti). **Swami Dayananda Saraswati** taught it.

So the match is **A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III**.

questions.question_md:
Match the **LIST-I** with **LIST-II**

| LIST-I | LIST-II |
|---|---|
| A. Gilbert Ryle | I. Definite Description |
| B. Bertrand Russell | II. Dogma of Empiricism |
| C. W. V. O. Quine | III. Descriptive Metaphysics |
| D. P.F. Strawson | IV. Ghost in the machine |

Choose the ***correct*** answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
- **A – IV. Gilbert Ryle: "ghost in the machine".** In *The Concept of Mind*, Ryle uses this phrase to mock Descartes' mind–body dualism.
- **B – I. Bertrand Russell: theory of definite descriptions** ("On Denoting", 1905).
- **C – II. W. V. O. Quine: "Two Dogmas of Empiricism"** (1951). The two dogmas are the analytic–synthetic distinction and reductionism.
- **D – III. P. F. Strawson: descriptive metaphysics.** In *Individuals*, he describes the actual structure of our thought about the world.

So the match is **A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III**.

questions.question_md:
Match the **LIST-I** with **LIST-II**

|---|---|
| A. *Being and Time* | I. Franz Brentano |
| B. *Being and Nothingness* | II. Martin Heidegger |
| C. *Otherwise than Being* | III. Jean-Paul Sartre |
| D. *On the Several Senses of Being in Aristotle* | IV. Immanuel Levinas |

Choose the ***correct*** answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
- **A – II.** *Being and Time* (1927) is by **Martin Heidegger**.
- **B – III.** *Being and Nothingness* (1943) is by **Jean-Paul Sartre**.
- **C – IV.** *Otherwise than Being or Beyond Essence* (1974) is by **Emmanuel Levinas**.
- **D – I.** *On the Several Senses of Being in Aristotle* (1862) is **Franz Brentano's** dissertation. It inspired Heidegger's interest in the question of Being.

So the match is **A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I**.

questions.question_md:
Match the **LIST-I** with **LIST-II**

| A. *Saam* | I. Gift |
| B. *Daam* | II. Division |
| C. *Daṇḍa* | III. Persuasion |
| D. *Bheda* | IV. Force |

Choose the ***correct*** answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
These are the four classic means (*upāyas*) of statecraft in Indian political thought:

- **A – III. Sāma:** persuasion or conciliation by friendly talk.
- **B – I. Dāna (Daam):** gifts or bribes.
- **C – IV. Daṇḍa:** force or punishment.
- **D – II. Bheda:** division, that is, creating splits in the enemy's side.

questions.question_md:
Match the **LIST-I** with **LIST-II**

| LIST-I | LIST-II |
|---|---|
| A. Justice as shaped by free market | I. Multiculturalism |
| B. Justice as to affirm group identity | II. Communitarianism |
| C. Justice as entitlement | III. Liberalism |
| D. Justice as shared understanding | IV. Libertarianism |

Choose the ***correct*** answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
- **A – IV. Libertarianism.** Justice is what results from free exchange in the market. The state must not redistribute.
- **B – I. Multiculturalism.** Justice requires recognising and affirming the identity of cultural groups.
- **C – III. Liberalism.** Liberal justice gives each person rights and fair **entitlements**, set by just institutions.
- **D – II. Communitarianism.** Michael Walzer says that justice depends on the **shared understandings** of a community.

So the key gives **A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-II**.

Note: Nozick calls his libertarian view an "entitlement theory". So C could also suggest libertarianism. But A fits libertarianism most clearly. Only this option matches B and D correctly.

questions.question_md:
Match the **LIST-I** with **LIST-II**

| B. *The Idea of Justice* | II. John Rawls |
| C. *Liberalism and the Limits of Justice* | III. Amartya Sen |
| D. *Anarchy State and Utopia* | IV. Michael Sandel |

Choose the ***correct*** answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
- **A – II.** *A Theory of Justice* (1971) is by **John Rawls**.
- **B – III.** *The Idea of Justice* (2009) is by **Amartya Sen**.
- **C – IV.** *Liberalism and the Limits of Justice* (1982) is by **Michael Sandel**. It is a communitarian critique of Rawls.
