The trap: many students think ~(Q · R) gives ~Q. But a conjunction is false when only one conjunct is false. Here R is false, so nothing follows about Q.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following valid moods according to their figures, from the first figure to the fourth figure :

A. Felapton

B. Camestres

C. Fresison

D. Celarent

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
The traditional mnemonic verses group the valid moods by figure.

- First figure: Barbara, **Celarent**, Darii, Ferio. So D comes first.
- Second figure: Cesare, **Camestres**, Festino, Baroco. So B is second.
- Third figure: Darapti, Disamis, Datisi, **Felapton**, Bocardo, Ferison. So A is third.
- Fourth figure: Bramantip, Camenes, Dimaris, Fesapo, **Fresison**. So C is fourth.

The order is D, B, A, C. The tempting option "D, B, C, A" swaps Felapton and Fresison. Felapton is third figure, while its look-alike Fesapo is fourth figure.

questions.question_md: In the traditional square of opposition, if the proposition "Some poets are critics" is given as false, then which one of the following is correct ?
options: A is false; E is true; O is undetermined
A is false; E is true; O is true
A is undetermined; E is true; O is true
A is false; E is undetermined; O is true
questions.explanation:
The given proposition is an I proposition, and it is false.

- E ("No poets are critics") is the contradictory of I. Contradictories have opposite truth values. So E is true.
- A ("All poets are critics") is the superaltern of I. If the subaltern is false, the superaltern must be false. So A is false.
- O ("Some poets are not critics") is the subcontrary of I. Subcontraries cannot both be false. So O is true.

All three values are fixed. The tempting option says O is undetermined. That would be right only if I were given as true, not false.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statement forms are tautologous ?

A. p ⊃ (q ⊃ p)

B. (p ⊃ q) ⊃ (q ⊃ p)

C. [(p ⊃ q) · ~q] ⊃ ~p

D. (p · ~p) ⊃ q

E. (p ∨ q) ⊃ (p · q)

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
A tautology is true in every row of its truth table. Look for a row that makes each form false.

- A. Tautology. To be false, p must be true and q ⊃ p false. But q ⊃ p cannot be false when p is true.
- B. Not a tautology. With p false and q true, p ⊃ q is true and q ⊃ p is false. The whole form is false.
- C. Tautology. It is the statement form of Modus Tollens, a valid argument form.
- D. Tautology. The antecedent p · ~p is never true, so the conditional is never false.
- E. Not a tautology. With p true and q false, p ∨ q is true and p · q is false.

B is the trap. It looks like a law, but converting a conditional is not valid.

questions.question_md:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as **Assertion A** and the other is labelled as **Reason R**.

**Assertion A :** In the Boolean interpretation, the inference from "All S is P" to "Some S is P" is not valid.

**Reason R :** In the Boolean interpretation, universal propositions assert that their subject class has at least one member.

In the light of the above statements, choose the **most appropriate** answer from the options given below :
options: Both **A** and **R** are correct and **R** is the correct explanation of **A**
Both **A** and **R** are correct but **R** is NOT the correct explanation of **A**
**A** is correct but **R** is not correct
**A** is not correct but **R** is correct
questions.explanation:
In the Boolean (modern) interpretation, only particular propositions (I and O) have existential import. Universal propositions (A and E) do not.

- A is correct. "All S is P" only says that there is nothing that is S and not P. It is true even if the class S is empty. But "Some S is P" says that at least one S exists. So subalternation fails. Copi calls this mistake the existential fallacy.
- R is not correct. It gives the traditional (Aristotelian) view of universals. The Boolean view denies existential import to universals.

The tempting choice is "both correct, R explains A". In fact, the opposite of R is the reason why A is true.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** (Thinker) with **LIST-II** (Work) :

| LIST-I | LIST-II |
|---|---|
| A. Aldo Leopold | I. *The Case for Animal Rights* |
| B. Peter Singer | II. *A Sand County Almanac* |
| C. Tom Regan | III. *Silent Spring* |
| D. Rachel Carson | IV. *Animal Liberation* |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Each work is the best-known book of its author.

- A–II. Aldo Leopold wrote *A Sand County Almanac* (1949). Its last essay, "The Land Ethic", states his land ethic.
- B–IV. Peter Singer wrote *Animal Liberation* (1975). He argues against speciesism on utilitarian grounds.
- C–I. Tom Regan wrote *The Case for Animal Rights* (1983). He argues that animals are "subjects-of-a-life" with rights.
- D–III. Rachel Carson wrote *Silent Spring* (1962). It shows the harm of pesticides such as DDT.

The tempting option "A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III" swaps Singer and Regan. Singer is a utilitarian and does not base his view on rights. Regan is the rights theorist.

questions.question_md:
"A thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of the biotic community. It is wrong when it tends otherwise."

The above maxim is the central principle of which one of the following ?
questions.explanation:
Aldo Leopold states this maxim in "The Land Ethic", in *A Sand County Almanac* (1949). The key words are "biotic community". Leopold enlarges the community to include soils, waters, plants and animals, or collectively, the land.

- The maxim is holistic. It judges acts by their effect on the whole community, not on single organisms.
- Naess's deep ecology is the closest distractor. But Naess speaks of self-realisation and the equal intrinsic value of all life. He does not use the "integrity, stability, and beauty" formula.
- Schweitzer's reverence for life values each individual living being.
- Singer's view concerns the interests of individual sentient animals.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements about euthanasia are correct ?

A. Voluntary euthanasia is carried out at the request of a competent patient.

B. Non-voluntary euthanasia is carried out on a competent patient against his expressed wish.

C. Involuntary euthanasia is carried out on a person who is capable of giving consent but has not consented.

D. Passive euthanasia consists in withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment.

E. James Rachels held that the bare difference between killing and letting die is, in itself, morally important.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Peter Singer's *Practical Ethics* gives the standard three-way division.

- A. Correct. In voluntary euthanasia, the patient asks for death.
- B. Not correct. This describes involuntary euthanasia. Non-voluntary euthanasia applies to a person who cannot consent, such as an infant or a patient in an irreversible coma.
- C. Correct. In involuntary euthanasia, the person could consent but is not asked or refuses.
- D. Correct. Passive euthanasia lets the patient die by not giving or by stopping treatment. Active euthanasia takes a direct step to cause death.
- E. Not correct. In "Active and Passive Euthanasia" (1975), Rachels argued the opposite. He said the bare difference between killing and letting die is not morally important.

The main trap is B, which mixes up non-voluntary and involuntary.

questions.question_md: In H.L.A. Hart's *The Concept of Law*, the secondary rule that lays down the criteria for identifying the valid rules of a legal system is called the :
questions.explanation:
Hart says a legal system is a union of primary and secondary rules. Primary rules impose duties. Secondary rules are rules about the primary rules.

- The rule of recognition gives the criteria of legal validity. It tells officials which rules count as law. It cures the "uncertainty" of a simple set of primary rules.
- The rule of change lets people introduce new rules and remove old ones. It cures the "static" quality.
- The rule of adjudication gives power to decide whether a rule has been broken. It cures "inefficiency".

The basic norm (Grundnorm) is the tempting distractor. It also grounds legal validity, but it belongs to Hans Kelsen's pure theory of law, not to Hart.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements about the philosophy of technology are correct ?

A. Hans Jonas, in *The Imperative of Responsibility*, argued that the scale of modern technology calls for a new ethics of responsibility towards future generations.

B. Don Ihde introduced the 'device paradigm', in which devices hide their machinery and displace focal things and practices.

C. Langdon Winner, in "Do Artifacts Have Politics?", argued that technical artefacts can embody specific forms of power and authority.

D. Andrew Feenberg accepted the substantive view that technical design cannot be changed by democratic intervention.

E. Jacques Ellul, in *The Technological Society*, argued that technique has become autonomous and follows its own logic of efficiency.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- A. Correct. Hans Jonas (1979) said that modern technology has effects far in space and time. So ethics must include responsibility for future human life.
- B. Not correct. The 'device paradigm' belongs to Albert Borgmann, in *Technology and the Character of Contemporary Life* (1984). Don Ihde is known for postphenomenology and his types of human–technology relations.
- C. Correct. Winner (1980) argued that some artefacts, such as low bridges on Long Island, carry political arrangements.
- D. Not correct. Feenberg agrees that technology is not neutral. But he rejects the fatalism of the substantive view. He argues that citizens can change technical design. He calls this democratic rationalization.
- E. Correct. Ellul held that technique is autonomous. It grows by its own demand for efficiency, outside real human control.

B is the near-miss trap, because Ihde and Borgmann both work in post-Heideggerian philosophy of technology. D is tempting because Feenberg does accept one part of the substantive view.

questions.question_md: Which one of the following best expresses R. Edward Freeman's stakeholder theory of corporate governance ?
options: Managers must take account of all groups that can affect or are affected by the firm, and not only its shareholders.
The one social responsibility of business is to increase its profits while staying within the rules of the game.
A corporation is only a legal fiction and so cannot bear any moral responsibility.
Directors act as agents of the shareholders alone and owe fiduciary duties only to them.
questions.explanation:
Freeman set out stakeholder theory in *Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach* (1984). A stakeholder is any group or person who can affect, or is affected by, the firm's objectives. Examples are employees, customers, suppliers, local communities and shareholders. Managers must balance the legitimate interests of all these groups.

- The second option is Milton Friedman's famous claim (1970). It is the shareholder view, which Freeman opposes. It is the most tempting distractor because it is the best-known statement in business ethics.
- The third option denies corporate moral responsibility. Stakeholder theory assumes that firms have such responsibility.
- The fourth option states shareholder primacy, which is again the view that Freeman rejects.

questions.question_md: According to the passage, the Mīmāṃsā holds that the validity of a cognition is :
options: Produced by a special excellence (guṇa) in the causes of the cognition
Known later by inference from the success of the action it prompts
Produced and apprehended by the same conditions that give rise to the cognition itself
Never apprehended, since every cognition is open to doubt
questions.explanation:
The passage says that the conditions that produce a cognition also produce its validity. It also says that the cognition is known as valid as soon as it arises. So, for the Mīmāṃsā, both the origin (utpatti) and the knowledge (jñapti) of validity are intrinsic. This is svataḥ-prāmāṇya, the view of Kumārila.

- Option (1), a guṇa (excellence) in the causes, is the Nyāya account of how validity arises.
- Option (2), inference from successful action, is the Nyāya account of how validity is known.
- Option (4) is not in the passage. For the Mīmāṃsā, a cognition stays valid unless a later cognition contradicts it.

The trap is to mix the two schools. Options (1) and (2) are correct statements, but they belong to the Nyāya, not to the Mīmāṃsā.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements correctly present the Nyāya view as given in the passage ?

A. Validity arises from an excellence (guṇa) in the causes of the cognition.

B. Validity is known by inference when the action prompted by the cognition succeeds.

C. Invalidity is apprehended along with the cognition, as soon as the cognition arises.

D. Both validity and invalidity are extrinsic.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
The passage gives the Nyāya view of parataḥ-prāmāṇya (extrinsic validity).

- A is correct. Validity comes from a guṇa (excellence) in the causes, for example a sound sense-organ.
- B is correct. The Nyāya knows validity by inference, after the action that the cognition prompts succeeds.
- C is wrong. For the Nyāya, invalidity is also extrinsic. Nothing in the passage makes invalidity known along with the cognition. That kind of intrinsic invalidity is the Buddhist position in the passage.
- D is correct. The passage says "For the Nyāya, invalidity too is extrinsic". So both are parataḥ.

So A, B and D are correct. Option (3) is the tempting trap, because a student who reads C quickly can take it as a general claim about error. Standard texts (Datta and Chatterjee, *The Six Ways of Knowing*) give the same Nyāya account.

questions.question_md: Kumārila's objection that, on the rival view, "the process would never end" charges that view with which defect ?
questions.explanation:
The passage says that if each cognition needed a further cognition to certify it, the further one would need another. The series would never end. In Indian logic, this defect is called anavasthā (infinite regress).

- Ātmāśraya means that a thing depends on itself. The passage does not say this.
- Anyonyāśraya means that two things depend on each other. Here there is a chain, not a pair.
- Cakraka is a circle through three or more terms. A circle comes back to its start. The passage describes a chain with no end.

The Nyāya reply in the passage also shows the point. A cognition can prompt action before its validity is known, so "no endless series is needed". Nāgārjuna used the same kind of regress against the pramāṇas in the *Vigrahavyāvartanī*.

questions.question_md: Which of the following positions on validity (prāmāṇya) and invalidity (aprāmāṇya) is correctly attributed in the passage ?
options: Sāṃkhya : both validity and invalidity intrinsic
questions.explanation:
The passage gives four positions.

- Mīmāṃsā: validity intrinsic, invalidity extrinsic.
- Nyāya: both validity and invalidity extrinsic.
- Sāṃkhya: both validity and invalidity intrinsic.
- Buddhists: invalidity intrinsic, validity extrinsic.

So option (3) is the correct match for the Sāṃkhya.

- Option (1) gives the Mīmāṃsā view, not the Sāṃkhya view.
- Option (2) reverses the Buddhist view. The Buddhists make invalidity intrinsic and validity extrinsic.
- Option (4) gives the Buddhist view, not the Nyāya view. For the Nyāya, invalidity is also extrinsic.

This four-fold scheme is the standard summary in Indian doxography. Each distractor is a real position with the wrong school's name on it.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following can be correctly inferred from the passage ?

A. For the Mīmāṃsā, a cognition is to be accepted as valid unless it is contradicted or its causes are found defective.

B. For the Nyāya, a cognition can lead to action even before its validity has been established.

C. For the Mīmāṃsā, the authority of the Veda follows from the absence of an author in whom a defect could lie.

D. For the Nyāya, validity is apprehended by the same conditions that produce the cognition.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- A follows. For the Mīmāṃsā, validity is intrinsic. Invalidity is known only through a contradicting cognition (bādhaka-jñāna) or a discovered defect. So, until one of these appears, the cognition stands as valid.
- B follows. The passage says that a cognition can prompt action before its validity is known. This is the Nyāya answer to the regress.
- C follows. Invalidity comes only from a defect (doṣa) in the causes. The Veda has no author, so there is no defect in its source. Its intrinsic validity is therefore never overturned.
- D does not follow. This is the Mīmāṃsā view of how validity is known. The Nyāya knows validity later, by inference from successful action.

So A, B and C are correct. Option (4), "A and C only", is the main trap. A student who links the Nyāya only with "testing first" may wrongly reject B. But the passage states B directly.

questions.question_md: The central thesis defended in the passage is that :
options: Only primary qualities exist outside the mind
The existence of material substance can be proved by reason
The being of sensible things consists in their being perceived
Our ideas are copies of mind-independent objects
questions.explanation:
The passage builds to Berkeley's thesis "esse is percipi": for sensible things, to be is to be perceived. Sensible things are collections of ideas, and ideas exist only in minds. This is the core of Berkeley's immaterialism in *A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge* (1710).

- Option (1) is Locke's view, and Berkeley rejects it. He argues that primary qualities are as mind-dependent as secondary qualities.
- Option (2) is the opposite of the passage. Berkeley denies material substance.
- Option (4) is Locke's resemblance view. Berkeley answers it with "an idea can be like nothing but an idea".

The trap is option (1). It mentions primary qualities, which the passage discusses at length, but it states the view Berkeley attacks.

questions.question_md: According to the passage, one ground on which Berkeley rejects Locke's distinction between primary and secondary qualities is that :
options: Extension and motion cannot be conceived without some colour or other sensible quality
Secondary qualities exist in bodies just as primary qualities do
Primary qualities are known through innate ideas
Secondary qualities, unlike primary ones, do not vary from perceiver to perceiver
questions.explanation:
The passage says that Berkeley cannot frame the idea of an extended, moving body without giving it some colour or other sensible quality. So primary qualities cannot be separated from secondary qualities. If secondary qualities are in the mind, primary qualities are in the mind too. Berkeley gives this argument in the *Principles*, section 10.

- Option (2) is wrong. Berkeley does not put secondary qualities in bodies. He puts primary qualities in the mind.
- Option (3) is wrong. The passage says nothing about innate ideas. Innate ideas belong to rationalists such as Descartes.
- Option (4) reverses the passage. Heat and sweetness vary with the perceiver, and size and speed vary in the same way.

The trap is option (2). It also removes the distinction, but in the wrong direction, towards realism.

questions.question_md: In the passage, the remark that "an idea can be like nothing but an idea" is used to show that :
options: Our ideas cannot resemble or represent qualities in an unperceived material substance
All ideas are exactly alike in content
Every idea is a faint copy of an earlier impression
Ideas are produced in us by the motion of material particles
questions.explanation:
Locke said that our ideas of primary qualities resemble qualities in matter. Berkeley replies that an idea can resemble only another idea. A colour can be like only a colour, and a shape can be like only a perceived shape. Matter is supposed to be unperceived, so nothing in it can be like an idea. The resemblance claim of representative realism therefore fails. This is the *Principles*, section 8.

- Option (2) misreads "like". Berkeley does not say all ideas are the same.
- Option (3) is Hume's copy principle (impressions and ideas). The passage is about Berkeley.
- Option (4) is the causal account of perception that Berkeley rejects. For him, God produces the ideas of sense.

The trap is option (3). It is a famous empiricist slogan about ideas, but it belongs to Hume and answers a different question.

questions.question_md: Which of the following is NOT a claim made in the passage ?
options: Ideas are passive, and only spirits are active
The regular order in which ideas of sense are excited is what we call the laws of nature
The ideas of sense are produced by the will of the finite perceiver
Berkeley denies matter but not the reality of things
questions.explanation:
The passage says the opposite of option (3). The ideas of sense do not depend on my will. Because of this, another spirit, God, must produce them. In the *Principles*, sections 28–30, Berkeley contrasts these ideas with the ideas of imagination, which I can make at will.

- Option (1) is in the passage: "Ideas are passive; only spirits are active."
- Option (2) is in the passage. The regular order in which God excites ideas is what we call the laws of nature.
- Option (4) is in the passage. Berkeley says that he denies matter, not the reality of things.

The trap is that option (3) sounds like a natural form of idealism. If all things are ideas, a student may think that the perceiver makes them. Berkeley rejects this. It would turn his view into solipsism.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following can be correctly inferred from the passage ?

A. Berkeley denies that trees and tables are real.

B. A tree that no human being sees continues to exist because God perceives it.

C. For Berkeley, what cannot exist apart cannot be conceived apart either.

D. For Berkeley, the mind is nothing but a bundle of perceptions.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- A is wrong. The passage ends by saying that Berkeley denies matter, not the reality of things. Trees and tables are real, but they are collections of ideas.
- B is correct. The passage says that an unseen tree still exists, because God perceives it.
- C is correct. Berkeley attacks abstract ideas, because they let the mind separate in thought what cannot exist apart. So, for him, inseparable things cannot be conceived apart. His argument about extension and colour uses the same point.
- D is wrong. The "bundle of perceptions" theory of the self is Hume's view. For Berkeley, the mind is an active spirit, not a collection of ideas.

So only B and C are correct. Option (1) is the main trap. Many students think idealism means that things are unreal. Berkeley explicitly denies this. Option (3) tempts students who mix up the two empiricists.

groups.md:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow :

In *The Concept of Mind* (1949), Gilbert Ryle attacks what he calls the "official doctrine" about the mind, which he traces chiefly to Descartes. On this doctrine every person has both a body and a mind. The body is in space, obeys mechanical laws and can be observed by anyone. The mind is not in space, and its workings are private: only their owner knows them directly, by a kind of inner perception. Ryle calls this view, "with deliberate abusiveness", the dogma of the Ghost in the Machine. He argues that it rests on a category-mistake. It presents the facts of mental life as if they belonged to one logical type or category, when they actually belong to another. A foreigner who has been shown the colleges, libraries and offices of Oxford and then asks, "But where is the University?" makes such a mistake. He takes the University to be one more building, when it is only the way in which all that he has already seen is organized. In the same way, the dualist treats the mind as an extra, hidden thing behind a person's behaviour. For Ryle, to describe someone as intelligent or vain is largely to describe how he is disposed to act and react. He also argues that knowing how to do something cannot be reduced to knowing that certain propositions are true.

Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow :

Aristotle opens the *Nicomachean Ethics* by observing that every art, every inquiry and every action aims at some good. Some ends are sought for the sake of other ends, but there must be a highest end, desired for its own sake and never for the sake of anything else. Nearly everyone agrees that this end is *eudaimonia*, usually translated as "happiness" but better rendered as "flourishing" or "living well". People disagree, however, about what it consists in. The many identify it with pleasure, men of action with honour, and others with wealth, which Aristotle sets aside because it is merely useful for getting something else. To settle the question, he asks what the function (*ergon*) of a human being is. Life, nutrition and growth are shared with plants, and perception with horses and oxen. What is peculiar to man is an active life of the part of the soul that has reason. The human good is therefore activity of the soul in accordance with virtue, and this "in a complete life", for one swallow does not make a summer. Virtue of character is not implanted in us by nature. We acquire it by habituation: we become just by doing just acts, and brave by doing brave acts. It is a settled state concerned with choice, lying in a mean relative to us, as courage lies between rashness and cowardice.

questions.question_md:
Read the following statements about Robert Nozick's *Anarchy, State, and Utopia* carefully :

A. Justice in holdings is set out by principles of just acquisition, just transfer and the rectification of injustice.

B. The Wilt Chamberlain example is meant to show that liberty upsets patterns of distribution.

C. Nozick defends a patterned principle: distribute to each according to his need.

D. Nozick holds that taxation of earnings from labour is on a par with forced labour.

E. The minimal state is presented as a framework for utopia.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
options: A, B, D and E only
A, B, C and D only
A, C, D and E only
questions.explanation:
Nozick's entitlement theory is historical, not patterned.

- A is correct. A holding is just if it comes from just acquisition or just transfer. Past injustice is corrected by rectification.
- B is correct. Fans freely pay to watch Wilt Chamberlain. He becomes rich, and the starting pattern is upset by free choices.
- C is wrong. Nozick rejects all patterned and end-state principles. "To each according to need" is the kind of principle he attacks.
- D is correct. Nozick says that taxing earnings is like forcing a person to work some hours for another.
- E is correct. Part III argues that the minimal state is a framework within which many communities can pursue their own idea of utopia.

Options (2), (3) and (4) all include C, the false statement.

questions.question_md:
Read the following statements on Heidegger's analysis of Dasein in *Being and Time* :

A. The being of Dasein shows itself as care (*Sorge*).

B. When Dasein lives as the 'they-self' (*das Man*) in its everyday life, it exists authentically.

C. Death is Dasein's ownmost, non-relational possibility, and being-towards-death individualises Dasein.

D. Thrownness (*Geworfenheit*) means that Dasein freely chooses the world into which it comes.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
In *Being and Time*, Heidegger describes the basic structures of Dasein (human existence).

- **A – true.** In §41, Heidegger says that the being of Dasein is care (*Sorge*).
- **B – false.** The 'they-self' (*das Man*) is the everyday, anonymous self. Heidegger calls this mode **inauthentic**. Dasein lives as 'one' lives.
- **C – true.** Death is Dasein's ownmost, non-relational possibility. Nobody can die for me. So being-towards-death takes Dasein out of the 'they' and individualises it.
- **D – false.** Thrownness means the opposite. Dasein finds itself already in a world that it did not choose.

So only A and C are correct. The option 'A and B only' is a trap. It confuses the everyday 'they-self' with authentic existence.

questions.question_md: Which pragmatist philosopher wrote *The Varieties of Religious Experience*, the Gifford Lectures that study religion through the personal experiences of individuals ?
questions.explanation:
William James gave the Gifford Lectures at Edinburgh in 1901–1902. He published them in 1902 as *The Varieties of Religious Experience*. The book studies religion as the feelings, acts and experiences of individual people. It discusses conversion, saintliness and mysticism. James judges religious experience by its fruits in life, not by its roots.

- **John Dewey** wrote *A Common Faith* (1934) on religion. He did not write the *Varieties*.
- **C. S. Peirce** founded pragmatism as a theory of meaning. He did not write this book.
- **F. C. S. Schiller** was a British pragmatist (humanism). He did not write this book.

The tempting option is Dewey, because he also wrote on religion. But his book is *A Common Faith*.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I (Thinker) | LIST-II (Concept) |
|---|---|
| A. Muhammad Iqbal | I. Jīvan-devatā (the Lord of one's life) |
| B. Sri Aurobindo | II. The Absolute in the alternative forms of Truth, Freedom and Value |
| C. K. C. Bhattacharyya | III. Mard-i-Momin (the perfect man) |
| D. Rabindranath Tagore | IV. The psychic being (caitya puruṣa) |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Each thinker has one well-known concept.

- **A-III:** Iqbal calls the ideal human being *Mard-i-Momin* (the perfect man). This person has a strong ego (khudi) and is close to God.
- **B-IV:** Sri Aurobindo calls the divine spark in the individual the *psychic being* (caitya puruṣa). It grows through many lives and guides inner change.
- **C-II:** K. C. Bhattacharyya wrote *The Concept of the Absolute and its Alternative Forms*. He says that the Absolute appears as Truth, Freedom or Value. These forms are alternatives, and we cannot unite them in one concept.
- **D-I:** Tagore uses *Jīvan-devatā* (the Lord of one's life) for the inner divine presence that shapes his life and poetry.

The option A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II is the most tempting. It changes only C and D. But the 'alternative forms of the Absolute' is a term from KCB's logic of the Absolute, not from Tagore's poetry. The option A-IV, B-III mixes the two 'higher self' ideas of Iqbal and Aurobindo.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I (Name in the *Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad*) | LIST-II (State of the self) |
|---|---|
| A. Vaiśvānara | I. The self in the dream state (svapna) |
| B. Taijasa | II. The fourth, non-dual self beyond the three states |
| C. Prājña | III. The self in the waking state (jāgrat) |
| D. Turīya | IV. The self in the state of deep sleep (suṣupti) |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
The *Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad* says that the self (Ātman) has four quarters (pāda). It gives a name to each one.

- **A-III:** Vaiśvānara is the self in the waking state (jāgrat). It knows outer objects.
- **B-I:** Taijasa is the self in the dream state (svapna). It knows inner objects.
- **C-IV:** Prājña is the self in deep sleep (suṣupti). It is a mass of consciousness and full of bliss.
- **D-II:** Turīya is "the fourth". It is not one more state. It is the non-dual self that lies under the three states.

The most tempting wrong option is A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II. It swaps Taijasa and Prājña. Remember that *taijasa* means "made of light": the dreamer sees inner images. Prājña is the sleeper who is "one mass of knowing".

questions.question_md:
The following categorical syllogism is invalid :

All metals are conductors.

All metals are elements.

∴ All elements are conductors.

Which rule of the valid categorical syllogism does it break ?
options: The middle term must be distributed at least once
A term distributed in the conclusion must be distributed in its premise
At least one premise must be affirmative
If the conclusion is negative, one premise must be negative
questions.explanation:
The terms are: major term P = conductors, minor term S = elements, middle term M = metals. The form is AAA in the third figure.

- **Middle term rule**: "metals" is the subject of an A proposition, so it is distributed. This rule is kept.
- **Distribution rule**: "elements" is the subject of the A conclusion, so it is distributed there. In the minor premise it is the predicate of an A proposition, so it is undistributed. This rule is broken. The name of this fallacy is illicit minor.
- **Affirmative premise rule**: both premises are affirmative, so this rule is kept.
- **Negative conclusion rule**: the conclusion is affirmative, so this rule does not apply.

The middle-term rule tempts many candidates. But "metals" is the subject of both premises, and the subject of an A proposition is always distributed.

questions.question_md: According to St. Thomas Aquinas, in which one of the following are essence and existence really identical ?
questions.explanation:
In *De Ente et Essentia*, Aquinas holds that in every creature, essence (what a thing is) differs from existence (that it is). A creature receives its existence from another. Only in God is essence the same as existence. God is *ipsum esse subsistens*, subsistent being itself.

- Option (1) is the tempting trap. Angels have no matter, so they are pure forms. But Aquinas says that their essence still differs from their existence. This composition makes them creatures.
- Option (2): the human soul is a created form. Its existence comes from God.
- Option (3): prime matter is pure potentiality. It cannot exist by itself, so it cannot be identical with existence.

questions.question_md: Which one of the following correctly describes the way of life that Plato prescribes for the guardians in the ideal state of the *Republic* ?
options: They hold no private property and no private families; wives and children are held in common.
They hold no private property, but each guardian keeps a private family of his own.
They keep private families and land, but they are barred from all trade and commerce.
They may possess gold and silver, but they may not own any land or houses.
questions.explanation:
Plato wants the guardians to care only for the good of the whole city.

- At the end of Book III, he says that guardians must own no private property. They live and eat together, and they must not touch gold or silver.
- In Book V, he adds that among the guardians, wives and children are held in common. No parent knows his own child.

So the guardians have neither private property nor private families. Option (1) is correct.

- Option (2) is the near miss. It keeps the first rule but drops the second.
- Option (3) allows both families and land, which Plato forbids.
- Option (4) reverses Plato's rule. Gold and silver are exactly what the guardians must not possess.

questions.question_md: The doctrine of *homo mensura*, which makes each person's perception the standard of what is true for that person, is associated with which Sophist ?
questions.explanation:
Protagoras of Abdera said that man is the measure of all things. Plato discusses this saying in the *Theaetetus*. It expresses a relativism about knowledge. What seems true to each person is true for that person.

- Gorgias is known for the nihilist theses: nothing exists; if it exists, we cannot know it; if we know it, we cannot communicate it.
- Prodicus is known for the exact distinction of word meanings.
- Thrasymachus, in the *Republic*, says that justice is the interest of the stronger.

questions.question_md: Reality is of two kinds: independent (*svatantra*) and dependent (*asvatantra*). God (Viṣṇu) alone is independent; souls and matter depend on Him. Difference (*bheda*) is real and five-fold — between God and soul, God and matter, soul and soul, soul and matter, and matter and matter. This view is held by :
questions.explanation:
Madhva divides all reality into two classes. Viṣṇu is the only independent (svatantra) reality. Souls (jīva) and matter (jaḍa) are dependent (asvatantra). Madhva also teaches that five kinds of difference (pañca-bheda) are real and eternal. These two doctrines are the marks of Dvaita Vedānta.

- Rāmānuja also makes souls and matter depend on God. But for him they are the body of Brahman. He does not teach a real five-fold difference. He teaches a qualified non-difference.
- Nimbārka holds that souls and matter are both different and not different from Brahman (bhedābheda).
- Vallabha holds that the world is Brahman itself, without change (pure non-dualism).

So only Madhva makes difference itself the nature of things. The near-miss is Viśiṣṭādvaita, because it shares the idea of dependence.

questions.question_md:
Jaina epistemology recognises five kinds of knowledge (*jñāna*). Umāsvāti's *Tattvārthasūtra* lists them in a fixed order.

Arrange the following kinds of knowledge in the order in which the *Tattvārthasūtra* lists them :

A. Avadhi-jñāna

B. Mati-jñāna

C. Kevala-jñāna

D. Manaḥparyāya-jñāna

E. Śruta-jñāna

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
*Tattvārthasūtra* 1.9 lists the five kinds as mati, śruta, avadhi, manaḥparyāya and kevala. The list goes from the least direct to the most complete.

- **B. Mati:** ordinary knowledge through the senses and the mind. It is indirect (parokṣa).
- **E. Śruta:** knowledge from words and signs. It depends on mati, so it comes second.
- **A. Avadhi:** direct knowledge of distant forms, such as clairvoyance.
- **D. Manaḥparyāya:** direct knowledge of the thoughts of other minds. It is finer than avadhi.
- **C. Kevala:** perfect knowledge of all things. Only a liberated soul has it.

So the order is B, E, A, D, C.

The closest wrong option is B, E, D, A, C. It puts manaḥparyāya before avadhi. Avadhi is the lower kind, because its range is only material forms. The option E, B, A, D, C is wrong because śruta needs mati first.

questions.question_md: In the Nyāya five-membered inference (*parārthānumāna*) about fire on a hill, which member is the statement "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen" ?
questions.explanation:
The Nyāya inference for others has five members (avayava):

1. Pratijñā: "The hill has fire." This states the thesis.
2. Hetu: "Because it has smoke." This gives the reason.
3. Udāharaṇa: "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen." This states the universal rule (vyāpti) with an example.
4. Upanaya: "This hill has smoke that always goes with fire." This applies the rule to the case.
5. Nigamana: "Therefore the hill has fire." This is the conclusion.

The given sentence has both a universal rule and a familiar example (the kitchen). So it is the udāharaṇa. Upanaya is the tempting wrong option, because it also speaks of smoke and fire. But upanaya applies the rule to this hill only. It does not state the rule.

questions.question_md: According to the divine command theory, a form of ethical super-naturalism, what makes an action morally obligatory ?
options: Its conformity to the moral code accepted by the agent's society
Its tendency to produce the greatest happiness of the greatest number
Its being right in itself, which God only recognises and reports
Its being commanded by God, whose will alone makes it obligatory
questions.explanation:
Ethical super-naturalism grounds morality in God. Its main form is the divine command theory. This theory says that an act is obligatory *because* God commands it. God's will is the source of the duty.

- Conformity to the code of one's society is cultural relativism.
- The greatest happiness of the greatest number is the principle of utility.
- The option "right in itself, which God only recognises" is the near-miss. It is the second horn of the Euthyphro dilemma. On that view, rightness exists before and apart from God's command. God only reports it. So the command does not make the act right. The divine command theorist rejects this view, because it makes morality independent of God.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following rules of replacement are correctly stated ?

A. De Morgan's theorem : ~(p · q) ≡ (~p ∨ ~q)

B. Exportation : [(p · q) ⊃ r] ≡ [p ⊃ (q ∨ r)]

C. Transposition : (p ⊃ q) ≡ (~q ⊃ ~p)

D. Material implication : (p ⊃ q) ≡ (p ∨ ~q)

E. Distribution : [p · (q ∨ r)] ≡ [(p ∨ q) · (p ∨ r)]

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
A rule of replacement is correct only when its two sides have the same truth value in every row.

- **A** is correct. The denial of a conjunction is the disjunction of the denials.
- **B** is wrong. Exportation is [(p · q) ⊃ r] ≡ [p ⊃ (q ⊃ r)]. Take p, q true and r false: the left side is F, but p ⊃ (q ∨ r) is T.
- **C** is correct. A conditional is equivalent to its contrapositive.
- **D** is wrong. Material implication is (p ⊃ q) ≡ (~p ∨ q). Take p false and q true: p ⊃ q is T, but p ∨ ~q is F.
- **E** is wrong. It mixes the two forms of Distribution. The correct form is [p · (q ∨ r)] ≡ [(p · q) ∨ (p · r)]. Take p false, q and r true: the left side is F, but the right side is T.

So only A and C are correct. Option "A, B and D only" tempts, because B and D each change only one symbol of a real rule.

questions.question_md:
Read the following statements on Swami Vivekananda's idea of universal religion :

A. Vivekananda holds that we should not only tolerate other religions but accept all religions as true.

B. For Vivekananda, the universal religion will come when one religion replaces all the others.

C. He compares the different religions to streams that rise in different places but mix their waters in the same sea.

D. He holds that the ideal religion must make room for philosophy, devotion, mysticism and work.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Vivekananda's universal religion is unity in variety. It does not remove the different religions.

- **A is correct.** At Chicago in 1893 he said: "We believe not only in universal toleration, but we accept all religions as true."
- **B is not correct.** He says that the Christian need not become a Hindu, and the Hindu need not become a Christian. Each religion must keep its own nature and grow by learning from the others.
- **C is correct.** He quotes a hymn: streams rise in different sources but mix in the sea. In the same way, different paths lead to the one God.
- **D is correct.** In "The Ideal of a Universal Religion" he wants a religion for the philosopher, the devotee, the mystic and the worker. These correspond to jñāna, bhakti, rāja and karma yoga.

So A, C and D are correct. Options with B are wrong, because Vivekananda rejects the idea that one creed must win over all others.

questions.question_md: David Hume holds that every simple idea is copied from a corresponding impression. Which one of the following does he himself admit as a possible exception to this principle ?
options: The idea of a missing shade of blue
The idea of a golden mountain
questions.explanation:
Hume gives his own counter-example in the *Treatise* (1.1.1) and in the *Enquiry* (Section II). Suppose a person has seen all shades of blue except one. Place the shades in order from dark to light. The person sees a gap. Hume says that this person can form the idea of the missing shade without the impression. He calls the case singular and keeps his principle.

- Option (1): Hume traces necessary connection to an internal impression, the felt determination of the mind by custom. So it is not an exception.
- Option (3): Hume finds no impression of a simple, constant self. So he denies that we have such an idea.
- Option (4): a golden mountain is a complex idea. The mind compounds it from the simple ideas of gold and mountain.

questions.question_md:
Annambhaṭṭa's *Tarkasaṃgraha* divides cognition (*buddhi*) into memory and experience (*anubhava*), and divides experience into valid and non-valid. Which of the following are the kinds of non-valid experience (*ayathārtha anubhava*) according to this text ?

A. Saṃśaya

B. Anumiti

C. Smṛti

D. Tarka

E. Viparyaya

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Annambhaṭṭa says that non-valid experience is of three kinds: saṃśaya, viparyaya and tarka.

- **A. Saṃśaya (doubt):** correct. The mind wavers between two alternatives.
- **B. Anumiti (inferential knowledge):** not correct. It is one of the four kinds of valid experience. The others are pratyakṣa, upamiti and śābda.
- **C. Smṛti (memory):** not correct. The text puts memory outside experience (anubhava). So it cannot be a kind of non-valid experience.
- **D. Tarka (hypothetical reasoning):** correct. An example is "If there were no fire, there would be no smoke." It supposes something that is not the fact.
- **E. Viparyaya (error):** correct. An example is the cognition of silver in a shell.

So the answer is A, D and E only. The trap is C. Memory can be true or false, but Annambhaṭṭa does not count it as anubhava. The other trap is to leave out tarka, because tarka helps inference.

questions.question_md: Who stated that "the great and chief end of men's uniting into commonwealths, and putting themselves under government, is the preservation of their property" ?
questions.explanation:
The sentence comes from Locke's *Second Treatise of Government* (§124). For Locke, 'property' has a broad sense. It covers a person's life, liberty and estate. People leave the state of nature because it lacks a known law, an impartial judge and a power to enforce judgments. So they form a government to protect their property.

- Option (1), Hobbes, is the near miss. He also explains why people form a commonwealth. But for Hobbes the chief end is security and peace, not property.
- Option (3): Rousseau stresses the general will and the freedom of the citizen.
- Option (4): Bentham rejects the social contract and bases government on utility.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I (Debt) | LIST-II (Means of repaying it) |
|---|---|
| A. Deva-ṛṇa | I. Study and teaching of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) |
| B. Ṛṣi-ṛṇa | II. Performance of sacrifices (*yajña*) |
| C. Pitṛ-ṛṇa | III. Hospitality to guests and fellow men |
| D. Manuṣya-ṛṇa | IV. Begetting and raising offspring |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
The Vedic texts say that every person is born with debts (ṛṇa). The *Taittirīya Saṃhitā* names three. The *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* adds a fourth, the debt to men.

- **A-II:** The debt to the gods (deva-ṛṇa) is paid by sacrifice (yajña).
- **B-I:** The debt to the seers (ṛṣi-ṛṇa) is paid by Vedic study (svādhyāya). The seers gave the Veda, so one keeps it alive.
- **C-IV:** The debt to the ancestors (pitṛ-ṛṇa) is paid by having children. This continues the family line and its offerings.
- **D-III:** The debt to men (manuṣya-ṛṇa) is paid by hospitality.

The tempting wrong option is A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III. It gives sacrifice to the seers and study to the gods. But the gods receive the offerings of a yajña. The seers receive the study of the texts they saw.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements are true of G. E. Moore's position in "A Defence of Common Sense" ?

A. Moore claims to know with certainty many truisms, for example that the earth existed for many years before his body was born.

B. Moore holds that we can know a common-sense proposition to be true without knowing its correct analysis.

C. Moore holds that common-sense beliefs are only probable hypotheses which philosophy must first prove.

D. Moore holds that all material things are ideas that exist only in some mind.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
In "A Defence of Common Sense" (1925), Moore gives a list of truisms. He says that he knows them with certainty.

- **A – true.** One truism is that the earth existed for many years before his body was born.
- **B – true.** Moore separates two questions. Is the proposition true? What is its correct analysis? He is sure of the first. He is doubtful about the second.
- **C – false.** For Moore, these beliefs are known, not mere hypotheses. Philosophy does not need to prove them first.
- **D – false.** This is idealism. Moore rejects it and holds that material things exist independently of minds.

So A and B only are true. The option 'A and C only' is tempting, but C makes common sense depend on philosophical proof.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I (Text) | LIST-II (Doctrine) |
|---|---|
| A. *Hind Swaraj* | I. Hinduism is more a way of life than a form of thought. |
| B. *The Hindu View of Life* | II. Modern civilisation, which makes bodily welfare the object of life, is irreligion. |
| C. *Philosophy of Hinduism* | III. All prophets taught one and the same dīn (Waḥdat-i-Dīn). |
| D. *Tarjumān al-Qur'ān* | IV. A religion must be judged by the tests of justice and social utility. |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Each text carries one central claim.

- **A-II:** In *Hind Swaraj* (1909), Gandhi says that modern civilisation makes bodily welfare the object of life. He calls it irreligion.
- **B-I:** In *The Hindu View of Life* (1926), S. Radhakrishnan says that Hinduism is more a way of life than a form of thought. It has no single fixed creed.
- **C-IV:** In *Philosophy of Hinduism*, B. R. Ambedkar tests a religion by justice (liberty, equality, fraternity) and by social utility. He finds that Hinduism fails both tests.
- **D-III:** In *Tarjumān al-Qur'ān*, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad teaches *Waḥdat-i-Dīn*. All prophets taught one dīn (religion). Only the outer laws and rites are different.

The most tempting wrong option is A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV. It swaps the two texts on religion in general. But the unity of all religions is Azad's thesis, while the tests of justice and utility are Ambedkar's.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following writings of Karl Marx (some written with Friedrich Engels) in the order in which they were written :

A. *Capital*, Volume I

B. *Manifesto of the Communist Party*

C. *Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts*

D. *A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy*

E. *The German Ideology*

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
The dates of writing are:

- C. *Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts*: 1844, in Paris.
- E. *The German Ideology*: 1845–46, with Engels.
- B. *Manifesto of the Communist Party*: 1847–48, with Engels.
- D. *A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy*: 1859.
- A. *Capital*, Volume I: published in 1867.

So the order is C, E, B, D, A.

The trap is the publication date. The *Manuscripts* and *The German Ideology* were first published only in 1932. But the question asks for the order of writing. Option (1) puts the *Manifesto* before *The German Ideology*. Option (4) puts *Capital* before the *Contribution*, which was its forerunner.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following are limbs of the Noble Eightfold Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgika mārga*) taught in the fourth Noble Truth ?

A. Samyak dāna

B. Samyak vyāyāma

C. Samyak saṅkalpa

D. Samyak śraddhā

E. Samyak ājīva

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
The fourth Noble Truth is the path that ends suffering. It has eight limbs: right view (dṛṣṭi), right resolve (saṅkalpa), right speech (vāk), right action (karmānta), right livelihood (ājīva), right effort (vyāyāma), right mindfulness (smṛti) and right concentration (samādhi).

- **A. Samyak dāna:** not a limb. Dāna (giving) is a virtue and a pāramitā, but it is not in the eightfold list.
- **B. Samyak vyāyāma (right effort):** a limb.
- **C. Samyak saṅkalpa (right resolve):** a limb.
- **D. Samyak śraddhā (right faith):** not a limb. Faith is important in Buddhism, but it is not one of the eight.
- **E. Samyak ājīva (right livelihood):** a limb.

So the answer is B, C and E only. Option "B, D and E only" is tempting, because "right faith" sounds like a Buddhist term. But faith is not one of the eight limbs.

questions.question_md: Which of the following combinations correctly represents Gandhi's idea of swadeshi in the spheres of religion, politics and economics ?
options: Ancestral religion, indigenous political institutions, foreign goods of better quality
Ancestral religion, indigenous political institutions, goods made by immediate neighbours
Ancestral religion, a centralised modern state, goods made by immediate neighbours
Conversion to a reformed faith, indigenous political institutions, goods made by immediate neighbours
questions.explanation:
In his Madras speech of 1916, Gandhi defines swadeshi as the spirit that limits us to the use and service of our immediate surroundings. He then applies it in three spheres.

- **Religion:** a person should keep to his ancestral religion and remove its defects.
- **Politics:** a person should use the indigenous institutions and serve them by curing their defects.
- **Economics:** a person should use only goods made by his immediate neighbours and make those industries efficient.

So the correct combination is ancestral religion, indigenous institutions and goods of the neighbours.

- "Foreign goods of better quality" breaks the economic part.
- "A centralised modern state" breaks the political part. Gandhi did not trust centralised state power.
- "Conversion to a reformed faith" breaks the religious part.

Each wrong option keeps two correct parts. So the candidate must check all three spheres.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following objections does Aristotle raise against Plato's theory of Ideas (Forms) in Book A of the *Metaphysics* ?

A. The Ideas contribute nothing to our knowledge of sensible things, since they are not in those things.

B. The Ideas cannot explain the movement and change of sensible things.

C. To say that things 'participate' in the Ideas is to use empty words and poetic metaphors.

D. To posit the Ideas is like trying to count things more easily by first adding to their number.

E. There are no universals at all; only individual things can be known.

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
options: A, B, C and D only
questions.explanation:
In *Metaphysics* A.9, Aristotle lists several objections to the separate Ideas of Plato.

- A is correct. The Ideas are not in the things, so they do not help us to know them.
- B is correct. The Ideas are unchanging. So they cannot cause the movement and change that we see.
- C is correct. Aristotle calls 'participation' and 'pattern' empty words and poetic metaphors.
- D is correct. Aristotle compares the Platonist to a man who cannot count a few things, so he doubles them first.
- E is wrong. Aristotle does not deny universals. He holds that the universal exists in the particular things, not apart from them. Science is of the universal.

Option (3) is the near miss. It leaves out B, but Aristotle stresses that the Ideas explain no motion. Options (1) and (2) include E, which makes Aristotle a nominalist.

questions.question_md: Which one is the correct order in which Kaṇāda's *Vaiśeṣika Sūtra* (1.1.4) lists the six positive categories (*padārtha*) ?
options: Dravya, Karma, Guṇa, Sāmānya, Samavāya, Viśeṣa
Guṇa, Dravya, Karma, Viśeṣa, Sāmānya, Samavāya
Dravya, Guṇa, Karma, Sāmānya, Viśeṣa, Samavāya
Dravya, Guṇa, Karma, Viśeṣa, Sāmānya, Samavāya
questions.explanation:
*Vaiśeṣika Sūtra* 1.1.4 names the categories in this order: dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa and samavāya. Abhāva (non-existence) was added as a seventh category by later writers.

The order has a logic:

- Dravya (substance) comes first, because it is the substrate of all others.
- Guṇa (quality) and karma (action) exist only in a substance.
- Sāmānya (universal) unites many things. Viśeṣa (particularity) separates eternal things. Sāmānya comes before viśeṣa.
- Samavāya (inherence) is the relation that ties these categories together. It comes last.

The closest wrong option swaps sāmānya and viśeṣa. Another wrong option puts karma before guṇa. Both break the order of the sūtra.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements are true of Wittgenstein's *On Certainty* ?

A. Wittgenstein wrote these notes in response to G. E. Moore's defence of common sense and his proof of an external world.

B. Wittgenstein agrees that Moore refutes the sceptic correctly when he says "I know that here is a hand".

C. Some propositions are exempt from doubt and are like hinges on which our questions and doubts turn.

D. The game of doubting itself presupposes certainty, so a doubt that doubted everything would not be a doubt.

E. Hinge propositions are empirical hypotheses that we accept because the evidence for them is very strong.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
*On Certainty* contains notes from the last eighteen months of Wittgenstein's life (1949–1951). It was published in 1969.

- **A – true.** The notes discuss Moore's "A Defence of Common Sense" and "Proof of an External World".
- **B – false.** Wittgenstein says that Moore misuses "I know" here. Moore's mistake is to answer the sceptic by saying "I do know it".
- **C – true.** In §341, some propositions are 'exempt from doubt'. They are like hinges on which questions turn.
- **D – true.** In §115, the game of doubting presupposes certainty. In §450, a doubt that doubted everything would not be a doubt.
- **E – false.** Hinges are not hypotheses supported by evidence. They form the groundless framework within which we give and test evidence.

So A, C and D only are true. The option 'A, B and C only' is the near miss. Wittgenstein agrees with Moore's certainties, but not with his claim to *know* them.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I (Kind of definition) | LIST-II (Description) |
|---|---|
| A. Ostensive definition | I. States that a word applies to a thing when a stated test gives a stated result |
| B. Synonymous definition | II. Names a wider class and the specific attribute that marks off the members of the defined term |
| C. Operational definition | III. Points to or gestures at examples of the things the term denotes |
| D. Definition by genus and difference | IV. Gives another word, already understood, that has the same meaning |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Copi divides definitions by the two kinds of meaning of a term. Extensional (denotative) definitions use the objects that the term denotes. Intensional (connotative) definitions use the attributes that the term connotes.

- **A-III**: an ostensive definition is extensional. It points to examples, such as "this is a desk".
- **B-IV**: a synonymous definition gives a word with the same meaning, such as "*Gift* means present".
- **C-I**: an operational definition states a test and its result. Example: one mineral is harder than another if it scratches it.
- **D-II**: a definition by genus and difference names the wider class (genus) and the mark (difference). Example: "a triangle is a plane figure with three sides".

The option A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I swaps C and D. Both describe connotative definitions, so a careless reader may swap them.

questions.question_md:
Which one of Mill's methods of experimental inquiry is used in the following reasoning ?

"Astronomers found that the observed path of Uranus did not match the path calculated from the pull of the Sun and the known planets. They traced this remaining deviation to an unknown planet, and this led to the discovery of Neptune."
questions.explanation:
The method of residues subtracts from a phenomenon the part already explained by known causes. Then it attributes the remaining part (the residue) to the remaining antecedent.

Here the astronomers subtracted the effects of the Sun and the known planets. A part of the deviation of Uranus was still unexplained. They traced this residue to a further cause, the then-unknown planet Neptune (discovered in 1846). Copi uses this case as a standard example of the method of residues.

- Agreement looks for one circumstance common to many cases of the effect.
- Difference compares a case where the effect occurs with a case where it does not.
- Concomitant variation finds two phenomena that vary together. This is the tempting option, because the orbit "varies". But the reasoning works by subtraction of known effects, not by tracking joint variation.

questions.question_md: According to R. M. Hare, a genuine moral judgement such as 'You ought to keep your promise' is :
options: a statement that sense experience can verify or falsify
a report of the speaker's own feeling of approval
prescriptive and also universalizable to all similar cases
a description of a simple and non-natural property
questions.explanation:
R. M. Hare (*The Language of Morals*, *Freedom and Reason*) holds that moral judgements have two marks.

- They are **prescriptive**. Like imperatives, they tell us what to do.
- They are **universalizable**. If I say that you ought to do X here, I must say the same of any relevantly similar case.

This makes the third option correct.

- Verification by sense experience is the logical positivist test of meaning. Ayer used it to deny that moral judgements are factual.
- A report of the speaker's feeling of approval is subjectivism.
- A simple, non-natural property is Moore's account of "good". Hare is a non-cognitivist, so he does not say that moral judgements describe properties.

questions.question_md: Which of the following models of the doctor–patient relationship makes the physician the patient's guardian, who decides the best treatment while the patient is expected simply to accept it ?
questions.explanation:
Ezekiel and Linda Emanuel (1992) describe four models of the doctor–patient relationship.

- **Paternalistic model:** the physician acts as the patient's guardian. He decides what is best for the patient. The patient's role is to give assent. This puts beneficence above autonomy.
- **Informative model:** the physician is a technical expert. He gives all the facts, and the patient makes the choice.
- **Interpretive model:** the physician acts as a counsellor. He helps the patient find out his own values and then choose.
- **Deliberative model:** the physician acts as a teacher or friend. He discusses which health values are worth having, but the patient makes the final choice.

The deliberative model is the most tempting option, because the physician gives his view in it. But he only persuades. He does not decide in place of the patient.

questions.question_md: In *After Virtue*, Alasdair MacIntyre explains the core concept of a virtue in three successive stages. Which one of the following gives these three stages correctly ?
options: Pleasure, utility and the greatest happiness of society
Duty, maxims and the kingdom of ends
Practices, natural rights and the social contract
Practices, the narrative unity of a human life and a moral tradition
questions.explanation:
In chapters 14 and 15 of *After Virtue* (1981), MacIntyre builds the concept of a virtue in three stages.

1. A **practice**: a cooperative activity, such as chess or farming, with goods internal to it. A virtue lets us achieve these internal goods.
2. The **narrative unity of a human life**: virtues support the good of a whole life, understood as a story.
3. A **moral tradition**: virtues sustain the traditions that give practices and lives their context.

- The option with "natural rights and the social contract" is the near-miss. It starts correctly with practices. But MacIntyre rejects natural rights. He calls belief in them belief in "witches and unicorns".
- Pleasure and utility belong to utilitarianism.
- Duty, maxims and the kingdom of ends belong to Kant.

questions.question_md: Which one of the following statements correctly expresses John Locke's notion of substance in general ?
options: It is a supposed but unknown support of the qualities that produce simple ideas in us.
It is nothing but a bundle or collection of different perceptions.
It is that which is in itself and is conceived through itself.
It is a simple, windowless centre of force that mirrors the universe.
questions.explanation:
In the *Essay* (II.xxiii.2), Locke says that the idea of pure substance in general is only "a supposed, but unknown, support" of qualities. We find that some simple ideas always go together. We cannot imagine how they exist alone, so we suppose a substratum that holds them. Locke says that we know it only as "something, he knew not what".

- Option (2) is Hume's account of the mind as a bundle of perceptions.
- Option (3) is Spinoza's definition of substance in the *Ethics*.
- Option (4) describes the monad of Leibniz.

The trap is to confuse Locke's empiricist view with the views of other modern thinkers.

questions.question_md: Spinoza's proposition in the *Ethics* that "the order and connection of ideas is the same as the order and connection of things" expresses the doctrine of :
questions.explanation:
This is *Ethics* Part II, Proposition 7. For Spinoza, thought and extension are two attributes of one substance, God or Nature. A mode of extension and the idea of that mode are one and the same thing, expressed in two ways. So mental events and bodily events run in parallel, without any causal action between them. This is psycho-physical parallelism.

- Option (1): pre-established harmony is Leibniz's view. God sets up separate monads so that they agree.
- Option (2): occasionalism is the view of Malebranche and Geulincx. God is the only true cause on each occasion.
- Option (4): interactionism is Descartes' view. Mind and body act on each other at the pineal gland.

All four are answers to the Cartesian mind–body problem, so the distractors are close.

questions.question_md: In his essay "Philosophy as Rigorous Science" (1911), Husserl argues against two positions that, in his view, prevent philosophy from becoming a rigorous science. Which are these two positions ?
questions.explanation:
Husserl published "Philosophy as Rigorous Science" in the journal *Logos* in 1911. In this essay he criticises two positions.

- **Naturalism** treats consciousness and ideas as parts of nature. It tries to study them by the methods of natural science. So it destroys the ideal norms of logic and knowledge.
- **Historicism** treats every philosophy as a product of its historical period. It leads to relativism and to 'world-view philosophy' (*Weltanschauung* philosophy).

Against both, Husserl asks for a phenomenology of pure consciousness. It must give strict, timeless knowledge.

The tempting option is 'Psychologism and formalism'. Husserl attacked psychologism in the *Logical Investigations* (1900–1901). But formalism is not his target, and the essay names naturalism and historicism. 'Rationalism and empiricism' and 'Idealism and realism' are not the targets of this essay.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following are marks of the *sthitaprajña* (the person of steady wisdom) as described in the second chapter of the *Bhagavadgītā* ?

A. He withdraws his senses from their objects as a tortoise draws in its limbs.

B. He gives up all actions and lives as a wandering renouncer.

C. He neither rejoices nor hates when he meets with good or evil.

D. He casts off all desires of the mind and is content in the self alone.

E. He keeps a relish (*rasa*) for sense-objects even after he sees the Supreme.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Arjuna asks Kṛṣṇa for the marks of the sthitaprajña in *Gītā* 2.54. Kṛṣṇa answers in verses 2.55–72.

- **A. Correct.** Verse 2.58 uses the image of the tortoise that draws in its limbs.
- **B. Not correct.** The *Gītā* does not ask for the giving up of action. It asks for action without attachment. The sthitaprajña is free from desire, not free from work.
- **C. Correct.** Verse 2.57 says that he does not rejoice or hate when good or evil comes.
- **D. Correct.** Verse 2.55 says that he casts off all desires and is content in the self by the self.
- **E. Not correct.** Verse 2.59 says that even the relish (rasa) goes away when he sees the Supreme. Fasting removes only the objects.

So the answer is A, C and D only. B is the trap, because it confuses steady wisdom with renunciation of action.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements correctly present Descartes' proofs for the existence of God in the *Meditations* ?

A. The idea of an infinite and perfect being must be caused by a being that actually has all the perfection the idea represents.

B. Everything that moves is moved by another, so there must be a first unmoved mover.

C. Existence can no more be separated from the essence of God than a valley can be separated from a mountain.

D. The existence of God cannot be proved by reason and must be accepted by faith alone.

E. I, who have the idea of God, could not exist as I do unless God existed.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Descartes gives three proofs.

- A is correct. This is the causal (trademark) argument of Meditation III. The cause of an idea must have at least as much reality as the idea represents.
- B is wrong. The argument from motion is the First Way of Aquinas, after Aristotle. Descartes does not use it.
- C is correct. This is the ontological argument of Meditation V. Descartes uses the mountain–valley and triangle comparisons.
- D is wrong. Descartes proves God by reason. God's existence then guarantees clear and distinct perceptions.
- E is correct. This is the second proof of Meditation III. A finite being with the idea of God could not cause or keep itself in existence.

Option (2) is the tempting one, because the argument from motion is a famous proof. But it belongs to Aquinas.

questions.question_md: Which one of the following best expresses 'negative liberty' as Isaiah Berlin uses the term ?
options: Self-mastery, in which one's rational or 'higher' self controls one's lower desires
Taking part in the making of the laws under which one lives
Freedom from interference by other persons within a certain area of action
Having the material resources needed to achieve one's chosen ends
questions.explanation:
In "Two Concepts of Liberty" (1958), Berlin separates two questions. Negative liberty asks: what is the area within which a person is left to do what he can, without interference by others? So negative liberty is freedom from interference. Option (3) is correct.

- Option (1) is positive liberty. It answers the question "Who governs me?" and is linked to self-mastery. This is the main trap.
- Option (2) is the democratic, participatory idea that Berlin also links with positive liberty.
- Option (4) is closer to the ability or capability to act. Berlin says that a lack of means is not in itself a lack of liberty.

questions.question_md: Which one of the following schools of Buddhism holds that the ultimate reality (*tattva*) is free from the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi-vinirmukta*) — it cannot be called existent, non-existent, both or neither — and that all things are empty (*śūnya*) of own-nature because they arise dependently ?
questions.explanation:
Nāgārjuna's Mādhyamika school uses the four-cornered negation (catuṣkoṭi). Reality is not "is", not "is not", not "both" and not "neither". It is beyond all views. Nāgārjuna also says that dependent arising (pratītyasamutpāda) is emptiness (śūnyatā). A thing that arises in dependence has no own-nature (svabhāva).

- Vaibhāṣika and Sautrāntika are realist schools. They accept real momentary dharmas with their own nature.
- Vijñānavāda (Yogācāra) denies outer objects, but it says that consciousness (vijñāna) is real. So it affirms one kind of being.

Vijñānavāda is the tempting option, because it is also a Mahāyāna school and it also uses the word śūnya. But only Mādhyamika makes reality free from all four alternatives.

questions.question_md: According to Immanuel Kant, a hypothetical imperative is one that :
options: commands an action as good in itself, without reference to any end
is the supreme principle of morality, binding on all rational beings
commands an action as a means to some end that the agent desires
expresses the agent's own feeling of approval towards the action
questions.explanation:
In the *Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals*, Kant divides imperatives into two kinds.

- A **hypothetical imperative** commands an action as a means to an end that the agent wants. Example: "If you want to be trusted, keep your word." It binds only those who want the end.
- A **categorical imperative** commands an action as good in itself, without any further end. It binds every rational being.

So the third option is correct.

- The first and second options describe the categorical imperative. These are the tempting distractors, because they use Kant's own terms.
- A feeling of approval is the emotivist or subjectivist account. Kant does not ground any imperative in feeling.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements are true of A. J. Ayer's account of knowledge in *The Problem of Knowledge* (1956) ?

A. If someone knows that p, then p must be true.

B. If someone knows that p, then he must be sure that p.

C. If someone knows that p, then he must have the right to be sure that p.

D. Knowing is a special state of mind which infallibly reveals its object to the knower.

E. Being completely sure that p is, by itself, sufficient for knowing that p.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
options: A, B, C and E only
questions.explanation:
At the end of chapter 1 of *The Problem of Knowledge*, Ayer gives three conditions for knowing that something is the case. What one knows must be true. One must be sure of it. One must have the right to be sure.

- **A – true.** This is the truth condition.
- **B – true.** This is the condition of being sure.
- **C – true.** This is the condition of the right to be sure. Ayer says that this right can be earned in different ways.
- **D – false.** Ayer rejects this view. He argues that knowing is not a special mental state that guarantees its own truth.
- **E – false.** A person can be completely sure and still be wrong. Also, he may have no right to be sure. So being sure is not sufficient.

So A, B and C only are true. 'A and B only' is the near miss, because it leaves out the right to be sure.

questions.question_md: Which of the following statements reflects Bhīṣma's view, in the *Śānti Parva* of the *Mahābhārata*, on the relation between the king and the age (yuga) ?
options: The age decides the conduct of the king, and the king cannot change it.
The king and the age both depend only on the past karma of the subjects.
The age is fixed by the gods, and the king can only read its signs.
The king is the cause of the age; his use of daṇḍanīti can bring about the Kṛta age.
questions.explanation:
In the *Śānti Parva* (Rājadharma section), Bhīṣma takes up a doubt: is the age the cause of the king, or is the king the cause of the age? His answer is clear: "The king is the cause of the age" (*rājā kālasya kāraṇam*).

He explains this through daṇḍanīti (the science of governance and punishment).
- When the king applies daṇḍanīti fully, the Kṛta age comes.
- When he gives up a part of it, the Tretā and Dvāpara ages follow.
- When he gives it up entirely, the Kali age comes.

So the king is responsible for the moral condition of his time.

The first option is the most tempting, because it is the view that Bhīṣma raises as a doubt. He then rejects it. The options on karma and on the gods take responsibility away from the king. This is the opposite of the Rājadharma teaching.

questions.question_md:
Which among the following statements are true with reference to Russell's philosophy of logical atomism ?

A. An atomic fact consists of a particular that has a quality, or of particulars that stand in a relation.

B. Russell holds that the world consists of things and not of facts.

C. Molecular propositions are formed from atomic propositions by words such as "or", "and" and "if".

D. In the strict logical sense, the only names are words like "this" and "that", which stand for particulars known by acquaintance.

E. The simples at which analysis finally arrives are the material atoms studied by physics.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Russell gave the lectures "The Philosophy of Logical Atomism" in 1918.

- **A – true.** The simplest facts are atomic facts. A particular has a quality, or two or more particulars stand in a relation.
- **B – false.** For Russell, the world contains facts. Facts make propositions true or false. They are not mere things.
- **C – true.** Molecular propositions contain words like "or", "and" and "if". They are built from atomic propositions.
- **D – true.** Ordinary names are disguised descriptions. Logically proper names are words like "this" and "that". They name particulars known by acquaintance.
- **E – false.** Russell says that his atoms are atoms of logical analysis, not of physical analysis.

So A, C and D only are true. 'A, B and C only' is tempting, but B reverses Russell's view that the world contains facts.

questions.question_md: Jaina ethics names three jewels (*tri-ratna*) which together form the path to liberation. Which one of the following gives these three jewels correctly ?
options: Right knowledge, right effort and right meditation
Right faith, right knowledge and right austerity
Right faith, right knowledge and right conduct
Right conduct, right livelihood and right faith
questions.explanation:
The first sūtra of Umāsvāti's *Tattvārthasūtra* says: "samyag-darśana-jñāna-cāritrāṇi mokṣa-mārgaḥ". Right faith, right knowledge and right conduct together are the path to liberation.

- Right faith (samyag-darśana) is belief in the Jaina truths (tattvas).
- Right knowledge (samyag-jñāna) is correct and complete knowledge of these truths.
- Right conduct (samyak-cāritra) is the practice of the vows and the avoidance of harm.

All three must be present together. One alone cannot give liberation.

- "Right effort", "right meditation" and "right livelihood" are not Jaina jewels. They are terms of Buddhist ethics.
- "Right austerity" is the near-miss. Tapas is a means of shedding karma, but it is not one of the three jewels.
