questions.explanation:
Heraclitus of Ephesus taught that everything is in flux (*panta rhei*). A river keeps its name, but new water always flows in. So the river we step into the second time is not the same. Change is the basic fact of the world. A hidden *logos* keeps a measure and order in this change.

- **Parmenides** says the opposite. Being is one and unchanging, and change is an illusion.
- **Zeno of Elea** defends Parmenides with paradoxes against motion.
- **Thales** takes water as the first principle, but he does not give the river saying.

The tempting distractor is Thales, because the fragment mentions water.

questions.question_md: According to St. Thomas Aquinas, which one of the following truths about God exceeds the power of natural reason and can be known only through revelation ?
options: That God is a Trinity of three Persons
That God is the first efficient cause
questions.explanation:
In the *Summa contra Gentiles* (I.3), Aquinas divides truths about God into two kinds.

- Some truths exceed all the power of human reason. His example is that God is three and one (the Trinity). We know them only through revelation, by faith.
- Other truths natural reason can reach. His examples are that God exists and that God is one. Philosophers such as Aristotle proved them by reason.

So reason and faith do not conflict. Reason proves the ‘preambles of faith’, and revelation adds the mysteries.

- **God exists** and **God is the first efficient cause**: the Five Ways prove these by reason.
- **God is one**: Aquinas names this as a truth that reason can prove.

The near-miss is ‘God is one’. It sounds like a doctrine of faith, but Aquinas puts it on the side of reason.

questions.question_md: Spinoza defines substance as ‘that which is in itself and is conceived through itself’. According to the *Ethics*, which of the following does **not** follow from this definition ?
options: Two or more substances can have the same attribute.
It belongs to the nature of substance to exist; it is the cause of itself.
One substance cannot be produced by another substance.
questions.explanation:
Spinoza proves in *Ethics* Part I, Proposition 5, that there cannot be two or more substances of the same nature or attribute. If two substances shared an attribute, nothing could distinguish them. So the statement in option 2 contradicts his system.

- **Necessarily infinite** (I P8): a finite substance would be limited by another of the same nature, and this is impossible.
- **Exists by its own nature** (I P7): substance cannot be produced by anything else, so it is self-caused (*causa sui*).
- **Not produced by another** (I P6): two substances have nothing in common, so one cannot cause the other.

The tempting wrong answer is option 1, because people think of many finite things. But for Spinoza finite things are modes, not substances.

questions.question_md: In the Vedānta account of the law of karma, the portion of past karma that has already begun to bear fruit, and that has produced the present body, is called :
questions.explanation:
The Vedānta divides karma into three stocks by the time of its fruit.

- *Prārabdha* karma has already started to give fruit. It has produced the present body and life. Even knowledge does not stop it; it ends only when it is used up.
- *Sañcita* karma is the stored karma of past lives that has not yet started to give fruit.
- *Āgāmi* (or *kriyamāṇa*) karma is the new karma made in this life, which will give fruit in the future.
- *Niṣiddha* karma is a Mīmāṃsā term for forbidden acts. It is not one of the three stocks.

*Sañcita* is the most tempting, because it is also past karma. But sañcita karma has not yet begun to bear fruit.

questions.question_md: In Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika ethics, the merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) that an action leaves in the self, and that later bring about its fruits, are together called :
questions.explanation:
In Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, good actions produce *dharma* (merit) and bad actions produce *adharma* (demerit). Both are qualities of the self. They cannot be seen, so together they are called *adṛṣṭa* (the unseen). Adṛṣṭa brings the fruits of actions to the agent at the right time, in this life or in a later life.

- *Saṃskāra* in Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika is a separate quality, such as the impression that causes memory.
- *Vāsanā* (latent tendency) is a term used mainly in Yoga and Buddhism.
- *Ṛta* is the Vedic cosmic and moral order, not a quality of the self.

*Saṃskāra* is the most tempting, because it is also a trace left in the self. But Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika lists dharma and adharma apart from saṃskāra.

questions.question_md: Among the four *puruṣārthas*, which one is the regulating principle that should guide the pursuit of *artha* and *kāma* ?
questions.explanation:
The Indian tradition accepts wealth (*artha*) and pleasure (*kāma*) as proper goals of life. But a person must seek them within the limits of *dharma* (moral and social duty). Dharma controls the means and the measure of these goals. So wealth and pleasure become good only when dharma guides them.

- *Kāma* and *artha* are the goals that dharma regulates. They do not regulate themselves.
- *Mokṣa* is the final goal of life. It is freedom from the cycle of birth and death. It is not the rule that controls daily pursuits.

*Mokṣa* is the most tempting, because it is the highest puruṣārtha. But the regulating role belongs to dharma.

questions.question_md: The thesis that no 'ought' conclusion can be validly derived from premises that state only what 'is' the case is classically associated with :
questions.explanation:
David Hume stated this thesis in *A Treatise of Human Nature* (Book III, Part I, Section I). He noticed that moral writers move from 'is' statements to 'ought' statements without any explanation. He said that this new relation needs a reason, because it cannot be deduced from the old ones. Later writers call this point the is–ought gap or 'Hume's Law'.

- **G. E. Moore** is the most tempting distractor. His 'naturalistic fallacy' (1903) is a related but different thesis. It says that 'good' cannot be defined by any natural property. Moore came about 160 years after Hume.
- **Aristotle** bases ethics on human nature and its function, so he does not separate fact and value in this way.
- **Kant** separates empirical facts from the moral law, but the 'is–ought' formulation belongs to Hume.

questions.question_md: Which among the following most appropriately defines **rule utilitarianism** ?
options: An act is right if it produces more good for the agent himself than any other act open to him.
An act is right if its own consequences are better than those of any other act open to the agent.
An act is right if its maxim can be willed as a universal law, whatever its consequences may be.
An act is right if it conforms to a rule whose general acceptance would produce the best consequences.
questions.explanation:
Rule utilitarianism judges an act in two steps. First, it asks which rules would produce the best consequences if people generally accepted them. Then it calls an act right when the act conforms to such a rule. So utility tests the rule, and the rule tests the act.

- Option 2 is the most tempting distractor. It defines **act utilitarianism**, which applies the principle of utility directly to each single act.
- Option 1 defines **ethical egoism**, because it counts only the agent's own good.
- Option 3 states Kant's test of universalizability. It ignores consequences, so it is deontological, not utilitarian.

questions.question_md: “Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains. One thinks himself the master of others, and still remains a greater slave than they.” With whom is the above statement associated ?
questions.explanation:
These are the opening lines of Chapter 1 of Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s *The Social Contract* (1762). Rousseau asks how the bonds of society can become legitimate. His answer is a contract in which each person places himself under the supreme direction of the general will.

- **Hobbes** describes the state of nature as a war of all against all. He does not use this line.
- **Locke** writes about natural rights to life, liberty and property in the *Second Treatise*.
- **Marx** speaks of chains in the *Communist Manifesto*: workers “have nothing to lose but their chains”. That is a different line.

Marx is the tempting distractor because of the word ‘chains’.

questions.question_md: According to Swami Vivekananda, religion is the manifestation of :
options: the knowledge stored in the scriptures
the fear of a personal God
questions.explanation:
Vivekananda gives two short definitions. They are easy to mix up.

- "Religion is the manifestation of the Divinity already in man."
- "Education is the manifestation of the perfection already in man."

So, for religion, the key word is *Divinity*. For Vivekananda, every soul is potentially divine. Religion does not add something new to man. It brings out the divine nature that is already present.

Why the other options are wrong:

- "The perfection already in man" is his definition of education, not of religion. This is the tempting trap.
- Religion is not book learning. Vivekananda says that religion is realisation, not doctrines or books.
- He rejects a religion based on fear. He calls fear a weakness and wants a religion of strength.

questions.question_md: In Deendayal Upadhyaya's *Integral Humanism*, what is the name for the innate nature or 'soul' of a nation, which decides what is acceptable to its culture ?
questions.explanation:
Upadhyaya calls the innate nature of a nation its **Chiti**. Chiti is like the soul of the nation. It is present from the birth of the nation. It decides which ideas and practices the culture accepts and which it rejects.

Why the other options are wrong:

- **Virāṭ** is the vital power of the nation. It gets its energy from Chiti, and it keeps the nation strong and united. It is the tempting option, because the two ideas always appear together.
- **Antyodaya** means the rise of the last person. It is a goal of economic policy, not the soul of the nation.
- **Dharma-rājya** is a state governed by dharma. It is a political ideal, not the innate nature of a people.

questions.question_md: Who among the following philosophers wrote *The Will to Believe* (1896), which defends our right to adopt a religious belief when the evidence cannot settle the question ?
questions.explanation:
William James wrote "The Will to Believe" in 1896. It is a lecture, and it also gives its name to his 1897 book of essays.

James says that some choices are "genuine options". A genuine option is live, forced and momentous. When the intellect cannot settle such an option, our passional nature may lawfully decide it. Religious belief is his main example.

- **Peirce** founded pragmatism as a theory of meaning. He did not write this essay.
- **Dewey** developed instrumentalism. His work on religion is *A Common Faith*.
- **Royce** was an absolute idealist. He was a colleague of James, but he criticised the pragmatist theory of truth.

questions.question_md: Which among the following philosophers holds that "subjectivity is truth", and that truth for an existing individual lies in passionate, inward commitment rather than in objective knowledge ?
questions.explanation:
Søren Kierkegaard states this thesis in the *Concluding Unscientific Postscript* (1846), under the name Johannes Climacus.

For Kierkegaard, objective thought asks only *what* is true. Existential truth asks *how* a person relates to what he believes. Truth for the existing individual is "an objective uncertainty held fast in the most passionate inwardness". This is the basis of his idea of faith.

- **Husserl** wants philosophy to be a rigorous science. He does not praise subjective passion.
- **Heidegger** studies the Being of Dasein. He does not use this slogan.
- **Nietzsche** is the tempting option because of his perspectivism. But perspectivism is a claim about interpretation, not about inward faith.

questions.question_md: In *Being and Time*, Heidegger says that idle talk (*Gerede*), curiosity (*Neugier*) and ambiguity (*Zweideutigkeit*) characterise the everyday Being of Dasein. Which basic way of Being of Dasein do these three show ?
questions.explanation:
In *Being and Time* (§§35–38), Heidegger first describes idle talk, curiosity and ambiguity. Then he says that together they show "falling" (*Verfallen*).

In falling, Dasein is absorbed in the everyday world of the "they" (*das Man*). Idle talk repeats what "one" says. Curiosity seeks novelty for its own sake. Ambiguity hides what is really understood. Falling is not a moral fall. It is a basic, inauthentic way of everyday existence.

- **Thrownness** is the most tempting option. It is the fact that Dasein finds itself already delivered over to a world. It is not the everyday absorption in the "they".
- **Resoluteness** is the authentic response to the call of conscience. It is the opposite of falling.
- **Being-towards-death** individualises Dasein. It pulls Dasein out of the "they".

questions.question_md: Which of the following is the motto that Husserl gave to phenomenology, as a call to describe what is given in experience before any theory ?
questions.explanation:
Husserl's motto is "To the things themselves" (*Zu den Sachen selbst*). He uses it in the *Logical Investigations* (1900–01).

The motto asks the philosopher to turn away from inherited theories and empty words. The philosopher must go back to the phenomena as they are given in intuition and describe them faithfully.

- **"Back to Kant"** was the slogan of the neo-Kantian movement (Otto Liebmann, 1865). Husserl did not adopt it.
- **"Existence precedes essence"** is Sartre's formula for human existence.
- **"To be is to be perceived"** (*esse est percipi*) is Berkeley's principle of idealism.

questions.question_md: In *The Problems of Philosophy*, Russell argues that Berkeley's case for idealism rests on an equivocation in the word "idea". Between which two things does Berkeley fail to distinguish ?
options: The act of apprehending and the object that is apprehended
Knowledge by acquaintance and knowledge by description
The primary qualities and the secondary qualities of things
The sense of an expression and its reference
questions.explanation:
In chapter 4 ("Idealism") of *The Problems of Philosophy* (1912), Russell refutes Berkeley's argument.

Russell says that "idea" can mean two things. It can mean the mental act of apprehending a thing. It can also mean the thing that the act apprehends. The act is surely in the mind. Berkeley then moves, by an unconscious equivocation, to the claim that the apprehended object is also in the mind. So the argument for idealism is fallacious.

- **Acquaintance and description** is Russell's own distinction (chapter 5). It is the near-miss option, but it is not his diagnosis of Berkeley.
- **Primary and secondary qualities** is Locke's distinction. Berkeley rejects it, but Russell does not use it here.
- **Sense and reference** is Frege's distinction.

questions.question_md: In "Two Dogmas of Empiricism", what view does W. V. O. Quine put forward in place of the dogma of reductionism ?
options: Each synthetic statement has its own unique range of confirming and disconfirming experiences.
Analytic statements are true come what may, and only synthetic statements can be revised.
Our statements about the external world face the tribunal of experience as a corporate body, not one by one.
A statement is meaningful only if experience can conclusively verify it.
questions.explanation:
Quine's positive view in the last section of "Two Dogmas" (1951) is holism. He says that "our statements about the external world face the tribunal of sense experience not individually but only as a corporate body".

Our knowledge is a man-made fabric (or web) that touches experience only at its edges. A conflict with experience forces some change in the system. But we have choices about which statements to revise.

- **Option 1** is the most tempting. But it states the dogma of reductionism itself, which Quine rejects.
- **Option 2** is false for Quine. He says that no statement is immune to revision, not even the laws of logic.
- **Option 4** is the strong verification principle of logical positivism. Quine's holism rejects the idea of testing statements one at a time.

questions.question_md: In "Proof of an External World" (1939), G. E. Moore states the conditions that make his proof a rigorous one. Which of the following is **NOT** one of those conditions ?
options: The premiss is different from the conclusion.
The premiss is something that Moore knows to be the case, and not merely something that he believes.
The conclusion really follows from the premiss.
The premiss has itself been proved from other, more certain premisses.
questions.explanation:
Moore's proof is "Here is one hand, and here is another". He says that it is perfectly rigorous because it meets three conditions:

- **Option 1:** the premiss is different from the conclusion. This is a condition.
- **Option 2:** Moore knows the premiss. He does not merely believe it, and it is not merely true by luck. This is a condition.
- **Option 3:** the conclusion ("two external things exist") really follows from the premiss. This is a condition.
- **Option 4** is **not** a condition. Moore admits that he cannot prove his premisses. He says that he knows them all the same. He holds that we can know many things that we cannot prove.

Option 2 is the tempting distractor. Some students think that Moore only claims common-sense belief. In fact he claims knowledge, and knowledge without proof is the centre of his reply to the sceptic.

questions.question_md: Nietzsche calls for a radical overturning of the moral values that Christianity and its Platonic heritage have handed down. What does he call this project ?
questions.explanation:
Nietzsche names this project the "revaluation of all values" (*Umwertung aller Werte*). He uses the phrase in *The Antichrist* and *Ecce Homo* (1888).

Nietzsche holds that Christian and Platonic morality are hostile to life. The revaluation must replace them with values that affirm life.

- **Will to power** is the tempting option. It is the basic drive in all life. It is the standard by which values are judged, not the name of the project.
- **Eternal recurrence** is the thought that one's life will repeat itself endlessly. It is a test of affirmation.
- **Amor fati** (love of fate) is the attitude of accepting everything that happens, without wishing anything to be different.

questions.question_md: In the *Arthaśāstra*, Kauṭilya advises the king to test the integrity of his ministers by secret tests (upadhā). Besides the tests based on dharma, artha and kāma, what is the fourth test based on ?
questions.explanation:
Kauṭilya discusses these tests in Book 1 of the *Arthaśāstra*. The king uses secret agents to tempt each minister. The four tests are:

- **Dharmopadhā:** a test with a religious or moral appeal.
- **Arthopadhā:** a test with an offer of money.
- **Kāmopadhā:** a test with the temptation of love or desire.
- **Bhayopadhā:** a test with fear, for example a threat of danger.

The king then gives each minister work that fits the tests that he has passed. This is part of Kauṭilya's system of internal security.

Why the other options are wrong:

- **Mokṣa** is the tempting trap. Dharma, artha and kāma are three puruṣārthas, so mokṣa looks like the natural fourth. But Kauṭilya's list is about practical loyalty, and fear replaces liberation.
- **Mantra** is counsel. It is not one of the tests.
- **Yaśas** (fame) is not one of the tests.

questions.question_md: The words 'socialist' and 'secular' were added to the Preamble of the Constitution of India by which one of the following ?
questions.explanation:
Parliament passed the 42nd Amendment Act in 1976, during the Emergency. It added three words to the Preamble: 'socialist', 'secular' and 'integrity'. So India became a "sovereign socialist secular democratic republic".

The Constitution already had secular features before 1976. Articles 25 to 28 protect freedom of religion. The amendment only made the secular ideal explicit in the Preamble.

Why the other options are wrong:

- **The 44th Amendment (1978)** is the tempting trap. It changed many Emergency-era provisions. But it kept the new words in the Preamble.
- **The 24th Amendment (1971)** dealt with the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution.
- **The 52nd Amendment (1985)** added the anti-defection law.

questions.question_md: In John Rawls’s original position, the parties rank the alternatives by their worst possible outcomes and choose the alternative whose worst outcome is better than the worst outcomes of all the others. This rule of choice is called the -----
questions.explanation:
In *A Theory of Justice* (§26), Rawls says the parties behind the veil of ignorance follow the **maximin rule**. The name means ‘maximum minimorum’: maximise the minimum. The parties do not know their place in society. So they choose the principles whose worst result is the least bad. Rawls uses this rule to argue for his two principles rather than for utilitarianism.

- **Principle of average utility**: Rawls rejects it. It may sacrifice some people for a higher average.
- **Pareto principle**: a test of efficiency, not this rule of choice under uncertainty.
- **Principle of insufficient reason**: it gives equal chances to every outcome. Rawls rejects it in the original position.

The near-miss is the principle of insufficient reason. It also concerns choice under uncertainty, but it leads to average utility.

questions.question_md: Who among the following philosophers holds that cities will have no rest from evils until philosophers become kings or kings become philosophers ?
questions.explanation:
Plato says this in the *Republic* (Book V, 473c–d). In his ideal state, political power and philosophy must come together. Only the philosopher knows the Form of the Good, so only he can rule justly.

- **Aristotle** prefers a mixed constitution (polity). He does not make philosophers the rulers.
- **Hobbes** gives power to an absolute sovereign by covenant, whatever his wisdom.
- **Rousseau** puts sovereignty in the general will of the people.

Aristotle is the tempting distractor because he is also a Greek theorist of the ideal state.

questions.question_md: Which among the statements best explains ‘dialectical materialism’ in Marxist philosophy ?
options: Matter is primary and develops through the struggle of opposites; consciousness is a product of matter.
Absolute Spirit develops through the struggle of opposites; matter is only its outward expression.
Matter consists of unchanging atoms that combine mechanically, without any inner contradiction.
Moral ideas are the main force of social change and develop apart from economic conditions.
questions.explanation:
Dialectical materialism joins two ideas. Marx and Engels took the dialectic from Hegel: reality develops through the struggle and unity of opposites. But they made it materialist: matter is primary, and mind or consciousness is a product of matter. Marx says he found Hegel’s dialectic ‘standing on its head’ and set it right side up.

- **Option 2** is Hegel’s idealist dialectic. Spirit, not matter, is primary.
- **Option 3** is the old mechanical materialism. It has matter but no dialectic.
- **Option 4** is an idealist view of history. Marxism holds that ideas depend on material conditions.

Option 2 is the near-miss. It keeps the dialectic but reverses the relation of matter and spirit.

questions.question_md: A deductive argument that is valid and has all true premises is called :
questions.explanation:
A sound argument is a valid deductive argument whose premises are all true. Because it is valid, true premises guarantee a true conclusion. So every sound argument has a true conclusion.

- **Cogent** is the most tempting distractor. Many logic books use it for a strong *inductive* argument with true premises. It does not apply to a valid deductive argument.
- **Consistent** describes a set of statements that can all be true together. It does not describe an argument that is valid and has true premises.
- **Tautologous** describes a statement form that is true for every assignment of truth values.

questions.question_md: In quantification theory, an expression that contains at least one free individual variable is neither true nor false. Which one of the following expressions is of this kind ?
questions.explanation:
A propositional function contains at least one free (unbound) individual variable. So it is neither true nor false. It becomes a proposition when we put a constant for the variable or bind the variable with a quantifier.

- **Fx · Ga:** the variable x is free because no quantifier binds it. So this is a propositional function.
- **(x)(Fx ⊃ Gx):** the universal quantifier binds both occurrences of x. So this is a general proposition.
- **(∃x)(Fx · Gx):** the existential quantifier binds x. So this is also a general proposition.
- **Fa ⊃ Gb:** it has only the individual constants a and b, and no variables. So it is a compound singular proposition.

The trap is that 'Fx · Ga' contains the constant a. A constant in one part does not bind the free x in the other part.

questions.question_md: Who argued, in *Respect for Nature* (1986), that every living organism is a 'teleological centre of life' with inherent worth, and so deserves moral respect ?
questions.explanation:
Paul W. Taylor wrote *Respect for Nature: A Theory of Environmental Ethics* (1986). His view is called biocentric egalitarianism.

Each living thing pursues its own good in its own way. So each organism is a teleological centre of life. For Taylor, all such organisms have equal inherent worth. Humans are not superior to other living things.

Why the other options are wrong:

- **Aldo Leopold** is the tempting trap. But his land ethic is holistic. It values the biotic community as a whole, not each single organism.
- **J. Baird Callicott** defended and developed Leopold's holistic land ethic.
- **Arne Naess** founded deep ecology. He stressed self-realisation and the identification of the self with nature.

questions.question_md: A surrogacy arrangement in which the surrogate mother receives no payment or reward, apart from her medical expenses and insurance cover, is called :
questions.explanation:
Surrogacy is classified in two different ways.

1. By payment:
   - **Altruistic surrogacy:** the surrogate gets only her medical costs and insurance. She gets no fee.
   - **Commercial surrogacy:** the surrogate gets a fee or reward beyond these costs.
2. By genetic link:
   - **Traditional surrogacy:** the surrogate's own egg is used, so she is the genetic mother.
   - **Gestational surrogacy:** an embryo from other people is placed in her womb. She has no genetic link to the child.

The question is about payment, so the answer is altruistic surrogacy. India's Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021 allows only this type.

Gestational and traditional surrogacy are tempting only if you mix the two ways of classifying surrogacy.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following limbs of Patañjali's *aṣṭāṅga yoga* in the order in which the *Yoga Sūtra* lists them :

A. Pratyāhāra

B. Āsana

C. Dhāraṇā

D. Niyama

E. Prāṇāyāma

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
*Yoga Sūtra* 2.29 lists the eight limbs: *yama, niyama, āsana, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna* and *samādhi*.

- D. Niyama (observances) comes second, after yama.
- B. Āsana (posture) is third.
- E. Prāṇāyāma (control of breath) is fourth.
- A. Pratyāhāra (withdrawal of the senses) is fifth.
- C. Dhāraṇā (concentration) is sixth. It starts the inner limbs (*antaraṅga*).

So, the order is D, B, E, A, C.

The fourth option swaps pratyāhāra and dhāraṇā. The first option swaps āsana and prāṇāyāma. Both are adjacent swaps.

questions.question_md:
According to the Vaiśeṣika theory of atomic causation (*paramāṇu-kāraṇavāda*), arrange the following from the simplest to the most complex, in the building up of a gross element :

A. Tryaṇuka (triad)

B. Paramāṇu (atom)

C. Caturaṇuka (tetrad)

D. Dvyaṇuka (dyad)

E. Mahābhūta (gross element)

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
In Vaiśeṣika, the eternal atoms (*paramāṇu*) are the material cause of the physical world. Gross things are built up step by step.

- B. Paramāṇu: the partless, eternal atom comes first.
- D. Dvyaṇuka: two atoms join to form a dyad.
- A. Tryaṇuka: three dyads join to form a triad. The triad is the smallest perceptible thing.
- C. Caturaṇuka: four triads join to form a tetrad.
- E. Mahābhūta: larger and larger wholes then make the gross element.

So, the order is B, D, A, C, E.

The fourth option swaps the triad and the tetrad. The first option puts the triad before the dyad. Both break the step-by-step order.

questions.question_md:
According to Leibnitz’s *Monadology*, arrange the following monads from the lowest to the highest:

A. Rational souls or spirits

B. Bare (naked) monads

C. Animal souls

D. God, the supreme monad

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Leibnitz ranks monads by the clearness of their perceptions.

- **B. Bare monads**: they have only confused, unconscious perceptions, as in a dreamless sleep.
- **C. Animal souls**: they have feeling and memory, so their perceptions are more distinct.
- **A. Rational souls (spirits)**: they also have reason and self-consciousness (apperception). They know necessary truths.
- **D. God**: the primary unity and supreme monad. His perceptions are fully clear and adequate.

So the order is B, C, A, D.

Option 1 swaps bare monads and animal souls. Option 4 gives the order from highest to lowest.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following stages of the prisoner’s ascent in Plato’s Allegory of the Cave, from the first to the last:

A. He looks at the sun itself and sees it as it is.

B. He sees only the shadows cast on the wall in front of him.

C. Outside the cave, he first sees shadows and reflections in water, and then the things themselves.

D. He turns round and sees the fire and the objects carried along behind him.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Plato gives this allegory in *Republic* Book VII.

- **B**: the chained prisoners see only shadows on the cave wall and take them to be reality.
- **D**: a freed prisoner turns round. He sees the fire and the objects whose shadows he saw.
- **C**: he is dragged out of the cave. His eyes are weak, so he first looks at shadows and reflections in water, then at the things.
- **A**: last of all, he can look at the sun itself. The sun stands for the Form of the Good.

So the order is B, D, C, A.

Option 3 puts the outside world before the fire. But the prisoner must first turn round inside the cave.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following steps of St. Anselm’s ontological argument in *Proslogion* II in their logical order:

A. Therefore, that than which nothing greater can be conceived exists both in the understanding and in reality.

B. Even the fool, when he hears the words ‘that than which nothing greater can be conceived’, understands what he hears.

C. Then that than which nothing greater can be conceived would be something than which a greater can be conceived, which is a contradiction.

D. Whatever is understood is in the understanding, so this being exists at least in the understanding.

E. Suppose it exists in the understanding alone; then it can be thought to exist in reality as well, which is greater.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Anselm’s argument in *Proslogion* II is a *reductio ad absurdum*.

- **B**: even the fool (who says there is no God) understands the phrase.
- **D**: what is understood is in the understanding. So the being exists at least there.
- **E**: suppose it exists only in the understanding. A being that also exists in reality is greater.
- **C**: then we could conceive something greater than the greatest conceivable being. This is a contradiction.
- **A**: so the supposition is false. The being exists both in the understanding and in reality.

So the order is B, D, E, C, A.

Option 4 states the contradiction before the supposition that produces it. Option 1 makes the supposition before the being is shown to be in the understanding.

questions.question_md:
Identify the correct chronological order of publication of the works given below :

A. *Freedom from the Known*

B. *Rāja Yoga*

C. *The Buddha and His Dhamma*

D. *The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam*

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Link each work to its author and date.

- B. *Rāja Yoga* by Swami Vivekananda came out in 1896.
- D. *The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam* by Muhammad Iqbal came out in 1930. It collects his Madras lectures. An enlarged edition followed in 1934.
- C. *The Buddha and His Dhamma* by B. R. Ambedkar came out in 1957, after his death in 1956.
- A. *Freedom from the Known* by J. Krishnamurti came out in 1969.

So the order is B, D, C, A.

The tempting wrong option is "B, C, D, A". It puts Ambedkar before Iqbal. But Iqbal died in 1938, so his lectures came long before Ambedkar's last book. The options that start with D are wrong because Vivekananda's book is the oldest.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following ethical ideas based on the chronology of their emergence :

A. Ethics of care as a 'different voice' in moral reasoning

B. Hedonic calculus for measuring pleasures and pains

C. Ataraxia, or freedom from mental disturbance, as the goal of life

D. Justice as fairness, chosen behind a veil of ignorance

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Place each idea with its thinker and date.

- **C** – Epicurus (341–270 BCE) taught that ataraxia (calm of mind) and freedom from bodily pain make the happy life.
- **B** – Jeremy Bentham gave the hedonic (felicific) calculus in *An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation* (1789).
- **D** – John Rawls gave 'justice as fairness' and the veil of ignorance in *A Theory of Justice* (1971).
- **A** – Carol Gilligan described the ethics of care in *In a Different Voice* (1982).

So the order is C, B, D, A.

Option 'C, B, A, D' is the most tempting wrong order. It swaps the two modern ideas. Rawls (1971) came about eleven years before Gilligan (1982). Option 'B, C, D, A' wrongly puts Bentham before the ancient Greek Epicurus.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following grades of theoretic consciousness, according to K. C. Bhattacharyya, from the lower to the higher :

A. Spiritual thought

B. Empirical thought

C. Transcendental thought

D. Pure objective thought

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
K. C. Bhattacharyya ranks theoretic consciousness in four grades. Each grade is freer from the object than the one before it.

- B. **Empirical thought** is about facts that we can perceive. It is the thought of science.
- D. **Pure objective thought** is about objects that we cannot perceive but can still think. It is the philosophy of the object, for example logic and metaphysics.
- A. **Spiritual thought** turns to the subject itself. It is the philosophy of the spirit.
- C. **Transcendental thought** is the highest grade. It is the philosophy of truth, which goes beyond subject and object.

So the order is B, D, A, C.

The tempting wrong option is "B, D, C, A". It puts transcendental thought below spiritual thought. For Bhattacharyya, the transcendental is the last and highest grade.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following stages of the triple transformation in Sri Aurobindo's Integral Yoga in the order in which they take place :

A. Supramental transformation

B. Psychic transformation

C. Spiritual transformation

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
In *The Life Divine*, Sri Aurobindo describes a triple transformation of the human being.

- B. **Psychic transformation** comes first. The psychic being (the soul within) comes forward and guides mind, life and body.
- C. **Spiritual transformation** comes next. Light and force from higher planes of the spirit descend into the whole nature.
- A. **Supramental transformation** comes last. The Supermind transforms the whole being, including the body.

So the order is B, C, A.

The tempting wrong option is "B, A, C". It starts correctly with the psychic stage. But the supramental change is the final step, not the middle one.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following propositions in the order in which they appear in Wittgenstein's *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus* :

A. A logical picture of facts is a thought.

B. What we cannot speak about we must pass over in silence.

C. The world is all that is the case.

D. A thought is a proposition with a sense.

E. What is the case – a fact – is the existence of states of affairs.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
These are main numbered propositions of the *Tractatus* (Pears–McGuinness translation):

- **C** is proposition 1: "The world is all that is the case."
- **E** is proposition 2: a fact is the existence of states of affairs.
- **A** is proposition 3: a logical picture of facts is a thought.
- **D** is proposition 4: a thought is a proposition with a sense.
- **B** is proposition 7, the last one: what we cannot speak about we must pass over in silence.

So the order is C, E, A, D, B.

The book moves from the world, to facts, to pictures of facts (thoughts), to propositions, and finally to silence. The tempting option "C, E, D, A, B" reverses thought and proposition. But Wittgenstein first defines a thought as a picture (3). Then he says that a thought is a proposition with a sense (4).

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following works in the order of their first publication, from the earliest to the latest :

A. Frege, "On Sense and Reference"

B. Quine, "Two Dogmas of Empiricism"

C. Russell, "On Denoting"

D. Wittgenstein, *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus*

E. Moore, "The Refutation of Idealism"

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
The dates of first publication are:

- **A.** Frege, "Über Sinn und Bedeutung" (On Sense and Reference) – 1892.
- **E.** Moore, "The Refutation of Idealism", in *Mind* – 1903.
- **C.** Russell, "On Denoting", in *Mind* – 1905.
- **D.** Wittgenstein, *Tractatus* – 1921 in German (English edition 1922).
- **B.** Quine, "Two Dogmas of Empiricism", in *The Philosophical Review* – 1951.

So the order is A, E, C, D, B.

The close trap is "A, C, E, D, B". It puts Russell before Moore. But Moore's essay (1903) came two years before Russell's (1905). Frege is clearly the earliest, and Quine is clearly the latest.

questions.question_md:
Sequence the following stages in Thomas Hobbes’s account of the origin of the commonwealth in *Leviathan*:

A. Each man covenants with every other man to give up his right of governing himself to one man or to an assembly.

B. In the state of nature there is a war of every man against every man.

C. The multitude so united in one person is called a commonwealth, the great Leviathan.

D. Fear of death leads reason to suggest the laws of nature, the first of which is to seek peace.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Hobbes builds the state step by step in *Leviathan*.

- **B**: without a common power, life is a war of every man against every man (Chapter 13).
- **D**: fear of death makes men seek peace. Reason suggests the laws of nature, and the first is to seek peace (Chapter 14).
- **A**: to secure peace, each man covenants with every other man. Each gives up his right to govern himself to one sovereign (Chapter 17).
- **C**: the united multitude becomes one person, the commonwealth or Leviathan (Chapter 17).

So the order is B, D, A, C.

Option 2 puts the covenant before the laws of nature. But the covenant is how men follow the law of nature to seek peace.

questions.question_md:
The following lines make up a formal proof of validity for the argument whose only premise is P ⊃ (R · Q) and whose conclusion is P ⊃ R. Put the lines in the order in which they occur in the proof, beginning with the premise :

A. ~P ∨ R

B. P ⊃ (R · Q)

C. P ⊃ R

D. (~P ∨ R) · (~P ∨ Q)

E. ~P ∨ (R · Q)

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
The proof runs as follows.

1. **B:** P ⊃ (R · Q) — the premise.
2. **E:** ~P ∨ (R · Q) — from 1, by Material Implication.
3. **D:** (~P ∨ R) · (~P ∨ Q) — from 2, by Distribution.
4. **A:** ~P ∨ R — from 3, by Simplification.
5. **C:** P ⊃ R — from 4, by Material Implication.

So the order is B, E, D, A, C.

Option 'B, D, E, A, C' puts the distributed form before the disjunction. But Distribution needs the disjunction ~P ∨ (R · Q) first. Option 'B, E, A, D, C' uses Simplification before there is a conjunction to simplify.

questions.question_md:
What is the correct sequence of steps in proving the validity of an argument whose conclusion is a conditional statement by the rule of Conditional Proof (C.P.) ?

A. Assume the antecedent of the conclusion as an additional premise

B. Derive the consequent of the conclusion by the rules of inference and replacement

C. Infer the conditional conclusion by C.P. and discharge the assumption

D. Write down the given premises of the argument

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
The rule of Conditional Proof works in four steps.

1. **D:** Write the given premises first.
2. **A:** Assume the antecedent of the conditional conclusion as an additional premise. This starts the scope of the assumption.
3. **B:** From the premises and the assumption, derive the consequent of the conclusion by the rules.
4. **C:** Infer the whole conditional 'antecedent ⊃ consequent' by C.P. This step discharges the assumption and ends its scope.

So the order is D, A, B, C.

Option 'D, B, A, C' is the most tempting distractor. In C.P., we cannot derive the consequent before we make the assumption, because the derivation uses it. Options that start with A put the assumption before the given premises.

questions.question_md:
Find the correct order in the development of the philosophical conception of God in the history of western philosophy:

A. God is the unmoved mover, whose activity is thought thinking itself.

B. The Demiurge brings order into a pre-existing chaos and so makes the cosmos.

C. The existence of God is a postulate of pure practical reason.

D. God created time together with the world, so there was no time before creation.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Each idea belongs to a thinker, and the thinkers follow a clear historical order.

- **B. Demiurge**: Plato, *Timaeus* (4th century BCE).
- **A. Unmoved mover, thought thinking itself**: Aristotle, *Metaphysics* Book XII (Lambda). Aristotle was Plato’s pupil.
- **D. Time created with the world**: St. Augustine, *Confessions* Book XI (about 400 CE).
- **C. God as a postulate of practical reason**: Kant, *Critique of Practical Reason* (1788).

So the order is B, A, D, C.

Option 2 puts Aristotle before his teacher Plato. Option 3 puts Augustine before Aristotle.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements about the three orders of reality (*sattā*) in Advaita Vedānta are correct ?

A. Brahman alone has *pāramārthika sattā* (absolute reality).

B. The son of a barren woman has *prātibhāsika sattā*, just like the snake seen in a rope.

C. The world of everyday experience has *vyāvahārika sattā* (empirical reality).

D. The snake seen in a rope has *prātibhāsika sattā* (apparent reality).

E. Objects with *vyāvahārika sattā* are sublated by another ordinary waking perception.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Advaita grades things by whether and when they are sublated (*bādha*).

- A is correct. Brahman is never sublated, so it alone is absolutely real.
- B is not correct. The son of a barren woman is never experienced at all. Advaita calls it *tuccha* or *alīka* (wholly unreal). It has no sattā of any kind.
- C is correct. The world is real for all practical purposes until one knows Brahman.
- D is correct. The rope-snake appears only for a short time. It is real only while it appears.
- E is not correct. A later perception sublates the rope-snake. Only the knowledge of Brahman sublates the empirical world.

So, the answer is A, C and D only.

B is the most tempting, because both the rope-snake and the barren woman's son are unreal. But the rope-snake appears, and the other never appears.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following are among the Four Noble Truths (*ārya-satya*) taught by the Buddha ?

A. Duḥkha-nirodha – the cessation of suffering

B. Kṣaṇikatva – the momentariness of all things

C. Duḥkha – suffering

D. Śūnyatā – the emptiness of all things

E. Duḥkha-samudaya – the origin of suffering

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
The Buddha's first sermon gives the Four Noble Truths: *duḥkha* (suffering), *duḥkha-samudaya* (the origin of suffering), *duḥkha-nirodha* (the cessation of suffering) and *duḥkha-nirodha-gāminī pratipad* (the path to its cessation).

- A is correct. Cessation is the third truth.
- B is not correct. Momentariness is a later Buddhist doctrine (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*), not one of the four truths.
- C is correct. Suffering is the first truth.
- D is not correct. Emptiness is a Mādhyamika doctrine, not one of the four truths.
- E is correct. The origin of suffering is the second truth.

So, the answer is A, C and E only. B and D are tempting, because they are real Buddhist doctrines. But they are not among the four truths.

questions.question_md:
Which among the following statements are in accordance with Aristotle’s doctrine of form and matter, and of potentiality and actuality ?

A. Matter is the principle of potentiality and form is the principle of actuality.

B. The form of a sensible thing exists in a separate world, apart from the thing.

C. An acorn is potentially an oak tree, and the full-grown oak is its actuality.

D. Actuality is prior to potentiality in definition and in substance.

E. In a sensible thing, it is matter, not form, that makes the thing knowable and definable.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Aristotle explains change and being through form and matter, and through potentiality and actuality.

- **A. Correct.** Matter is what can become something. Form makes it actually something.
- **B. Incorrect.** This is Plato’s theory of separate Forms. For Aristotle, the form of a sensible thing exists in the thing.
- **C. Correct.** This is a standard example. The acorn has the potentiality, and the oak is its actuality.
- **D. Correct.** In *Metaphysics* IX (Theta) 8, Aristotle says actuality is prior in definition and in substance. We define ‘able to build’ through ‘building’.
- **E. Incorrect.** For Aristotle, form makes a thing knowable and definable. Matter as such is unknowable.

So A, C and D are correct. Option 2 is tempting, but it includes B, which is Plato’s doctrine.

questions.question_md:
Read the following statements about the Sophists and choose the correct statements:

A. Protagoras was the first to ask for payment for teaching, and he claimed to make his pupils good citizens.

B. Gorgias argued that nothing exists; that if anything existed, it could not be known; and that if it were known, it could not be communicated.

C. The Sophists held that there is one absolute truth, the same for all men, which reason can know.

D. Protagoras said that about the gods he could not know whether they exist or not.

E. Gorgias held that speech has no real power over the soul, so rhetoric is a useless art.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
The Sophists were paid teachers of the 5th century BCE. They taught rhetoric and success in public life.

- **A. Correct.** In Plato’s *Protagoras*, Protagoras openly asks for fees. He promises to teach the art of politics.
- **B. Correct.** This is Gorgias’ three-step thesis in *On Not-Being*.
- **C. Incorrect.** The Sophists were relativists or sceptics. They denied one absolute truth for all.
- **D. Correct.** This is Protagoras’ famous agnostic fragment about the gods.
- **E. Incorrect.** In the *Encomium of Helen*, Gorgias calls speech a ‘mighty lord’. It works on the soul like a drug.

So A, B and D are correct. Statement C is the trap: absolute, universal truth is the aim of Socrates and Plato, not of the Sophists.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements about the kinds of *vidhi* (injunction) in Pūrva Mīmāṃsā are correct ?

A. A *niyama-vidhi* forbids an act outright, as in "*na kalañjaṃ bhakṣayet*".

B. An *apūrva-vidhi* enjoins an act that cannot be known through any other means.

C. A *niyama-vidhi* makes one means compulsory where several means could serve the purpose, as in "*vrīhīn avahanti*".

D. A *parisaṅkhyā-vidhi* works by excluding what it does not mention, as in "*pañca pañcanakhā bhakṣyāḥ*".

E. A *parisaṅkhyā-vidhi* enjoins an act that is not known at all from any other source.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Mīmāṃsā manuals such as the *Arthasaṃgraha* name three kinds of vidhi by their function.

- A is not correct. "One should not eat kalañja" is a *niṣedha* (prohibition), not a niyama-vidhi.
- B is correct. An *apūrva-vidhi* teaches something that no other pramāṇa can tell us.
- C is correct. Rice can be husked by pounding or with the nails. "One should pound the rice" makes pounding compulsory. This is a *niyama-vidhi* (restrictive rule).
- D is correct. "Five five-clawed animals may be eaten" excludes the eating of other five-clawed animals. This is a *parisaṅkhyā-vidhi* (exclusive rule).
- E is not correct. It describes an apūrva-vidhi, not a parisaṅkhyā-vidhi.

So, the answer is B, C and D only.

E is the most tempting, because it describes a real kind of vidhi. But the definition belongs to apūrva-vidhi.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements about the *bodhisattva* ideal in Mahāyāna Buddhism are correct ?

A. A bodhisattva seeks only his own release from suffering, as the arhat does.

B. A bodhisattva vows to work for the liberation of all suffering beings.

C. *Upāya-kauśalya* (skill in means) is the ability to adapt the teaching to the need and capacity of each hearer.

D. *Upāya-kauśalya* requires that one fixed form of the teaching be given to all hearers alike.

E. Compassion (*karuṇā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are the twin marks of the bodhisattva.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
In Mahāyāna, the bodhisattva seeks enlightenment for the good of all beings, not for himself alone.

- A is not correct. Seeking only one's own release is the ideal that Mahāyāna criticises in the arhat. The bodhisattva goes beyond it.
- B is correct. The bodhisattva vows to help all beings reach liberation.
- C is correct. *Upāya-kauśalya* means skilful means. The teacher fits the teaching to the person, as a doctor fits the medicine to the patient.
- D is not correct. This is the opposite of skill in means.
- E is correct. Karuṇā moves the bodhisattva to help others. Prajñā lets him see the emptiness of all things.

So, the answer is B, C and E only. A is tempting for a candidate who confuses the bodhisattva with the arhat ideal.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements are true of Kant ?

A. Kant treats freedom of the will, immortality of the soul and the existence of God as postulates of practical reason.

B. Kant holds that a good will is good only because of what it achieves or brings about.

C. Kant commands us to treat humanity, in ourselves and in others, never merely as a means but always at the same time as an end.

D. Kant holds that an action is right when its consequences produce the greatest happiness.

E. Kant derives the supreme principle of morality from an empirical study of human nature.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Statements A and C are true of Kant.

- **A – True.** In the *Critique of Practical Reason*, Kant postulates freedom, immortality and God. The moral law needs these postulates, but theoretical reason cannot prove them.
- **B – False.** In the *Groundwork*, a good will is good in itself. It would 'shine like a jewel' even if it achieved nothing.
- **C – True.** This is the formula of humanity, which is one form of the categorical imperative.
- **D – False.** This is the utilitarian standard. Kant judges an act by its maxim, not by its consequences.
- **E – False.** Kant says that the moral law must be found a priori in pure reason. It does not come from experience of human nature.

Option 'C, D only' is tempting because C is true, but D states the consequentialist view that Kant rejects.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements are true of the *Tirukkural* of Thiruvalluvar ?

A. It is divided into three books, on aṟam (virtue), poruḷ (wealth) and inbam (love).

B. It contains 1330 couplets, arranged in 133 chapters of ten couplets each.

C. It contains a separate fourth book on vīḍu (final liberation).

D. Its first book deals with the virtues of the householder as well as those of the ascetic.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
The *Tirukkural* is a Tamil ethical classic written in short couplets (kuṟaḷ).

- **A is true.** It has three books: Aṟattuppāl (virtue), Poruṭpāl (wealth) and Inbattuppāl or Kāmattuppāl (love).
- **B is true.** It has 133 chapters. Each chapter has ten couplets, so there are 1330 couplets.
- **C is false.** There is no fourth book on vīḍu. The work covers only three of the four puruṣārthas. Scholars often note this feature.
- **D is true.** The book on virtue has sections on domestic virtue (illaṟam) and on ascetic virtue (tuṟavaṟam).

So A, B and D are true.

The tempting wrong statement is C, because Indian texts often list four goals of life. Thiruvalluvar does not give liberation a separate book.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements about Greek ethics are correct ?

A. In the *Republic*, Plato names wisdom, courage, temperance and justice as the cardinal virtues.

B. For Plato, justice in the soul consists in each of its three parts doing its own work, with reason ruling.

C. Plato assigns the virtue of courage to the appetitive part of the soul.

D. The Stoics hold that virtue is the only good and is sufficient for happiness.

E. Aristotle denies that akrasia (weakness of will) is possible, since no one knowingly does wrong.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Statements A, B and D are correct.

- **A – Correct.** *Republic* Book IV gives these four virtues. Later writers call them the cardinal virtues.
- **B – Correct.** Plato divides the soul into reason, spirit and appetite. Justice is the harmony in which each part does its own work under reason.
- **C – Incorrect.** Courage belongs to the spirited part (thumos). Temperance concerns the agreement of all parts, with appetite obeying reason.
- **D – Correct.** For the Stoics, virtue is the only good. Health and wealth are only 'indifferents'.
- **E – Incorrect.** Socrates denies akrasia ('no one does wrong willingly'). Aristotle discusses akrasia in *Nicomachean Ethics* Book VII and accepts that it happens.

Option 'A, D, E only' is the most tempting distractor. It wrongly gives the Socratic view to Aristotle.

questions.question_md:
Which among the following statements are true of J. S. Mill ?

A. Mill argues that the only evidence that something is desirable is that people actually desire it.

B. Mill holds that the ultimate sanction of morality is an internal one, the feeling of duty or conscience.

C. Mill holds that the utilitarian standard is the agent's own greatest happiness alone.

D. Mill holds that justice is wholly independent of utility.

E. Mill holds that utilitarianism requires the agent to be as impartial as a disinterested and benevolent spectator.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Statements A, B and E are true of Mill. All three come from his *Utilitarianism* (1861).

- **A – True.** In Chapter IV, Mill says that the only proof that a thing is desirable is that people actually desire it.
- **B – True.** In Chapter III, Mill accepts external sanctions too. But the ultimate sanction is internal: a feeling of duty in our own mind, which is conscience.
- **C – False.** The standard is the greatest happiness of all concerned, not only the agent's happiness.
- **D – False.** In Chapter V, Mill grounds justice in utility. He calls it the most important part of social utility.
- **E – True.** In Chapter II, Mill says the agent must be strictly impartial between his own happiness and that of others.

Option 'A, B, C only' is tempting because Mill's proof starts from each person's desire for his own happiness. But Mill's standard is the general happiness.

questions.question_md:
Choose the correct combination of statements about M. N. Roy from those given below :

A. Roy called his mature philosophy Radical Humanism or New Humanism.

B. For Roy, the physical universe is a law-governed system, and man is a part of this system.

C. Roy accepted the Marxist view that economic factors alone decide the course of history.

D. For Roy, reason in man is an echo of the harmony of the law-governed universe.

E. Roy held that a strong party system is necessary for radical democracy.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
M. N. Roy started as a Marxist. Later he built his own philosophy of freedom.

- **A is true.** He named it Radical Humanism or New Humanism. He set it out in the *22 Theses* (1946).
- **B is true.** His metaphysics is materialist. The universe is a self-contained system that follows its own laws. Man grows out of this physical world.
- **C is false.** Roy rejected economic determinism. He held that ideas also move history.
- **D is true.** Roy said that reason in man is an echo of the harmony of the universe. So man is rational because nature is law-governed.
- **E is false.** Roy rejected party politics. He wanted a partyless democracy based on local people's committees. He dissolved his own Radical Democratic Party in 1948.

So A, B and D are true.

Statement C is the tempting trap, because Roy began his career as a communist.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements are true of John Dewey ?

A. Dewey calls his version of pragmatism instrumentalism.

B. For Dewey, education is only a preparation for future adult life and has no value as present experience.

C. Dewey holds that ideas are instruments, or plans of action, for solving problematic situations.

D. Dewey wrote *Democracy and Education* (1916).

E. Dewey holds that truth is a fixed, eternal correspondence that does not depend on inquiry.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- **A – true.** Dewey names his pragmatism instrumentalism (he also calls it experimentalism).
- **B – false.** In *My Pedagogic Creed* (1897), Dewey says that education is a process of living. It is not a preparation for future living. Learning must grow out of the child's present experience.
- **C – true.** For Dewey, ideas are tools. They are hypotheses that guide action in a problematic situation. They are tested by whether they resolve it.
- **D – true.** *Democracy and Education* (1916) is his main work on the philosophy of education.
- **E – false.** Dewey rejects a fixed, ready-made truth. Truth is the result of successful inquiry. He prefers the term "warranted assertibility".

So A, C and D are true. Option "A, B and C only" is tempting, but statement B reverses Dewey's view of education.

questions.question_md:
Who among the following were members of the Vienna Circle ?

A. Moritz Schlick

B. Rudolf Carnap

C. Edmund Husserl

D. Otto Neurath

E. Gilbert Ryle

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
The Vienna Circle was the group of logical positivists that met in Vienna from the 1920s.

- **A – member.** Moritz Schlick led the group. It formed around his chair at the University of Vienna.
- **B – member.** Rudolf Carnap was its leading logician. He wrote *Der logische Aufbau der Welt* (1928).
- **C – not a member.** Edmund Husserl founded phenomenology. His method is quite different from logical positivism.
- **D – member.** Otto Neurath was a founder of the movement. He wrote much of the 1929 manifesto and promoted the unity of science.
- **E – not a member.** Gilbert Ryle was an Oxford ordinary-language philosopher.

So the members are A, B and D. A. J. Ayer visited the Circle and spread its ideas in England, but he is not in this list.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements are correct about Bhīṣma's account of the origin of kingship in the *Śānti Parva* of the *Mahābhārata* ?

A. In the beginning there was no king and no daṇḍa; people protected one another through dharma.

B. The king stands above dharma, and the people may never resist even an unrighteous king.

C. When dharma declined, Brahmā composed a vast treatise of one hundred thousand chapters on dharma, artha and kāma.

D. Pṛthu was called 'rājā' because he pleased (rañjita) the people.

E. This account is narrated by Vidura to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Yudhiṣṭhira asks Bhīṣma how kingship began. Bhīṣma answers in the Rājadharma section of the *Śānti Parva*.

- **A is correct.** In the beginning there was no state, no king and no punishment. People protected one another through dharma.
- **B is incorrect.** The king must rule by dharma. The epic even says that people may kill a king who does not protect them.
- **C is correct.** Greed and delusion destroyed this order. The gods went to Brahmā. He composed a treatise of one hundred thousand chapters on dharma, artha and kāma, with daṇḍanīti.
- **D is correct.** Pṛthu, son of Vena, promised to rule by dharma. He pleased (rañjita) the people, so he was called rājā.
- **E is incorrect.** Bhīṣma teaches this to Yudhiṣṭhira from his bed of arrows.

So A, C and D are correct.

Statement B is the tempting trap. It sounds like a theory of absolute kingship. But the epic always places the king under dharma.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following together constitute *vārttā* (economics) according to Kauṭilya ?

A. Ānvīkṣikī

B. Kṛṣi (agriculture)

C. Vaṇijyā (trade)

D. Trayī

E. Paśupālya (cattle-rearing)

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Kauṭilya names four sciences (vidyā): ānvīkṣikī, trayī, vārttā and daṇḍanīti. He then defines vārttā as agriculture, cattle-rearing and trade.

- **A. Ānvīkṣikī** is not part of vārttā. It is the separate science of reasoning (philosophy).
- **B. Kṛṣi** is part of vārttā.
- **C. Vaṇijyā** is part of vārttā.
- **D. Trayī** is not part of vārttā. It is the separate science of the three Vedas.
- **E. Paśupālya** is part of vārttā.

So B, C and E are correct.

Vārttā gives the state grain, cattle, money and labour. So Kauṭilya says it supports the treasury and the army.

The tempting wrong option is "B, C and D only". It mixes one of the four vidyās with the parts of vārttā.

questions.question_md:
Which among the following statements are true about Amartya Sen’s capability approach ?

A. Capabilities are the real freedoms that a person has to achieve various combinations of functionings.

B. Sen judges a person’s well-being mainly by income and by the commodities that the person owns.

C. Functionings are the various ‘beings and doings’ that a person may value, such as being well nourished.

D. Sen draws up one fixed list of ten central capabilities that every just constitution must guarantee.

E. In *Development as Freedom*, Sen treats freedom both as the primary end and as the principal means of development.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Sen moves the focus from resources to what people can actually do and be.

- **A. True.** A capability is a real freedom or opportunity to achieve functionings.
- **B. False.** Sen criticises income and commodity measures. People convert resources into well-being in different ways.
- **C. True.** Functionings are ‘beings and doings’, such as being healthy or taking part in community life.
- **D. False.** Martha Nussbaum gives a list of ten central capabilities. Sen deliberately refuses one fixed list. He leaves the choice to public reasoning.
- **E. True.** Sen calls freedom the primary end (constitutive role) and the principal means (instrumental role) of development.

So A, C and E are true. Statement D is the trap, because it belongs to Nussbaum’s version of the approach.

questions.question_md:
Which among the following claims are characteristic of ethical descriptivism, as defended by Philippa Foot against Hare's prescriptivism ?

A. The meaning of a moral term is fixed by descriptive criteria for its correct use.

B. Moral judgements are statements that can be true or false.

C. A person may call anything at all 'good', provided he is ready to universalize his prescription.

D. Facts about human good and harm set limits to what can count as a moral evaluation.

E. Moral words serve only to express the speaker's feelings and to arouse feelings in others.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Descriptivism says that moral terms have descriptive meaning that fixes their correct use. Philippa Foot defended it in 'Moral Arguments' and 'Moral Beliefs' (1958).

- **A – Yes.** For the descriptivist, the conditions for applying a moral word belong to its meaning.
- **B – Yes.** Descriptivism is a cognitivist theory. A moral judgement can be true or false, like a factual one.
- **C – No.** This is the prescriptivist view that Foot attacks. For Hare, the speaker's will to universalize decides what he calls good.
- **D – Yes.** Foot argues that a person cannot make just any act a virtue. An evaluation needs a link to human good and harm.
- **E – No.** This is emotivism (Ayer, Stevenson), which is a non-cognitivist theory.

Option 'A, B and C only' is tempting because Hare's universalizability sounds like a 'criterion'. But Foot rejects it as the source of moral meaning.

questions.question_md:
Using truth tables, identify the statement forms that come out false under every assignment of truth values to their variables, that is, the self-contradictory forms :

A. (p ⊃ q) · (p · ~q)

B. (p · q) ⊃ p

C. ~(p ⊃ p)

D. (p ∨ q) · ~p

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
A self-contradictory form is false in every row of its truth table.

- **A – Self-contradictory.** p · ~q is true only when p is T and q is F. In that row, p ⊃ q is F. So the whole conjunction is never true.
- **B – Not self-contradictory.** It is a tautology, because when p · q is true, p is true. It is the form of Simplification.
- **C – Self-contradictory.** p ⊃ p is a tautology, so its negation is false in every row.
- **D – Not self-contradictory.** It is contingent. It is T when p is F and q is T, and F when p is T.

So A and C are self-contradictory.

Option 'C, D only' is tempting because D contains ~p beside p. But q can make p ∨ q true when p is false.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following are correct applications of the rules of quantification (as given by Copi) ?

A. From (x)(Fx ⊃ Gx), infer Fa ⊃ Ga by Universal Instantiation.

B. From Fa, where a names a particular individual, infer (x)Fx by Universal Generalization.

C. From (∃x)Fx and (∃x)Gx, infer Fa and then Ga by Existential Instantiation, using the same constant a both times.

D. From Fa · Ga, infer (∃x)(Fx · Gx) by Existential Generalization.

E. From Fy, where y denotes any arbitrarily selected individual, infer (x)Fx by Universal Generalization.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Statements A, D and E are correct applications.

- **A – Correct.** UI lets us infer any substitution instance of a universal quantification.
- **B – Incorrect.** UG works only from an instance about an arbitrarily selected individual (y). A fact about one named individual (a) does not hold for everything.
- **C – Incorrect.** EI may use only a constant with no earlier occurrence in the proof. 'Something is F' and 'something is G' do not show that the same thing is both.
- **D – Correct.** EG lets us infer an existential quantification from any true substitution instance.
- **E – Correct.** This is the proper form of UG: φy / ∴ (x)φx, where y is any arbitrarily selected individual.

Option 'A, C, D only' is the main trap. Each EI step in C looks correct, but the second step reuses the constant a. Option 'A, B, D, E only' fails because UG from a named constant (B) is invalid.

questions.question_md:
Which among the following are true of philosophical counselling ?

A. Gerd B. Achenbach opened a philosophical practice in Germany in 1981.

B. Lou Marinoff wrote *Plato, Not Prozac!*

C. Philosophical counselling treats mental illness mainly through medication.

D. Philosophical counselling helps clients to examine the assumptions, values and arguments behind their everyday problems.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Philosophical counselling uses philosophical dialogue to help people with everyday problems.

- **A is true.** Gerd B. Achenbach opened his philosophical practice near Cologne in 1981. This is usually taken as the start of the modern movement.
- **B is true.** Lou Marinoff wrote *Plato, Not Prozac!* (1999). The book made the field known to the public.
- **C is false.** Philosophical counsellors do not prescribe drugs. They do not claim to treat mental illness. They refer such cases to doctors.
- **D is true.** The counsellor helps the client to clarify concepts, test arguments and examine values and world-views.

So A, B and D are true.

Statement C is the trap. Marinoff's title itself contrasts Plato (philosophy) with Prozac (a medicine).

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I | LIST-II |
|---|---|
| A. Duḥkha-trayābhighātāj jijñāsā tad-abhighātake hetau | I. *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, Nāgārjuna |
| B. Vijñaptimātram evaitad asad-arthāvabhāsanāt | II. *Vaiśeṣikasūtra*, Kaṇāda |
| C. Yato'bhyudaya-niḥśreyasa-siddhiḥ sa dharmaḥ | III. *Sāṃkhyakārikā*, Īśvarakṛṣṇa |
| D. Yaḥ pratītyasamutpādaḥ śūnyatāṃ tāṃ pracakṣmahe | IV. *Viṃśatikā*, Vasubandhu |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Each line comes from a well-known verse or sūtra.

- A–III. *Sāṃkhyakārikā* 1 starts with the three kinds of suffering (*duḥkha-traya*). The enquiry is into the means to remove them.
- B–IV. The first verse of Vasubandhu's *Viṃśatikā* says that all this is "mere representation" (*vijñapti-mātra*). Non-existent objects only appear.
- C–II. *Vaiśeṣikasūtra* 1.1.2 defines dharma as that from which worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) come.
- D–I. *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* 24.18 says that dependent origination is what Nāgārjuna calls emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

So, the answer is A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I.

The second option is tempting. It swaps B and D, because both are Mahāyāna verses. But *vijñapti-mātra* is a Yogācāra term, and *śūnyatā* links the verse to Nāgārjuna.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I | LIST-II |
|---|---|
| A. *Monadology* | I. St. Augustine |
| B. *Ethics, Demonstrated in Geometrical Order* | II. Spinoza |
| C. *A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge* | III. Leibnitz |
| D. *Confessions* | IV. Berkeley |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Each work is a standard text of its author.

- **A. *Monadology*** (1714) – Leibnitz (III). It sets out the doctrine of monads and pre-established harmony.
- **B. *Ethics*** (1677) – Spinoza (II). He sets it out in the geometrical order, with definitions, axioms and propositions.
- **C. *Principles of Human Knowledge*** (1710) – Berkeley (IV). It defends immaterialism.
- **D. *Confessions*** (about 400 CE) – St. Augustine (I). It is his spiritual autobiography.

So the key is A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I.

Option 1 swaps the two rationalists, Leibnitz and Spinoza. It is the most tempting wrong option.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I | LIST-II |
|---|---|
| A. Faith seeking understanding | I. Hume |
| B. Nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the senses, except the intellect itself | II. Kant |
| C. Commit it then to the flames: for it can contain nothing but sophistry and illusion | III. Anselm |
| D. Thoughts without content are empty, intuitions without concepts are blind | IV. Leibnitz |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- **A. Faith seeking understanding** (*fides quaerens intellectum*) – Anselm (III). It was the first title of his *Proslogion*.
- **B. ‘… except the intellect itself’** – Leibnitz (IV). In the *New Essays* he adds this phrase to the empiricist maxim. He uses it to defend innate ideas against Locke.
- **C. ‘Commit it then to the flames’** – Hume (I). This is the end of the *Enquiry*. A book with no abstract reasoning about quantity and no experimental reasoning about matters of fact is worthless.
- **D. ‘Thoughts without content are empty …’** – Kant (II), *Critique of Pure Reason*. Knowledge needs both sensibility and understanding.

So the key is A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

Option 2 is the tempting one. It gets A and B right but swaps Hume and Kant.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I | LIST-II |
|---|---|
| A. H. A. Prichard | I. Equal consideration of the interests of all beings capable of suffering |
| B. Francis Hutcheson | II. Conscience as a reflective principle with natural authority over self-love and the passions |
| C. Joseph Butler | III. Obligation is known directly and is not derived from any good that the act produces |
| D. Peter Singer | IV. Moral approval arises from an inner 'moral sense' |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- **A-III:** H. A. Prichard wrote 'Does Moral Philosophy Rest on a Mistake?' (1912). He says that we see our obligations directly. We do not derive them from the good that an act produces.
- **B-IV:** Francis Hutcheson is the classic moral-sense theorist. For him, an inner sense approves of benevolent acts.
- **C-II:** Joseph Butler, in his *Fifteen Sermons* (1726), makes conscience the supreme principle in human nature. It has authority over self-love and the particular passions.
- **D-I:** Peter Singer, in *Practical Ethics* and *Animal Liberation*, defends equal consideration of interests for all beings that can suffer.

Key: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I.

The most tempting wrong option swaps Hutcheson and Butler (B-II, C-IV). Both are 18th-century British moralists who answered egoism. But the reflective, ruling conscience belongs to Butler. The 'moral sense' belongs to Hutcheson. Another option swaps Prichard and Hutcheson, because both speak of an immediate moral awareness.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I (Kantian term) | LIST-II (Meaning) |
|---|---|
| A. Autonomy | I. A will that necessarily conforms to the moral law, so that 'ought' does not apply to it |
| B. Heteronomy | II. The property of the will by which it is a law to itself |
| C. Holy will | III. The subjective principle on which an agent acts |
| D. Maxim | IV. The will being determined by some object outside it, such as inclination |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
All four terms come from Kant's *Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals* (1785).

- **A-II:** Autonomy is the property of the will by which it is a law to itself. It is the supreme principle of morality.
- **B-IV:** Heteronomy is the opposite. The will takes its law from an object outside it, such as inclination or happiness.
- **C-I:** A holy (perfectly good) will always acts in accord with the moral law by its own nature. So imperatives and 'ought' do not apply to it.
- **D-III:** A maxim is the subjective principle of volition, the rule on which the agent actually acts. The objective principle is the practical law.

Key: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

The first option swaps autonomy and heteronomy, which is the most common confusion. The third option swaps holy will and maxim. The fourth option gives autonomy the meaning of the holy will. But a human autonomous will still feels the moral law as an 'ought'.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I (Works) | LIST-II (Authors) |
|---|---|
| A. *The Synthesis of Yoga* | I. S. Radhakrishnan |
| B. *Gitanjali* | II. K. C. Bhattacharyya |
| C. *Eastern Religions and Western Thought* | III. Rabindranath Tagore |
| D. *Studies in Vedāntism* | IV. Sri Aurobindo |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- **A–IV.** Sri Aurobindo wrote *The Synthesis of Yoga*. It first appeared in his journal *Arya* from 1914.
- **B–III.** Rabindranath Tagore wrote *Gitanjali*. Its English version won him the Nobel Prize in 1913.
- **C–I.** S. Radhakrishnan wrote *Eastern Religions and Western Thought* (1939). It came from his Oxford lectures.
- **D–II.** K. C. Bhattacharyya wrote *Studies in Vedāntism* (1909). It was his first major work.

So the match is A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II.

The tempting wrong option is "A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I". It swaps Radhakrishnan and Bhattacharyya. Both men wrote on Vedānta. But the comparative study of Eastern and Western religion is Radhakrishnan's book.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I (Thinkers) | LIST-II (Ideas/Institutions) |
|---|---|
| A. J. Krishnamurti | I. Navayāna Buddhism |
| B. B. R. Ambedkar | II. "Back to the Vedas" |
| C. Rabindranath Tagore | III. "Truth is a pathless land" |
| D. Swami Dayananda Saraswati | IV. Viśva-Bhāratī |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- **A–III.** J. Krishnamurti said "Truth is a pathless land" in 1929. He said it when he dissolved the Order of the Star. No organisation, creed or guru can lead a person to truth.
- **B–I.** B. R. Ambedkar's form of Buddhism is called Navayāna (the new vehicle). He gave it a social and ethical meaning.
- **C–IV.** Rabindranath Tagore founded Viśva-Bhāratī at Santiniketan in 1921. It was a university for the meeting of world cultures.
