Arrange the following organisations in the chronological order of their founding :

A. Arya Samaj (Swami Dayananda Saraswati)

B. Satyashodhak Samaj (Jyotiba Phule)

C. Sri Narayana Dharma Paripalana Yogam (under Narayana Guru)

D. Ramakrishna Mission (Swami Vivekananda)

E. Radical Democratic Party (M. N. Roy)

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Date each organisation.

- B. Jyotiba Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj in Pune in 1873.
- A. Swami Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in Bombay in 1875.
- D. Swami Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission in Calcutta in 1897.
- C. The Sri Narayana Dharma Paripalana (SNDP) Yogam started in 1903. Narayana Guru was its first president.
- E. M. N. Roy founded the Radical Democratic Party in 1940.

So the order is B, A, D, C, E.

The most tempting wrong option is "A, B, D, C, E". The Arya Samaj is very well known, so students often put it first. But Phule's Samaj came two years earlier. "B, A, C, D, E" is also wrong. The Ramakrishna Mission came six years before the SNDP Yogam.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements are true of Deendayal Upadhyaya's view of the puruṣārthas ?

A. Man is an integrated unity of body, mind, intellect and soul, and the four puruṣārthas together answer to his needs.

B. Dharma is the regulating puruṣārtha, and artha and kāma are to be pursued within its limits.

C. The State is the source of dharma, and so the State stands above dharma.

D. Both the absence of wealth (arthābhāva) and its excess or dominance (arthaprabhāva) harm dharma.

E. Man is basically an economic being who acts only from self-interest.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Upadhyaya set out these ideas in his *Integral Humanism* lectures of 1965.

- **A is true.** He sees man as a whole of body, mind, intellect and soul. Dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa together meet the needs of this whole person.
- **B is true.** He calls dharma the basic puruṣārtha. Artha (wealth) and kāma (desire) are good only when dharma controls them.
- **C is false.** For Upadhyaya, dharma is above the State. The State must serve dharma. This is his ideal of Dharma Rājya.
- **D is true.** He warns that poverty (arthābhāva) and too much wealth or power (arthaprabhāva) both destroy dharma.
- **E is false.** He rejects the Western picture of man as only an economic being. He criticises both capitalism and communism for this view.

So A, B and D are true. The tempting wrong option is "A, C and D only". It treats the State as the master of dharma. That reverses his view.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements are true of Swami Vivekananda's views on religious experience and rituals ?

A. Every religion has three parts: philosophy, mythology and ritual.

B. Images and rituals have no use at any stage of spiritual life and must be given up at once.

C. Ritual is the most concrete part of religion and gives a visible form to its philosophy.

D. Religion is realisation, a matter of being and becoming, and not mere assent to doctrines.

E. Rāja Yoga asks the student to accept its claims on faith before any personal trial.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- **A is true.** In his lecture on the ideal of a universal religion, Vivekananda says that each religion has three parts. These are philosophy, mythology and ritual.
- **B is false.** He calls rituals and images the kindergarten of religion. They help beginners, and the mind outgrows them only slowly. He does not ask anyone to drop them at once.
- **C is true.** He calls ritual the most concrete part of religion. It is philosophy made concrete, so that ordinary people can grasp it.
- **D is true.** For Vivekananda, religion is not talk or belief. It is direct realisation of the Divine.
- **E is false.** In *Rāja Yoga*, he says that the student must not believe anything on faith. Each person must test the claims by practice and experience.

So A, C and D are true. The tempting wrong option is "A, B and C only". B sounds like a reformer's rejection of idol worship. But Vivekananda gave rituals a lower yet real place.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I (Works) | LIST-II (Authors) |
|---|---|
| A. *Ātmopadeśa Śatakam* | I. M. N. Roy |
| B. *Stuti Chintāmaṇi* | II. Jyotiba Phule |
| C. *Shetkaryacha Asud* | III. Narayana Guru |
| D. *Reason, Romanticism and Revolution* | IV. Sant Kabi Bhima Bhoi |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- **A–III.** Narayana Guru wrote *Ātmopadeśa Śatakam* (One Hundred Verses of Self-Instruction). It sets out his Advaita teaching in Malayalam.
- **B–IV.** Sant Kabi Bhima Bhoi wrote *Stuti Chintāmaṇi*. It is the main poetic text of Mahimā Dharma in Odia.
- **C–II.** Jyotiba Phule wrote *Shetkaryacha Asud* (The Cultivator's Whipcord) in 1883. It describes how priests and officials exploit the peasant.
- **D–I.** M. N. Roy wrote *Reason, Romanticism and Revolution*. It traces the history of European thought from the viewpoint of Radical Humanism.

So the match is A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I.

The tempting wrong option is "A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I". It swaps Narayana Guru and Bhima Bhoi. Both were saint-poets who taught one formless God and opposed caste. But the hundred verses of *Ātmopadeśa Śatakam* are Narayana Guru's, and *Stuti Chintāmaṇi* is the Mahimā Dharma scripture.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I (Texts) | LIST-II (Ideas) |
|---|---|
| A. *The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam* | I. The vows of the āśrama, such as truth, non-violence and non-possession |
| B. *Karma Yoga* | II. Work for work's sake, without attachment to its fruits |
| C. *Sādhanā* | III. Evil is not permanent; it is the passing imperfection of the finite in its growth |
| D. *From Yeravda Mandir* | IV. Nature and history, besides inner experience, as sources of knowledge |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- **A–IV.** In *The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam*, Muhammad Iqbal says that inner experience is only one source of knowledge. The Qur'ān points to two more sources: nature and history.
- **B–II.** In *Karma Yoga*, Swami Vivekananda teaches work for work's sake. One must work without attachment to the results.
- **C–III.** In *Sādhanā*, Rabindranath Tagore discusses the problem of evil. He says that evil is not absolute. It is the imperfection of the finite, which is always moving towards perfection.
- **D–I.** Mahatma Gandhi wrote *From Yeravda Mandir* in prison in 1930. It explains the vows of his āśrama, such as truth, ahiṃsā and non-possession.

So the match is A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I.

The tempting wrong option is "A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-II". It swaps Vivekananda and Gandhi. Both taught selfless action. But *Karma Yoga* gives the general ideal, while *From Yeravda Mandir* lists the concrete vows.

questions.question_md: In *Being and Time*, Heidegger holds that Dasein is not a worldless subject that must first prove that an outer world exists. Which expression does he use for this basic state (*Grundverfassung*) of Dasein ?
questions.explanation:
Heidegger calls the basic state of Dasein **Being-in-the-world** (*In-der-Welt-sein*). He writes it with hyphens to show one unified phenomenon. Dasein is always already involved with things and with others. So the self and the world are not two separate items that we must later join.

For this reason, Heidegger says that the real "scandal of philosophy" is not the lack of a proof of the outer world. The scandal is that people keep asking for such proofs.

- **Being-for-itself** and **Being-in-itself** are Sartre's terms for consciousness and for non-conscious things.
- **Being-towards-death** is a feature of Dasein's authentic existence in Division II. It is not the name of its basic state.

questions.question_md: France has no king at present. According to Bertrand Russell's theory of descriptions in "On Denoting" (1905), what is the status of the sentence "The present King of France is bald" ?
options: It is true, because its subject is an object that subsists without existing.
It is false, because it asserts that exactly one present King of France exists.
It is neither true nor false, because its presupposition of a king is not met.
It is meaningless, because its subject phrase does not denote anything at all.
questions.explanation:
Russell analyses a definite description into quantified claims. "The present King of France is bald" says three things:

1. At least one thing is a present King of France.
2. At most one thing is a present King of France.
3. Whatever is a present King of France is bald.

The first claim is false, so the whole sentence is **false**. The sentence still has a meaning. The phrase "the present King of France" has no meaning in isolation, but the full sentence does.

- "Subsists without existing" is Meinong's view, which Russell rejects.
- "Neither true nor false" because a presupposition fails is P. F. Strawson's reply in "On Referring" (1950). This is the most tempting option, but it is not Russell's view.
- "Meaningless" is wrong. Russell's analysis keeps the sentence meaningful and gives it a truth-value.

questions.question_md:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as **Assertion A** and the other is labelled as **Reason R** :

**Assertion A :** On the position that Kai Nielsen called "Wittgensteinian fideism", religious beliefs cannot be judged irrational from a standpoint outside religious life.

**Reason R :** On this position, the criteria of intelligibility and rationality are internal to each form of life and its language-games, so there is no neutral standard above all of them.

In the light of the above statements, choose the **most appropriate** answer from the options given below :
options: Both **A** and **R** are correct and **R** is the correct explanation of **A**
Both **A** and **R** are correct but **R** is NOT the correct explanation of **A**
**A** is correct but **R** is not correct
**A** is not correct but **R** is correct
questions.explanation:
Kai Nielsen used the label "Wittgensteinian fideism" in a 1967 paper. He applied it to thinkers such as D. Z. Phillips, Peter Winch and Norman Malcolm, who used the later Wittgenstein's ideas.

- **A is correct.** On this view, religion is a distinct mode of discourse. An outsider cannot call it irrational or incoherent by standards from science or metaphysics.
- **R is correct.** The view holds that each form of life, with its language-games, has its own criteria of what makes sense. No neutral, universal standard stands above all forms of life.
- **R explains A.** Religious belief is immune from outside criticism *because* the criteria for judging it are internal to religious practice.

Option 2 is wrong because R is not an extra, unrelated fact. It gives the very ground of A. Nielsen himself criticised this position, but the question asks only what the position holds.

questions.question_md:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as **Assertion A** and the other is labelled as **Reason R** :

**Assertion A :** According to Sartre in *Being and Nothingness*, the café waiter whose movements are a little too precise and too eager is in bad faith.

**Reason R :** The waiter denies his facticity and treats himself as a pure freedom that no fixed role or situation can limit.

In the light of the above statements, choose the **most appropriate** answer from the options given below :
options: Both **A** and **R** are correct and **R** is the correct explanation of **A**
Both **A** and **R** are correct but **R** is NOT the correct explanation of **A**
**A** is correct but **R** is not correct
**A** is not correct but **R** is correct
questions.explanation:
In *Being and Nothingness*, Sartre describes a waiter who "plays at being a waiter in a café". His movements are a little too quick and too exact.

- **A is correct.** Sartre uses the waiter as a standard example of bad faith (*mauvaise foi*). The waiter tries to be a waiter in the way that an inkwell is an inkwell.
- **R is not correct.** The waiter does the reverse. He tries to turn himself into a fixed thing, a being-in-itself. So he denies his **transcendence** (his freedom), and he hides in his **facticity** (his role and situation).

For Sartre, a human being is both facticity and transcendence. Bad faith plays one against the other. One pattern denies transcendence, as the waiter does. The other pattern denies facticity. R describes this second pattern and wrongly gives it to the waiter.

So the most tempting option, "both correct", fails because R reverses the direction of the waiter's self-deception.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following works of Edmund Husserl in the order of their first publication, from the earliest to the latest :

A. *Ideas Pertaining to a Pure Phenomenology* (Book I)

B. *The Crisis of European Sciences and Transcendental Phenomenology* (Parts I and II)

C. *Logical Investigations*

D. *Cartesian Meditations* (French edition)

E. "Philosophy as Rigorous Science"

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
The publication dates are:

- **C.** *Logical Investigations*: 1900–1901. This is Husserl's breakthrough work.
- **E.** "Philosophy as Rigorous Science": 1911, in the journal *Logos*.
- **A.** *Ideas I*: 1913. It presents the phenomenological reduction and transcendental phenomenology.
- **D.** *Cartesian Meditations*: 1931, in French. These came from the Paris lectures of 1929. The German text appeared only in 1950.
- **B.** *Crisis*: Parts I and II appeared in 1936 in the journal *Philosophia* (Belgrade).

So the order is **C, E, A, D, B**.

- "C, A, E, D, B" puts *Ideas I* before the *Logos* essay. This is the closest trap.
- "C, E, A, B, D" puts the late *Crisis* before *Cartesian Meditations*.
- "E, C, A, D, B" puts the 1911 essay before the 1900–1901 work.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements are true of William James's account of the pragmatic method in *Pragmatism* (1907) ?

A. The pragmatic method tries to settle metaphysical disputes by tracing the practical consequences of each notion.

B. If no practical difference follows whichever alternative is true, the alternatives mean practically the same thing and the dispute is idle.

C. James uses a dispute about whether a man goes round a squirrel to show how the method settles a quarrel by a distinction.

D. The pragmatic method stands for fixed results and decides which theory is true before any consequences are examined.

E. James traces the principle of pragmatism to C. S. Peirce's article "How to Make Our Ideas Clear" (1878).

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
options: A, B, C and E only
questions.explanation:
In Lecture II of *Pragmatism*, James presents pragmatism first as a method for settling disputes about meaning.

- **A is true.** The method interprets each notion by tracing its practical consequences.
- **B is true.** If no practical difference follows, the alternatives mean the same thing, and the dispute is idle.
- **C is true.** In the squirrel story, the answer depends on what "going round" means in practice. A distinction ends the quarrel.
- **D is false.** James says the method stands for no special results. It is only a method and an attitude of looking towards consequences.
- **E is true.** James credits Peirce, who introduced the principle in "How to Make Our Ideas Clear" (1878).

So the answer is **A, B, C and E only**. Any option that contains D is wrong.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements are true of Heidegger's position in "The Question Concerning Technology" (1954) ?

A. The essence of technology is by no means anything technological.

B. The instrumental definition of technology as a human means to an end gives the full truth about its essence.

C. Modern technology is a challenging-forth that sets upon nature and demands that it supply energy that can be extracted and stored.

D. Under the rule of modern technology, nature shows itself as standing-reserve (*Bestand*).

E. Modern technology reveals in the same way as the bringing-forth (*poiēsis*) of the ancient craftsman.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- **A is true.** Heidegger opens the essay with this claim. The essence of technology is a way of revealing, not a machine or a tool.
- **B is false.** Heidegger calls the instrumental definition "correct". But he says that the merely correct is not yet the true, so it does not reach the essence.
- **C is true.** Modern technology is a challenging-forth (*Herausfordern*). His example is the hydroelectric plant on the Rhine.
- **D is true.** Nature is ordered to stand by as standing-reserve (*Bestand*), a stock that waits to be used.
- **E is false.** Ancient *technē* was a bringing-forth (*poiēsis*), like the old wooden bridge or windmill. The revealing in modern technology is a challenging, not a bringing-forth in this sense.

So the answer is **A, C and D only**. The close traps are B, which Heidegger calls correct but not true, and E, which merges the two modes of revealing.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I | LIST-II |
|---|---|
| A. Thoughts belong to a "third realm", apart from both outer things and inner ideas | I. Rudolf Carnap |
| B. Heidegger's "The Nothing itself nothings" is a pseudo-statement | II. Gottlob Frege |
| C. "Linguistic phenomenology" as a name for the study of ordinary words | III. Moritz Schlick |
| D. "The meaning of a proposition is the method of its verification" | IV. J. L. Austin |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- **A-II.** In "The Thought" (1918), Frege says that thoughts are neither things of the outer world nor ideas. A "third realm" must be recognised.
- **B-I.** In "The Elimination of Metaphysics through Logical Analysis of Language" (1932), Carnap uses this sentence from Heidegger's "What is Metaphysics?" as an example of a metaphysical pseudo-statement.
- **C-IV.** In "A Plea for Excuses" (1956), Austin suggests "linguistic phenomenology" as a name for his method. We look at words to sharpen our perception of the phenomena.
- **D-III.** Schlick states this principle in "Meaning and Verification" (1936).

So the key is **A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III**.

The most tempting wrong option swaps Carnap and Schlick. Both were leaders of the Vienna Circle and both defended verificationism. But the attack on Heidegger is Carnap's famous paper.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I | LIST-II |
|---|---|
| A. *Amor fati* | I. Kierkegaard |
| B. Indirect communication | II. Merleau-Ponty |
| C. The look (*le regard*) | III. Nietzsche |
| D. The flesh (*la chair*) | IV. Sartre |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- **A-III.** *Amor fati* (love of fate) is Nietzsche's formula for greatness: to want nothing to be different, and to love what is necessary. It appears in *The Gay Science* and *Ecce Homo*.
- **B-I.** Kierkegaard uses indirect communication, for example through pseudonyms. He holds that ethical and religious truth cannot be handed over as a result. The reader must take it up inwardly.
- **C-IV.** In *Being and Nothingness*, Sartre analyses the look of the Other. When another person looks at me, I become an object, and I feel shame.
- **D-II.** In *The Visible and the Invisible*, Merleau-Ponty uses "flesh" for the common element of the seer and the seen.

So the key is **A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II**.

The tempting trap is to give "the look" to Merleau-Ponty, the philosopher of perception. But the look as a relation to the Other is Sartre's analysis.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I | LIST-II |
|---|---|
| A. *Contingency, Irony, and Solidarity* | I. John Dewey |
| B. *Humanism of the Other* | II. Richard Rorty |
| C. *Experience and Nature* | III. Friedrich Nietzsche |
| D. *Twilight of the Idols* | IV. Emmanuel Levinas |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- **A-II.** Richard Rorty wrote *Contingency, Irony, and Solidarity* (1989). It presents the liberal ironist.
- **B-IV.** Emmanuel Levinas wrote *Humanism of the Other* (*Humanisme de l'autre homme*, 1972). It defends a humanism based on responsibility for the other person.
- **C-I.** John Dewey wrote *Experience and Nature* (1925). It sets out his naturalistic metaphysics of experience.
- **D-III.** Friedrich Nietzsche wrote *Twilight of the Idols* (1889), with the subtitle "How to Philosophize with a Hammer".

So the key is **A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III**.

The tempting wrong option swaps Rorty and Dewey. Rorty saw himself as a follower of Dewey, and both are pragmatists. But *Experience and Nature* is Dewey's, and *Contingency, Irony, and Solidarity* is Rorty's.

questions.question_md: Bhīṣma's teaching in the *Śānti Parva* of the *Mahābhārata* falls into three sections. Which section deals with how a king must act in times of distress and calamity ?
questions.explanation:
The *Śānti Parva* is the twelfth book of the *Mahābhārata*. In it, Bhīṣma teaches Yudhiṣṭhira from his bed of arrows. The teaching has three sections:

- **Rājadharma** gives the normal duties of a king.
- **Āpaddharma** gives the rules for times of distress (āpad). For example, it covers a weak king, an empty treasury or a strong enemy. In such times, some normal rules may be relaxed.
- **Mokṣadharma** deals with liberation and spiritual knowledge.

So the section on distress is Āpaddharma.

The most tempting wrong option is Rājadharma. It is the best-known section on kingship, but it covers normal times. Anuśāsana is wrong because it is not a section of the *Śānti Parva*. The *Anuśāsana Parva* is the next book, the thirteenth, where Bhīṣma's teaching continues.

questions.question_md:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as **Assertion A** and the other is labelled as **Reason R** :

**Assertion A :** Article 15(4) of the Constitution of India, added by the First Amendment in 1951, allows the State to make special provisions for the advancement of socially and educationally backward classes, and of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

**Reason R :** The Supreme Court of India now holds that such affirmative action is opposed to the principle of equality, and is allowed only as a reluctant exception to Article 14.

In the light of the above statements, choose the **most appropriate** answer from the options given below :
options: Both **A** and **R** are correct and **R** is the correct explanation of **A**
Both **A** and **R** are correct but **R** is NOT the correct explanation of **A**
**A** is correct but **R** is not correct
**A** is not correct but **R** is correct
questions.explanation:
- **A is correct.** In 1951, the Supreme Court struck down a communal quota in *State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan*. Parliament then added clause (4) to Article 15 by the First Amendment. It allows special provisions for backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
- **R is not correct.** An early case (*M. R. Balaji*, 1963) did call Article 15(4) an exception. But the Court no longer treats such measures as opposed to equality. In *State of Kerala v. N. M. Thomas* (1976), the Court held that reservation is a part of equality, not an exception to it. *Indra Sawhney* (1992) confirmed this view. The Constitution aims at substantive equality, and unequal groups may need unequal help.

So A is correct but R is not correct.

The tempting wrong option is the first one. A student may think that every special provision must be an exception to equal treatment. But Indian law treats affirmative action as a means to real equality.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following elements (prakṛtis) of the State in the order in which Kauṭilya lists them in the *Arthaśāstra* :

A. Janapada

B. Kośa

C. Svāmī

D. Durga

E. Amātya

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Kauṭilya opens Book 6 of the *Arthaśāstra* with this list: "svāmī, amātya, janapada, durga, kośa, daṇḍa and mitra are the prakṛtis". He discusses them in this order and, in Book 8, weighs each one against the next.

- C. Svāmī (the king) comes first.
- E. Amātya (the minister) comes second.
- A. Janapada (the territory with its people) comes third.
- D. Durga (the fort) comes fourth.
- B. Kośa (the treasury) comes fifth.

Daṇḍa (the army) and mitra (the ally) follow, but they are not in the list here.

So the order is C, E, A, D, B.

The most tempting wrong option is "C, E, D, A, B". It puts the fort before the territory. The fort protects the land, so the swap looks natural. But Kauṭilya names the janapada before the durga.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements are correct about B. R. Ambedkar's scheme of State Socialism in *States and Minorities* (1947) ?

A. Key and basic industries should be owned and run by the State.

B. State Socialism should be left to ordinary laws that each new legislature can change.

C. Agriculture should be a State industry, with land let out to villagers for collective farming.

D. Parliamentary democracy should be suspended until State Socialism is fully set up.

E. State Socialism should be laid down in the Constitution itself, beyond the reach of a mere legislative majority.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Ambedkar wrote *States and Minorities* in 1947 as a memorandum to the Constituent Assembly.

- **A is correct.** He wanted key industries and basic industries to be owned and run by the State. Insurance was also to be a State monopoly.
- **B is false.** He did not want to leave the scheme to the will of the legislature. A new majority could undo it.
- **C is correct.** He proposed that agriculture be a State industry. The State would let out land to groups of villagers for collective farming, without caste distinction.
- **D is false.** He wanted State Socialism without giving up parliamentary democracy. He rejected dictatorship as the price of socialism.
- **E is correct.** He wanted State Socialism fixed by the law of the Constitution. Then no ordinary act of the legislature or executive could change it.

So A, C and E are correct. The tempting wrong option is "A, B and C only". B sounds democratic, but Ambedkar wanted constitutional protection, not ordinary law.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I (Officers in the *Arthaśāstra*) | LIST-II (Main charge) |
|---|---|
| A. Samāhartā | I. Trade and the sale of State goods |
| B. Sannidhātā | II. Collection of revenue from all sources |
| C. Sītādhyakṣa | III. Cultivation of the crown lands |
| D. Paṇyādhyakṣa | IV. The treasury and the State storehouses |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- **A–II.** The Samāhartā is the chief collector of revenue. He gathers income from forts, the countryside, mines, forests, herds and trade routes.
- **B–IV.** The Sannidhātā is the chief of the treasury and storehouses. He builds and guards the treasury, the granary and the armoury.
- **C–III.** The Sītādhyakṣa is the superintendent of agriculture. He has the crown lands sown and harvested.
- **D–I.** The Paṇyādhyakṣa is the superintendent of trade. He fixes the prices and handles the sale of State goods.

So the match is A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I.

The most tempting wrong option is "A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I". It swaps the Samāhartā and the Sannidhātā. Both are top financial officers. But the Samāhartā brings revenue in, while the Sannidhātā keeps and stores it.

questions.question_md: Will Kymlicka accepts minority rights that protect a group against the decisions of the wider society, but he rejects minority rights that let a group limit the basic liberties of its own members. What does he call these two kinds of claim, respectively ?
options: Special representation rights and polyethnic rights
questions.explanation:
In *Multicultural Citizenship* (1995), Kymlicka separates two kinds of group claim.

- **External protections** protect a minority from the decisions of the larger society. An example is language rights, which reduce the group's weakness against the majority. A liberal can accept them.
- **Internal restrictions** let a group limit the liberty of its own members, for example to stop dissent. Kymlicka rejects them, because they violate individual autonomy.

The stem gives the accepted kind first and the rejected kind second. So the answer is 'external protections and internal restrictions'.

- 'Internal restrictions and external protections' gives the same two terms in reverse order. It is the closest trap.
- **Self-government, polyethnic and special representation rights** are Kymlicka's three *forms* of group-differentiated rights. They are not the two kinds of claim in the stem.

questions.question_md: In Plato's *Republic*, the 'noble lie' (the myth of the metals) teaches the citizens that :
options: The god mixed silver in the rulers, gold in the auxiliaries, and iron and bronze in the farmers and craftsmen
The god made all citizens of one and the same metal, so that every citizen is equally fit to rule
The god mixed gold in those fit to rule, silver in the auxiliaries, and iron and bronze in the farmers and craftsmen
The god fixed each child's class by the metal of its parents, so that no child may ever move to another class
questions.explanation:
In *Republic* Book III, Socrates proposes a 'noble lie' to make the citizens accept the three classes.

All citizens are told that they are brothers, born of the same earth. But the god mixed **gold** in those fit to rule, **silver** in the auxiliaries, and **iron and bronze** in the farmers and craftsmen.

- The first option swaps gold and silver between rulers and auxiliaries.
- The second option is wrong. The citizens share one mother, the earth, but not one metal.
- The fourth option is the most tempting trap. Children usually resemble their parents. But Plato says that a gold or silver child born to bronze parents must be raised up. A bronze or iron child born to rulers must be moved down. So class depends on the child's own nature, not on birth.

questions.question_md:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as **Assertion A** and the other is labelled as **Reason R** :

**Assertion A :** Locke holds that in the state of nature every man has the right to punish those who break the law of nature.

**Reason R :** Locke holds that a man makes a thing his property by mixing his labour with it.

In the light of the above statements, choose the **most appropriate** answer from the options given below :
options: Both **A** and **R** are correct and **R** is the correct explanation of **A**
Both **A** and **R** are correct but **R** is NOT the correct explanation of **A**
**A** is correct but **R** is not correct
**A** is not correct but **R** is correct
questions.explanation:
**A is correct.** See the *Second Treatise* (§§7–8). In the state of nature, the execution of the law of nature is put into every man's hands. Each person may punish an offender, so far as calm reason and conscience direct. Locke calls this the executive power of the law of nature.

**R is correct.** In chapter V, Locke says that every man has property in his own person. When he mixes his labour with something in the common stock, he makes it his property.

**R does not explain A.** The right to punish rests on the law of nature itself. That law would be in vain if nobody could enforce it. It does not rest on the labour theory of property.

‘R is the correct explanation of A’ is tempting because both claims come from the same book about the state of nature. But one does not give the reason for the other.

questions.question_md:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as **Assertion A** and the other is labelled as **Reason R** :

**Assertion A :** In the *Critique of the Gotha Programme*, Marx holds that in the first phase of communist society each producer receives back from society, after deductions, according to the amount of labour he has given.

**Reason R :** This first phase has just emerged from capitalist society, and so it is still stamped with the birthmarks of the old society.

In the light of the above statements, choose the **most appropriate** answer from the options given below :
options: Both **A** and **R** are correct and **R** is the correct explanation of **A**
Both **A** and **R** are correct but **R** is NOT the correct explanation of **A**
**A** is correct but **R** is not correct
**A** is not correct but **R** is correct
questions.explanation:
**A is correct.** In the *Critique of the Gotha Programme* (1875), Marx describes the first phase of communist society. The producer gets a certificate for the labour he has given. After deductions for common funds, he draws from the social stock an equal amount of goods. So the measure is labour, not need.

**R is correct.** Marx says that this society has not developed on its own foundations. It has just emerged from capitalism, so it still carries the birthmarks of the old society.

**R explains A.** Marx draws the labour standard *from* these birthmarks. The principle of equal exchange (bourgeois right) survives in the first phase because the old society is not yet overcome. Only in the higher phase can society write: 'From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs!'

‘A is not correct but R is correct’ is the trap. A candidate who knows only the slogan about needs may think A is false.

questions.question_md:
Each of the following thinkers wrote a classic of Western social and political philosophy. Put the authors in historical sequence, from the oldest to the most recent :

A. Isaiah Berlin, 'Two Concepts of Liberty'

B. Karl Marx, *Capital*

C. Michael Sandel, *Liberalism and the Limits of Justice*

D. Plato, *Republic*

E. John Locke, *Two Treatises of Government*

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
The authors lived, and their works appeared, in this order:

1. **D. Plato** (about 428–348 BCE), author of the *Republic*.
2. **E. John Locke** (1632–1704), author of the *Two Treatises of Government*.
3. **B. Karl Marx** (1818–1883), author of *Capital*.
4. **A. Isaiah Berlin** (1909–1997), author of 'Two Concepts of Liberty'.
5. **C. Michael Sandel** (born 1953), author of *Liberalism and the Limits of Justice*.

So the key is D, E, B, A, C.

Option D, E, A, B, C puts Berlin before Marx. This is wrong, because Berlin was born after Marx died. Berlin even wrote a biography of Marx (1939).

questions.question_md:
In *A Theory of Justice*, Rawls describes a four-stage sequence for applying the principles of justice. Arrange the stages in their proper order :

A. The legislative stage, at which just laws and policies are enacted within the limits of the constitution

B. The original position, at which the parties choose the principles of justice behind a veil of ignorance

C. The application of rules to particular cases by judges and administrators, and the following of rules by citizens

D. The constitutional convention, at which delegates choose a just constitution

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Rawls sets out the four-stage sequence in *A Theory of Justice* (§31). At each stage the veil of ignorance is partly lifted.

1. **B. Original position.** The parties choose the two principles of justice. They know no particular facts about themselves.
2. **D. Constitutional convention.** Delegates design a just constitution. They now know the general facts about their society.
3. **A. Legislative stage.** Laws and policies are judged from the standpoint of a representative legislator, within the constitution.
4. **C. Application.** Judges and administrators apply the rules to particular cases, and citizens follow them. Now everyone has full knowledge of the facts.

So the key is B, D, A, C.

Option B, A, D, C is tempting. But Rawls puts the constitution before ordinary legislation, because laws must fit the constitution.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements are true of Charles Taylor's essay 'The Politics of Recognition' ?

A. Taylor distinguishes a politics of equal dignity from a politics of difference.

B. For Taylor, misrecognition can do real harm, and can imprison a person in a false and reduced mode of being.

C. Taylor holds that a person forms his identity monologically, independently of any dialogue with others.

D. Taylor defends a strictly 'difference-blind' procedural liberalism as the only acceptable form of liberal society.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
In 'The Politics of Recognition' (1992), Taylor argues that identity needs recognition by others.

- **A – true.** The politics of equal dignity stresses what is the same in all citizens: equal rights. The politics of difference asks us to recognise the unique identity of a person or group.
- **B – true.** Taylor says that nonrecognition or misrecognition can be a form of oppression. It can imprison someone in a false, distorted and reduced mode of being.
- **C – false.** Taylor stresses the dialogical character of human life. We define our identity in dialogue with significant others.
- **D – false.** Taylor criticises a difference-blind, purely procedural liberalism. He defends a liberalism that can pursue collective goals, such as the survival of French culture in Quebec, while protecting basic rights.

So the key is A and B only. Option A and C only is tempting to a candidate who reads Taylor as a classical liberal individualist.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I (Concept) | LIST-II (Thinker) |
|---|---|
| A. The Lockean proviso on just acquisition | I. Ronald Dworkin |
| B. The distinction between brute luck and option luck | II. Robert Nozick |
| C. Open impartiality, using Adam Smith's impartial spectator | III. Bernard Williams |
| D. A warrior class opened to all by competition, to test equality of opportunity | IV. Amartya Sen |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- **A. Lockean proviso – Nozick (II).** In *Anarchy, State, and Utopia*, an acquisition is just only if it does not worsen the situation of others.
- **B. Brute luck and option luck – Dworkin (I).** Dworkin's equality of resources compensates for brute luck, which no one chose. It does not compensate for option luck from deliberate gambles.
- **C. Open impartiality – Sen (IV).** In *The Idea of Justice*, Sen uses Adam Smith's impartial spectator. He invites views from outside one's own society, not only from inside it.
- **D. Warrior class – Williams (III).** In 'The Idea of Equality', Williams imagines a warrior class opened to all by a test of strength. But only the well-fed rich can pass. So formal equality of opportunity can be empty.

So the key is A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

Option A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III swaps Nozick and Dworkin. Option A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV swaps Sen and Williams. These adjacent swaps are the main traps.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I (Work) | LIST-II (Theory of feminism) |
|---|---|
| A. Betty Friedan, *The Feminine Mystique* | I. Radical feminism |
| B. Shulamith Firestone, *The Dialectic of Sex* | II. Eco-feminism |
| C. Heidi Hartmann, 'The Unhappy Marriage of Marxism and Feminism' | III. Liberal feminism |
| D. Maria Mies and Vandana Shiva, *Ecofeminism* | IV. Socialist feminism |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- **A. Friedan – Liberal feminism (III).** *The Feminine Mystique* (1963) attacks the ideal of the happy housewife. Friedan sought equal rights and opportunities through reform and later founded NOW.
- **B. Firestone – Radical feminism (I).** *The Dialectic of Sex* (1970) treats sex class as the basic oppression. Firestone rooted it in biological reproduction.
- **C. Hartmann – Socialist feminism (IV).** Her essay (1979) argues that Marxism alone is sex-blind. She explains women's oppression by patriarchy and capitalism together.
- **D. Mies and Shiva – Eco-feminism (II).** *Ecofeminism* (1993) links the domination of women with the domination of nature.

So the key is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

Option A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II swaps radical and socialist feminism. Both Firestone and Hartmann use Marxist language, so this is the main trap.

questions.question_md: "Two statements that have the same truth value under every possible assignment of truth values to their simple components, so that the biconditional that joins them is a tautology" are called :
questions.explanation:
Copi separates two kinds of equivalence.
- Two statements are materially equivalent when they simply have the same truth value. For example, both are true. The biconditional 'p ≡ q' states this.
- Two statements are logically equivalent when they have the same truth value in every row of the truth table. Then their biconditional is a tautology. Examples are 'p' and '~~p', or '~(p · q)' and '~p ∨ ~q'.

The definition in the question says 'under every possible assignment' and 'is a tautology'. So it defines logical equivalence.

'Materially equivalent' is the trap. Material equivalence needs only the same actual truth value, not the same value in every row. 'Contradictory' statements always have opposite truth values. 'Consistent' statements can be true together.

questions.question_md:
On the Boolean interpretation of categorical propositions that Copi adopts, which fallacy does the following syllogism commit ?

All mammals are vertebrates.

All whales are mammals.

∴ Some whales are vertebrates.
questions.explanation:
The mood is AAI and the figure is the first (M–P, S–M).

Check the rules one by one:
- Three terms only: mammals, vertebrates, whales. No four terms.
- The middle term 'mammals' is distributed in the major premise (subject of an A proposition). No undistributed middle.
- The conclusion (an I proposition) distributes no term. So there can be no illicit major or illicit minor.
- No premise is negative.
- Both premises are universal, but the conclusion is particular.

On the Boolean interpretation, universal propositions have no existential import. They do not say that whales exist. But the particular conclusion does say that at least one whale exists. So the conclusion claims more than the premises give. This is the existential fallacy.

The trap is 'illicit minor'. 'Whales' is distributed in the minor premise, but it is not distributed in the conclusion, so the rule is not broken. (Traditional logic accepts this mood as Barbari, a weakened mood.)

questions.question_md:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as Assertion **A** and the other is labelled as Reason **R** :

**Assertion A :** In quantification theory, '(∃x)(Fx ⊃ Gx)' is not an adequate symbolisation of the proposition 'Some F are G'.

**Reason R :** '(∃x)(Fx ⊃ Gx)' is true when there is at least one thing that is not F, even if nothing is both F and G.

In the light of the above statements, choose the **most appropriate** answer from the options given below :
options: Both **A** and **R** are correct and **R** is the correct explanation of **A**
Both **A** and **R** are correct but **R** is NOT the correct explanation of **A**
**A** is correct but **R** is not correct
**A** is not correct but **R** is correct
questions.explanation:
Both statements are correct, and R explains A.

R is correct. A conditional 'Fa ⊃ Ga' is true whenever its antecedent 'Fa' is false. So if any individual 'a' is not F, then 'Fa ⊃ Ga' is true. By existential generalization, '(∃x)(Fx ⊃ Gx)' is then true. This holds even if no F is G at all.

A is correct. 'Some F are G' claims that at least one thing is both F and G. It is false when no F is G. Because '(∃x)(Fx ⊃ Gx)' can be true in that case, the two do not say the same thing. The correct symbolisation is '(∃x)(Fx · Gx)'.

R explains A. A is true *because* of the fact stated in R. The formula is made true too easily, by any non-F thing.

Option 2 is the tempting error for students who see R only as a separate fact about conditionals.

questions.question_md:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as Assertion **A** and the other is labelled as Reason **R** :

**Assertion A :** When the connotation (intension) of a term is increased, its denotation (extension) either decreases or remains the same.

**Reason R :** A term such as 'unicorn' has a connotation, but its denotation is empty.

In the light of the above statements, choose the **most appropriate** answer from the options given below :
options: Both **A** and **R** are correct and **R** is the correct explanation of **A**
Both **A** and **R** are correct but **R** is NOT the correct explanation of **A**
**A** is correct but **R** is not correct
**A** is not correct but **R** is correct
questions.explanation:
Both statements are correct, but R does not explain A.

A is correct. Connotation (intension) is the set of attributes that a term implies. Denotation (extension) is the class of things to which it applies. If we add attributes, fewer things or the same things fit the term. For example, 'person' → 'living person' → 'living person over 100 years old'. Copi states this law carefully: the extension decreases *or stays the same*. It does not always decrease.

R is correct. 'Unicorn' has a clear meaning (a horse-like animal with one horn). But no such animal exists. So its extension is the empty class.

R does not explain A. R shows that a term can have meaning without having members. It says nothing about how adding attributes changes the extension. So the answer is option 2. Option 1 is the trap, because both statements are about intension and extension.

questions.question_md:
Arrange the following valid syllogisms according to their figures, beginning with the first figure and ending with the fourth :

A. No hawks are herbivores. Some birds are herbivores. Therefore, some birds are not hawks.

B. Some philosophers are poets. All poets are writers. Therefore, some writers are philosophers.

C. No liars are trustworthy persons. Some salesmen are liars. Therefore, some salesmen are not trustworthy persons.

D. All whales are mammals. Some whales are toothed animals. Therefore, some toothed animals are mammals.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Find the major term (P, the predicate of the conclusion), the minor term (S, its subject) and the middle term (M). Then see where M stands.
- C – P = trustworthy persons, S = salesmen, M = liars. M–P, S–M: first figure (EIO-1, Ferio).
- A – P = hawks, S = birds, M = herbivores. P–M, S–M: second figure (EIO-2, Festino).
- D – P = mammals, S = toothed animals, M = whales. M–P, M–S: third figure (AII-3, Datisi).
- B – P = philosophers, S = writers, M = poets. P–M, M–S: fourth figure (IAI-4, Dimaris).

So the order is C, A, D, B.

'C, D, A, B' is the main trap. It swaps the second and third figures. In the second figure M is the predicate of both premises; in the third figure M is the subject of both. Students also misplace B, because its conclusion reverses the terms of its first premise.

questions.question_md:
The contrapositive of 'All S is P' is reached by a chain of obversion and conversion. Arrange the following propositions in the order in which they occur in this chain, beginning with the given proposition :

A. No non-P is S.

B. All S is P.

C. All non-P is non-S.

D. No S is non-P.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Contraposition is not a single basic step. It is obversion, then conversion, then obversion again.
1. B – 'All S is P' is the given A proposition.
2. D – Obvert B: change the quality (A → E) and replace the predicate by its complement. This gives 'No S is non-P'.
3. A – Convert D: an E proposition converts simply. This gives 'No non-P is S'.
4. C – Obvert A: change the quality (E → A) and complement the predicate. This gives 'All non-P is non-S', the contrapositive.

So the order is B, D, A, C.

'B, A, D, C' is the trap. It converts first. But 'All S is P' cannot be converted simply, so the chain must start with obversion.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following statements about representing standard-form categorical propositions by Venn diagrams are correct ?

A. To diagram 'All S is P', we shade the part of the S circle that lies outside the P circle.

B. To diagram 'Some S is not P', we shade the part of the S circle that lies outside the P circle.

C. To diagram 'No S is P', we shade the area where the S and P circles overlap.

D. To diagram 'Some S is P', we place an 'x' in the area where the S and P circles overlap.

E. Two overlapping circles for S and P divide the diagram into only three classes.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
In a Venn diagram, shading shows that a class is empty. An 'x' shows that a class has at least one member.
- A – Correct. 'All S is P' says that the class S·non-P is empty, so we shade it.
- B – Incorrect. 'Some S is not P' says that S·non-P has a member. We place an 'x' there; we do not shade it.
- C – Correct. 'No S is P' says that S·P is empty, so we shade the overlap.
- D – Correct. 'Some S is P' says that S·P has a member, so an 'x' goes in the overlap.
- E – Incorrect. Two overlapping circles inside a box give four classes: S·P, S·non-P, non-S·P and non-S·non-P. The region outside both circles also counts.

So A, C and D are correct. 'A, B and D only' is the trap. It treats the O proposition as if it were universal and so used shading.

questions.question_md:
Which of the following are standard-form categorical propositions ?

A. No reptiles are mammals.

B. Every bird has feathers.

C. Some musicians are not singers.

D. Only citizens are voters.

E. All triangles are three-sided figures.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
options: A, B, D and E only
questions.explanation:
A standard-form categorical proposition has four parts. These are a quantifier ('All', 'No' or 'Some'), a subject term, a copula ('are' or 'are not') and a predicate term.
- A – Standard form (E): 'No' + reptiles + are + mammals.
- B – Not standard. 'Every' is not a standard quantifier, and 'has feathers' is a verb phrase, not copula + term. Its standard form is 'All birds are feathered creatures'.
- C – Standard form (O): 'Some' + musicians + are not + singers.
- D – Not standard. It is an exclusive proposition. It means 'All voters are citizens'.
- E – Standard form (A): 'All' + triangles + are + three-sided figures.

So A, C and E are standard-form propositions. The trap is D. It looks like an A proposition, but 'only' reverses the subject and the predicate.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I (Fallacy) | LIST-II (Description) |
|---|---|
| A. Composition | I. Reasoning that what is true of a whole must also be true of each of its parts |
| B. Division | II. Asking a question in a way that takes for granted an answer to an earlier question that was never asked |
| C. Complex question | III. Moving from a few cases that are not typical to a general rule that covers all cases |
| D. Converse accident (hasty generalization) | IV. Reasoning that what is true of each part must also be true of the whole made up of those parts |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Each fallacy matches one description:
- A – Composition (IV): from the parts to the whole. Example: 'Each player is excellent, so the team is excellent.'
- B – Division (I): from the whole to the parts. Example: 'The university is famous, so each of its teachers is famous.'
- C – Complex question (II): 'Have you stopped cheating?' takes for granted an answer to the earlier question 'Did you cheat?'
- D – Converse accident, or hasty generalization (III): a general rule drawn from a few untypical cases.

So the key is A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.

'A-I, B-IV, C-II, D-III' is the trap. It reverses composition and division, which are mirror images of each other.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I (Statement form) | LIST-II (Truth-table result) |
|---|---|
| A. p · (q ∨ r) | I. True in three of the eight rows |
| B. (p ∨ q) ∨ r | II. True in five of the eight rows |
| C. p ⊃ (q · r) | III. True in six of the eight rows |
| D. (p ≡ q) ⊃ r | IV. True in seven of the eight rows |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Three variables give 2³ = 8 rows.
- A – p · (q ∨ r): p must be true (4 rows). Of these, q ∨ r is false only when q and r are both false. So 4 − 1 = 3 rows (I).
- B – (p ∨ q) ∨ r: false only when p, q and r are all false. So 8 − 1 = 7 rows (IV).
- C – p ⊃ (q · r): true in the 4 rows where p is false. When p is true, it is true only if q and r are both true (1 row). So 4 + 1 = 5 rows (II).
- D – (p ≡ q) ⊃ r: p ≡ q is true in 4 rows: p and q agree, and r is T or F. The conditional is false only when p ≡ q is true and r is false: 2 rows. So 8 − 2 = 6 rows (III).

So the key is A-I, B-IV, C-II, D-III.

'A-I, B-IV, C-III, D-II' is the closest trap. It comes from counting p ⊃ (q · r) as false in only two rows.

questions.question_md: Which philosopher held that a legitimate authority gives its subjects pre-emptive reasons for action, and that such authority is justified when following its directives helps them to conform better to reasons that already apply to them (the 'normal justification thesis') ?
questions.explanation:
Joseph Raz set out the "service conception" of authority, mainly in *The Morality of Freedom* (1986).

- His **pre-emption thesis** says that an authority's directive does not simply add one more reason. It replaces some of the reasons that the subject would otherwise weigh.
- His **normal justification thesis** says when authority is legitimate. Authority is legitimate if its directives help a person to follow the reasons that apply to him. He must do better this way than on his own judgement.

- Robert Paul Wolff is wrong. In *In Defense of Anarchism* (1970), he argued that autonomy and legitimate authority cannot go together.
- H. L. A. Hart is the most tempting wrong option. He was Raz's teacher and also a legal positivist. But Hart is known for the rule of recognition and for primary and secondary rules, not for this thesis.
- Ronald Dworkin is wrong. He saw law as integrity and attacked positivism.

questions.question_md: A doctor gives a dying patient large doses of morphine to relieve severe pain. She foresees, but does not intend, that the doses may shorten the patient's life. Which principle is most often used to justify her act ?
options: The distinction between ordinary and extraordinary means
The principle of the sanctity of life
questions.explanation:
The doctrine of double effect deals with one act that has a good effect and a bad effect. The act is allowed under these conditions:

- The act itself is not wrong. Giving pain relief is not wrong.
- The agent intends only the good effect, here relief of pain. She only foresees the bad effect, here an earlier death.
- The bad effect is not the means to the good effect. The relief does not come through death.
- There is a serious reason that balances the bad effect.

The morphine case meets all four conditions.

- The ordinary–extraordinary means distinction is the most tempting wrong option. It decides when a doctor may withhold or withdraw treatment. Here the doctor gives a drug, so it does not apply.
- The sanctity of life principle forbids intentional killing. It cannot by itself justify an act that may shorten life.
- Non-maleficence tells the doctor not to harm. It creates the problem here; it does not solve it.

questions.question_md: Who, in an essay of 1890 in the *Harvard Law Review*, argued that the law must protect privacy as 'the right to be let alone' ?
questions.explanation:
Samuel Warren and Louis Brandeis published "The Right to Privacy" in the *Harvard Law Review* in 1890. They wrote against the press of their time. New cameras and gossip papers had begun to invade private life. They argued that the law must protect a person's "right to be let alone". This essay is the starting point of modern privacy law and media ethics.

- Judith Jarvis Thomson is the most tempting wrong option. She also wrote an essay called "The Right to Privacy". But she wrote it in 1975. She argued that the right to privacy is a cluster of other rights.
- James Rachels is wrong. His essay "Why Privacy Is Important" (1975) links privacy to our ability to keep different relationships.
- John Stuart Mill is wrong. *On Liberty* (1859) defends a private sphere through the harm principle. But it does not contain this 1890 legal argument.

questions.question_md:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as **Assertion A** and the other is labelled as **Reason R** :

**Assertion A :** Patrick Devlin held that a society may use the criminal law to protect its shared morality, because a common morality is part of what holds that society together.

**Reason R :** The Wolfenden Report (1957), to which Devlin was replying, recommended that homosexual acts between consenting adults in private should remain criminal offences.

In the light of the above statements, choose the **most appropriate** answer from the options given below :
options: Both **A** and **R** are correct and **R** is the correct explanation of **A**
Both **A** and **R** are correct but **R** is NOT the correct explanation of **A**
**A** is correct but **R** is not correct
**A** is not correct but **R** is correct
questions.explanation:
- **A is correct.** Devlin gave his Maccabaean Lecture, "The Enforcement of Morals", in 1959. He argued that a shared morality holds a society together. An attack on that morality is like treason. So society may use the law to protect it.
- **R is not correct.** The Wolfenden Report recommended the opposite. It said that homosexual acts between consenting adults in private should no longer be crimes. Its reason was that there is a realm of private morality that is "not the law's business". Devlin wrote to reject this reasoning.

So A is correct but R is not correct.

H. L. A. Hart replied to Devlin in *Law, Liberty and Morality* (1963). He defended the Wolfenden view by using Mill's harm principle.

The tempting wrong option is the first one. A student may think that Devlin agreed with Wolfenden, because both were part of the same debate. In fact Devlin attacked its principle.

questions.question_md:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as **Assertion A** and the other is labelled as **Reason R** :

**Assertion A :** Tom Regan holds that only moral agents can be subjects-of-a-life, and so only moral agents have inherent value.

**Reason R :** Regan holds that all beings who have inherent value have it equally.

In the light of the above statements, choose the **most appropriate** answer from the options given below :
options: Both **A** and **R** are correct and **R** is the correct explanation of **A**
Both **A** and **R** are correct but **R** is NOT the correct explanation of **A**
**A** is correct but **R** is not correct
**A** is not correct but **R** is correct
questions.explanation:
Regan set out his "rights view" in *The Case for Animal Rights* (1983).

- **A is not correct.** For Regan, a subject-of-a-life has beliefs, desires, memory, feelings, a sense of the future and a welfare of its own. Moral patients can meet this test. These include human infants and many mammals. They cannot act morally, but they still have inherent value. So inherent value is not limited to moral agents.
- **R is correct.** Regan holds that inherent value is a categorical concept. A being either has it or does not. All who have it have it equally. It does not depend on intelligence, skill or usefulness to others.

So A is not correct but R is correct.

The most tempting wrong option is "A is correct but R is not correct". Students who know Kant's view may think that only rational agents have inherent value. Regan rejects this exactly to include animals.

questions.question_md:
Match **LIST-I** with **LIST-II** :

| LIST-I (Thinkers) | LIST-II (Ideas on technology) |
|---|---|
| A. Jacques Ellul | I. Authoritarian and democratic technics |
| B. Lewis Mumford | II. Embodiment, hermeneutic, alterity and background relations |
| C. Don Ihde | III. The infosphere |
| D. Luciano Floridi | IV. Technique as an autonomous, self-augmenting force |

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- **A–IV.** Jacques Ellul, in *The Technological Society*, argues that "technique" has become autonomous. It grows by its own logic and is no longer under human control.
- **B–I.** Lewis Mumford, in "Authoritarian and Democratic Technics" (1964), contrasts two kinds of technics. One is small-scale and person-centred. The other is large, centralised and system-centred, like his "megamachine".
- **C–II.** Don Ihde, a postphenomenologist, names four human–technology relations: embodiment, hermeneutic, alterity and background relations.
- **D–III.** Luciano Floridi, a philosopher of information, describes the infosphere. It is the whole environment of information in which we now live.

So the match is A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.

The tempting wrong option is "A-I, B-IV, C-II, D-III". It swaps Ellul and Mumford. Both are critics of large-scale technology. But the thesis of autonomous technique is Ellul's.

questions.question_md:
Which pair of the following statements is most acceptable to Milton Friedman's view of the social responsibility of business ?

A. The one social responsibility of business is to use its resources to increase its profits, within the rules of the game.

B. A manager who spends the owners' money on general social causes is, in effect, imposing taxes without authority.

C. Managers must balance the claims of all stakeholders, such as employees, suppliers and the local community.

D. A corporation, as a legal person, has a moral duty to put social welfare above returns to its owners.

E. Business ethics must be imposed by the State, since firms cannot be trusted to obey any rules.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Milton Friedman set out his view in "The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits" (*New York Times Magazine*, 1970).

- **A fits.** These are nearly his words. Business must stay within the rules of the game, that is, open and free competition without deception or fraud.
- **B fits.** Friedman says that an executive is the agent of the owners. If he spends their money on social causes, he taxes them and spends the tax without any democratic authority.
- **C does not fit.** This is the stakeholder theory of R. Edward Freeman, which Friedman's view opposes.
- **D does not fit.** Friedman says that only people have responsibilities. A corporation is an artificial person and has no moral duties of its own.
- **E does not fit.** Friedman wants limited government. He trusts law and market competition, not State-imposed ethics.

So the pair is A and B. The tempting wrong option is "A and C only". C sounds like a mild form of responsibility, but it belongs to the rival stakeholder view.

questions.question_md:
Which pair of the following statements is true of Judith Jarvis Thomson's argument in "A Defense of Abortion" (1971) ?

A. She grants, for the sake of argument, that the foetus is a person from the moment of conception.

B. She concludes that abortion is wrong in every case, because the foetus has a right to life.

C. She holds that the right to life includes the right to be given the use of another person's body.

D. Her violinist example aims to show that unplugging oneself from another person need not be unjust killing.

E. She rests her case mainly on the claim that the foetus cannot feel pain.

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
- **A is true.** Thomson does not argue about when the foetus becomes a person. She grants the opponent's premise that it is a person from conception.
- **B is false.** She argues that, even if the foetus is a person, abortion is permissible in many cases, for example after rape.
- **C is false.** This is the claim she denies. The right to life is not a right to use another person's body. It is only a right not to be killed unjustly.
- **D is true.** In her example, you wake up connected to a famous violinist who needs your kidneys for nine months. She says you may unplug yourself, even though he will die. Doing so does not violate his right to life.
- **E is false.** Her argument does not depend on sentience. It depends on bodily autonomy and the limits of the right to life.

So the pair is A and D. The tempting wrong option is "A and B only". A student may think that if the foetus is a person, abortion must be wrong. Thomson's whole point is that this inference fails.

questions.question_md:
"For the Nyāya, God is the efficient cause of the world, but not its material cause".

Which among the following offers the best explanation for this statement ?
options: The world is only an appearance of God, as a snake is an appearance of a rope.
The world is a real transformation of God's own body, as curd is of milk.
God first produces the atoms out of nothing and then leaves them to combine.
The atoms and other eternal substances already exist, and God only combines and arranges them.
questions.explanation:
The passage says that the material of the world is the eternal atoms and other eternal substances. God does not create them out of nothing. He only combines and arranges them, as a potter shapes clay that he did not make. So God is the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), and the atoms are the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).

- Option 1 is the Advaita view of *vivarta* (apparent change). The Nyāya is a realist school and treats the world as real.
- Option 2 is the most tempting. It is a *pariṇāma* (real transformation) view, like that of Rāmānuja. On that view God is also the material cause, which the Nyāya denies.
- Option 3 contradicts the passage. The Nyāya atoms are eternal, so nobody produces them.

questions.question_md:
"Finite souls cannot be the maker of the world".

Which among the following offers the best explanation for this statement, as given in the passage ?
options: Finite souls are made up of parts, and so they are themselves effects.
Finite souls come into being together with the bodies that they occupy.
Finite souls have limited knowledge and cannot perceive the invisible atoms.
Finite souls have no *adṛṣṭa*, and so they cannot direct the atoms.
questions.explanation:
The causal proof says that every effect needs an agent who knows its material. The material of the world is the invisible atoms. The passage says that finite souls have limited knowledge and cannot perceive these atoms. So they cannot make the world, and the maker must be omniscient.

- Option 1 is wrong. For the Nyāya, the soul is an eternal substance without parts. It is not an effect.
- Option 2 gives a Cārvāka-like view. The Nyāya holds that the soul is eternal and does not start with the body.
- Option 4 is the most tempting, because it uses a term from the passage. But the passage says that souls do acquire *adṛṣṭa* through their actions. Also, the passage does not use *adṛṣṭa* to explain why souls cannot make the world.

questions.question_md:
"*Adṛṣṭa* can by itself give to each soul the fruits that fit its actions".

Pick out the correct option from below with reference to the above :
options: Accepted by the Nyāya, since *adṛṣṭa* is itself a conscious power.
Accepted by the Nyāya, since the law of karma needs no guide.
Rejected by the Nyāya, since *adṛṣṭa* is unintelligent and needs an intelligent director.
Rejected by the Nyāya, since the fruits of actions come to souls by mere chance.
questions.explanation:
The passage gives the second proof of God. *Adṛṣṭa* is unintelligent. An unintelligent thing cannot by itself give each soul the pleasures and pains that fit its deeds. So an intelligent being, God, must direct it. The Nyāya therefore rejects the statement.

- Option 1 is wrong. The passage says that *adṛṣṭa* is unintelligent, not conscious.
- Option 2 is the most tempting. Schools such as the Mīmāṃsā and the Jaina hold that karma works without God. The Nyāya rejects this view, and that is why it uses the argument from *adṛṣṭa*.
- Option 4 is wrong. The Nyāya says that the fruits fit the deeds. They do not come by chance.

questions.question_md: Examine the causal proof for the existence of God given in the passage and choose the correct option from below.
options: The world has no beginning in time, and so it does not require any maker.
The atoms are made up of parts, and so the atoms also require a maker.
Things made up of parts are effects, and every effect requires an intelligent agent.
The world is an effect, and so God must be the material out of which it is made.
questions.explanation:
The causal proof in the passage has two steps. First, mountains, rivers and bodies are made up of parts, and so they are effects, like a pot. Second, every effect needs an intelligent agent. So the world needs an intelligent maker.

- Option 1 is an objection of the Mīmāṃsā, which denies a creator. It is not the Nyāya proof.
- Option 2 is the most tempting. But the Nyāya atoms have no parts, and the passage calls them eternal. Only composite things are effects.
- Option 4 is wrong. The passage says that God is the efficient cause, not the material cause.

questions.question_md: What is *adṛṣṭa* ?
options: The invisible atom out of which all composite things are made
The unseen merit and demerit that souls acquire through their actions
The unseen intelligent being who directs the atoms into combination
The eternal relation that binds a whole to its parts
questions.explanation:
*Adṛṣṭa* means 'the unseen'. In the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, it is the store of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) that a soul acquires through its actions. It later gives the soul pleasures and pains that fit its deeds. The passage gives this meaning directly.

- Option 1 describes the atom (*paramāṇu*). Atoms are also invisible, but they are the material of the world.
- Option 3 describes God (*Īśvara*), who directs *adṛṣṭa* and the atoms.
- Option 4 describes *samavāya* (inherence), another padārtha. It is a relation, not a store of merit and demerit.

questions.question_md: According to the passage, the Manichaeans explained evil by :
options: The weakness of matter that resists form
The anger of God against sinners
A second eternal principle opposed to the good
Mere ignorance of the true good
questions.explanation:
The passage says that the Manichaeans explained evil by a second eternal principle. This principle is a kingdom of darkness at war with the kingdom of light. Augustine followed this dualism for some years and later rejected it.

- Option 1 is close to a Platonic and Neoplatonic idea that matter resists form. The passage does not give it to the Manichaeans.
- Option 2 is not in the passage.
- Option 4 is close to the Socratic view that wrongdoing comes from ignorance. It is not the Manichaean view.

questions.question_md: What among the following can be implied correctly from the passage ?
options: Evil exists as a positive reality side by side with the good.
The lesser, changeable goods are evil in themselves.
A wholly evil being could exist, since evil is self-subsistent.
Evil can exist only in a thing that is, in some respect, good.
questions.explanation:
The passage says that evil is the privation (lack) of good. A thing can lose good only because it has good to lose. A thing that lost all its good would cease to be. So evil needs a subject that still has some good. Evil can exist only in something that is, in some respect, good.

- Option 1 is the Manichaean view that the passage rejects. Evil is not a substance.
- Option 2 reverses the passage. It says that the lesser goods are not bad, and the fault lies in the disordered turning of the will.
- Option 3 is the most tempting reversal. A thing with no good at all would not exist, so a wholly evil being cannot exist.

questions.question_md: In saying that to seek the efficient cause of an evil will is like trying to see darkness, what among the following can be implied correctly ?
options: The evil will is efficiently caused by the lesser goods that it desires.
The evil will is caused by God, since God gave the creature its will.
The evil will is a falling away from good, not a positive effect of some cause.
The evil will cannot be known, so the creature is not responsible for it.
questions.explanation:
Darkness is not a thing that we see. It is only the absence of light. In the same way, an evil will is not a positive product of some cause. It is a defect, a falling away from the unchangeable good. So it has a 'deficient' cause, not an efficient one.

- Option 1 is the most tempting. But the passage says that the lesser goods are not bad. The fault lies in the turning of the will, not in its objects.
- Option 2 is wrong. The passage says that the will is a good gift and its misuse is not the Creator's fault.
- Option 4 is wrong. The analogy is about the kind of cause, not about knowledge. The passage puts the fault on the creature.

questions.question_md: In this passage Augustine primarily contrasts :
options: Changeable goods with the unchangeable good
Evil as an independent principle with evil as a lack of good
questions.explanation:
The passage starts with the problem of evil. It states the Manichaean answer, which makes evil a second eternal principle. Augustine rejects this dualism. He says that evil is not a substance but the privation of good. The rest of the passage develops this privation view. So the main contrast is between evil as an independent principle and evil as a lack of good.

- Option 1 is a theme of Augustine and Aquinas, but this passage does not discuss it.
- Option 2 is not in the passage. The passage speaks of moral evil only.
- Option 3 is the most tempting. The passage mentions changeable and unchangeable goods. But they only explain how moral evil arises. They are not the main contrast.

questions.question_md: Why, according to the passage, is God not to be blamed for the evil done by a free will ?
options: Because the misuse of free will is needed to make the whole universe beautiful.
Because evil is a mere privation, and so no real wrong is ever done by anyone.
Because the will of the creature comes from the principle of darkness, not God.
Because the will is a good gift needed to live rightly, and its misuse is the creature's fault.
questions.explanation:
The passage says that the will itself is a good gift. Without free will no one could live rightly. When a creature misuses this gift, the fault is the creature's and not the Creator's. So God is not to blame for the evil that a free will does.

- Option 1 is the most tempting. The passage does say that what seems evil in a part may serve the order of the whole. But it does not say that the misuse of the will is needed for beauty.
- Option 2 goes too far. Evil is a privation, but the passage still speaks of real moral evil and real fault.
- Option 3 gives the Manichaean dualism that Augustine rejects. God made all things, including the will.

groups.md:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow :

In the opening chapters of *The Life Divine*, Sri Aurobindo describes two negations that have kept human thought from a complete view of existence. The materialist denies the Spirit and accepts Matter as the only reality. The ascetic affirms the Spirit but refuses the world. Aurobindo sees a strong form of this refusal in the Māyāvāda of Advaita, which he calls Illusionism. For Śaṅkara, Brahman alone is real. The world of names and forms (*nāma-rūpa*) is superimposed on Brahman through ignorance, as a snake is seen in a rope. The appearance of the snake brings no change in the rope, and it vanishes when the rope is known. In the same way, the world-appearance brings no change in Brahman and is removed by the knowledge of Brahman. Its cause, *māyā*, is called *anirvacanīya*. Aurobindo accepts the Upaniṣadic teaching that Brahman is one, but he rejects the conclusion that the world is unreal. If Brahman is the one reality, all that Brahman manifests must share in that reality, for 'all this is Brahman'. *Māyā*, in his reading, is not a power of illusion. It is the consciousness-force of the Divine that measures out and forms the many from the One. The goal of life is therefore not escape from the world but its divine transformation.

Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow :

Knowledge is nothing but the perception of the agreement or disagreement of any of our ideas. Where this perception is lacking, we may guess or believe, but we do not know. Knowledge has degrees, and these depend on the way in which the agreement is perceived. Sometimes the mind sees the agreement of two ideas immediately, by themselves, without the help of any other idea. Thus it sees that white is not black and that three is more than two. This is intuitive knowledge, the clearest and most certain that human frailty can reach. At other times the mind cannot compare two ideas at once. It must then use other ideas, called proofs, to bring out their agreement, and this is demonstration. Every step of a demonstration must have intuitive certainty. Demonstrative knowledge is therefore certain, but it is less clear, and in a long chain a step is easily missed. A third degree reaches beyond our ideas to the particular existence of finite things outside us. This sensitive knowledge falls short of the other two. Yet it deserves the name of knowledge, for no one is in earnest so sceptical as to doubt the things he sees and feels. Where knowledge fails, the mind must rely on judgement and probability.

questions.question_md:
In the opening chapter of the *Metaphysics*, Aristotle traces how human knowing rises from its lowest to its highest form. Arrange the following in ascending order :

A. Experience (*empeiria*)

B. Wisdom (*sophia*)

C. Sense-perception (*aisthēsis*)

D. Art (*technē*)

E. Memory (*mnēmē*)

Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
In *Metaphysics* A.1, Aristotle shows a ladder of knowing. Each step uses the step below it.

- **C. Sense-perception** comes first. All animals have it.
- **E. Memory** comes from perception. Some animals have it, and memory makes them able to learn.
- **A. Experience** comes from many memories of the same thing. It knows *that* something is so.
- **D. Art** comes when one universal judgement forms from many experiences. Art knows the *why*, the cause, so it can be taught.
- **B. Wisdom** is the highest. It is knowledge of the first causes and principles.

So the order is C, E, A, D, B.
